title: Women-Empowered Home-Based Agri-Processing: A Sustainable Approach for Rural Economic Development in Afghanistan
abstract: Conflict and turmoil over the last 50 years have impaired Afghanistan’s agricultural and water infrastructure and threatened rural livelihoods and economic stability. This study assesses value-added, home-based, women-empowered agri-processing in Afghanistan as a sustainable strategy to promote rural economic development, empower women, and enhance food security. By analyzing existing literature, global reports, and regional case studies, this paper highlights the roles of adaptable technologies, microcredit mechanisms, and market linkages in building resilient rural economies and overcoming limitations such as land fragmentation, low technology inputs, and poor agri-infrastructure. The main growth drivers would be harnessing adaptable technology, building rural infrastructure, adopting efficient agricultural practices, and connecting to skilled education. The findings underscore the significance of supportive policies and investments in home-based value-added agri-processing to foster sustainable growth, poverty reduction, and economic inclusivity in Afghanistan.

title: Women as Landowners: Implications for Household Food Security in Ethiopia
abstract: The study explores whether female landownership (sole or joint) alters the self-reported household food security in Ethiopia following decades of implementing land reform. The distinction among various types of landownership has received limited attention in the literature. The study uses data from households that own agricultural plots of land from the Ethiopian Socioeconomic Panel Survey (ESPS 2021/22) and uses the Food Insecurity Experience Scale (FIES) as the indicator of household food security status. Using multivariable logistic regression models, we find that female landownership, especially joint ownership of female with other male members, is associated with an increase in the likelihood of being food-secure. Female landownership was associated with a 7.3% reduction in food insecurity and a 5.5% reduction in severe food insecurity. Female landownership through joint ownership was associated with a 7.4% reduction in food insecurity and a 7% reduction in severe food insecurity. Regional differences in household food insecurity risk have been identified as a significant factor related to food insecurity. Land allocation programs granting joint female and male landownership offer a viable approach to sustain the family, reducing the food insecurity risk.

title: Network Fragility and Sustainability of a Territorial Yam Supply Chain for Food Security in the Colombian Caribbean
abstract: The sustainability of territorial agri-food systems depends on whether high-value produce can reach a paying market. The yam supply chain of Montes de María, a post-conflict subregion of the Colombian Caribbean, sorts its product into a non-substitutable export grade and a local grade. This study identifies the structural conditions under which single-point dependence transforms a demand shock into food loss, integrating network analysis with a household survey of the territory. The chain is modeled as a weighted directed graph in three layers: value concentration, structural criticality via Menger edge connectivity, and a differential-equation model of export-grade erosion under a demand shock with saturating absorption and storage; a parallel food-insecurity and dietary-diversity survey sets the baseline. Results, reported as conditional scenarios, show the export value hangs on a single non-redundant channel: one cut disconnects it. Under a shock, permanent loss nears 18% of diverted product versus 50% without storage, while the export-income collapse (40–57%) is not buffered. With 41% of surveyed households food-insecure, this fragility can erode rural livelihoods through economic access. Diversifying the export outlet and strengthening local storage emerge as levers for a resilient and sustainable chain, supporting the access dimension of food security that underpins territorial peace.

title: Global Supply Chain Shocks and Inflation in a Diversifying Oil Economy: Sustainability Implications for Saudi Arabia
abstract: This study examines the effects of global supply chain shocks on inflation in Saudi Arabia, using monthly data from January 2014 to March 2026. Supply chain resilience has emerged as a critical dimension of economic sustainability, yet its inflationary consequences in commodity-dependent economies remain insufficiently understood. The analysis applies both Structural Vector Autoregression (SVAR) and Local Projection (LP) models to estimate impulse response functions. Inflation is measured using the wholesale price index (WPI) and its primary components. Findings from both methodologies are consistent, demonstrating that global supply chain shocks have positive, statistically significant impacts on most measures of wholesale price inflation in the short to medium term. The magnitude and persistence of these effects differ across components. In proportional terms, the most pronounced responses are found in ores and minerals and agricultural products—sectors closely tied to food security and sustainable resource management. However, their contribution to the aggregate WPI depends on their relative weights, with higher-weight categories, particularly metal products, machinery and equipment and food-related products, contributing more to aggregate wholesale price movements. Although the effects diminish in statistical significance over longer horizons, the cumulative responses indicate that supply chain disruptions can leave a persistent upward effect on wholesale price levels across specific categories, even after the direct inflationary impulse has subsided. These findings underscore the importance of building supply chain resilience as part of broader strategies for sustainable economic stability, with direct implications for monetary policy and inflation management in resource-dependent economies.

title: Talca no es Santiago: Moral geography, rurality, and infrastructure of possibility in LGBTIQA+ violence and survival
abstract: Background Violence against LGBTIQA+ individuals is not limited to discrete acts of aggression. It also constitutes a territorial ecology that unevenly distributes habitability, safety, and recognition. This study examines how the statement “Talca is not Santiago” works as more than a comment on city size: it names a moral geography where reputation, social surveillance, and uneven access to infrastructure produce distinct thresholds of visibility, risk, and agency. Methods We used Reflexive Thematic Analysis (RTA) following Braun and Clarke to analyze a subcorpus of seven individual interviews and one focus group (n = 7) conducted in Talca and one focus group (n = 5) conducted in Santiago, drawn from a broader research project according to predefined criteria (density of territorial references and representation of both study sites). Reporting follows COREQ guidelines (S1 Checklist). We recruited participants through LGBTIQA+ organizations and social networks; participants self-identified with non-hegemonic sexual-gender identities, were over 18, and reported subjective experiences of violence. The analytical sample is composed predominantly of young (19–35 years) university-educated participants, with representation of cisgender, transmasculine, and non-binary identities and no trans women. We calibrate the scope of our conclusions accordingly. Results We constructed three themes: (1) Infrastructure of possibility—LGBTIQA+ life becomes practicable or precarious depending on available circuits of information, networks, and spaces; (2) Surveillance and reputation—in medium-sized cities and rural environments, social legibility intensifies daily control and shrinks the margin to maneuver, which also affects the possibility of leaving violent relationships; (3) Mobility and education as partial territorial rupture—moving for studies and traveling through urban circuits reconfigures future horizons without erasing access asymmetries. Conclusions Within the scope of a young, predominantly cisgender, university-educated sample, territorial scale operates as a constitutive condition of violence and survival, not as a backdrop. Interventions on LGBTIQA+ violence therefore need to address territorial conditions: connectivity, information circulation, community spaces, and confidentiality safeguards adapted to medium-sized cities and ruralities.

title: Perceived Value and Organic Food Purchase Intention for Sustainable Agricultural Development: An Extended Theory of Planned Behavior in Shandong, China
abstract: Understanding consumer demand for organic food is important for the development of sustainable agricultural markets and the broader transition toward more sustainable food systems. This study examines how health, safety, environmental, social, and hedonic values, together with subjective product knowledge, are associated with attitudes and purchase intention (PI) toward organic food. An extended Theory of Planned Behavior (TPB) framework was tested using an online non-probability quota survey of 733 adult consumers in Shandong Province, China. Structural equation modeling was employed to examine the proposed associations. The results show that health, safety, environmental, social, and hedonic values are positively associated with attitudes toward organic food, with health and safety values showing the largest standardized associations. Attitude, subjective norms, and perceived behavioral control are positively associated with PI, with subjective norms showing the largest direct association. In contrast, subjective product knowledge shows a positive but statistically non-significant association with attitude. These findings highlight the importance of health-, safety-, and environment-related value perceptions in shaping consumer evaluations of organic food. From a demand-side perspective, the results provide insights for organic food market development and sustainable agricultural policy. By strengthening consumer recognition of differentiated organic products, demand-side development may help create more favorable market conditions for producers participating in higher-value and sustainability-oriented agricultural value chains, providing a demand-side perspective relevant to organic food market development and potentially to sustainable agricultural value chains.

title: Do Agricultural Machinery Services Promote Grain-Oriented Land Use? The Countervailing Role of Farmland Rent in Rural China
abstract: Rural labor out-migration and low comparative returns to grain challenge food security in China. This study examines the association between agricultural machinery services (AMS) and the allocation of sown land between grain and economic crops, and whether farmland rent is linked to a countervailing pattern. Using data from the 2021 China Household Finance Survey (CHFS) for 421 villages and 5496 farming households, supplemented by the 2019 wave for the instrumental-variable analysis and additional diagnostics, we estimate province fixed-effects and instrumental-variable models. Greater AMS coverage is associated with a lower economic-crop share. Grain-specific service intensity is positively associated with relative gross sales revenue from grain and with farmland rent. Higher rent is positively associated with the economic-crop share in villages with active rental markets, but the estimated rent-related indirect association is imprecise: its bootstrap confidence interval includes zero. The data do not provide robust evidence that the rent association diminishes at higher rent levels. The association between AMS coverage and the economic-crop share is more negative in villages with better irrigation. These findings suggest that machinery services are linked to grain-oriented cropping, while the possible land-market feedback requires further investigation.

title: Study on Spatiotemporal Evolution, Decoupling Characteristics and Driving Mechanism of Agricultural Carbon Emissions from Technological Progress—Panel Evidence from 21 Prefectures (States) in Sichuan Province, China
abstract: Against the dual goals of agricultural and rural carbon emission reduction, carbon sequestration and food security guarantee, this paper uses municipal panel data of 21 prefectures in Sichuan Province from 2015 to 2024 to calculate agricultural carbon emissions from multiple dimensions including farmland utilization, paddy field methane, crop cultivation, straw burning and livestock breeding. The standard deviational ellipse model (SDE) is adopted to reveal the spatiotemporal pattern of agricultural carbon emissions, and the Tapio decoupling model is applied to identify the decoupling relationship between agricultural carbon emissions and the agricultural economy. A panel model is constructed. The Breusch–Pagan Lagrange Multipkier (LM) test and Hausman test are performed to select the random-effects model to examine the impact of agricultural technological progress on agricultural carbon emissions. Robustness tests and grouped heterogeneity analysis are carried out. Furthermore, mediation and moderation models are introduced to identify the internal transmission paths and boundary conditions. The results show that: (1) From 2015 to 2024, the total agricultural carbon emissions in Sichuan Province generally declined. Animal husbandry was the primary emission source while carbon emissions from crop cultivation showed an upward trend, and carbon emission intensity kept decreasing. The spatial pattern of agricultural carbon emissions presented strong path dependence; the emission centroid remained stable in the central basin with a northeast–southwest spatial distribution. (2) The relationship between agricultural carbon emissions and the agricultural economy in Sichuan Province fluctuated alternately between strong decoupling and weak decoupling. Sustained and stable strong decoupling has not yet been achieved, and the incremental emissions from crop cultivation constitute a key factor disturbing the decoupling state. (3) Benchmark regression results indicated that agricultural technological progress significantly curbed regional agricultural carbon emissions, and urbanization also exerted emission-reduction effects. The proportion of primary industry, land scale operation and grain planting ratio significantly increased agricultural carbon emissions, whereas rural residents’ income and agricultural industrial structure showed no significant impacts. The carbon emission reduction effect of agricultural technological progress, constrained by regional endowments, presented notable regional heterogeneity. The emission reduction effect of technological progress was significant in plain and non-ethnic farming areas, while it was difficult to achieve emission reduction merely by relying on mechanization in ethnic regions and non-plain mountainous areas. (4) Mechanism tests demonstrated that fertilizer application intensity played a partial mediating role between agricultural technological progress and agricultural carbon emissions. Agricultural technological progress can indirectly reduce carbon emissions by lowering fertilizer application intensity. The multiple cropping index exerted a positive moderating effect. The higher the multiple cropping index, the stronger the inhibitory effect of agricultural technological progress on agricultural carbon emissions. This paper identified key regions, core emission reduction targets and directions for technological optimization for differentiated low-carbon agricultural governance in Sichuan Province, and provided empirical evidence for developing agriculture-specific carbon emission reduction plans tailored to local conditions. It also clarified the limits of the emission reduction effectiveness of agricultural technological advancements across different regions. The research findings can provide precise guidance for the green and low-carbon transformation of regional agriculture, assist local governments in addressing weaknesses in agricultural emission reduction efforts and mitigate risks such as rising emissions from crop cultivation and rebound effects from decoupling.

title: Vision-spectroscopy cooperative sensing and cold atmospheric plasma inactivation for early warning and management of agricultural product diseases
abstract: Abstract Pathogen-induced disease causes heavy post-harvest losses and threatens food safety, yet routine inspection rarely identifies an infection before it becomes visible. This study evaluates multimodal sensing, threshold-based early warning and plasma-based decontamination for post-harvest disease management in strawberry (Fragaria × ananassa cv. ‘Hongyan’). A dual-branch network, pairing a ResNet-34 visual encoder with a one-dimensional convolutional spectral encoder through bidirectional cross-modal attention, fuses RGB imagery with near-infrared hyperspectral reflectance. Across five severity grades the fused model reached 93.5 ± 0.7% accuracy over fifteen cross-validation runs and 94.2% on a fruit-level held-out test set of 260 samples (95% CI 91.4 to 97.1), with a weighted F1 score of 0.938 and a Cohen’s Kappa of 0.927. Its 2.7-point margin over an unweighted late-fusion baseline did not reach significance after correction for eleven held-out comparisons (continuity-corrected McNemar $$\:{\chi\:}^{2}$$ = 4.00, Holm-adjusted $$\:p$$ = 0.140). Alarms preceded the expert-confirmed transition to a visible lesion by 52.0 ± 9.6 h in the 80-fruit monitoring cohort. Cold atmospheric plasma parameters were screened systematically: 1.5 W/cm 2 in Ar/O 2 for 180 s delivered more than a 3.5-log reduction for Botrytis cinerea , Colletotrichum gloeosporioides and Aspergillus niger ; the measured quality attributes did not differ significantly from untreated controls under the tested conditions. Leakage assays and a sigmoidal dose-response model support membrane damage associated with oxidative stress. The proposed progression from membrane peroxidation through enzyme disruption to DNA damage remains a mechanistic hypothesis. Sensing and treatment were evaluated separately; the present evidence is limited to one commodity, laboratory conditions and no integrated pilot-scale trial.

title: Low diet quality increases the genetic risk of high blood cholesterol levels in Asian Indian adults [CURES – 165]
abstract: Background Asian Indians face an increased burden of cardiometabolic diseases, yet the interplay between genetic predisposition and diet quality in this population remains underexplored. This study aimed to examine their interaction on cardiometabolic traits in this population. Methods We conducted a cross-sectional analysis of 1,020 adults (452 men, 568 women; aged 25–80 years) from the Chennai Urban Rural Epidemiology Study (CURES). A genetic risk score (GRS) of three variants: TCF7L2 rs7903146, FTO rs8050136, and FTO rs1588413 was constructed. Diet quality was evaluated using the Indian Diet Quality Score, based on the intake of eight food groups. Associations between the GRS and cardiometabolic traits, as well as the interactions between the GRS and diet quality score, were assessed. Results A high GRS was significantly associated with higher fasting plasma glucose ( p = 0.005) and glycated haemoglobin ( p = 0.006). Significant interactions between the GRS and the diet quality score were observed on total cholesterol (P interaction = 0.003) and low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (P interaction = 0.005) concentrations, after correction for multiple testing. At the low diet quality score level, individuals with a high GRS had significantly higher total cholesterol and low-density lipoprotein cholesterol concentrations than those with a low GRS ( p < 0.001, for all comparisons). Conclusion This study provides novel evidence for the effect of gene–diet quality interactions on lipid outcomes in Asian Indians. Individuals with higher genetic risk may be more vulnerable to lipid abnormalities when adhering to a low-quality diet, emphasising the value of integrating genetic and dietary data into personalised nutrition strategies for lipid-related cardiometabolic risk prevention.

title: Combining Ability and Hybrid Performance of Cowpea Landraces Under Semiarid Conditions
abstract: Cowpea (Vigna unguiculata (L.) Walp.) plays a key role in food security and income generation in semiarid regions, particularly for smallholder farming systems in the Brazilian semiarid. However, productivity remains low because of environmental limitations, genetic constraints, and traditional crop management practices. We evaluated diallel crosses among cowpea landraces to identify superior parents and cross combinations in terms of earliness and grain yield under semiarid conditions. Six landrace accessions, previously selected through participatory prospecting for adaptability and yield stability, were crossed in a complete diallel design to produce 15 F1 hybrids and their reciprocal crosses. The hybrids were evaluated under field conditions in the semiarid region during the 2023 growing season using a randomized complete block design with ten replications. The evaluations were conducted according to each genotype’s developmental stage and immature pod formation. Early-maturing varieties were harvested at 60 days, intermediate and late varieties between 65 and 75 days. At physiological maturity, early and intermediate genotypes were harvested at 80 days, while late genotypes were harvested between 85 and 90 days. General combining ability (GCA) and specific combining ability (SCA) were estimated using Griffing’s Method I (fixed-effects model), and treatment means were compared using the Scott–Knott test at the 5% significance level. Significant GCA and SCA effects (p < 0.05) were detected for 12 of the 14 evaluated traits, whereas reciprocal effects were significant for seven traits. The hybrid combinations L1 × L4, L1 × L5, and L4 × L5, and their reciprocal crosses, exhibited superior agronomic performance, highlighting their potential as valuable genetic resources for cowpea breeding under semiarid environments.

title: Prevalence and determinants of cesarean section delivery among Somali women: a multivariable analysis of a nationally representative survey
abstract: Background Cesarean section is a life-saving obstetric intervention when medically indicated, yet access remains severely limited in Somalia, where maternal morbidity and mortality are high.Objective(s) To determine the magnitude of cesarean section delivery and identify factors associated with its utilization among Somali women using nationally representative survey data.Methods A secondary analysis of the 2020 Somali Health and Demographic Survey was conducted using data from 23,445 women aged 15–49 years. Odds ratios (ORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were reported, with statistical significance set at p < 0.05.Results The prevalence of cesarean section was 0.3% (61/23,445). Compared with women aged ≥ 35 years, those aged 25–34 years (OR = 6.483; 95% CI: 2.160–19.458; p = 0.001) and <25 years (OR = 6.293; 95% CI: 2.422–16.351; p < 0.001) had statistically significantly higher odds of cesarean delivery. Rural residence (OR = 0.177; 95% CI: 0.091–0.346; p < 0.001) and low household wealth (OR = 0.243; 95% CI: 0.097–0.611; p = 0.003) were statistically significantly associated with lower odds of cesarean delivery. Women with ≥6 children had statistically significantly higher odds of cesarean delivery (OR = 3.960; 95% CI: 2.072–7.569; p < 0.001). Breastfeeding was not significantly associated with cesarean delivery (p = 0.079).Conclusions Cesarean section utilization in Somalia remains extremely low, indicating substantial inequities in access to emergency obstetric care. Maternal age, parity, place of residence, and household wealth were associated with cesarean delivery.

title: From rules to learning: A GIS-integrated agent-based reinforcement learning framework for simulating farmers’ land-use decisions and sustainable policy design
abstract: Developing countries face critical tensions between farmland-use policies prioritizing food security and environmental sustainability, and farmers’ livelihood-centered land-use strategies. To address these challenges, this study develops a human-centered agent-based model that integrates dual-layer Q-learning with GIS-based spatial representation. This framework simulates farmers’ adaptive decision-making under dynamic policy and environmental conditions while formalizing behavioral heterogeneity through Theory of Planned Behavior (TPB)-informed typologies. Agents dynamically evolve land-transfer and cropping strategies via perception–action–feedback learning cycles. Applied to and validated against empirical observations from a representative Chinese case, the model reveals non-linear scale–efficiency relationships, with medium-scale farms exhibiting the comparatively balanced performance across yield and multiple resource-use efficiency dimensions. The analysis further identifies evolutionary pathways of adaptive behavior under policy incentives and quantifies trade-offs among area-weighted crop output, resource-use efficiency, and regional gross income. Scenario simulations show that rice-oriented subsidies increase rice output but reduce resource-use efficiency, rapeseed output, and gross income, whereas rotation-oriented incentives increase gross income while maintaining rice output near the baseline level. These findings support performance-linked subsidies based on multidimensional outcomes, tiered land-transfer regulation, and diversified cropping incentives. By linking adaptive behavioral dynamics with spatial and institutional constraints, this study provides a robust analytical framework for evaluating land-use policies and supports more effective governance strategies for balancing food security, environmental sustainability, and rural livelihoods.

title: Fractional-Order Epidemiological Model for Banana Bunchy Top Disease Integrating Memory Effects and Optimal Control Strategies
abstract: Banana Bunchy Top Disease (BBTD) is caused by Banana Bunchy Top Virus (BBTV), poses a significant threat to global banana farming and results in substantial yield losses and economic instability for smallholder farmers. Extensively, Classical compartmental models are used in plant diseases while overlooking the hereditary effects intrinsic to biological systems. Throughout this paper, an innovative fractional-order epidemiological model for BBTD is formulated using Caputo-type derivatives to integrate memory effects in plant–vector interactions. In this model, the host plant population is partitioned into five distinct compartments—susceptible, exposed, infected, treated, and recovered—whereas the vectors are classified into susceptible, infectious, and removed states. By applying the next-generation matrix, the local stability of the disease-free equilibrium is established. The sensitivity analysis of BBTD reveals that transmission and progression parameters act as the essential determinants of disease persistence within the ecosystem. The Numerical simulations are executed using the modified Euler method that illustrates the impact of fractional-order dynamics includes infection peaks, treatment effectiveness, and recovery delays. Using Optimal control strategies and Pontryagin’s Maximum Principle, preventive measures, vector management, and treatment interventions for BBTD are developed. These strategies demonstrate that integrated controls significantly reduce the infection prevalence while maintaining cost-effectiveness. These findings underscore the efficacy of fractional calculus in plant disease epidemiology, offering superior predictive precision and actionable insights for sustainable, long-term BBTD management.

title: Climate-Smart Agricultural Practice Adoption and Its Determinants Among Smallholder Farmers in West Belesa District, Northwest Ethiopia
abstract: Climate change represents a profound global crisis and the most significant threat to contemporary agricultural systems. This study evaluates the adoption status of Climate-Smart agricultural (CSA) practices among smallholder households and identifies the key factors influencing their adoption in the West Belesa district of Northwest Ethiopia. This study justifies the gaps in CSA adoption. Using a stratified random sampling technique, 400 respondents were selected. The research employed a mixed-methods approach, collecting primary quantitative data through structured surveys, which were then cross-verified with qualitative insights from Focus Group Discussions (FGDs) and Key Informant Interviews (KIIs). Data analysis was performed using descriptive statistics and a binary logistic regression model to isolate the specific economic and institutional drivers of adoption. The results show that 56.3% of the sampled households have adopted at least one CSA practice. However, a significant gender gap was identified, with only 50.5% of female-headed households adopting these practices compared to higher rates among their male counterparts (62%). The binary logit model reveals that adoption is positively, negatively and significantly influenced by farming experience (B = 0.104, odds = 1.110), age (B = −0.065, odds = 0.937),family size (B = −0.216,odds = 0.805), frequency of extension contact (B = −1.721,odds = 0.179), and access to credit (B = −2.073,odds = 0.126). Furthermore, the decision to adopt is strongly tied to the farmer’s information needs and their perception of the technology’s ability to boost productivity.

title: Self‐Help Group‐Bank Linkage Programme as Driver of Rural Financial Inclusion: A Conceptual Analysis and Enhanced Framework
abstract: ABSTRACT Self‐Help Group (SHG)‐Bank Linkage Programmes have emerged as an important mechanism for promoting rural financial inclusion by connecting underserved communities with formal banking institutions. Despite significant progress in expanding banking outreach, many rural households, particularly women and low‐income groups, continue to experience barriers in accessing formal credit, savings facilities, and financial services. This study examines the role of SHG‐Bank Linkage Programmes in strengthening financial inclusion through a conceptual analysis of existing research, institutional reports, and secondary evidence. The study focuses on four major dimensions: access to formal credit, savings behaviour and financial literacy, women's empowerment, and community‐level economic development. The analysis highlights that SHG‐bank partnerships reduce credit barriers through collective savings, peer accountability, and group‐based lending mechanisms. These programmes also contribute to women's economic participation by improving financial confidence, leadership capacity, and involvement in household and community decision‐making. However, challenges such as regional disparities, digital barriers, uneven SHG performance, and sustainability concerns remain significant. Based on the evidence reviewed, the study proposes an enhanced SHG‐Bank Linkage framework incorporating digital financial services, financial literacy initiatives, entrepreneurship support, and stronger institutional coordination. The proposed framework provides a conceptual pathway for strengthening inclusive and sustainable rural financial systems. The result shows that the enhanced version of the model achieves better financial reach by expanding credit access for SHG members from 58% to 85%. The future scope of SHG‐Bank linkage programmes lies in leveraging digital technologies to expand outreach and enhance financial literacy, thereby deepening financial inclusion in rural areas.

title: Evaluating the influence of water bank on water market, farmer’s participation, and reallocation efficiency through agent-based modeling
abstract: Chronic water scarcity in many river basins has intensified the need for effective mechanisms to improve the allocation of water resources. Water markets are widely promoted as a means of reallocating water toward higher-value uses. Within this framework, water banks, functioning as intermediary institutions, can enhance market efficiency by facilitating transactions, managing fluctuations in supply and demand, and generating economic incentives. This study employs an agent-based model (ABM) to assess the effects of a water bank on market dynamics, farmer decision-making, agricultural value added, and broader economic outcomes in basin scale resulting from water reallocation among agricultural users. In the model, the water bank is represented as an autonomous, strategically behaving market agent operating alongside heterogeneous farmers. The model is applied to the Lenjan sub-basin of Iran’s Zayandeh-Rud River basin. Farmers' participation in the market, involving three crop types, namely barely, rice, and almonds, is simulated over the period 2000–2024 under three scenarios: no market (NM), a decentralized market without a water bank (NB), and a market supported by a water bank (WB). The results of these scenarios are then compared. The findings indicate that the water bank substantially improves market efficiency, sustainability, and allocative efficiency relative to the direct-transaction scenario (NB). Acting as an intertemporal buffer, the bank absorbed surplus water during wet years and released it during droughts, thereby reducing excess supply and demand imbalances by 54% and 61%, respectively. This buffering capacity mitigates market failures associated with the absence of storage-based intermediation. The presence of a water market clearly raises overall income up to 170%. However, the water bank also led to a fairer redistribution of profits among different farmer groups. The total value added per unit of water increased by 12% under the NB scenario and by 40% under the WB scenario, suggesting that the water bank enhances the economic efficiency of water allocation through its influence on price formation and its role in equilibrating supply and demand. In the water market, the bank purchased approximately 1210 million cubic meters of water and resold half, while retaining the remaining 600 million cubic meters in storage equivalent to 18% of total available water. This stored volume could potentially support environmental flows for the Zayandeh-Rud River, as well as meet industrial and part of the urban water demand in the region. These findings underscore that the value of a water bank lies not merely in facilitating trade, but in its capacity to transform competing claims on scarce water into coordinated, incentive-compatible reallocation. This provides evidence that strategic storage and institutional intermediation should be integral components of water market design.

title: Action collective et formes locales de gouvernance en contexte de conflit armé en Colombie
abstract: In Colombia, in the context of armed conflict, peasant and rural organizations have developed forms of local governance that interact with the action of the State and with the armed actors. Despite the signing of a peace agreement between the Colombian government and the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia-People's Army (FARC-EP) in November 2016, guerrillas, territory, land, and fairer distribution of agricultural land remain central to theirs demands. Interviews conducted in the late 2010s in Caquetá and in North Cauca, two regions marked by confrontation between military forces and insurgent groups, reveal the existence of mechanisms such as the Community Action Committee (JAC) and the Peasant Reserve Zones (ZRC). These mechanisms constitute collective actions and local forms of bottom-up governance that are built through interaction at various levels with the State, but also through often tense “arrangements” with the still-present armed actors.

title: Knowledge, perceived benefits and willingness to adopt telehealth among women of reproductive age attending selected rural primary health care centres in Ibadan, Oyo State, Nigeria
abstract: Nigeria contributes nearly one-third of global maternal deaths, and rural women bear a disproportionate burden due to understaffed primary health centres (PHCs), geographic barriers, and limited access to skilled care. Telehealth has been identified as a scalable strategy for improving access to maternal and reproductive health services. However, evidence on demand-side readiness, specifically the knowledge and perceived benefits that drive willingness to adopt telehealth, remains limited among rural women of reproductive age in Nigeria. A facility-based descriptive cross-sectional study was conducted among 336 women of reproductive age (15–49 years) attending nine rural PHCs across three Local Government Areas (Ido, Oluyole, and Ona Ara) in Ibadan zone, Oyo State, using multistage probability sampling. Data were collected using the validated bilingual Rural Telehealth Adoption Assessment Questionnaire (R-TAAQ), grounded in the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), Health Belief Model (HBM), and UTAUT. Descriptive statistics, chi-square tests, Pearson correlation, and binary logistic regression were employed. The response rate was 93.6%. The majority demonstrated high knowledge of telehealth (62.8%; mean = 5.80 ± 2.34/8) and positive perceived benefits (82.4%; mean = 25.6 ± 7.52/30). Willingness to adopt was high (83.9%; mean = 11.1 ± 3.24/15). Perceived benefits were the only variable significantly associated with willingness to adopt (χ² = 46.774, p < 0.001). Knowledge ( p = 0.428), facilitating conditions ( r = 0.037, p = 0.493), and all socio-demographic variables ( p > 0.05) were not significant. Binary logistic regression confirmed perceived benefits as the sole significant predictor (AOR = 11.274, 95% CI: 5.427–23.422, p < 0.001; Nagelkerke R² = 0.254; classification accuracy = 84.5%). Women with 3–4 children were significantly less likely to be willing to adopt (AOR = 0.073, p = 0.027). Rural women demonstrated high knowledge and strong willingness to adopt telehealth for maternal care. Perceived benefits, not knowledge, infrastructure, or demographics, is the primary determinant of adoption intention. Telehealth promotion in rural PHC settings should prioritise benefit-focused communication while simultaneously addressing structural barriers to enable sustained engagement.

title: Association between smartphone and tablet ownership, usage diversity, and physical function in community-dwelling older adults in rural Japan: A cross-sectional study
abstract: BACKGROUND: Evidence on digital engagement and physical function in rural older adults remains limited. We examined associations between smartphone or tablet ownership, including the diversity of their usage, and physical function among rural community-dwelling older adults. METHODS: This cross-sectional study included 248 men and 359 women aged ≥65 years and residing in Japanese rural towns in 2025. Data on smartphone or tablet ownership and usage diversity (e.g., voice calls, LINE, email, Internet, electronic payments, and applications) were collected via a questionnaire. Physical function was objectively measured using handgrip strength, skeletal muscle index, and gait speed. Multiple regression and logistic regression models were used to calculate unstandardized coefficients (B) and odds ratios (ORs). RESULTS: Smartphone or tablet ownership was reported by 81.9% of men and 82.2% of women. Ownership was significantly associated with higher gait speed in men (B = 0.09, 95% CI: 0.02, 0.17) and women (B = 0.12, 95% CI: 0.06, 0.18). Usage diversity was positively associated with grip strength in men (B = 0.54, 95% CI: 0.06, 1.02), gait speed in men (B = 0.02, 95% CI: 0.01, 0.04) and women (B = 0.03, 95% CI: 0.01, 0.05); conversely, it was inversely associated with sarcopenia in men (OR = 0.59, 95% CI: 0.37, 0.95). CONCLUSIONS: Smartphone or tablet ownership and more diverse usage may contribute to the maintenance of physical function in older adults living in rural areas. Thus, digital engagement could serve as a practical means of supporting physical function in rural settings, where structural barriers can restrict opportunities to connect with others and obtain health information.

title: Social Dynamics Are Associated with Plant-Based Dietary Consumption Patterns Among Rural Adults in the U.S.
abstract: Background/Objectives: Social dynamics are known to influence eating behaviors and differ across geographic contexts. Some evidence suggests healthy plant-based diets (PBDs) are associated with reduced risk of chronic diseases, morbidity and mortality, and have lower environmental burdens. This paper examines the role of social influence, expectations, and pressures in consumption of PBDs among rural residents in the United States, with attention to gender differences. Methods: National survey data from rural adults (n = 2210) were analyzed using adjusted logistic regression models including an interaction between social beliefs and gender, and qualitative interviews (n = 55) thematically explored gendered social influences on PBD patterns. Results: Results showed that perceived expectations from important members of the respondents’ social network were positively associated with PBD adherence (p < 0.001), without a significant overall interaction with gender (p = 0.163). Perceived social pressure was also associated with PBD adherence overall (p = 0.009), and the association differed by gender (interaction p = 0.001), but did not show a consistent trend across levels of agreement. Qualitative findings suggested that family members influenced the feasibility of PBD, while friends were more commonly described as supportive. Women appeared to face challenges to enacting a PBD when family members (especially male partners) were not supportive. Conclusions: These results suggest social relationships have complex and gendered roles in shaping PBD among rural residents in the United States.

title: Empowerment and resistance: A study on the impacts of informal institutions on the interactions between tourism enterprise and rural residents
journal: Journal of Hospitality and Tourism Management
abstract: The interactions between tourism enterprises and rural residents have attracted increasing attention, but existing studies have rarely explored the influence of informal institutions on such interactions or the dynamic evolution of the roles of tourism enterprises. A systematic and nuanced theoretical and empirical elaboration on this topic remains lacking. A qualitative approach, including nonparticipant observations, semistructured interviews, and thematic analysis, was used to investigate the impacts of informal institutions on tourism enterprise–rural resident interactions and the role evolution of the enterprise during such interactions. The findings reveal dual heterogeneous effects of informal institutions on the interactions between tourism enterprise and rural residents, including the positive effects of guanxi and the negative effects of mianzi and distrust as components of informal institutions. The positive impact of such interactions is often accompanied by implicit conflicts, which local residents employ ideological confrontation and behavioral opposition to shift onto tourism enterprise. Jointly shaped by compound forces, the enterprise undergoes role overload that triggers its role entrenchment , thus transforming multiple roles into its ontological identity as a business operator and manager. Suggestions for sustainable rural tourism development are also presented.

title: “This Isn’t as Bad as I Thought”: Rural QTBIPOC Students’ Narratives of School Counseling
abstract: Rural queer and transgender Black, Indigenous, and People of Color (QTBIPOC) youth navigate layered inequities that shape academic, social/emotional, and mental health outcomes. This narrative inquiry explored how six rural QTBIPOC students perceived and experienced school counseling, with particular attention to help-seeking related to sexual/affectional and/or gender identity. Participants completed a brief written reflection and a semi-structured interview; data were analyzed through iterative narrative and cross-case analysis. Six themes described how counseling became (or failed to become) a viable support: (a) students often interpreted the school counselor role as vague and primarily academic; (b) help-seeking operated as risk management in close-knit rural contexts where disclosure could invite judgment, minimization, or exposure; (c) counselor identity and perceived competence shaped expectations of being understood versus the burden of translation; (d) perceptions shifted over time through direct encounters and peer-shared narratives; (e) positive experiences were anchored in rapport, validation, and active privacy practices; and (f) students framed advocacy as “small but radical” actions that increased safety and visibility under constraint. Implications are offered for rural school counselors and counselor education to strengthen culturally responsive, queer-affirming practice and reduce barriers to support.

title: Competing Mortality, Not Breast-Cancer Mortality, Explains the Survival Deficit of Breast Cancer After a Prior Non-Breast Cancer: A SEER Competing-Risks Analysis
abstract: Background and Objectives: Women who develop breast cancer after a previous cancer of another site have poorer overall survival, yet it is unsettled whether the breast cancer itself is more lethal or whether the deficit reflects competing causes of death in an older, previously treated population. We decomposed this survival deficit by cause of death, defining every endpoint identically across groups. Materials and Methods: Using the Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results (SEER) database (17 registries, 2010 to 2020), we studied women with invasive breast cancer as a single primary (n = 473,073), as a second or later primary after a non-breast index cancer (second primary breast cancer, SPBC; n = 26,832), and as a second breast primary (n = 40,252). Cause of death was assigned from the SEER cause-of-death-to-site recode, applied identically across cohorts. Cohorts were compared using cause-specific and Fine–Gray models weighted by an inverse-probability propensity score for age, race and ethnicity, subtype, grade, stage, nodal status, year, marital status, income, and rurality. Results: Breast-cancer mortality was not higher in SPBC than in single-primary disease, and was if anything lower (10-year cumulative incidence 12.0 versus 13.6 percent; weighted cause-specific hazard ratio 1.06). The deficit fell almost entirely to competing, non-breast mortality (35.3 versus 13.5 percent). In a five-way decomposition, cardiovascular disease was not the leading competing cause; non-cancer causes and the index cancer each accounted for more deaths. Once patient factors were balanced, cardiovascular and other non-cancer hazards were near unity (1.05 and 1.07), leaving further cancer death as the main excess. Conclusions: A breast cancer arising after a non-breast cancer is not intrinsically more lethal. Its survival deficit is competing mortality, driven mainly by further cancer death and, to a smaller and largely age-explained degree, by cardiovascular and other non-cancer causes.

title: Cultivating agricultural career intentions through behavioral drivers among students
abstract: This study applies the Theory of Planned Behavior to examine factors influencing Indian students’ intentions to pursue agricultural careers. Conducting a survey of 285 students from two universities via Google Forms, it analyzes proclivity for five career paths: Government jobs, Researcher/Professor, Farming, Agripreneurship, and civil services using multinomial logistic regression. Government jobs emerged as the most preferred, shaped by positive attitudes and perceived social norms. Language competency correlated with interest in farming and Agripreneurship, while self-efficacy negatively influenced structured roles. Gender and institutional background significantly affected choices. The findings underscore the role of psychological readiness and socio-cultural context in career decisions. The study recommends career awareness programs, attitude-building initiatives, and land-leasing schemes to promote youth engagement in agriculture.

title: Differences in disability-free life expectancy among Chinese older adults by combined body mass index and waist circumference categories
abstract: Weight management is an important component of strategies to promote healthy aging. However, the associations of body shapes and fat distribution with disability-free life expectancy (DFLE) among older adults have not been adequately evaluated. Data were obtained from the 2011–2018 waves of the Chinese Longitudinal Healthy Longevity Survey (CLHLS). Participants were categorized according to a combined classification of body mass index (BMI) and waist circumference (WC). Microsimulation was used to estimate life expectancy (LE) and DFLE across the different BMI–WC categories. Subgroup analyses were further conducted by sex and, within each sex, by urban-rural residence. Z tests were used to assess whether differences in DFLE between groups were statistically significant ( P < 0.05). At baseline, the mean age of the participants was 85.49 ± 10.98 years. At age 65, DFLE was 14.25 years (95% confidence interval (CI): 13.38–15.05) in the low BMI group, 15.47 years (95% CI: 14.72–16.37) in the appropriate BMI with central obesity group, and 15.82 years (95% CI: 14.27–17.20) in the high BMI group; all were lower than that in the appropriate BMI with normal WC group (16.02 years, 95% CI: 15.32–16.74). Among participants aged 73–95 years in the appropriate BMI with central obesity group, men had significantly shorter DFLE than women ( P < 0.05). Among women aged 76–95 years in the low BMI group, those living in urban areas had significantly shorter DFLE than their rural counterparts ( P < 0.05). Older adults with low BMI or appropriate BMI with central obesity had shorter DFLE, suggesting that weight management in later life should consider both BMI and fat distribution. Although older women had longer LE, they spent a smaller proportion of their remaining life disability-free. In particular, urban older women with low BMI may experience a greater burden of disability.

title: School-Based Rescued Produce Distribution, and Changes in Parental Fruit Intake and Household Dietary Behaviors: A Non-Randomized Controlled Cluster Trial
abstract: Background/Objectives: Fruit and vegetable intake remains below recommended levels, particularly among families facing socioeconomic constraints. School-based food access interventions may improve household dietary behaviors. This study evaluated the association between participation in the “Leket Health” school-based rescued produce distribution program and changes in parental fruit and vegetable intake, nutrition-related parenting practices, and household food security. Children’s fruit and vegetables intake was assessed as a secondary exploratory outcome. Methods: A non-randomized controlled cluster trial was conducted among parents (n = 281) of 4th–5th-grade students at three elementary schools in a peripheral town in Israel, with one school per study arm (three clusters in total). Schools were assigned to full intervention (biweekly fruit and vegetable boxes and nutrition education), partial intervention (boxes only), or control. Parent data were collected at baseline and after 7 months using both self-reported fruit and vegetable portions and a validated food frequency questionnaire (FFQ), food security questionnaire, and parental behavior questionnaire. Child intake was assessed using a study-specific FFQ. Primary analyses used a complete-case approach, supplemented by an allocation-based multiple-imputation sensitivity analysis among 269 identifiable participants. The trial was not registered in a public registry. Results: A total of 70% of enrolled participants completed the study. The two parental intake measures yielded discordant findings: categorical changes in parent-reported daily fruit servings differed across study groups in the complete-case analysis (p = 0.028), whereas FFQ-derived fruit and vegetable intake (g/day) showed no statistically significant between-group differences. The overall parenting-practices score showed no statistically significant change (p = 0.770) or between-group difference (p = 0.297). Household food insecurity increased from 8.7% to 14.3% and worsened across all study arms, with no significant between-group difference in deterioration (p = 0.810). No primary dietary endpoint was prespecified. In the allocation-based multiple-imputation analysis, adjusted follow-up fruit intake was higher than control by 0.38 portions/day (95% CI 0.04–0.71) in the full-intervention arm and 0.25 portions/day (95% CI −0.10 to 0.61) in the partial-intervention arm; estimates were attenuated under more adverse assumptions regarding missing outcomes. In an exploratory post-allocation adherence analysis, each additional produce box collected was associated with 6.7% higher odds of a parent-reported increase in fruit intake (OR = 1.067, 95% CI 1.003–1.135; p = 0.040). Among intervention participants, parent-reported improvements in nutrition-related parenting practices were associated with parent-reported increases in household vegetable variety (OR = 2.219, 95% CI 1.057–4.656; p = 0.035). These exploratory associations do not establish intervention effects. The overall parenting-practices score showed no statistically significant change (p = 0.770) or between-group difference (p = 0.297). Household food insecurity increased from 8.7% to 14.3% and worsened across all study arms, with no significant between-group difference in deterioration (p = 0.810). Among children, no significant changes were observed in FFQ-derived intake. Conclusions: Program participation was associated with higher parent-reported fruit servings, although the magnitude of between-arm differences varied across missing-data assumptions. No significant changes were observed in parental vegetable servings or FFQ-derived fruit and vegetable intake among parents or children. Given the single-school-per-arm design, these findings should be interpreted as exploratory and require confirmation in studies with multiple schools per arm.

title: Understanding the Impacts of Photovoltaic Panel Type on Cilantro, Calendula, and Chile Pepper Production in a Containerized Agrivoltaic System
abstract: New Mexico farmers face challenges from drought and pollution, while many residents experience food insecurity. Combining strategies to reduce natural resource consumption, increase income, and produce food for local communities is an important consideration. Agrivoltaics (AV), the co-location of agricultural production and photovoltaic (PV) panels, can be used to generate electricity and provide shade to crops. This is important in hot, arid climates that are adopting solar energy, since AV can increase soil moisture and moderate temperature peaks. Providing demonstrations to the community of the dual use of PV panels and agriculture will be helpful in integrating AV into residential use, therefore a containerized agrivoltaics (CAV) project was established in Farmington, NM. Four different solar panel treatments, ranging in price, were installed onto traditional garden boxes and compared with a full sun control. Cilantro (Coriandrum sativum) ‘Santo’, chile peppers (Capsicum anuum) ‘NuMex Primavera’, and calendula (Calendula officinalis) ‘Alpha’ were grown in the system. In addition to yield and other plant parameters, microclimates were monitored. Generally, plant yield, quality, and stomatal conductance were comparable in the PV treatments and the full sun control for all three crops. Continuing efforts to improve the livelihood of New Mexicans will require an interdisciplinary and applied scientific approach that considers the communities’ perspective and values.

title: Recommendations for HIV care continuity during droughts and floods with key populations living with HIV in Kampala, Uganda: Qualitative insights
abstract: Background Climate change and extreme weather events increasingly threaten HIV care continuity, yet evidence centering the lived experiences of key populations living with HIV remains limited. To address this knowledge gap, this qualitative study elicited recommendations for strengthening HIV service delivery during droughts and floods with young men who have sex with men (MSM) and female sex workers (FSW) living with HIV in Kampala, Uganda. Methods This community-based qualitative study involved semi-structured interviews with a purposive sample of young people (aged 18-24) living with HIV (8 MSM, 8 FSW) and 20 key informants from community leadership, climate, and HIV sectors from May-July 2024. Data were analyzed using framework thematic analysis and organized across institutional, community, and household level strategies. Results The 36 participants included 16 people living with HIV (8 MSM, 8 FSW; median age 23.5) and 20 key informants (7 women, 13 men) representing community leadership ( n = 4), climate and environmental issues ( n = 8), and HIV expertise ( n = 8). Participants identified multi-level and interconnected strategies to sustain HIV care during droughts and floods. Institutional-level recommendations included decentralizing and mobilizing antiretroviral therapy (ART) delivery, expanding multi-month dispensing, maintaining emergency drug buffers, integrating nutritional support to address food insecurity, and equipping frontline workers for adverse weather conditions. Community-level strategies emphasized livelihood and savings initiatives, environmental management, infrastructure improvements, peer support networks, and targeted outreach during weather-related disruptions. Household-level strategies included strengthening food and water security, diversifying income sources, planning ahead for treatment continuity, and using practical transport solutions, such as bicycles, to overcome flood-related barriers. Conclusions Sustaining HIV care during weather-related disruptions requires coordinated responses that extend beyond the health sector. Climate-resilient HIV programmes should integrate service delivery adaptations with social protection, livelihood support, infrastructure investments, and community-led interventions to enable uninterrupted HIV care for young Ugandan key populations with HIV in climate-affected settings.
keywords: young men who have sex with men

title: Resilience, market transparency, and farmer performance: an information processing perspective on fragmented agricultural markets
abstract: Farmers’ value realization is restricted by structural uncertainty, institutional fragmentation, and information asymmetry in the agricultural markets of developing economies. Previous studies have largely conceptualized resilience through disruption and recovery perspectives, while less attention has been given to its role in information processing and coordination within fragmented agricultural systems. Building on Information Processing Theory (IPT), this conceptual study reconceptualizes Agricultural Supply Chain Resilience as a distributed information-processing capacity and proposes that it influences farmer performance through market execution capability, with market transparency acting as a boundary condition. Market execution capability reflects the ability to convert coordinated information into market processes, including grading, pricing, auctioning, and settlement. By reducing informational ambiguity and enhancing the reliability and interpretability of market information, market transparency moderates the extent to which execution ability converts into farmer outcomes. By positioning resilience as a distributed information processing capability, the study’s framework advances IPT beyond primary hierarchical organizational settings to fragmented agricultural systems. This study indicates a multi-faceted approach to policy interventions that should combine digital market platforms and transparency mechanisms with institutional capacity, farmer organizations, and support for market access and bargaining conditions.

title: Unpacking the drivers of improved crop technology adoption and intensity among smallholder farmers in Ethiopia’s Amhara Region
abstract: Agricultural transformation in sub-Saharan Africa depends critically on the adoption of improved crop technologies, yet uptake remains limited despite sustained dissemination efforts. This study unpacks the drivers influencing smallholder farmers’ decisions to adopt and intensify the use of improved agricultural technologies in Ethiopia’s Amhara Region, an area characterized by diverse agro-ecologies and persistent food insecurity. Utilizing cross-sectional household survey data from 486 randomly selected farm households across three zones, we employ a generalized double-hurdle model with correlated errors to analyze two sequential decision-making processes: the initial adoption decision and the intensity of adoption, measured by land area allocated to improved technologies. We also estimate a Multivariate Probit model to account for joint adoption of technology packages, and conduct sub-sample analyses to examine household-level heterogeneity. The results reveal that adoption is a multi-phase process, with distinct drivers influencing each stage. Household-level characteristics, including education, agricultural experience, and social network participation, significantly affect the initial adoption decision. In contrast, resource endowments such as livestock holdings and farm size predominantly determine the intensity of technology use. Institutional factors, including access to extension services and credit, play significant roles across both decision stages. The correlation between the two hurdles is positive and significant (ρ = 0.42, p < 0.01), confirming the presence of selection bias and justifying the generalized specification. Adoption rates vary substantially by technology type, from 78% for inorganic fertilizer to 23% for improved crop varieties. Heterogeneity analysis reveals that credit constraints bind more tightly for small farms and female-headed households, while extension services substitute for formal education among less educated farmers. The findings underscore the importance of distinguishing between adoption and intensity when designing agricultural extension and technology dissemination policies. Tailored interventions that address both entry-level behavioral barriers and resource constraints are essential for scaling up improved crop technologies. By disaggregating the adoption process, this study provides nuanced insights for policymakers and development practitioners seeking to foster sustainable agricultural transformation in resource-constrained, climate-vulnerable settings.

title: Data Fusion of GPS Trackers and Activometers Mounted on Milking Cows for Alpine Pasture Exploitation Monitoring
abstract: Extensive grazing in alpine environments represents a livestock management strategy that contributes to landscape conservation, animal welfare, and allows the production of high-quality dairy products. Digital technologies offer a potential solution to these challenges by supporting farmers and facilitating generational turnover. In this work, 20 lactating cows were monitored during the grazing season using GPS devices to track movements across the pasture area and activometers composed of an accelerometer-based collar that recorded cow neck movements continuously, classifying them into three possible behaviours: rumination, feeding and resting. Data provided by the activometers were collected with a resolution of 15 min intervals, reporting the duration of each activity, while GPS data were collected at an average frequency of 5 min. GPS data were filtered for potential outliers and subsequently aligned with activometers data through a Visual Basic for Applications (VBA) algorithm. This data fusion optimization enabled the creation of a robust integrated dataset in which each GPS position was associated with the animal’s predominant activity, allowing the analysis of grazing patterns and the generation of high-resolution grazing maps. The combination of these two digital tools proved effective in assessing animal behaviour in mountainous environments, providing operational indicators to support pasture management and improve forage biomass utilisation.

title: From downstream demand to upstream innovation: how a digital platform coordinates agri-food value chain upgrading—the case of Taotian Digital Agriculture
abstract: Digital platforms are becoming increasingly involved in upstream agricultural production, yet existing research offers limited explanation of why consumer-facing platforms move beyond transaction intermediation or how they coordinate innovation across fragmented agri-food value chains. This study addresses this question through an in-depth case study of Taotian Group’s ready-to-eat kiwifruit project in China, drawing on interviews, field observations, internal corporate documents, government materials, and public sources. The case evidence indicates that upstream involvement followed the platform’s recognition that unstable fruit quality, inadequate postharvest technologies, and weak market rewards for quality improvement were constraining downstream value creation. Taotian Digital Agriculture responded by translating consumer demand into a clearly defined product target and coordinating the technological and organizational adjustments required across production, processing, storage, logistics, and sales. Demand forecasting, product grading, and differentiated market channels further reduced uncertainty over innovation returns and reinforced upstream investment. The study identifies a demand-to-innovation mechanism through which downstream market capabilities are converted into upstream innovation and coordination capabilities. The case further indicates that the durability and inclusiveness of platform-led upgrading may depend on stable economic returns, accessible local services, manageable compliance costs, risk-sharing arrangements, and platform governance. The study therefore clarifies how a consumer-facing platform can link demand interpretation, upstream innovation coordination, and market-value realization, while identifying economic and social conditions that warrant further empirical examination.

title: Contestation Between the State, Oil and Fishers in Trinidad and Tobago: (Re)producing ‘Edge’ Populations on the Post‐Plantation Extraction Frontier
abstract: ABSTRACT Successive waves of extraction in the Caribbean—from plantation monocultures to oil and gas—have reshaped overlapping agrarian, coastal and marine environments, undermining the socio‐ecological foundations of small‐scale fisher livelihoods and generating ongoing conflict between the state, energy sector and fishing communities. Yet despite the importance of fishing to post‐colonial island economies, these tensions are rarely examined through a post‐plantation lens. Bringing Caribbean plantation scholarship together with more recent work on race, social reproduction and exclusion, this article examines the enduring colonial logics structuring such contestation in Trinidad and Tobago. Drawing on historical, ethnographic and interview research, it argues that historically entrenched systems of valuation and dispossession remain fundamental to understanding how some people and places become devalued and how this, in turn, facilitates continued extraction. Small‐scale fishers and marine environments are conceptualised as ‘edge’ populations and spaces whose marginality is continually (re)produced by state‐mediated capital accumulation rooted in colonial legacies and oriented towards export‐driven extraction, rather than rural development or domestic food security. In Trinidad, extractive capitalism intensifies processes of devaluation, expropriation and exclusion, while sustaining an illusion—or ‘masquerade’—of inclusion. Understanding fishers' position in this way reveals the cyclical nature of their struggles and demonstrates that their marginalisation and depletion are implicated in, rather than peripheral to, post‐colonial capitalist development. Consequently, these frontier spaces and the marginal communities that populate them remain important sites of social reproduction and negotiation over legitimacy and control.

title: Pork Price Fluctuations in China: Epidemic Associations, Storage and Release Operations, and Forecasting
abstract: Pork remains a cornerstone of many food systems, and fluctuations in its price are a critical concern for the economic sustainability of agricultural supply chains. This study connects epidemic associations, reserve-operation case studies and forecasting to examine pork price fluctuations in China using average retail prices in 36 major cities. Linear and nonlinear regressions examine epidemic conditions, while reserve cases compare price changes and pig-to-grain ratios. Chronological out-of-sample forecasts compare seven models at one-, three- and six-week horizons, with ordinary least squares as the principal benchmark. Direct-price and cumulative-change approaches are evaluated on the original price scale. The epidemic index exhibits a nonlinear association in the five-knot specification with year controls despite limited linear explanatory power. Reserve episodes show differing adjustment paths, and higher pig-to-grain ratios are not consistently accompanied by lower dispersion. Univariate autoregressive integrated moving average (ARIMA) achieves the lowest root mean squared error in most comparisons, while market indicators improve selected forecasts. Support vector regression using price history and slaughter profits under the cumulative-change approach yields the lowest three-week errors among the evaluated main-sample configurations. These findings inform market monitoring and the selection of forecasting indicators and models.

title: Determinants of climate smart agricultural practices adoption and their implications for household food security in Musanze District, Rwanda
abstract: Climate change threatens smallholder agriculture in Sub-Saharan Africa. In Musanze District, this study assessed Climate Smart Agriculture (CSA) adoption and its impact on household food security. A cross-sectional survey of 422 households used HFIAS and HDDS indicators. CSA adoption was high (91.7–100%), though constrained by land fragmentation. All households were food secure, with a mean HDDS of 10.78. Higher adoption intensity was associated with greater dietary diversity, measured using the Household Dietary Diversity Score (HDDS). Farmers perceived gains in income and diet, but not affordability. While CSA supports food security, addressing land fragmentation, input access and market challenges is essential for sustained impact.

title: The Impact of Digital Skills on Common Prosperity for Rural and Pastoral Households in Underdeveloped Regions
abstract: With the rapid development of artificial intelligence and digital tools, the digital economy has become an important driving force for socioeconomic development, and digital skills have become a crucial capability for achieving common prosperity. Based on 804 pieces of micro-survey data from agricultural and pastoral areas in Xizang, this study explores common prosperity from the objective material dimension and subjective spiritual dimension, starting with the economic effect and social effect of digital skills. It constructs a dual-path analysis framework of “digital skills–economic behavior–common prosperity” and “digital skills–social psychology–common prosperity” to theoretically analyze and empirically test the logical relationship and mechanism of action of digital skills on the common prosperity of agricultural and pastoral households in underdeveloped regions. The research indicates that digital skills significantly promote the common prosperity of agricultural and pastoral households in underdeveloped regions, with a greater impact on spiritual common prosperity than material common prosperity. Heterogeneity analysis reveals that the promotion effect of digital skills on common prosperity is more pronounced in villages located in relatively economically developed agricultural areas, indicating the existence of certain digital poverty and a digital divide. The mechanism analysis shows that digital skills affect common prosperity through two paths: non-agricultural employment in economic behavior and fairness perception in social psychology. Therefore, it is necessary to improve digital infrastructure in agricultural and pastoral areas and enhance the digital skills of agricultural and pastoral households in underdeveloped regions; improve the information release and transmission mechanism of digital platforms to promote non-agricultural employment; enhance digital social inclusiveness and digital cultural regulation to improve fairness perception; and leverage the empowering and converging effects of the digital economy, harness the economic effect and social effect of digital skills, and enhance both material and spiritual common prosperity to achieve comprehensive common prosperity.

title: A Study on the Spatial Differentiation Mechanisms and Optimization Pathways for the Synergistic Integration of Multifunctional Homestead Sites and Rural Revitalization—A Case Study of Deqing County, China
abstract: Existing studies rarely investigate the relationship between the diversity of homesteads and rural revitalization at the county scale, and the attention given to the spatial differentiation mechanism and differentiation optimization paths of the two is still insufficient. As land that guarantees farmers’ housing security and their core asset, rural homesteads are vital for rural revitalization. This study examines the relationship between homestead diversity and rural development, focusing on spatial differentiation mechanisms and possible optimization paths. Based on field surveys in 103 villages and questionnaire data from farmers and officials in Deqing County, this study explores the multifunctionality of homesteads, rural revitalization, and their spatial coupling and symbiosis mechanisms. Results provide the following observations: (1) From 2015 to 2020, both homestead multifunctionality and rural revitalization improved. Their coupling coordination followed a “high-west, low-east” pattern, with primarily coordinated areas expanding, synergy index high-value zones shifting eastward, regional disparities narrowing, and symbiotic coefficients exhibiting spatial complementarity. (2) Homestead multifunctionality lagged mainly around the county seat, while rural revitalization lagged mostly along administrative boundaries. (3) For regions with differing levels of homestead development and rural revitalization, differentiated optimization strategies are proposed across four dimensions: political, economic, social, and technological. In areas where homestead development lags, a dual-track approach combining policy incentives and market mechanisms is recommended, together with improvements in infrastructure and public services. In areas where rural revitalization lags, five key strategies are proposed: industry-led development, talent cultivation, cultural empowerment, ecological livability, and organizational strengthening. This study developed an analytical framework for the coordinated integration of homestead diversity and rural revitalization at the county scale, revealing the mechanisms underlying their differentiated symbiotic relationship and advancing the theoretical understanding of the synergies between homestead diversity and rural revitalization. In practice, a differentiated optimization path of zoning and classification is proposed to provide practical guidance for coordinating the advancement of county-level homestead reform and rural revitalization.

title: The synergistic effect of internet-based health communication on health promotion: the chain-mediating effect of health literacy and health education
abstract: Next-generation internet technologies, represented by artificial intelligence, are reshaping the nationwide health information distribution system; this study examines the synergistic benefit effect of online health communication on health promotion. The analysis utilizes 5,333 data points from the 2023 China General Social Survey (CGSS), which employed a nationally stratified, multi-stage sampling design. Using the Hayes PROCESS Model 6 serial chain mediation model, 2,000 bias-correction Bootstrap samples were generated to conduct baseline OLS regression, mediation effect decomposition, multidimensional heterogeneity analysis, and an IPW inverse probability weighting robustness test. The baseline OLS regression reveals a significant positive overall association between online health communication and health promotion. The chain mediation model identified three indirect pathways: a single health literacy mediation pathway, a single digital health education mediation pathway, and a core serial synergistic pathway (“Online Health Communication → Health Literacy → Digital Health Education → Health Promotion”); the confidence intervals for all three pathways do not include zero. The heterogeneity analysis uncovered the distribution pattern of the digital health gap: the serial chain effect is slightly higher in urban areas than in rural areas, and slightly higher among women than among men (though the intergroup difference is not statistically significant); the strongest effect is observed among the middle-aged population aged 31–60 years, while the serial transmission chain tends to weaken among groups with lower educational attainment. Multiple robustness tests, including IPW inverse probability weighting, support the reliability of the core findings. The positive association between online health communication and residents’ health promotion can be explained through the independent and serial mediation statistical pathways involving health literacy and digital health education; this observation reveals a “progressive synergy” relationship among the three factors.

title: Morphological, Agronomic and Genetic Characterization of Northern Italian Polenta Maize Landraces
abstract: Agrobiodiversity encompasses the diversity of plants, animals, and microorganisms that sustain agricultural ecosystems and underpin global food security. Within agrobiodiversity, Plant Genetic Resources for Food and Agriculture (PGRFA) play a central role in enhancing the adaptability and resilience of cropping systems. However, the transition to modern, high-yielding cultivars during the Green Revolution led to widespread genetic erosion, particularly affecting landraces. Although extensive ex situ conservation efforts have been undertaken, complementary in situ and on-farm strategies remain essential to maintain evolutionary potential and local adaptation. In Northern Italy, numerous maize landraces are currently threatened by extinction, especially in Alpine and pre-Alpine areas where materials are poorly documented and often absent from seed banks.
