The study reveals the following: (1) Both ARM and ARG levels in Jilin Province showed upward trends, with the pace of ARM development generally outpacing that of ARG; (2) Development levels exhibited east-west disparities, with Da’an and Zhenlai counties ranking highest in ARM and Changling and Wangqing counties highest in ARG; (3) Coupling coordination increased annually, transitioning from low to intermediate coordination, with the ranges of primary and intermediate coordination steadily expanding; (4) Spatial clustering was evident in coupling coordination, exhibiting a distinct ‘high in the west, low in the east’ gradient. This research advances theoretical understanding of the coordination between ARM and ARG and provides empirical support for China’s rural revitalization goal.

title: Local ecological knowledge, governance and commercialisation in mangrove–oyster fisheries of the Gambia
abstract: Oyster harvesting within mangrove ecosystems represents a critical livelihood activity for coastal communities in the Gambia, particularly for women. This study examines governance arrangements, harvesting practices, and livelihood dynamics from the perspective of oyster harvesters. Increasing commercialisation has progressively shifted oyster harvesting from primarily subsistence-orientated use toward an important source of household income, creating new interactions among livelihood needs, resource use, and mangrove management. Using a qualitative case study approach, we interviewed 60 female oyster harvesters in two key oyster harvesting sites, the urban Tanbi Wetland complex and the rural Foni Bullock catchment area. Individual interviews, complemented by two focus group discussions, were analysed to explore interactions among ecological conditions, governance mechanisms, local ecological knowledge, and livelihood strategies. Oyster harvesting remained an important livelihood activity across both sites, with broadly comparable patterns of sole and diversified livelihood dependence. Harvesting practices were strongly shaped by local ecological knowledge of tidal cycles, seasonal variation, oyster availability, and mangrove conditions, with knowledge transmitted predominantly through families. Participants reported increasing harvesting pressure and declining oyster abundance, alongside the growing importance of formalised governance measures such as seasonal closures, harvesting restrictions, and collective monitoring. Commercialisation was reflected in changing processing practices and market interactions, although market access and governance implementation differed between the urban Tanbi and rural Foni Bullock systems. The findings highlight the need for integrated governance approaches that recognise the interconnections among ecological conditions, local ecological knowledge, community institutions, commercialisation, and gendered livelihood strategies. Strengthening community-based governance, women’s participation in decision-making, sustainable harvesting practices, and equitable access to training and markets will be important for supporting the long-term sustainability and resilience of mangrove–oyster fisheries in The Gambia.

title: The role of rural tourism in promoting small farmer’s income: Evidence from the sub-Himalayan region of Eastern India
journal: Local Economy The Journal of the Local Economy Policy Unit
abstract: Rural tourism is increasingly recognised as a viable non-farm livelihood strategy for small and marginal farmers, especially in regions with strong tourism potential. However, despite its growing policy relevance, empirical evidence on its role in improving farmers’ income in the sub-Himalayan region of Eastern India remains limited. This study examines the determinants of farmers’ participation in tourism-led livelihood activities and estimates the impact of this participation on household income. Primary data were collected from 400 households across eight villages in the Jalpaiguri and Alipurduar districts of West Bengal, India. A binary probit model was used to analyse participation decisions, while a two-stage least squares instrumental variables approach was used to estimate income effects. The findings reveal that access to credit, housing conditions, marital status, migration, and primary occupation significantly influence participation. Participation in tourism has a positive and statistically significant impact on farmers’ income. Additionally, gender, age, education, landholding size, migration, and family structure are positively associated with income among participating households. The study highlights key drivers and constraints of tourism participation. It emphasises the need to promote rural tourism alongside supportive policies such as improved access to credit, skill development, and local employment opportunities to ensure inclusive and sustainable livelihood outcomes.

title: Nitrogen Management for Mitigating Agricultural N2O Emissions in Semi-Arid Morocco: A Comparative Review
abstract: Morocco’s semi-arid farms are under growing pressure to lower nitrous oxide (N2O) emissions while maintaining crop yields and soil health. Agriculture is a major anthropogenic source of N2O emissions in Morocco; improved nitrogen management is therefore relevant to the country’s broader climate mitigation efforts. This review examines regulatory, technical, and economic measures that have reduced nitrogen losses or agricultural N2O emissions in other countries and assesses their potential relevance to Morocco’s smallholder-dominated farming systems. In 2018, Moroccan managed soils released 13,108 Gg of carbon dioxide equivalents (CO2-eq) according to the national inventory, highlighting the importance of improved nitrogen management for agricultural climate mitigation. The study compares peer-reviewed research, policy documents, and regulatory frameworks from four benchmark countries: Denmark, the Netherlands, the United Kingdom, and Brazil. It addresses three questions: which nitrogen management strategies have evidence of reducing agricultural N2O emissions in contexts relevant to Morocco; which institutional, regulatory, and socioeconomic barriers may constrain their adoption; and how these strategies could be incorporated into a phased national framework. For each intervention, the review synthesizes reported outcomes, the agronomic and climatic conditions under which they were obtained, and their potential transferability to Morocco’s semi-arid agricultural systems. Outcomes are differentiated as direct N2O measurements, nitrogen loss or fertilizer use indicators, agronomic feasibility evidence, or policy and enabling evidence. The review also identifies gaps in Morocco’s fertilizer governance under Law No. 53-18 and considers national enabling assets, including soil fertility mapping, emerging organic-fertilizer supply chains, conservation agriculture initiatives, and existing agricultural-support programmes. The review presents an author-proposed Integrated Nitrogen Management Framework (INMF) based on three complementary pillars: regulatory reform, field-level technical measures, and economic instruments. It presents three implementation periods—2027–2029, 2029–2032, and 2032–2035—for testing, validating, and progressively scaling these measures under Moroccan conditions. The INMF is a conceptual, phased implementation framework rather than a quantitative national mitigation model. It does not estimate an aggregate agricultural N2O emission reduction because the reviewed interventions differ in their production context, evidence type, and measured outcome. Morocco’s unconditional Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC) provides the broader policy context, but its economy-wide target is not interpreted as a sector-specific target for agricultural N2O emissions. The review discusses implementation challenges, including data limitations, institutional capacity constraints, and smallholder adoption barriers. It identifies priorities for Morocco: field measurement of N2O emissions and emission factors, multi-site evaluation of mitigation practices, strengthened monitoring and advisory systems, and socioeconomic assessment of farmer adoption and policy feasibility.

title: Beyond impulsivity: cultural scripts and social learning of female suicide in rural northern China
abstract: Beginning in the late 1990s, China drew global attention for its high suicide rates and an unusual pattern of elevated suicide among rural women. Much of the literature attributed these deaths to impulsivity. However, such accounts understate the structural pressures and cultural scripts through which interpersonal distress is transformed into suicidal behavior. This study examines the cultural context of suicidal behavior among rural Chinese women in the early 2000s. This study re-analyzes ethnographic data collected between 2004 and 2006 in rural northern China, where female suicide rates were unusually high. The oral life histories of 11 women who had survived a suicidal act in which the suicidal behavior appeared to be impulsive were examined together with related participant observation and in-depth interview materials drawn from ethnographic data on 62 villagers, including bereaved family members. Six focus group interviews were also reviewed to identify local explanatory frameworks. Three main patterns observed. First, the regional maxim about female suicide—“First cry, second make a fuss, and if that fails, hang oneself”—functioned as a culturally recognized script for women responding to conflict. Second, female suicide became familiar and socially learned through repeated exposure to female suicidal acts among close kin and neighbors. Third, local discourse explained suicide as a symptom of women’s impulsivity and “narrow-mindedness,” thereby obscuring its meaning of protest against constrained agency within patriarchal household relations and broader systems. This study’s findings suggest that the seemingly impulsive patterns of suicidal behavior among rural Chinese women in the early 2000s are better understood through a context and cultural-script lens rather than through an individual psychopathology lens. In patriarchal settings that leave women few legitimate means to voice grievances, female suicidal behavior becomes a culturally available, socially learned response to express distress and protest. Female suicide prevention everywhere should address the context and the cultural scripts that shape women’s suicidality.

title: Gendered landscapes of loss: climate change, disaster, and women's resilience in rural India
abstract: This article examines the gendered dimensions of climate-induced disasters in rural India through a systematic archival analysis of five community testimonies published by the People's Archive of Rural India (PARI). Drawing on stories from Odisha, Maharashtra, Assam, and Kerala, the study analyses how climate change manifesting as erratic monsoons, intensifying floods, accelerating riverbank erosion, and catastrophic landslides disproportionately impacts women in agrarian and indigenous communities. The article employs a qualitative methodology combining systematic archival analysis with a structured three-phase coding protocol (deductive, inductive, and cross-case thematic synthesis) and an intersectionality framework to trace how gender intersects with caste, indigeneity, and rural marginality to shape differential vulnerabilities. The five PARI narratives are situated within a broader analytical organization informed by the Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction (2015–2030) and feminist political ecology. Findings reveal three interconnected themes: (1) the erosion of women's agricultural knowledge systems and seed sovereignty under climate stress; (2) the gendered burden of displacement, care work, and livelihood loss during and after flood disasters; and (3) women's emergent roles as agents of climate adaptation through agroecological practice and community-based resilience. The article argues that community-authored narratives constitute a vital but underutilised epistemological resource for disaster scholarship, offering situated, intersectional knowledge that complements quantitative risk assessments. It concludes with policy recommendations for gender-responsive disaster risk reduction (DRR) in India that centre local women's knowledge and agency.

title: Advancements in Applied Food Biotechnology: Integrated Approaches in Biopreservatives, and Probiotic Delivery Systems, Two Years of Journal Experience
publisher: Shahid Behehsti University of Medical Sciences
abstract: Background and Aim: Faced with rising antimicrobial resistance, environmental concerns, and growing consumer demand for clean-label food products, applied food biotechnology plays a pivotal role in establishing sustainable, resilient, and health-oriented food networks. This manuscript synthesizes recent advancements across three interconnected domains: natural antimicrobials, industrial fermentation, and probiotic delivery systems. Material and Methods: Critical analysis of the manuscript publiched in last years from Applied Food Biotechnology was performed. Results and Conclusion: In biopreservation, natural antimicrobials, including plant essential oils, polyphenols, lytic bacteriophages, and microbial bacteriocins, offer non-toxic alternatives to synthetic chemical additives. These bioactive compounds disrupt cell membranes and suppress quorum sensing, effectively controlling persistent pathogens such as Staphylococcus aureus, Escherichia coli O157:H7, and Listeria monocytogenes without promoting cross-resistance. Furthermore, innovations in functional food microbiology have accelerated the development of plant-based probiotics, postbiotics, and advanced encapsulation matrices. These delivery systems safeguard microbial viability during thermal processing and gastrointestinal transit, facilitating targeted delivery to support gut homeostasis, immune modulation, and metabolic regulation. Together, these multidisciplinary strategies bridge fundamental microbiology with industrial applications to build safer, sustainable food systems. INTRODUCTION Knowledge is rarely built in isolation; it thrives at the intersection of diverse disciplines. In multidisciplinary fields like applied food biotechnology, progress depends on bridging microbiology, biochemistry, food engineering, and green technology. Applied Food Biotechnology is a journal that welcomes a wide variety of topics acting as a vibrant ecosystem of ideas. By bringing together research on natural biopreservatives, precision fermentation, strain engineering, and bio-nanotechnology, it reflects a core truth: variety is the foundation of modern understanding. Embracing a spectrum of perspectives breaks rigid scientific silos, encouraging cross-pollination where a discovery in one domain sparks innovation in another. Ultimately, celebrating thematic breadth equips us to navigate complex global food challenges with agility, creativity, and lasting resilience. The modern landscape of food science, human health, and agricultural sustainability faces unprecedented challenges. The global rise of antimicrobial resistance (AMR), driven by the overuse of conventional antibiotics, poses a major threat to public health and clinical medicine. Concurrently, changing climate patterns, expanding international supply chains, and evolving consumer demands are forcing the food industry to transition away from synthetic chemical additives, artificial preservatives, and environmentally detrimental manufacturing work-flows. In response to these pressing global issues, the integration of natural antimicrobials, food microbiology, and functional probiotic delivery systems has emerged as a crucial paradigm for the next generation of safe, resilient, and health-oriented food systems. At the center of this paradigm shift is the exploitation of natural antimicrobial compounds derived from plants, animals, and beneficial microorganisms. Bioactive molecules, such as plant essential oils, polyphenols, microbial bacteriocins, and lytic bacteriophages, offer potent, non-toxic alternatives to traditional chemical pesticides and synthetic food preservatives. Unlike single-target synthetic drugs, natural antimicrobials frequently operate via complex, multi-target mechanisms, such as bacterial cell membrane disruption, cell wall lysis, or the suppression of quorum sensing gene expression, which drastically lowers the likelihood of target pathogens developing cross-resistance. Integrating these natural biopreservatives into food matrices effectively inhibits persistent foodborne pathogens (including Staph. aureus, Escherichia coli O157:H7, Listeria monocytogenes, and Clostridium species) while extending product shelf-life and ensuring consumer safety. Finally, the convergence of food microbiology and probiotic research continues to expand the therapeutic landscape of functional nutrition. Beyond traditional fermented dairy products, innovative plant-based matrices, postbiotic supernatants, and advanced microencapsulation technologies (e.g., electrospun nanofibers, bio-nanocomposites, and chitosan complexes) are critical for preserving microbial viability against thermal processing and gastrointestinal stress. These delivery vehicles enable targeted intestinal release, supporting host gut homeostasis, immune modulation, and metabolic regulation, such as dyslipidemia and blood glucose control [1]. Collectively, recent advancements in applied food biotechnology bridge fundamental biological research with practical industrial applications. By uniting bio-preservation, metabolic strain engineering, bioprocess optimization, and targeted functional delivery, scientific innovation continues to build sustainable, safe, and health-promoting global food networks for the future. ANTIMICROBIALS Studying natural antimicrobial compounds derived from plants, fungi, bacteria, and marine organisms is critical in addressing some of modern medicine's greatest challenges. On other side, as conventional antibiotics face declining efficacy due to the global rise of antimicrobial resistance (AMR), drug-resistant superbugs threaten public health. Natural products provide a vast, untapped chemical landscape containing unique bio-active molecules that can serve as templates for next-generation pharmaceuticals. Beyond human medicine, research into natural antimicrobials plays a vital role in agriculture and food security. Applications of natural antimicrobials is essential in production of food products where help to reduce traditional chemical preservatives and to respond to the demands for more natural and healthier food commodities. Plant-based essential oils, polyphenols, and microbial bacteriocins offer non-toxic alternatives to synthetic chemical pesticides and artificial food preservatives. Integrating these bio-preservatives helps inhibit foodborne pathogens, extend shelf life, and reduce consumer exposure to synthetic chemicals. Furthermore, natural antimicrobials often exhibit complex mechanisms of action, such as targeting bacterial cell membranes or disrupting quorum sensing, making it harder for microbes to develop resistance compared to single-target synthetic drugs. Investigating these compounds unlocks sustainable solutions across medicine, agriculture, and industry [2-4]. Thus, is not surprising that in last one year, several papers published in Applied Food Biotechnology were available on exploring different aspects of natural antimicrobials as effective tools in controls of pathogens and spoilages in food and clinical areas. Staph. aureus is one of the most cited pathogens related to clinical and food safety aspects that poses persistent food safety challenges due to its widespread prevalence and heat-resistant enterotoxins [5]. Finding appropriate antimicrobials to control Staph. aureus is challenge. Wang et al. [5] suggested applications of purified egg-white lysozyme and reported on strong catalytic activity log-phase Staph. aureus. Authors [5] reported on that expressed mode of action can be considered as primarily bacteriolytic, hydrolyzing peptidoglycan bonds in the bacterial cell wall, which results in membrane collapse and intracellular leakage. In addition, thermal modification under optimized conditions (90 oC for 15 min at pH 6.2) can significantly enhance this antibacterial performance, boosting overall inhibition against S. aureus by 35.1 % to achieve 82.5 % total efficacy compared to the native enzyme. Moreover, authors explored possibilities for synergistic interactions with phenolic compounds, combining ferulic acid with lysozyme provides superior inhibition. And reported in possible mechanisms on activations of effective enzymatic cascade. Talking about food borne pathogens, one of the serious problems is contamination with E. coli O157:H7, extremely low infectious dose (fewer than 10 to 100 CFU), and capacity of this painvolvedto be involve in severe human illness such as hemorrhagic colitis and hemolytic-uremic syndrome [6]. In perspective on rise of antimicrobial resistance and the limitations of traditional chemical or physical decontamination methods, application of lytic bacteriophages can be a solution for control of E. coli O157:H7, as phages can offer a highly specific, natural alternative for biocontrol in food, including meat systems. In work of Molaei Gharamaleki et al. [6], authors evaluated single-phage treatments and demonstrate strong, dose-dependent bactericidal action. Even with high initial contamination level of 107 CFU/mL of E. coli O157:H7 on beef, application of single-phage treatment (phage tf1) at a multiplicity of infection (MOI) of 0.1 eliminates 65 % of bacteria within 20 minutes at room temperature, while increasing the dose to an MOI of 100 achieves a 99 % reduction. Moreover, if exposure period was increased to over 60-minute, single-phage application yields a 93.5 % reduction at MOI 10, a 99 % reduction at MOI 100, and complete (100 %) bacterial elimination at MOI 1000. All these results served as proof for efficacity of phage treatment. Moreover, authors suggested that phage cocktails (comprising phages tf1, tf2, and sc) can be even more effective, bringing cell counts below clinical transmission thresholds. title: Women at the Helm: Female Top Managers and Business Process Innovation in Ecuadorian Firms
abstract: Women’s participation in senior management has increased, yet evidence regarding its relationship with different forms of business innovation remains inconclusive, particularly in emerging economies. This study examines whether formal Ecuadorian firms with a woman as their top manager are more likely to report business process innovation than firms led by men. A quantitative, non-experimental, cross-sectional design was applied to firm-level data from 345 enterprises included in the World Bank Enterprise Survey Ecuador; 66 firms (19.1%) reported a female top manager. Process innovation was measured from WBES item H5, which asks whether the establishment introduced a new or improved process during the preceding three years, including production or service methods, logistics/delivery/distribution, or supporting activities. Weighted logit models with firm controls and sector and region fixed effects were estimated. In the main specification (n = 327), female top management was associated with higher odds of process innovation (OR = 3.475; 95% CI [1.570, 7.688]; p = 0.002), and the direction remained positive across robustness checks. No statistically significant association was found with product innovation, R&D expenditure, or green-practice adoption. The findings therefore support a differentiated interpretation: female top management is associated with internal process change, but not uniformly with every innovation outcome. Because the data are cross-sectional and the female-manager group is comparatively small, the estimates are associational, their precision and heterogeneity are limited, and generalization is restricted to the formal non-agricultural private-sector population represented by the WBES sampling frame.

title: Building capacity for short food supply chains through food processing workshops: Experience from the Horizon Europe RURBANIVE project
abstract: Background Short food supply chains (SFSCs) are increasingly recognised as a means of improving the sustainability, resilience and economic viability of local food systems. However, many farmers and small-scale food producers lack the technological knowledge required to develop value-added products for direct sale. The Horizon Europe RURBANIVE project addresses these challenges through knowledge exchange, capacity building and innovation. Within this framework, practical food processing workshops were designed as multi-actor learning activities promoting collaboration between academia, farmers, food producers and public authorities and building their capacities. This study evaluated participants’ perceptions of the workshops and the potential contribution of those practical courses and digital learning platform for shortening the food supply chains. Methods Between 2025 and 2026, eight practical workshops on dairy, bakery, meat and brewing technologies were organised at the Czech University of Life Sciences Prague. The workshops combined theoretical lectures with hands-on demonstrations on pilot-scale processing lines. Overall, 122stakeholders participated, but only 92 (75.4%) of them completed an anonymous post-workshop questionnaire evaluating nine aspects of the educational activities. Digital learning platform Moodle has been developed as a follow-up of the workshops but cannot be evaluated yet. Results Participant satisfaction was very high. Almost all respondents were satisfied with the workshops, considered the objectives clear and highly rated the facilitators. The duration of the workshops and the balance between theory and practice were positively evaluated, while 77.2% of respondents expressed interest in attending similar events in the future. The workshops resulted in the development of digital learning platform with four production courses and one product marketing course. Conclusions Practical workshops effectively supported knowledge transfer and strengthened participants’ capacity to develop value-added products suitable for direct sales channels. Combined with digital learning tool, they provide a transferable model for supporting short food supply chains and more resilient local food systems.

title: Unlocking Innovation in European Plant Breeding: A Perspective on the New Genomic Techniques Framework
abstract: New genomic techniques (NGTs), including targeted mutagenesis and cisgenesis, can accelerate plant breeding and support the development of crops adapted to abiotic stresses associated with climate change and to biotic stresses such as pests and diseases, resource limitations and changing societal needs. Their application in the European Union has nevertheless been constrained by legislation adopted before these technologies became available, especially Directive 2001/18/EC, and by the regulatory gap following the 2018 decision on Case C-528/16 of the Court of Justice of the European Union. The recent Regulation (EU) 2026/1388 establishes a dedicated framework that differentiates NGT plants with changes comparable to those obtainable naturally or by conventional breeding from plants carrying more complex modifications. This Perspective welcomes the shift towards greater scientific proportionality and considers how it can translate European research strength into varieties and products reaching farmers, value chains and consumers. Although only few genome-edited crops have reached commercial application to date, they do not necessarily predict the future direction of genome-edited crop development. Nevertheless, they illustrate that genome editing is already being applied to a diverse range of product concepts beyond experimental research. We argue, however, that regulatory reform alone will not unlock innovation. Success will require harmonised implementation, practical and affordable access to enabling technologies, intellectual property and breeding germplasm, participation by public institutions and smaller breeders, and transparent evaluation of environmental, social and economic outcomes. The forthcoming European Biotech Act II also offers an opportunity to develop coherent, application-specific approaches for NGT microorganisms and industrial biotechnology.
keywords: Court of Justice of the European Union

title: Are cooperatives associated with more resilient financial architectures? Evidence from Spanish agricultural firms
journal: Journal of Co-operative Organization and Management
abstract: This study examines whether cooperative organization is associated with a distinct financial resilience profile among agricultural firms. Financial resilience is conceptualized as the combination of ex-ante buffering capacity (liquidity and working-capital slack, together with the operating flow that replenishes these buffers) and ex-post downside exposure (the realized incidence of accounting losses). Drawing on the literature on cooperative governance, organizational purpose and financial flexibility, the paper argues that cooperatives should not be evaluated only through average profitability, because their organizational logic may be more visible in liquidity preservation, working-capital slack and downside-risk exposure. Using firm-level panel data on Spanish agricultural firms for 2014–2024, the study compares cooperatives with investor-owned firms through models with province and year fixed effects, firm-level controls and several robustness checks based on stricter sample comparability, propensity-score weighting and balanced-panel restrictions. The results show no robust cooperative differential in return on assets. However, cooperative firms exhibit higher cash intensity, greater working-capital slack, stronger EBITDA-based operating performance in several specifications and a lower probability of reporting losses. These findings suggest that the cooperative form is associated less with systematically higher mean returns than with a more protective short-term financial architecture. The paper contributes to research on cooperation-based organizations by documenting that organizational form is systematically associated with the way firms structure financial buffers and limit downside exposure. It also extends cooperative performance research by shifting attention from profitability comparisons to resilience-oriented accounting outcomes.

title: Effects of Adding a Structured Exercise Programme to Ergonomics Training in Women Dairy Farmers: A Randomised Controlled Trial
abstract: Background/Objectives: Milking exposes women dairy farmers to sustained trunk flexion and repetitive upper-limb loading, producing a high burden of musculoskeletal disorders. Ergonomics education is the conventional preventive strategy, but added benefit from structured exercise is untested in this population. Methods: In this assessor-blinded randomised controlled trial, 50 women who had milked cows for ≥5 years were allocated to ergonomics training alone (control, n = 25) or ergonomics training plus a 12-week, home-based, equipment-free exercise programme (experimental, n = 25). The primary outcome was pain intensity (NRS), designated as primary only after data collection, so all analyses are exploratory; secondary outcomes were musculoskeletal symptoms (Nordic Questionnaire, seven-day recall at both assessments), upper-limb function (QuickDASH), depression (BDI) and quality of life (WHOQOL-BREF). Continuous outcomes were analysed by mixed-model ANOVA and ANCOVA. Results: All participants completed the trial, with self-reported exercise adherence of 100%. Time × group interactions favoured the combined intervention for pain (F1,48 = 55.19, p < 0.001; baseline-adjusted mean difference −1.25, 95% CI −1.58 to −0.92), upper-limb function, depressive symptom scores and three WHOQOL-BREF domains (all p < 0.05), but not social relationships (p = 0.896). Mean NRS reduction was −3.76 ± 0.66 versus −2.24 ± 0.78 (d = −2.10), and symptomatic body regions fell by −2.64 ± 0.70 versus −1.20 ± 1.53 (p < 0.001). Conclusions: Both groups improved, and adding a 12-week equipment-free exercise programme was associated with greater short-term, self-reported gains. These exploratory findings from a small single-region sample need confirmation in larger trials with objective adherence measures and longer follow-up.

title: A systems-oriented framework for wise, equitable, and sustainable digital agricultural transformation in sub-Saharan Africa: A critical review
abstract: CONTEXT Sub-Saharan Africa (SSA) faces mounting food security pressures amidst accelerating digital agricultural investment. Digital agricultural solutions in the region are growing rapidly, yet adoption remains uneven, often excluding women, resource-constrained smallholders, and remote rural communities. The prevailing ‘smart farming’ paradigm, which prioritizes technological optimization, has often failed to account for the structural, institutional, and social conditions that determine whether digital tools deliver durable outcomes. OBJECTIVE In this study, we argue that digital agricultural transformation in SSA requires fundamental reorientation, moving from technology-centric deployment to systems-oriented integration. We aim to operationalize the emerging concept of wise agricultural systems for the SSA context and to develop a framework that can guide more equitable, sustainable, and resilient digital agricultural transformation. METHODS We employ a critical narrative review, organizing the literature into five thematic strands covering digital advisory services and adoption, infrastructure, gender and equity, environmental sustainability, and data governance. Within each strand, we critically assess the evidence, examining underlying assumptions, identifying contradictions, and assessing where evidence is robust or remains limited. We use the wise agricultural systems concept and the Socio-Cyber-Physical System (SCPS) lens to organize our analytical structures. RESULTS We demonstrate that the primary barriers to effective digital agricultural transformation in SSA are systemic rather than technical. These barriers include weak rural road and connectivity infrastructure, fragmented, outdated, and non-interoperable public agricultural data resources, erosion of farmer trust through extractive platform design, institutional capacity deficits in extension and regulatory systems, a persistent gender digital divide affecting approximately half of SSA's smallholder farming population. These challenges are compounded by extractive platform designs that can erode farmer trust and data governance arrangements that concentrate value in corporate actors at the expense of farming communities. Digital tools that have generated durable benefits share common features, including proximity to farmer realities in design, integration with human advisory systems, and embedding within functional institutional arrangements. Drawing on these findings, we propose a four-component framework for wise digital agricultural transformation comprising ground-level integration, institutional infrastructure, equitable governance, and adaptive learning. CONCLUSIONS Wise digital agricultural systems in SSA are defined not by technological sophistication but by their demonstrated capacity to achieve balanced, resilient performance across socioeconomic viability, environmental sustainability, and social justice. Achieving this requires investment in the non-digital foundations of effective digital agriculture, including physical infrastructure, extension capacity, and data governance, and genuine participation of smallholder farmers in system design. SIGNIFICANCE In the study, we make a conceptual contribution by operationalizing the wise agricultural systems framework for SSA and by demonstrating that the persistent gap between digital agricultural promise and rural reality is a systemic rather than a technological problem. The proposed four-component framework offers actionable guidance for researchers, policymakers, development finance institutions, and platform designers seeking to redirect digital agricultural investment toward systems that serve people, sustainability, and justice.

title: The Genus Weissella: A Review of its Antimicrobial Potentials, Functional Characteristics and Uses in Food Biopreservation
publisher: Shahid Behehsti University of Medical Sciences
abstract: Background and Aim: Heterofermentative lactic acid bacteria belonging to the Genus Weissella possess unique metabolic capabilities with distinct value for natural food preservation. This review has synthesized current insights into the physiological characteristics, antibacterial pathways and antifungal mechanisms of Weissella species, with their practical uses within diverse food systems and safety problems restricting their commercial adoption. Material and Methods: A comprehensive literature search was carried out using PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science and Google Scholar for peer-reviewed literature published up to June 2026. The review covered Weissella taxonomy, ecological distribution, functional characteristics, antimicrobial activities and mechanisms, food biopreservation and biosafety. Relevant literature was critically screened and synthesized based on strain characteristics, bioactive metabolites, mechanisms of action, food-matrix uses, preservation outcomes and safety considerations. Results and Conclusion: The reviewed studies have indicated that Weissella shows strain-dependent antimicrobial activity mediated by multiple compounds, including organic acids, volatile organic compounds, bacteriocins and exopolysaccharides. These factors can inhibit foodborne and spoilage microorganisms through acidification, metabolic disruption and damage to fungal membranes and hyphae, with strains showing potentials for aflatoxin B1 adsorption. Antimicrobial effects have been reported against several bacterial and fungal pathogens, while food-model studies demonstrate decreases in microbial load and delayed visible spoilage in various food matrices. However, these effects cannot be generalized within Weissella because antimicrobial production, technological characteristics and safety characteristics differ within the strains. Therefore, further strain-specific safety assessment, standardized efficacy assessment, mechanistic studies and pilot and industrial-scale validation are needed before reliable use of Weissella-based biopreservation systems. INTRODUCTION Filamentous fungi are some of the most persistent and economically significant sources of food contamination in the global food supply chain. Fungal colonization within staple supplies such as dairy, cereals, grains and fresh produce causes progressive degradation of organoleptic characteristics, nutritional value and market acceptability [1,2]. Therefore, fungal contamination poses a significant challenge to the food industry compromising safety and quality of food products [3]. In addition to physical deterioration, filamentous fungi synthesize mycotoxins that represent critical biological hazards in foods. While ingestion of contaminated supplies triggers acute toxicosis [4], chronic dietary exposure is linked to severe long-term health consequences, including developmental delays and nutritional impairment in early childhood [5]. Foodborne diseases are still a major global public health concern, with the World Health Organization (WHO) estimating that approximately 866 million people were ill and 1.52 million died from foodborne diseases worldwide in 2021 [6]. Furthermore, fungal contamination and mycotoxin occurrence pose substantial challenges throughout the global food supply chain. Eskola et al. estimated that mycotoxins were detectable in up to 60–80% of food-crop samples, indicating that contamination at detectable levels is substantially more widespread than estimates based on regulatory exceedances alone [7]. Fresh fruits and vegetables are particularly susceptible to fungal deterioration during postharvest handling, storage and distribution. Despite advances in agricultural production and postharvest management, fungal diseases are still major constraints to food security because they decrease product quality, shorten storage life and decrease market value [8]. Postharvest vulnerability is further heightened in tropical and subtropical climates, where increased ambient temperatures and relative humidity accelerate fungal proliferation. Highly perishable climacteric fruits such as mango, banana, strawberry, pineapple and papaya are susceptible to contamination by Botrytis cinerea, Penicillium expansum, Colletotrichum species and Rhizopus stolonifer during handling, transport and storage [9,10]. These pathogens typically enter host tissues via physical wounds or natural openings, rapidly colonizing plant tissues and driving severe postharvest decay and economic loss [11]. Species within Aspergillus and Penicillium represent critical postharvest threats because they merge aggressive spoilage capability with potent mycotoxin synthesis [2], positioning fungal contamination as food security and public health concern. Adequate consumption of fruits and vegetables is an important component of a healthy diet. For example, WHO links insufficient fruit and vegetable intake to nearly 19% of gastrointestinal cancer deaths, nearly 31% of ischaemic heart disease deaths and nearly 11% of stroke deaths [12]. Nevertheless, postharvest preservation is still challenging because physiological processes associated with maturation and postharvest deterioration continue after harvest [13]. Quality retention is further compromised by transpiration-driven water loss, tissue senescence and opportunistic bacterial (Pseudomonas spp.) or fungal infections (Fusarium spp., Alternaria alternata and C. gloeosporioides), which routinely damage high-value crops such as tomatoes and avocados [9,11]. To lessen postharvest deterioration, conventional food preservation depends on physical treatments, modified atmosphere packaging and chemical additives such as sorbates, benzoates, propionates, ethanol and ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA). While these methods enhance microbial stability and extend shelf life, their long-term reliance faces increasing studies [14]. Nevertheless, exposure to chemical and biological preservatives can induce microbial stress responses and may contribute to the development of preservative-tolerant or antimicrobial-resistant microbial strains [15]. In contrast, physical preservation technologies may need substantial capital costs and potential degradation of organoleptic and nutritional quality [16]. These constraints have driven research to sustainable, natural preservation alternatives that balance broad-spectrum antimicrobial efficacy with consumer safety expectations [17]. Biopreservation uses beneficial microorganisms or their metabolites to suppress pathogens and spoilage organisms while preserving food quality. Compared with conventional chemical preservatives, this approach includes clean-label demand, although efficacy depends strongly on the food matrix, target organism and use conditions [18–20]. Lactic acid bacteria (LAB) are widely identified as promising biopreservative microorganisms due to their long-standing use in food fermentation and their ability to produce a range of antimicrobial and functional metabolites, including organic acids, bacteriocins, hydrogen peroxide and exopolysaccharides (EPS) [17,21]. Nevertheless, these characteristics are not necessarily shared by all Weissella strains, as their functional characteristics can vary significantly at the strain level. Although Weissella has been discussed in relation to taxonomy, fermentation and probiotic potential, the evidence connecting strain-level taxonomy, metabolite-mediated antibacterial and antifungal mechanisms, practical food uses and regulatory safety is still fragmented. This review has addressed that gap by integrating recent taxonomic developments including the separation of Periweissella with mechanistic evidence and use outcomes within fresh produce, bakery products and cereal matrices. Its novelty depends on extending previous Weissella-focused reviews by providing a strain-conscious framework that links antimicrobial metabolites and mechanisms of action with matrix-specific efficacy, biosafety considerations and experimental evidence needed for further use and regulatory translation [22,23]. Accordingly, this review has assessed the taxonomy, ecological distribution, physiological and functional attributes, antimicrobial mechanisms, biopreservation performance and biosafety of Weissella, with particular emphasis on antifungal efficacy and the requirements for safe, scalable, clean-label food preservation. As shown in Figure 1, the food biopreservation potential of Weissella should be assessed through an integrated strain-level framework that addresses taxonomy, ecology, bioactive metabolites, antimicrobial activity, practical preservation outcomes and safety requirements. MATERIALS AND METHODS 2.1. Literature Search Strategy To investigate the biotechnological landscape of Weissella, a comprehensive literature search was carried out using PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science and Google Scholar for relevant literature published up to June 2026. The retrieval strategy targeted peer-reviewed studies investigating Weissella taxonomy, ecological niches, functional characteristics, antimicrobial mechanisms, food preservation trials and biosafety assessments. The retrieval strategy combined controlled vocabulary and keyword terms, including Weissella, Weissella cibaria, Weissella confusa, "bacteriocins", "weissellicins", "antimicrobial activity", "antifungal activity", "biopreservation", "lactic acid bacteria", "EPS", "postharvest diseases", "volatile organic compounds" and "mycotoxins". Terms were linked using Boolean logic (AND/OR) and reference lists of retrieved articles were manually screened to capture additional eligible studies. 2.2. Study Selection Relevant peer-reviewed research articles, review articles and authoritative taxonomic resources were addressed. Non-peer-reviewed reports, conference abstracts, editorials and duplicate publications were excluded. title: Assessing climate change perceptions and climate-smart agriculture adoption among root, tuber and banana farmers in Eastern D.R. Congo
abstract: Perceptions shape human practices, including agricultural decisions, yet their influence on climate-smart agriculture adoption remains insufficiently understood in climate-vulnerable eastern Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC). This study compared farmers’ perceptions of climate change with empirical climate data of the past three decades across South-Kivu’s agroecological zones (AEZ), eastern DRC. It further assessed climate-smart agriculture (CSA) practices being used by smallholder root, tuber, and banana (RTB) farmers and factors driving their adoption. Data on climate change perception and drivers of CSA adoption was collected from 407 smallholder RTB farmers, selected through a multistage stratified random sampling, while climate data trends of the past three decades (1989–2024) were assessed using RClimDex 1.9. Farmers perceived increase in floods, drought, rainfall, wind speed, and lightning regardless of AEZ, though weather data could only confirm significant increase in rainfall. The study identified 24 CSA practices being used in RTB-based production systems, with varying adoption rates and drivers. Generally, farmer location, access to information and communication technologies (ICTs), and crop had the most significant effects on CSA adoption regardless of the practice. The findings, supported by both observed climate records and farmers’ perceptions, indicate that climate parameters are changing in eastern DRC and may adversely affect RTB production systems, although the perceived magnitude of these changes does not always correspond with observed trends. Therefore, there is need for context-specific interventions to foster a sustainable transition toward climate-smart RTB production systems, building upon and scaling up practices that are already adopted by smallholders.
keywords: eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo

title: Integrated Conversion of Coconut and Palm Oils into Bio-Based Chemicals via Hydrolysis and Kolbe Electrolysis
abstract: This study presents an integrated two-step synthetic protocol for the conversion of coconut and palm oils into high-value bio-based hydrocarbons, alcohols, and aldehydes. The process employs alkaline hydrolysis followed by Kolbe electrolysis. Under reflux in an EtOH-KOH system, both oils were quantitatively converted into their constituent fatty acid mixtures (C16–C18:1 for palm oil and C8–C18:1 for coconut oil) with yields up to 88% and 92%, respectively. The resulting intermediates were characterized via GC–MS. Subsequently, galvanostatic Kolbe electrolysis (100 mA) was performed using custom platinum electrodes in binary and ternary solvent systems. High substrate conversions (>86%) were obtained, and the organic product distribution reached up to 73% and 74% relative hydrocarbon selectivity for palm and coconut oil derivatives, respectively, in a ternary MeOH/EtOH/H2O system. However, operating under excess charge yielded isolated hydrocarbon mass yields of 8–20% (with up to 18% Kolbe dimers) alongside medium- and long-chain alcohols and aldehydes. This integrated protocol demonstrates a scalable and tunable route for converting vegetable oils into high-purity bio-based chemicals.

title: AgroNLP-SimAssist: a multilingual transformer-based decision support simulator for crop disease diagnosis, advisory generation, and market intelligence
abstract: Abstract There are three major shortcomings of agricultural NLP and need addressing, regardless of the recent developments in the field: (i) use of proprietary or small-scale datasets that affect reproducibility; (ii) one-task models that only focus on intent recognition but lack integration for crop disease diagnosis, advice, and market information; and (iii) the absence of simulators for evaluating the system’s performance during actual deployment. The application of precision agriculture is constrained by limitations in diverse farming environments. The study introduces AgroNLP-SimAssist, which represents a unified multilingual transformer architecture augmented by an easily deployable agricultural decision support simulator, as the proposed solution to overcome the challenges. The five major components constituting the proposed framework are: (1) domain-specific multilingual transformer embedding; (2) data collection and cleaning from publicly available agricultural datasets; (3) multiple prediction tasks including trend price estimation, crop disease detection, and advisory recommendation; (4) SHAP value explainability for expert validation; and (5) advisory simulation engine for evaluating latency and scalability. Multilingually available data sources, which include multilingual agricultural reports from the FAO organization, crop-disease descriptions from the PlantVillage knowledge base, and price-market narratives from the Agmarknet website, have been used for training and validation purposes. Among the 3,200 multilingual farmer queries dataset (in English, Hindi, and Kannada), there was an assignment of 70%, 15%, and 15% to the training, validation, and testing sets, respectively. In terms of accuracy compared to the existing classifiers, results from experiments yielded 96.1% disease classification, 94.3% advisory relevance, and 92.7% named entity recognition with F1-measure. The simulation system scaled up to 10,000 concurrent users with an inference latency of 0.35 s/query. The proposed data-driven AgroNLP-SimAssist framework facilitates extension services and precision agriculture through providing a scalable, reproducible, and interpretable solution for intelligent agricultural advisory systems.

title: Comparative Metabolome Analysis Reveals That MaOPR1 Is a Key Modulator of the Response to Banana Fusarium Wilt
abstract: Background: Banana Fusarium wilt inflicts enormous economic losses on global banana production; however, effective control strategies remain elusive. We previously demonstrated that overexpression of plantain (Musa paradisiaca) ICE1 (MpICE1) significantly enhances banana resistance to Fusarium wilt. This study aimed to screen and identify key resistance genes associated with banana Fusarium wilt resistance and further explore their molecular functions and regulatory mechanisms, so as to provide a solid theoretical basis for the genetic breeding and disease resistance improvement of banana. Methods: Based on our previous transcriptomic dataset and the current metabolomic analysis, we identified a key gene encoding 12-oxo-phytodienoic acid reductase, MaOPR1, involved in the linoleic acid metabolism pathway, and functionally validated its role via dsRNA-mediated gene silencing. Results: Silencing of MaOPR1 alleviated banana leaf-lesion response after Fusarium wilt. Conclusions: Integrating metabolomic and dsRNA-silencing evidence, MaOPR1 acts as a negative regulator of banana Fusarium wilt resistance, associated with alpha-linolenic acid metabolic reprogramming in the MpICE1-overexpressing background.

title: Layered conditionality in the global timber trade: Regulatory interoperability and the EUDR–FLEGT interface in Indonesia and Ghana
abstract: Demand-side forest regulations increasingly shape production beyond consumer markets through legality licensing, due diligence, traceability mandates and private certification. Existing research suggests that these instruments can disadvantage smallholders but typically evaluates each in isolation. This article develops the concept of layered conditionality to analyze how separate regulatory requirements interact at the point of production, and how the rules linking them allocate residual compliance costs. Layering is additive when requirements duplicate information and fixed costs, substitutive when compliance with one framework formally satisfies an element of another, and catalytic when existing institutions lower the marginal cost of meeting later rules. Using a structured, focused comparison of Indonesia and Ghana, the only two tropical timber exporters with operational Forest Law Enforcement, Governance and Trade (FLEGT) licensing, we examine how the European Union Deforestation Regulation (EUDR) interfaces with domestic legality systems and private certification. Because the EUDR's core obligations are not yet in application, the analysis identifies mechanisms and risks rather than realized outcomes. EUDR recognition of FLEGT licenses is confined to legality verification; it does not extend to deforestation-free production, plot geolocation or operators' risk assessment. Whether layering facilitates participation or increases exclusion risks is likely to depend on system interoperability, the distribution of fixed information costs, and smallholders' position in domestic value chains. The article develops propositions for future empirical assessment and identifies bounded policy options within the existing legal framework ahead of EUDR application in December 2026.

title: Impact of Cassava Producers’ Participation in Inclusive Agribusiness Models on Allocative Efficiency in Benin
abstract: This study examines the impact of cassava producers’ participation in inclusive agribusiness models (IAMs) on allocative efficiency in Benin, providing new microeconomic evidence on smallholder market integration in Sub-Saharan Africa. Using a sample of 1167 farmers across seven departments, we combine Stochastic Frontier Analysis (SFA) with an Endogenous Switching Regression (ESR) model to estimate efficiency while correcting for observable and unobservable selection bias. The results reveal moderate average allocative efficiency (0.646), indicating that producers remain about 35 percentage points below the cost-minimizing input allocation. IAM participants display higher allocative efficiency (0.700) than non-participants (0.620). The ESR model yields a positive and statistically significant treatment effect: participation is associated with an increase of 0.150 points in allocative efficiency among beneficiaries (ATT), while the potential effect for non-participants is smaller (ATU = 0.060). These results are corroborated by an Inverse-Probability-Weighted Regression Adjustment (IPWRA) robustness check, which yields a closely comparable treatment effect (ATT = 0.132). This ATT–ATU asymmetry reveals treatment-effect heterogeneity and positive selection on gains, as producers with the largest expected efficiency gains are the most likely to participate. Within IAMs, ordinary cooperative membership and the existence of a sales contract are associated with higher allocative efficiency, whereas extension contact and meeting participation, although the strongest predictors of participation, are associated with lower efficiency among participants, pointing to time-allocation trade-offs. The findings offer actionable evidence for designing inclusive value chain policies targeting the most marginalized smallholders and addressing structural constraints limiting efficiency across producer groups.

title: Perceived Equity: An Underlying Mechanism Between Sustainability Strategies Adopted by Businesses and Farmers' Well‐Being in Agri‐Food Value Chains
abstract: ABSTRACT To promote the well‐being of farmers, businesses across coffee, cocoa, and other agri‐food value chains are increasingly adopting sustainability strategies that go beyond classical certification schemes. Key strategies include corporate sustainability programs, social entrepreneurship, and farmer self‐organization in cooperatives. However, the links between these strategies and farmer well‐being vary considerably—and the mechanisms explaining these variations remain insufficiently understood, especially those operating in upstream links of agri‐food chains. This paper investigates how perceived equity in farmer–buyer first‐mile relationships and farmers' access to extension services differ across sustainability strategies, and to what extent these mechanisms explain well‐being differences across Peruvian coffee and cocoa farmers. We rely on descriptive and multivariate statistical analyses performed on a cross‐sectional dataset that compiles information on 623 farmers across three production areas. Our results demonstrate that equity as perceived by farmers from their first‐mile relationships plays a greater role in explaining well‐being differences than access to extension services. These well‐being connections vary across demographic groups, decreasing significantly for older and female farmer groups. Furthermore, farmers engaged in social enterprises are more likely to report higher levels of perceived equity compared to those affiliated with corporate sustainability programs or cooperatives. Despite the correlational design of this analysis, its results unveil important implications for business practices: while extension services are relatively standard across all examined strategies, practices aimed at strengthening perceived equity are currently not. Discussing these findings, we examine the challenges of scaling up perceived equity through social enterprises.

title: A thematic review of skill development for women’s empowerment and sustainable livelihoods under SDG 5 and SDG 8
abstract: Abstract Skill development and capacity-building programmes for women occupy the ground where SDG 5 (Gender Equality) and SDG 8 (Decent Work and Economic Growth) meet. The two goals are linked in structure, as the success of one is essential to the success of the other, and the evidence from skill-based interventions on middle- to long-term livelihood outcomes for women has been developing in different disciplines such as development economics, gender studies, and agricultural research, each addressing a part of the question, but none addressing the whole. That evidence is brought together in this review. The search was carried out using the guidance provided by PRISMA 2020 and Scopus was used as the search database; this is a limitation as it was decided to only use one search database. It returned 3,841 records. Deduplication and language filtering left 2,614 for title and abstract screening, of which 1,161 proceeded to full-text assessment. Sixty-three studies satisfied every pre-specified criterion; six were subsequently removed at re-screening, yielding a final corpus of 57 peer-reviewed journal articles published between 2005 and 2022. Quality was appraised using the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool, supplemented by five adapted criteria for designs outside its empirical scope. Ten thematic clusters were identified: vocational training and labour market outcomes; digital skills and technology-mediated empowerment; microfinance, financial inclusion and agency; entrepreneurship and self-employment; self-help group and cooperative models; rural livelihoods and agriculture; gender-responsive policy frameworks; decent work quality and SDG 8 alignment; SDG 5–SDG 8 interlinkages and synergies; and structural barriers and constraints. The synthesis indicates that integrated, multi-component programmes are associated with stronger empowerment and livelihood outcomes than standalone skills training. The review contributes an integrated four-level conceptual framework mapping skill development inputs, empowerment pathways, livelihood outcomes and policy moderators explicitly to specified SDG 5 and SDG 8 targets.

title: Climate Change and Water Management Nexus: An Integrated Assessment of Water-Use-Efficiency and Productivity Among Smallholder Wheat Farmers in Nigeria
abstract: This study addresses the persistent challenge of low wheat productivity and inefficient water use among smallholder farmers in North Western Nigeria, a region increasingly affected by water scarcity, climate variability, and weak irrigation infrastructure. Despite rising demand for wheat, local production remains inadequate, largely due to limited adoption of sustainable water management practices. The study aims to assess the determinants and conditional effects of adopting such practices on wheat yield and water-use efficiency. Primary data were collected from smallholder wheat farmers using a multi-stage sampling technique across Katsina, Kano, and Kaduna States. The study employed descriptive statistics, principal component analysis (PCA), multivariate probit (MVP) regression, and Bayesian linear regression to analyse adoption behaviour and its effects on productivity outcomes. PCA identified nine key components explaining 68.46% of the variation in water management practices. The MVP results revealed that gender, household size, cooperative membership, farm size, access to credit, and market distance significantly influence adoption decisions, while also highlighting substitutability among practices due to resource constraints. The Bayesian regression results show that adoption of sustainable water management practices were positively associated with wheat yield and water-use efficiency, confirming evidence of a positive association with enhancing productivity under water-limited conditions. The study concludes that improving wheat productivity requires integrated interventions that address both technological and institutional constraints. It recommends strengthening extension systems, promoting targeted agricultural financing, enhancing cooperative-based support, improving rural infrastructure, and adopting climate-smart, location-specific strategies to drive widespread adoption and build resilient agrifood systems.

title: Can rural collective economic development mitigate farmland abandonment in China? The roles of endogenous scale economies and exogenous financial incentives
abstract: Reducing farmland abandonment is of critical importance for the scientific management of land resources, safeguarding food security, and promoting sustainable agricultural development. Existing research on farmland abandonment has mostly focused on individual or policy factors, and the association between the rural collective economy and farmland abandonment has not been fully examined quantitatively. Based on the latest panel data from the China Labor-force Dynamics Survey, this paper empirically examines the statistical correlation and conditional mechanisms between rural collective economic development and farmland abandonment from the dual perspectives of endogenous scale economies and exogenous financial incentives. The study finds that the level of collective economic development is significantly and negatively correlated with both the area and proportion of farmland abandonment. From the perspective of endogenous scale economies, collective economic organizations possessing the dual characteristics of “farmland scale management” and “service scale management” are associated with a lower degree of farmland abandonment. From the perspective of exogenous financial incentives, in the groups of households that have obtained loans and have higher loan amounts, the negative correlation between collective economic development and abandonment is more pronounced. Heterogeneity analysis shows that in villages providing uniform irrigation and drainage, technical guidance, and planting planning services, the aforementioned negative correlation is more prominent. Based on this, the role of the collective economy in relation to farmland abandonment is noted, alongside associations of lower abandoned land with the cultivation of moderate-scale agricultural management and the optimization of rural financial supply.

title: From Competitiveness to Sustainable Security Capability: Spatial Patterns and Institutional Logic of China’s Rice Food Security Governance
abstract: Background: Global food supply chains face intensifying geopolitical and climate disruptions, posing significant threats to environmental sustainability and resource equity. Conventional competitiveness frameworks, which prioritize market share and export performance, inadequately capture the sustainable development logic of populous developing countries. China produces approximately 27% of global rice output but accounts for less than 1.5% of global exports, while maintaining a self-sufficiency rate exceeding 95%—a paradox that existing market-centric theories cannot coherently explain. Objective: This study proposes “Rice Food Security Capability (RFSC)” as an alternative conceptual framework to quantify and monitor the sustainability of staple-food systems, empirically examines its spatial distribution across China’s 31 provinces (2015–2023), and distills transferable lessons for developing countries. Methods: A five-dimensional evaluation system was constructed covering production, processing, industry integration, market, and policy dimensions. principal component analysis (PCA), exploratory spatial data analysis (ESDA), and Getis-Ord Gi hot spot analysis were applied to provincial-level data. Qualitative indicators were assessed via a six-expert panel with intraclass correlation coefficients (ICCs) of 0.87 and 0.82, exceeding the 0.75 good threshold. Results: Five principal components explained 91.51% of total variance in 2023. The Middle-Lower Yangtze River region (comprehensive score 0.52) and Northeast China (0.47) constitute high-capability agglomeration areas, highlighting regional disparities crucial for sustainable resource allocation, while Southwest China (0.22) and Northern China (0.13) exhibit lower capability. Global Moran’s I ranged from 0.241 to 0.310 (p < 0.01), confirming significant spatial clustering. Government strategic security capability (F4) exhibited negative spatial autocorrelation (I = −0.217, p < 0.05), revealing inter-regional policy compensation dynamics. Whole-industry-chain security capability (F1), explaining 57.33% of variance, is the primary pillar. Conclusion: China’s rice security capability rests on three mechanisms: government-led policy coordination, technology-driven innovation, and multi-agent whole-chain resilience. Four replicable lessons for achieving Sustainable Development Goal 2 (zero hunger) and promoting sustainable agriculture emerge: whole-chain thinking, institutional coordination priority, technology localization, and reliance on domestic supply. These findings provide a quantifiable tool for policymakers to assess and monitor the sustainability of food governance.

title: Farmers’ preferences and willingness to pay for agritourism development: Evidence from rural areas in the Qinba Mountains, China
abstract: Agritourism has emerged as an important mechanism for integrating agriculture and tourism, providing diversified recreational experiences while supporting rural economic revitalization. However, little evidence exists on how farmers value and trade off different attributes of agritourism development. Using a choice experiment (CE), this study examines farmers' preferences for agritourism participation through the lens of the motivation–opportunity–ability (MOA) framework. Using field survey data from 539 farmers in China's Qinba Mountain area, the study provides evidence from the mountainous region with rich agritourism resources. Farmers generally favoured agritourism development over the status quo. Within the choice experiment, the ecological environment had the highest estimated marginal willingness to pay (WTP), at 91.35 Chinese yuan (CNY) per household per year, followed by technical guidance and training at CNY 85.10 per household per year. Analysis incorporating the MOA dimensions and three variables extending the framework identifies heterogeneity in farmers' general inclination towards participation, while livelihood type, health status, and cooperative membership moderate preferences for specific development attributes. By integrating the MOA framework with a choice experiment, this study clarifies both what farmers value in agritourism development and why their general inclination towards participation differs.

title: Digital Inclusive Finance and Agricultural New-Quality Productive Forces: Dynamic Effects, Industrial-Chain Coordination, and Data-Element Thresholds
abstract: This study examines how digital inclusive finance promotes agricultural new-quality productive forces through agricultural industrial-chain coordination, data-element conditions, dynamic accumulation, and spatial spillovers. Based on a balanced panel of 30 Chinese provinces from 2013 to 2023, we estimate two-way fixed-effects, system GMM, mediation, panel-threshold, and spatial Durbin models. The results demonstrate that digital inclusive finance significantly increases agricultural new-quality productive forces. This finding remains robust to lagged specifications, system-GMM estimation, Oster bounds, and an independent agricultural green total factor productivity outcome. Agricultural industrial-chain coordination is positively associated with the outcome and is consistent with a partial transmission channel. Data-element agglomeration generates a double-threshold pattern, with the marginal contribution of digital inclusive finance increasing after the estimated thresholds have been crossed. The spatial estimates indicate positive associations with neighboring provinces under some weight matrices, with stronger associations in eastern China and in regions with greater industrial-chain coordination. By integrating organizational coordination, data factors, temporal dynamics, and spatial dependence, this study provides a unified account of digital financial empowerment in agriculture. The findings indicate the need to develop digital financial inclusion alongside agricultural data infrastructure and cross-stage industrial-chain coordination, which would support sustainable, regionally balanced agricultural modernization.

title: Village-Level Institutional Capacity and Farmers’ Willingness to Participate in Agricultural Water Governance
abstract: Insufficient farmer participation constrains sustainable agricultural water governance and collective action. Village-level agricultural water governance organizations connect institutional provision with farmers’ behavioral responses, but evidence on the association between their perceived institutional capacity (IC) and farmers’ willingness to participate in agricultural water governance (PW) remains limited. Using survey data from 1342 farmers across seven provincial-level regions in China, this study employed ordinary least squares with village-clustered standard errors, supplemented by multinomial logit analyses. The results show IC is positively and significantly associated with PW, with significant associations for relational resources and mobilization capacity but not knowledge resources. A significant indirect association through institutional trust suggests a potential pathway linking IC to PW. Cooperation level shows outcome-specific moderation: the IC association with the probability of reporting the highest willingness category is stronger at higher cooperation levels, whereas moderation on the PW score scale is not significant. Subgroup analysis indicates this association remains positive across groups defined by pollution-related harm experience, seasonal flow variability and village size. Further analysis shows that the association extends to information acquisition, decision-making involvement, governance monitoring, and pollution accountability willingness. These findings suggest the potential value of strengthening organizational capacities, institutional trust, cooperation, and diverse participation opportunities.

title: Microplastic contamination in agricultural systems: impacts on plant productivity, economic losses, and supply chain resilience
abstract: Microplastics (MPs) have transitioned from a predominantly marine concern to a defining threat facing terrestrial agroecosystems, where croplands now function as one of the largest global reservoirs of plastic particles. This review synthesizes evidence to construct an integrated narrative that links the entry of MPs into farmland with declining plant productivity, quantifiable economic losses, and the erosion of agricultural supply chain resilience. The synthesis is based on a documented search of Web of Science, Scopus, ScienceDirect and Google Scholar covering January 2018 to March 2026, with explicit inclusion and exclusion criteria reported in Section 1.1. Sources, fate and soil-phase processes are treated in condensed form, because they are already covered comprehensively elsewhere; we retain only the evidence that propagates into crop, economic and supply-chain outcomes. Building on these soil-level disturbances, we evaluate the phytotoxic consequences for crops, spanning inhibited germination, impaired root architecture, reduced photosynthetic efficiency, disrupted nutrient acquisition, and the uptake and translocation of nano-sized particles into edible tissues. A central contribution of this review is the explicit coupling of these biophysical impacts to their economic and systemic dimensions, because recent global meta-analyses estimate that MP-induced photosynthetic suppression alone may reduce staple crop production by tens to hundreds of millions of tons annually, translating into substantial revenue losses, quality downgrading, remediation expenditure, and heightened exposure of food supply chains to shocks. Rather than reporting these modelled outputs at face value, we dissect the inferential chain that produces them, from effect size to biomass to harvestable yield to price, and we identify the assumptions at each step that determine whether the resulting figures are decision-grade. We complement the global estimates with farm-level cost–benefit evidence showing that the private returns to plasticulture remain positive while the contamination externality contributes under one percent of the accounted benefits of current management, which explains the persistence of practices that degrade the productive base. Throughout, illustrative case studies from China, Chile, Australia, and Europe are embedded within each thematic section rather than treated in isolation, demonstrating how local contamination patterns propagate into landscape- and market-scale consequences. We further appraise mitigation and remediation options, ranging from source reduction and material substitution to biochar amendment, and we assess emerging governance instruments such as the FAO Voluntary Code of Conduct and circular-economy regulation. Finally, we identify persistent knowledge gaps concerning the calibration of field-realistic dose–response relationships, the construction of decision-grade economic estimates, and the severe geographical imbalance of the evidence base, in which South Asia, sub-Saharan Africa and Latin America are collectively represented by a small fraction of published field studies, and we outline research priorities to safeguard soil health and food security. The review argues that microplastic contamination should be reframed not merely as an ecotoxicological problem but as a slow-onset stressor with strategic implications for the stability of global food systems.

title: Explainable machine learning models for AI enabled credit scoring and financial inclusion in emerging markets
abstract: This study examines whether explainable machine-learning approaches can support more inclusive credit scoring while maintaining acceptable predictive performance, transparency, and fairness in an emerging-market microfinance setting. We analyzed a de-identified dataset of 2500 resolved loan applications obtained from participating microfinance institutions in the MENA region during 2022–2023. Nine supervised algorithms were compared, spanning classical benchmarks (Logistic Regression, Decision Tree, Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, Support Vector Machine, K-Nearest Neighbors) and modern gradient-boosting frameworks (XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost). Default (90 + days past due) was modeled as the positive class. Performance was evaluated on a held-out test set using ROC-AUC and PR-AUC with bootstrap confidence intervals, supported by repeated stratified cross-validation and DeLong tests. Interpretability was assessed with SHAP, including stability and cross-model consistency checks, and fairness was evaluated using disparate impact, equal opportunity, predictive parity, group-level calibration, and intersectional analysis. An ablation design isolated the incremental contribution of non-traditional indicators. CatBoost achieved the highest test-set discrimination (ROC-AUC = 0.783, 95% CI [0.741, 0.825]; PR-AUC = 0.506) but was statistically indistinguishable from regularized Logistic Regression (ROC-AUC = 0.780; DeLong p = .59), and no gradient-boosting model significantly outperformed the logistic benchmark. SHAP analysis identified Credit Score Category, Utility Payment Behavior, and Repayment History as the dominant predictors, with rankings highly stable under resampling (Spearman ρ = 0.999) and consistent across model families (ρ = 0.95–0.98 among tree ensembles).
