Wealth-related inequalities in both breast and cervical cancer screening are substantial and persist after adjustment for key demographic determinants in Kenya. Incorporating equity-oriented considerations into the planning and scale-up of screening services is urgently needed to expand access among economically disadvantaged women, particularly those residing in rural areas with low educational attainment.

title: Analysis of climate trend, variability and its implications on bread wheat (Triticum aestivum L.) productivity in central highlands of Ethiopia
abstract: Climate change is a global threat with localized geographic and socioeconomic impacts that directly related to agricultural productivity and sustainability. This study assessed the spatio-temporal variability and trend of rainfall, temperature and growing season characteristics and their impact on bread wheat in the central Highlands of Ethiopia. Long-term (1989–2020) daily rainfall and temperature data of the study locations were collected from Ethiopian Meteorological Institute. Climate variability was analyzed using Coefficient of Variation, Precipitation Concentration Index, and Standardized Anomaly Index indices. Trend analysis were determined by Mann–Kendall trend test and Sen’s slope tests. Growing seasons characterized by INSTAT+ 3.37 statistical software while impact of climate variability on wheat yield was assessed using combined multiple regression analysis. Rainfall was temporally and spatially variable and recorded below the long term mean in 58% of the study years. Both maximum and minimum temperatures were significantly increasing (p < 0.01) by 0.043–0.081 °C and 0.034–0.094 °C per year respectively, over the period 1989 to 2020. Analysis of growing season characteristics indicated the shifting of crop calendar in which the start of the rainy season ranged from June 13 (165 DOY)—July 6 (188 DOY). The end of the rainy season ranged from October 10 (284 DOY)—November 2 (307 DOY), and the length of the growing period ranged from 96–136 days. The results also indicated that assessed climate variables explain 17–83% of the change in wheat yield at selected study sites. These climate shifts disrupt farming calendars, trigger crop failures and threatening food security. To adapt, farmers must switch to early-maturing, drought-tolerant crop varieties and implement soil moisture conservation.

title: Infant and Young Child Feeding Practices and Their Determinants in Sagar District, Madhya Pradesh: A Facility-Based Cross-sectional Study
abstract: Abstract Background: Infant and young child feeding (IYCF) practices are essential for growth and development during the first two years. However, district-level evidence on IYCF practices and determinants remains limited in India. This study assessed IYCF practices, maternal knowledge, and determinants of IYCF indicators among children aged 0–23 months in Sagar, Madhya Pradesh. Methods: A facility-based cross-sectional study was conducted among 430 mother–child pairs attending immunization sessions at selected Anganwadi centers between March 2020 and October 2021. IYCF practices were assessed using World Health Organization (WHO) indicators, and maternal knowledge was evaluated using a pretested 17-item questionnaire. Logistic regression models were used to identify independent predictors of IYCF indicators. Results: Early initiation of breastfeeding, exclusive breastfeeding (EBF), continued breastfeeding at one year, and timely introduction of complementary feeding were reported in 73.5%, 86.1%, 98.1%, and 76.5% of children, respectively. However, only 12.5% achieved minimum dietary diversity (MDD), 33.9% minimum meal frequency (MMF), 7.8% minimum acceptable diet (MAD), and 2.3% consumed iron-rich or iron-fortified foods. Adequate maternal knowledge was observed in 22.6% of mothers. Normal vaginal delivery independently predicted early initiation of breastfeeding, whereas male children had lower odds of EBF. Adequate maternal knowledge regarding IYCF was positively associated with MMF, MDD, and MAD, while urban residence was independently associated with improved MDD and MAD. Conclusion: Despite satisfactory breastfeeding practices, complementary feeding remained suboptimal. Strengthening nutrition counseling through existing maternal and child health programs, with emphasis on maternal knowledge and rural populations, may improve IYCF practices.

title: Human-Hippopotamus conflicts and socio-ecological tensions in the Ruzizi plain: a one health and political ecology perspective
abstract: Introduction Human-wildlife conflicts have intensified in the Kamanyola and Katogota areas of South Kivu, Democratic Republic of Congo, leading to human fatalities, injuries, crop losses and retaliatory killings of hippopotamuses. These conflicts illustrate the need for integrated conservation approaches that account for biodiversity protection, livelihood security and ecosystem health. Methods We conducted a qualitative case study using individual semi-structured interviews, focus group discussions and non-participant field observations in conflict-affected areas. In total, 63 stakeholders, including residents (farmers), community leaders, wildlife managers and institutional/public authorities were interviewed. A further 24 individuals including all categories, participated in focus group discussions. We compared local ecological knowledge with institutional conservation frameworks to identify the main drivers of conflict and examine how different actors perceived and responded to them. Results Participants identified land pressure, weak environmental governance, limited legal awareness and divergent values attached to wildlife as the main drivers of the conflict. These factors were exacerbated by the absence of compensation mechanisms and by repressive conservation practices. Participants reported that the conflict contributed to food insecurity, economic marginalization, institutional mistrust, physical injuries, concerns about water quality, potential zoonotic exposure, and psychosocial stress. Discussion The findings support a participatory One Health governance model linking conservation, public health and local livelihoods. This approach is consistent with the One Health framework, which seeks to balance and optimize the health of people, animals and ecosystems through coordinated action across sectors. We recommend policy revision, community co-management, training of local eco-guards, fair compensation schemes and stronger coordination among health, veterinary and conservation services. Further quantitative research on hippopotamus populations, agricultural losses and health-risk mapping is needed to inform evidence-based coexistence strategies.

title: Harnessing Indigenous Knowledge for Climate-Smart Agri-Food Systems: A Review of Adaptation Strategies, Food Security, Ecosystem Services, Governance, and Digital Innovation in Sub-Saharan Africa
abstract: Sub-Saharan Africa (SSA) faces escalating climate challenges that threaten agricultural productivity, food security, ecosystem sustainability, and rural livelihoods. Indigenous knowledge (IK), developed through generations of interaction with local environments, offers context-specific and culturally embedded solutions for climate adaptation and resilient agri-food systems. This scoping review synthesizes evidence on the role of indigenous knowledge in advancing climate-smart agriculture (CSA) and resilient agri-food systems across SSA. Guided by the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses Extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR), the review analyzed 17 studies published between 2000 and 2026. The findings reveal that indigenous knowledge contributes significantly to climate resilience through traditional weather forecasting, crop diversification, indigenous seed preservation, agroforestry, water harvesting, soil fertility management, and community-based natural resource governance. These practices enhance food security, livelihood resilience, biodiversity conservation, and ecosystem service provision while strengthening adaptive capacity among smallholder farmers. The review further highlights the importance of inclusive governance frameworks, knowledge co-production, and policy support for integrating indigenous knowledge into climate adaptation and agricultural development strategies. Emerging digital technologies and innovation platforms also present opportunities for documenting, preserving, and scaling indigenous agricultural knowledge. However, challenges related to weak policy recognition, inadequate documentation, knowledge erosion, and limited digital infrastructure continue to constrain its effective utilization. The study concludes that integrating indigenous knowledge with scientific innovation is essential for building inclusive, sustainable, and climate-resilient agri-food systems in SSA.

title: Physicochemical tailoring of POME through mechanical pretreatment: Assessing nutrient uptake and biomass characteristics in mixotrophic Chlorella sp. cultivation
abstract: Palm oil mill effluent (POME) is organic, nutrient-rich wastewater which physicochemical properties can severely disrupt terrestrial and aquatic ecosystems when discharged untreated. This study investigates the effect of hydrothermal and ultrasonication pretreatments in enhancing nutrient release from POME for microalgae cultivation as an alternative organic-based medium. Liquid and solid fractions of raw POME were characterized prior to pretreatment. Lyophilized POME sludge comprised 35.86% extractives, while the extractive-free sludge consisted mainly of cellulose (28.3%), hemicellulose (13.8%), and lignin (16.1%) on mass weight basis. POME was pretreated at different range of temperature-time for hydrothermal (140, 180, 200, 220 °C; 60 and 120 min) and intensity-time for probe ultrasonication (50% and 100%; 2 and 10 min). Selected conditions were evaluated for Chlorella sp. cultivation and compared with R and BG-11 synthetic media representing mixotrophic and autotrophic growth. The liquid fraction of raw POME used as cultivation media in this study contained high levels of chemical oxygen demand (COD) (19,690 mg/L), total nitrogen (TN) (323 mg/L), total phosphorus (TP) (346 mg/L), corresponding to a COD:N:P mass ratio of 61:1:1. The highest TN consumption (74.99%) by Chlorella sp. was achieved in sonicated POME, while HT-POME yielded the greatest carbohydrate consumption (83.58%). Meanwhile, TP removal in all POME-based media exceeded 98.89%. Biomass productivity in POME-based media was comparable to R medium, although protein content was lower. Thermal analysis revealed increased structural condensation and thermal stability of residual sludge after pretreatment. Overall, US-pretreated POME supports efficient nutrient consumption, comparable microalgal growth, and offers integrated potential for wastewater treatment and downstream resource valorization.

title: Constraints Faced by Farmers in Using Social Media for Agricultural Information in Kanpur
journal: Journal of Scientific Research and Reports
abstract: Aims: This study identified the major constraints experienced by farmers in using social media for agricultural information and to document their suggestions for improving digital agricultural extension services. Study Design: An ex post facto research design was adopted. Place and Duration of Study: The study was conducted in Bilhaur block of Kanpur Nagar district, Uttar Pradesh, India, during 2023–2024. Methodology: A total of 120 smartphone-owning farmers were selected through simple random sampling from six villages of Bilhaur block. Primary data were collected through personal interviews using a structured and pre-tested interview schedule. The data were analysed using frequency, percentage, and rank-order techniques to identify the major constraints faced by farmers and their suggestions for improving the utilisation of social media for agricultural information. Results: The major constraints reported by farmers were lack of training on the use of social media (92.50%), language and cultural barriers (87.50%), low educational level (84.16%), lack of technical knowledge (81.66%), lack of trust in adopting social media (79.16%), and poor network connectivity (75.83%). Among the suggestions, ensuring a reliable and uninterrupted electricity supply (92.50%), improving village-level network connectivity (82.50%), providing financial support (80.00%), providing agricultural information in Hindi and other regional languages (75.83%), and providing training to improve farmers’ understanding of social media (75.83%) were the most frequently suggested measures. Conclusion: The findings indicate that farmers’ effective utilisation of social media for agricultural information is influenced by educational, technical, infrastructural, economic, language-related, and institutional constraints. Improving rural digital infrastructure, providing practical training, ensuring reliable electricity and network connectivity, providing agricultural information in Hindi and other regional languages, and strengthening linkages with agricultural extension services may help improve the effectiveness of social media as a complementary agricultural extension channel.

title: Circular Economy and Climate Resilience: Implications for Governance, Adaptation Strategies, and Economic Inclusion of Smallholder Farmers in Nigeria
abstract: Climate change, environmental degradation, and global supply chain disruptions highlight the urgency of advancing circular economy (CE) practices for sustainable agricultural transformation. However, in fragile governance contexts such as Nigeria, CE adoption among smallholder farmers remains uneven. This study investigates the role of governance quality, socioeconomic conditions, and climate variability in shaping CE implementation in Southwest Nigeria. Using survey data from smallholder farmers, we applied an instrumental-variable multivariate probit regression model to account for interdependencies across multiple CE practices, residue recycling, composting, and waste-to-energy. Governance quality was assessed through five indices: transparency, participation, enforcement, coordination, and service delivery. Socioeconomic (education, income, farm size) and climatic variables (rainfall, drought shocks) were included to capture enabling and constraining conditions. The results show that governance quality significantly affects CE adoption patterns: transparency strongly drives residue recycling, participation fosters composting, and enforcement enables capital-intensive waste-to-energy. Coordination and service delivery exert broad positive effects across multiple practices. Education, income, and farm size were positively associated with adoption, whereas climatic variability significantly influenced adoption decisions, reflecting farmers’ sensitivity to ecological shocks. The findings imply that scaling CE in Nigeria requires more than technical innovation; it demands transparent, participatory, and credible governance alongside inclusive socioeconomic support. Policy interventions should prioritize the strengthening of advisory systems, farmer cooperatives, regulatory enforcement, and integrated service delivery while embedding the CE within broader climate adaptation strategies. Through aligning governance quality with inclusive development, CE adoption can foster resilience, economic inclusion, and environmental sustainability in a fractured global order.

title: Digital capability and supply chain resilience in rural food tourism ventures: the role of food supply chain integration
abstract: Introduction Rural food tourism ventures coordinate perishable local supplies, food-service operations and fluctuating tourist demand. How digital capability and food supply chain integration relate to resource-saving practices and enterprise-level resilience remains unclear. Methods A four-wave matched survey of 467 women operators was analyzed using covariance-based structural equation modeling, bootstrap tests of statistical indirect associations and an ordinal-estimator sensitivity analysis. Public user-generated content was analyzed separately to characterize platform discourse. Results Digital capability was positively associated with food supply chain integration and enterprise-level supply chain resilience. Integration was positively associated with both the low-carbon-oriented and resource-saving food practices index and resilience. The direct association between the practices index and resilience was not statistically significant. Bootstrap estimates supported the indirect association between digital capability and the practices index through integration, but not the serial indirect association extending to resilience. Only the resilience text classifier met the prespecified reporting threshold; the remaining labels were retained as exploratory semantic cues. Discussion The findings distinguish resource-saving practices from disruption resilience and identify supply chain integration as an organizational correlate of both. Future research should test these associations in probability-based and gender-comparative samples and validate reported practices against measured energy use, food loss and emissions.

title: Asymmetric participation structures: The practical logic of gender norms in rural communities——A study of collective action among rural women in Jiangxi Province, China
abstract: Women's participation in village public affairs provides an important lens for understanding transformations in rural governance and gender relations in contemporary China. Drawing on fieldwork on two forms of women's collective action:collective homecoming activities among married-out women and collective gatherings organised by daughters-in-law in ten villages in Jiangxi Province, this article examines how village gender norms shape women's participatory identities and participation rights through the interpenetration of the public and private spheres. The findings show that village gender norms do not simply sustain existing arrangements by excluding women from public participation. Rather, they generate a practical logic marked by tensions between governance needs and ethical-cultural norms. In response to governance needs, villages enable women to gain participatory legitimacy and access to resources by mobilising their family and kinship relations to repair social ties and serve collective interests, thereby facilitating a flexible expansion of participatory identities. At the same time, ethical-cultural norms constrain the benefits, domains, and levels of women's participation through the prioritisation of household interests, the demarcation of the public–private boundary, and the differentiated allocation of responsibilities based on relational proximity. Women's participation rights consequently undergo a more rigid contraction. Village gender norms thus produce an asymmetric structure of participation characterised by the “flexible expansion of participatory identities and rigid contraction of participation rights.” This analysis extends research on rural women's public participation by distinguishing participation as identity from participation as rights, deepens understanding of the gendered consequences of public–private interpenetration, and reveals how gender norms adapt and persist amid rural social transformation.

title: Combining stated and revealed preferences to define smallholder cattle breeding objectives in northwest Ethiopia: Evidence for breeding program design
abstract: Identifying high-priority traits is essential for designing effective breeding programs in smallholder systems. This study employed both stated and revealed preference methods to identify priority traits for cattle breeding objectives among smallholders in northwest Ethiopia. Stated preferences were assessed using a discrete choice experiment (DCE), while revealed preferences were examined through a hedonic pricing approach. The two datasets were analyzed separately and their results compared to provide complementary insights. Data were collected between January and April 2024: 384 farmers participated in the choice survey across three districts (Farta = 91, Simada = 133, and Lay Gayint = 160), and 200 cattle transactions were recorded in three marketplaces-Debre Tabor, Simada, and Nefas Mewucha. Choice data were analyzed with a mixed logit model, and market data with a log-linear ordinary least squares regression. Results showed both convergence and divergence in trait preferences between methods. Farmers' strong preference for large body size in the DCE (p < 0.001) aligned with the significant positive effects of body condition and live body weight on market price (p < 0.001). However, traits not visually observable at sale-such as milk yield, docility, disease tolerance, libido, calving interval, and calf vigor-were highly valued in stated preferences but not captured in market prices due to observability constraints and information asymmetry. Conversely, the hedonic model revealed market structure effects not captured by the DCE, including higher prices paid by traders and premiums for slaughter animals. These findings demonstrate that employing both methods provides a more comprehensive evidence base for defining breeding objectives-capturing both invisible livelihood-critical traits valued by farmers and market dynamics that shape real-world prices. The identified priority traits provide a foundation for subsequent research to estimate genetic parameters and economic weights to design a breeding program.

title: Social Innovation for Digital Equity in Healthcare: A Descriptive Environmental Scan of Selected Digital Initiatives in India
abstract: Abstract Background Digital inequities continue to limit equitable access to healthcare and related services in India, particularly among underserved populations. Social enterprises and nongovernmental organizations increasingly employ digital tools and innovations to support healthcare delivery, communication, and community engagement; however, systematic descriptive evidence regarding such initiatives remains limited. Objectives: To describe the characteristics, scope, and patterns of digital initiatives implemented by selected social enterprises, nongovernmental organizations, and community-based organizations in India, with particular focus on digital health–related activities, beneficiary populations, and knowledge-exchange engagement. Methods: A cross-sectional descriptive environmental scan was conducted from February to July 2025 among 100 purposively selected organizations operating in India. Data were collected from organizational websites, publicly available reports, digital platforms, and direct communication using a structured data extraction tool developed from relevant literature and pilot reviewed before use. Quantitative data were analyzed using descriptive statistics with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for key proportions. Qualitative organizational descriptions were analyzed thematically to identify recurring domains of digital engagement using an inductive descriptive approach. Results: All organizations reported use of at least one digital platforms for communication or service delivery, and 96% (95% CI: 90.1–98.9) maintained official websites. Common organizational focus areas included women’s empowerment (93%; 95% CI: 86.1–96.8), health-related activities (72%; 95% CI: 62.3–80.1), and education (48%; 95% CI: 38.0–58.2). Among organizations reporting COVID-19–related digital initiatives (n = 96), telehealth services (75%) and online education platforms (50%) were most frequently described. Women/girls and rural populations were the predominant beneficiary groups. Although all organizations perceived their initiatives as having potential for replication or scale-up, these findings were based on organizational self-report and were not independently validated. Conclusion: This environmental scan describes widespread adoption of digital communication and service-delivery tools among selected social innovation organizations in India. Although digitally enabled initiatives frequently targeted underserved populations, the study did not assess effectiveness or direct impact on digital equity outcomes. Further evaluative research is needed to determine the effectiveness and scalability of these initiatives.

title: Planting subsidies or brand building? Policy thresholds and goal conflict in agribusiness-led contract farming
abstract: Introduction Under yield uncertainty and agribusiness-led contract farming, government intervention is important for sustaining agricultural production and supporting farmer profit. Yet production-side planting subsidies and demand-side brand-building policies operate through different mechanisms, leaving their relative advantages and applicable conditions unclear. This study examines how the government should choose between the two policies and how firm social responsibility shapes their relative performance. Methods We develop a sequential game involving a government, an agribusiness firm, and a farmer under stochastic yield. The firm's objective incorporates concern for farmer profit. Equilibrium decisions are derived by backward induction, and the policies are compared in terms of social welfare and farmer profit. Numerical analysis illustrates the analytical results. Results The planting subsidy policy directly strengthens the farmer's production incentive, whereas the brand-building policy expands market demand and induces the firm to offer a higher procurement price. The benefits of brand building depend critically on its cost-effectiveness. We identify two endogenous thresholds: a social-welfare threshold and a farmer-profit threshold, with the former strictly lower than the latter. As brand-building cost-effectiveness increases, policy preference shifts through three regions: planting-subsidy dominance, goal conflict, and brand-building dominance. In the intermediate region, brand building generates higher social welfare, while the farmer remains better off under planting subsidies. Yield risk, price sensitivity, and planting costs widen the goal-conflict region, whereas higher expected yield and stronger firm social responsibility narrow it. Market size affects absolute outcomes but does not change the relative policy ranking. Discussion These findings extend the agricultural-policy literature from the design of production subsidies to the choice between production-side and demand-side interventions. They show that improvements in aggregate welfare do not necessarily translate into greater benefits for farmers.

title: Carbon-intensive development and undernourishment in Africa: the role of non-hydro renewable energy in the climate–food security nexus
abstract: The study examines the relationship between carbon-intensive development, non-hydro renewable energy and undernourishment in 27 African countries between 2002 and 2021. The study focuses on whether non-hydro renewable electricity can reduce the link between greenhouse gas emissions and food insecurity in Africa. The analysis follows several stages. First, descriptive statistics, correlation analysis, panel unit-root tests and cointegration tests were conducted to evaluate the distributional properties, relationships, stationarity and long-term behavior of the variables under study. Secondly, a two-step System Generalized Method of Moments estimator was applied to a balanced panel of 540 observations in order to address the persistence of undernourishment, potential endogeneity, reverse causality and unobserved country-specific effects. Model reliability is then evaluated using Arellano–Bond serial correlation tests, Hansen and Sargan overidentification tests, and difference-in-Hansen tests of instrument exogeneity. The findings generally indicate that undernourishment is persistent and strongly influenced by structural, energy-related, demographic, environmental and economic factors. Dependence on fossil fuel-based electricity and continued population growth was associated with deteriorating food security outcomes, whereas the adoption of renewable energy and economic growth show potential to improve food security. The interaction term results between greenhouse gas emissions and renewable energy suggested that high carbon intensity may limit the food security benefits of expanding renewable energy. These findings emphasize the importance of integrated policies that accelerate decentralized investment in renewable energy, reduce dependence on fossil fuels and greenhouse gas emissions while strengthening climate-resilient agriculture and improving rural energy access. Lastly, coordinating energy, agricultural, climate, and population policies is essential for achieving sustainable development goals 2 and 7 in Africa.

title: Cost and Return Analysis of Green Gram in Sri Ganganagar District of Rajasthan, India
journal: Journal of Scientific Research and Reports
abstract: This study examined the cost of cultivation, yield, returns and profitability of green gram (Vigna radiata) cultivation among beneficiary and non-beneficiary respondents of Primary Agricultural Cooperative Societies (PACS) in Sri Ganganagar district of Rajasthan during the agricultural year 2024-25. Primary data were collected from 80 beneficiary and 80 non-beneficiary green gram growers, categorised into small, medium and large farm-size groups, using a pre-tested interview schedule. Costs of cultivation and returns were estimated on a per-hectare basis following standardised CACP cost concepts (Cost A1 to Cost C3). The results revealed that the average cost of cultivation was higher for beneficiary respondents (₹50,477.65/ha) than for non-beneficiary respondents (₹43,031.62/ha), mainly due to greater investment in quality inputs and timely farm operations facilitated by institutional credit. Beneficiary respondents recorded a higher grain yield (12.66 q/ha) and gross income (₹94,734.31/ha) than non-beneficiary respondents (10.04 q/ha and ₹74,244.88/ha, respectively). Despite higher cultivation costs, beneficiary respondents had a lower cost of production (₹3,868.02/q) than non-beneficiary respondents (₹4,287.09/q) and a higher return per rupee invested (1.92 compared with 1.73). The overall net income was also higher among beneficiary respondents (₹46,518.85/ha) than among non-beneficiary respondents (₹31,213.26/ha). The study concludes that access to institutional credit through PACS was associated with higher productivity, lower unit production costs and greater profitability in green gram cultivation.

title: A review on the recent trends in solar-biomass hybrid drying of agro and marine products in the context of sustainable development goals
abstract: Post-harvest losses remain a critical challenge in global food systems, pressing the need for efficient and sustainable drying technologies to ensure food preservation and food loss reduction. The primary objective of this review is to study solar hybrid drying (SHD) systems with respect to their performance, economic viability, and environmental impact. From recent advancements in the design configurations, modelling approaches, and case studies, the review work evaluates the scalability, economic feasibility, and climate resilience of SHD for food preservation. Particular attention was given to solar-biomass hybrid drying (SBHD) systems, which demonstrate a significant scope for future development. Scaling up SBHD systems can empower farmers, self-help groups, and allied organizations to produce value-added products and increase their income generation opportunities. Moreover, the main purpose of this review is to establish the linkage between drying technologies and Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), highlighting their importance in promoting sustainable energy use, ensuring food security and climate adaptation. Further, the findings indicate that the 12 SDGs and 36 targets support drying technology, predominantly focusing on zero hunger (SDG 2), clean and affordable energy (SDG 7), and climate action (SDG 13). The outcomes of this review will benefit researchers in the field of drying technology, which will enable them to focus on renewable energy, such as solar and biomass. Further, this encourages researchers to work towards an environmentally friendly path for alleviating food insecurity and track progress toward achieving SDGs.

title: Effectiveness of the electronic Community Health Information System on maternal continuum of care completion in rural East Shewa Zone, Eastern Ethiopia: A prospective controlled quasi-experimental study
abstract: Maternal mortality in Ethiopia remains high, and strengthening the continuum of maternal care is essential for reducing preventable deaths. The electronic Community Health Information System was introduced to improve service delivery through decision support, client tracking, and electronic referrals, but evidence of its effect in routine settings is limited. This study assessed the effect of the eCHIS's Reproductive, Maternal, Newborn, Child Health and Nutrition module intervention on completion of the maternal continuum of care. A prospective controlled pre-post quasi-experimental study design was conducted in Primary Health Care Units. Baseline data were collected from January 5 to February 5, 2025, enrolling pregnant women with twenty six weeks of gestation or earlier. Participants were followed for nine months, and end-line data collected that year. Maternal care outcomes came from antenatal, delivery, and postnatal registers, with verification interviews when records were incomplete. The primary outcome was completion of the maternal continuum of care. Intervention effects were estimated using a Difference in Differences fixed effects model with cluster robust standard errors. Follow-up was completed for 409 women in each group (97.5%). Baseline continuum of care completion was comparable across groups. By endline, completion increased from 19.6% to 47.7% in the intervention group versus 19.1% to 23.7% in controls. The eCHIS-RMNCHN intervention produced a 23.5% point improvement in full continuum of care completion (β = 0.235; 95% CI: [0.155-0.314]), with significant gains in ANC4+ and ANC4 + combined with SBA. Implementation of the eCHIS-RMNCHN module intervention was associated with substantial improvements in maternal continuum-of-care completion and key intermediate indicators. Strategies guided by the CFIR ERIC framework helped address local barriers to digital system use. Sustained implementation, leadership engagement, technical support, community involvement, and continuous performance monitoring are essential for maintaining these improvements and informing scale up efforts.

title: Household-level food-insecurity prediction from experience-scale surveys and open geospatial data: A reproducible machine-learning pipeline for Nigeria
abstract: This paper develops a reproducible machine-learning pipeline for household-level food-insecurity prediction in Nigeria using the 2024 NDHS FIES module and five open geospatial layers. Because the NDHS is a two-stage cluster sample, all evaluation uses cluster-grouped data splits in which no enumeration area contributes households to both training and test sets. On a held-out test set of 7,999 households from 276 enumeration areas, the random forest reaches AUROC 0.727 (cluster-bootstrap 95 percent CI 0.704 to 0.747) and gradient-boosted trees 0.714 (0.690 to 0.737), against 0.679 (0.653 to 0.702) for a logistic baseline. Under leave-zone-out validation, which scores entire geopolitical zones the model never saw, the logistic baseline outperforms both ensembles in all six zones. SHAP attribution assigns between 42 and 52 percent of predictive signal to contextual predictors depending on model and coordinate treatment, a larger share than prior DHS tree-ensemble work reports. Travel time to the nearest city is associated with lower food-insecurity risk, a pattern consistent with a subsistence-buffer channel during sharp naira depreciation that we present as a hypothesis requiring replication.

title: Toward sustainable cocoa production: technical efficiency as a transition path toward competitiveness in Colombia
abstract: The agricultural sector is an essential pillar for economic development and global food security. However, it faces challenges that compromise its viability, such as climate change, migration, and productivity variability. Colombia is among the main producing countries of fine and aromatic cocoa, and the department of Santander is the main producer of cocoa in the country; however, its production and commercialisation are affected by multiple factors, such as low access to competitive markets, a lack of infrastructure, and a low level of incorporation of technologies. In this study, the efficiency of cocoa on 500 farms located in five municipalities, Santander and Norte de Santander, Colombia, was analysed using a two-stage method with bootstrapped DEA and truncated regression. The results revealed 68.4% average technical efficiency and 21.5% scale efficiency. Efficiency is affected by technological limitations, training, and market factors. In addition, it was shown that gender gaps persist, with female producers showing significantly lower scale efficiency, suggesting structural barriers in access to productive resources, financing, and technical assistance, as well as a worrying lack of generational change.

title: Assessing the potential of agri-waste coarse aggregates for sustainable concrete production in Ghana
abstract: The increasing adoption of alternative construction materials is central to advancing sustainability in the construction industry, particularly in developing countries where agricultural waste presents both an environmental challenge and a resource opportunity. This study examined the factors influencing the preparedness of construction professionals in Ghana to adopt agricultural-waste coarse aggregates (AWCA) for sustainable concrete production. Specifically, the study assessed professionals’ knowledge and awareness of AWCA, their perceptions and intentions toward its use, as well as the key drivers and barriers affecting adoption. A structured questionnaire was administered to construction professionals, yielding 260 valid responses. The data were analysed using descriptive statistics and Structural Equation Modelling within the framework of the Theory of Planned Behaviour. The results indicate that while respondents exhibited moderate awareness of AWCA, their technical understanding of material processing, testing requirements, and performance standards was limited. Perceptions toward AWCA were generally cautious, with concerns related to durability, contamination risks, client acceptance, and the lack of local demonstration projects. SEM results showed that both knowledge and perception significantly influenced professionals’ intention to adopt AWCA, with perception emerging as the stronger predictor. The study further identified major barriers to adoption, including the absence of standards, inadequate testing infrastructure, supply-chain challenges, and limited policy support. These constraints persist despite the recognised environmental benefits of AWCA. The study concludes that improving AWCA adoption in Ghana requires targeted professional capacity-building initiatives, locally validated demonstration projects, and clear regulatory guidelines. Strengthening partnerships between academia and industry is also critical for building trust, reducing uncertainty, and advancing circular material practices. Overall, the findings highlight the transformative potential of agricultural waste utilisation in Ghana’s built environment.

title: Land System Couplings: From Telecoupling to an Integrated Framework and Its Application in Slovakia
abstract: Land-use change, climate change, and biodiversity loss require integrated analytical frameworks to address multi-scalar human–nature interactions. While the classical telecoupling framework effectively captures long-distance flows, it often overlooks the dense institutional and regional dynamics specific to the European context. This paper addresses this gap by synthesizing telecoupling research and operationalizing an integrated coupling framework rooted in metacoupling theory. Methodologically, a systematic literature review of 138 publications was conducted following PRISMA guidelines to evaluate contemporary indicators. The review revealed a strong predominance of quantitative methods in non-review articles and declared need to shift towards more complex, integrative models, while highlighting a critical scarcity of European-centered studies. Preliminary empirical application of the framework within the Horizon Europe Europe-LAND project—focusing on the LTSER Trnava region in Slovakia—indicates, based on interim findings, certain socioecological disparities and imbalances in decision-making influence. Specifically, highly land-dependent local actors appear to have limited leverage in legislative processes, which is further complicated by communication gaps between research institutions and primary land users. To achieve sustainable land management, European and national policies must transition from purely material flow analysis to causal institutional frameworks that counterbalance developer pressures and actively empower local agricultural practices.

title: Evaluating the Accuracy of Diseases of the Endometrium–evaluation and Risk Scoring as a Noninvasive screening Tool for Endometrial Pathologies in Abnormal Uterine Bleeding
abstract: A BSTRACT Background: Abnormal uterine bleeding (AUB) is one of the most common complaints among women’s visits to the gynecologist. The recent adoption of diseases of the endometrium–evaluation and risk scoring (DEERS) may help gynecologists to better screen patients for AUB. Objective: The objective of this study is to assess the reliability of DEERS in diagnosing specific endometrial pathologies. Materials and Methods: This prospective, observational study included 250 cases of AUB. The study took place from June 2022 to December 2023 at a tertiary care teaching hospital in Chengalpattu, Kanchipuram, Tamil Nadu. Patients in the study were scheduled for endometrial sampling, which involved endometrial curettage and biopsy. Results: Independent risk factors for disease incidence were identified. It was determined that individuals aged 40 years and above had a 13.44 times higher risk of developing the disease. Postmenopausal women were also identified as independent determinants of disease incidence with a 2.84 times higher risk. Moreover, obese women were found to have a 1.98 times higher risk of endometrial disease. Conclusion: The use of DEERS provided better screening of AUB patients and thereby improved the management of these patients from both urban and rural milieus.

title: The value of a family dinner from the perspective of subjective well-being
abstract: Based on data from the China Family Panel Studies ( CFPS ) 2014 and 2018 surveys, this paper investigates the association between family dinners and subjective well-being ( SWB ), analyzing it through the dual lenses of material and spiritual needs. The findings reveal that sharing meals with family members significantly enhances SWB —and that this positive effect has strengthened over time. Moreover, the magnitude of this effect exhibits notable heterogeneity across urban versus rural residence and across income groups. Employing the life satisfaction approach ( LSA ), the study further monetizes the value of family dinners. On average, residents are willing to pay CNY 11,585 annually for one additional family dinner per week—a willingness-to-pay figure that has also increased over time, again reflecting pronounced urban–rural and income-based disparities. Additional analysis uncovers a threshold effect in the relationship between family dinner frequency and SWB improvement, with the threshold varying by survey year, gender, marital status, and residential location (urban vs. rural).

title: Fertility in Ethiopia: factors associated with the number of live births —a survey—adjusted poisson regression analysis of the 2019 ethiopian mini demographic and health survey
abstract: Background Fertility is a key demographic and public health phenomenon reflecting actual childbearing within a population. It can be characterized using several measures, including total fertility rate, age-specific fertility rates, children ever born, and the number of births occurring within a defined reference period. These measures capture different dimensions of reproductive experience and are associated with a complex interplay of socioeconomic, demographic, cultural, biological, and policy-related factors. Methods By dividing the nine regions into urban and rural categories, twenty-one sampling strata were created. The survey employed a two-stage stratified cluster sampling design. In the first stage, 305 enumeration areas (EAs) were selected from the national sampling frame using probability proportional to size. A total of 8,885 women were included in the descriptive analysis, while the primary multivariable analysis was restricted to 6,585 ever-married/partnered women. A survey-adjusted Poisson regression model was used to examine associations between explanatory variables and the number of live births during the five years preceding the survey. Statistical significance was assessed using a two-sided p -value of <0.05. Result and conclusion The mean age of the participants was 27.6 years. More than four-fifths of women had either no formal education (40.4%) or primary education (41.7%). Compared with women aged 15–19 years, the expected number of recent live births was higher among women aged 20–24 years (aIRR = 2.129, 95% CI: 1.759–2.577). Women residing in Amhara had a lower expected number of recent live births than women residing in Tigray (aIRR = 0.765, 95% CI: 0.658–0.890). Lower expected counts were also observed in Addis Ababa (aIRR = 0.818, 95% CI: 0.684–0.979) and Dire Dawa (aIRR = 0.792, 95% CI: 0.659–0.952). An inverse association was observed between household wealth and recent live-birth counts. These findings highlight the multifactorial nature of recent live births in Ethiopia and suggest that fertility patterns are associated with a combination of individual, household, and contextual factors. These insights may help inform evidence-based reproductive health and family planning policies tailored to the Ethiopian context.

title: Historical redlining and breast cancer screening in a regional spatial analysis
abstract: BACKGROUND: Redlining, introduced in 1933 by the Homeowners' Loan Corporation, created enduring structural inequities in housing, health care access, and neighborhood investment. These historical patterns may contribute to persistent disparities in breast cancer screening. This study examines how historical redlining, alongside contemporary socioeconomic factors, shapes screening disparities across the University of Kansas Cancer Center (KUCC) catchment area. METHODS: We conducted a census tract-level spatial analysis across 123 counties (Kansas and western Missouri) by linking CDC PLACES breast cancer screening data with historical redlining maps. Explanatory variables included rurality, mammography facility availability, income inequality, gender pay gap, and uninsured rates. Logistic regression assessed overall associations, while geographically weighted binomial logistic regression evaluated spatial heterogeneity. RESULTS: Screening rates ranged from 56.9% to 84.5% across census tracts. Redlining was associated with lower screening odds in unadjusted models but was attenuated after accounting for socioeconomic and geographic factors. Rurality and income inequality were consistently associated with lower screening, whereas greater mammography facility availability was associated with higher screening rates. Spatial analyses revealed meaningful geographic variation, with localized negative associations of redlining and persistent, spatially varying effects of socioeconomic factors. CONCLUSION: Breast cancer screening disparities in this region reflect the combined influence of historical structural inequities and current socioeconomic conditions. Expanding access to mammography and implementing spatially targeted, equity-focused interventions may improve screening uptake and reduce disparities in underserved communities.

title: Association between anaemia and menopause-related quality of life in Tamil Nadu: a cross-sectional study
abstract: Anaemia and menopause are independently associated with reduced quality of life; however, empirical evidence on their intersection remains limited, particularly in the Indian context. This study aimed to assess the association between anaemia and menopause-related quality of life among postmenopausal women in Tamil Nadu. The study was conducted between May and June 2024 among 400 postmenopausal women aged 45–55 years in Chennai (urban) and Thiruvarur (rural) districts in Tamil Nadu as a community-based cross-sectional study using multistage sampling. A portable haemoglobin analyser was used to measure haemoglobin levels. The Menopause-Specific Quality of Life (MENQOL) questionnaire was used to measure menopause-related quality of life. Descriptive statistics, Mann–Whitney U tests, and multiple linear regression were used for the analysis. The prevalence of anaemia was 60.25%. Women aged over 50 years, with lower educational attainment, labour and wage-based workers were more likely to have anaemia. Multiple linear regression indicated no statistically significant association between haemoglobin levels and the vasomotor (adjusted B = − 0.005, p = 0.833), psychosocial (adjusted B = 0.004, p = 0.844), physical (adjusted B = 0.003, p = 0.840), or sexual (adjusted B = 0.032, p = 0.367) domains. A statistically significant association was observed in the unadjusted analysis for the sexual domain (B = 0.32, 95% CI 0.01–0.64, p = 0.047); however, this association was not retained after adjustment for age, education, occupation, marital status, residence, and physical activity level (adjusted B = 0.032, 95% CI − 0.037 to 0.100, p = 0.367). Anaemia was highly prevalent among postmenopausal women in Tamil Nadu, no statistically significant associations between haemoglobin levels and MENQOL domains were observed after adjustment for potential confounders. The unadjusted sexual-domain association should be considered exploratory and interpreted cautiously pending confirmation in future studies.

title: Determinants of Hypertension among Postmenopausal Women in Chengalpattu District, Tamil Nadu—A Cross-sectional Study
abstract: Abstract Background: Hypertension is a significant public health concern, especially among postmenopausal women, due to hormonal changes and age-related risk factors. This study aimed to estimate the prevalence of hypertension and identify its associated risk factors among postmenopausal women in Chengalpattu district, Tamil Nadu. Materials and Methods: A community-based cross-sectional study was conducted among 280 postmenopausal women in urban and rural areas of Chengalpattu district from January 2025 to June 2025. Participants were selected using a multistage sampling technique. Data were collected using a pre-tested structured questionnaire covering sociodemographic characteristics, dietary habits, lifestyle factors, and family history. Blood pressure was measured using standard procedures. Bivariate and Multivariable logistic regression analyses were performed using the software Statistical Package for Social Sciences version 23. Results: The prevalence of hypertension among postmenopausal women was found to be 37.1%. Significant sociodemographic determinants included higher educational status, urban residence, and not currently living with children. Behavioral and lifestyle-related factors such as duration since menopause, junk food consumption and family history of hypertension were identified as independent risk factors. Conclusion: Hypertension was common among postmenopausal women. Regular blood pressure screening and targeted interventions addressing unhealthy dietary habits and women with identified risk factors may improve cardiovascular health.

title: Prevalence of Inverted and Flat Nipples and Acceptance of Corrective Measures among Expectant Mothers in Rural Khordha
abstract: Abstract Introduction: Inverted or flat nipples, if not addressed during the antenatal period, can hinder successful breastfeeding. Women facing these issues often struggle with early initiation and may discontinue exclusive breastfeeding before six months. This study aimed to estimate the prevalence of inverted and flat nipples among pregnant women and to explore the factors that facilitate or hinder the acceptance of corrective interventions. Methodology: The community-based mixed-method explanatory study was conducted in the rural field practice area (RHTC) of a tertiary health center in Eastern India. A total of 156 participants were recruited by simple random sampling. A female physician performed breast examinations of the participants, maintaining privacy, and surgical grading was used for classification. Barriers and facilitators of acceptance of corrective measures were identified using a qualitative method involving multiple stakeholders. Results: One in 10 individuals (10.9%) in our study reported having a flat nipple. The majority of the participants (>80%) were under 30 years of age. Around one fifth (18.6%) of the mothers were aware of inverted or flat nipples, and 26.3% of mothers were detected as a high-risk pregnancy in the antenatal visits. Most mothers in our study had misconceptions about it or were unaware. The socio-cultural barriers played a significant role in the knowledge of the mothers regarding inverted or flat nipples and possible complications. Conclusion: The main reason for the lack of detection is lack of knowledge and socio-cultural determinants. Early identification of the anomalies and appropriate timely intervention will improve breastfeeding outcomes.

title: Prevalence and Predictors of Unhealthy Food Consumption among Children Aged 6–23 Months in Ajmer District, Rajasthan: A Community-based Cross-sectional Study
abstract: Abstract Introduction: Unhealthy food consumption (UFC) during early childhood is rising in India. It is associated with poor dietary diversity, increasing risks of obesity, and malnutrition. This study was conducted to assess the prevalence and predictors of UFC among children aged 6–23 months in Ajmer district, Rajasthan. Methods: This community-based, cross-sectional study was conducted between August 2024 and May 2025. A total of 300 children were selected through multistage random sampling. Data were collected using a pre-tested, semi-structured, interviewer-administered questionnaire. It was based on World Health Organization/United Nations Children’s Fund Infant and Young Child Feeding indicators. Data on sociodemographic characteristics, child feeding practices, household food environment, and maternal-child health services were collected. Statistical analysis was conducted using the Chi-square test, Fisher’s exact test, independent t -test, and multivariable logistic regression. Results: The prevalence of UFC was 77% (95% confidence interval [CI]: 72.2–81.8). Maternal screen time (adjusted odds ratio [aOR]: 3.23, P = 0.046), child age (aOR: 1.28, P < 0.01), low dietary diversity (aOR: 0.13, P < 0.01), use of food delivery applications (aOR: 4.23, P = 0.047), proximity to food outlets (aOR: 2.89, P = 0.041), low healthy food score (aOR: 0.53, P = 0.010), high unhealthy food score (aOR: 3.71, P < 0.01), food insecurity (aOR: 0.63, P = 0.034), visibility to unhealthy food (aOR: 3.79, P = 0.035), more post-natal care visits (aOR: 3.67, P = 0.027), fewer antenatal care visits (aOR: 0.62, P < 0.01), and fewer Accredited Social Health Activist visits (aOR: 0.30, P < 0.01) were found predictors of UFC. Conclusion: The high prevalence of UFC among young children suggests the need for targeted interventions. It should include behaviorial change communication, strengthening of routine health services, and strict regulation of digital food marketing.

title: Ecological constraints on sustainable agricultural development in palestine: A socio-ecological and environmental justice perspective
abstract: Agricultural sustainability in Palestine is increasingly shaped by the interaction of ecological stress, political restrictions, infrastructure fragility, and uneven institutional support. This study examines how ecological and governance-mediated constraints affect sustainable agricultural development in Palestine, using field evidence from the Gaza Strip and the West Bank. A mixed-methods design combined a structured survey of 250 farmers, semi-structured interviews with 17 experts, and secondary evidence from official statistics, GIS-based reports, policy documents, and peer-reviewed literature. Quantitative data were analyzed using SPSS through descriptive statistics, composite indices, non-parametric and categorical tests, rank correlations, and binary logistic regression, while expert interviews were analyzed thematically and integrated through triangulation. The findings show that ecological constraints are severe and multidimensional. The overall Ecological Constraint Severity Index reached 4.08 ± 0.61 on a five-point scale, with water-related constraints recording the highest severity score (4.34 ± 0.58), followed by regulatory-political constraints. These pressures were associated with declining production, reduced product quality, income losses, rising production costs, and weakened household food-security capacity. Adaptation practices, including drip irrigation, soil management, crop adjustment, solar pumping, rainwater harvesting, and water reuse, were present but unevenly adopted due to constraints in finance, infrastructure, energy, extension, technology, and institutional support. The study distinguishes resilience-building adaptation from distress coping, showing that responses such as reducing cultivated area may reflect shrinking livelihood options rather than sustainable transformation. The paper contributes to sustainability scholarship by framing ecological constraints as socio-ecological, governance-mediated, and political conditions requiring integrated and equity-oriented agricultural policy.

title: Tidal inundation type and soil chemical properties determine rice productivity in tropical acid sulfate swamp ecosystems
abstract: Ensuring sustainable rice (Oryza sativa L.) production in tidal swamp ecosystems is critical for strengthening food security in Indonesia.Soil chemical properties, tidal inundation type, and planting season strongly influence rice productivity in these systems.This study evaluated soil chemical characteristics and rice productivity across tidal swamp areas in Tanah Bumbu Regency, South Kalimantan, Indonesia, by inundation type and cropping season.Field surveys, soil analyses, and farmer interviews were conducted in five villages.Selimuran and Mudalang were classified as Type B tidal swamps.In contrast, Rantau Panjang, Api-api, and Segumbang were categorized as Type C. Type B soils were acidic, while Type C soils were very acidic.Although both types exhibited low organic C, total N, and exchangeable P, Type B soils had higher P and base cation availability and lower concentrations of exchangeable Al, Fe, sulfate, and pyrite.The pyritic layer was shallower in Type C soils, increasing oxidation risk.Rice productivity was significantly higher in Type B systems (5.43 t ha⁻¹) than in Type C systems (3.76 t ha⁻¹).Seasonal responses differed between tidal types.Yields in Type B fields declined by 0.95 t ha⁻¹ from the dry to the rainy season, whereas yields in Type C fields increased by 0.45 t ha⁻¹.These findings highlight the importance of site-and season-specific nutrient and water management to enhance productivity and sustainability in acid sulfate tidal swamp ecosystems.

summary_id.tujuan: Mengevaluasi karakteristik kimia tanah dan produktivitas padi di lahan rawa pasang surut tipe B dan C (tanah sulfat masam) menurut tipe genangan dan musim tanam di Kabupaten Tanah Bumbu, Kalimantan Selatan.
summary_id.metode: Survei lapangan dan analisis tanah laboratorium di lima desa (Selimuran, Mudalang, Rantau Panjang, Api-api, Segumbang) pada November 2021 hingga Maret 2022, dengan wawancara terstruktur terhadap lima petani per desa. Pengukuran muka air tanah dilakukan selama musim hujan. Analisis menggunakan statistik deskriptif, ANOVA (95%), uji post hoc, dan korelasi.
summary_id.temuan: Produktivitas padi tipe B lebih tinggi daripada tipe C (5,43 vs 3,76 t/ha; selisih 1,67 t/ha atau 37,13%). Hasil tipe B turun 0,95 t/ha dari musim kemarau ke hujan, sedangkan tipe C naik 0,45 t/ha. Lapisan pirit di tipe C lebih dangkal (rata-rata 37 cm vs 108 cm) dan Al dapat ditukar lebih tinggi (11,27-12,97 vs 5,20-6,00 cmol/kg). Temuan ini bersifat asosiatif, bukan kausal.
summary_id.keterbatasan: Tidak disebutkan secara eksplisit dalam bagian yang terbaca. Dari desain, jumlah unit sampel sangat kecil (lima desa, lima petani per desa), tipe genangan terkonfonding dengan lokasi, dan data hasil berasal dari wawancara petani. Hasil uji statistik ANOVA tidak tampak pada teks yang tersedia, dan teks penuh terpotong.
summary_id.relevansi: Temuan tentang biaya input (dolomit dan pupuk lebih tinggi di tipe C) dan variasi musim tanam penting untuk analisis kelayakan usaha tani padi rawa di Kalimantan Selatan. Studi ini dapat menjadi dasar pembanding untuk kajian ketahanan pangan lokal, tetapi fokusnya pada ilmu tanah dan agronomi, bukan pemasaran, kelembagaan, atau adopsi digital.

title: Advancing economic sustainability in smallholder agriculture: insights on financial inclusion, asset size, technology, and knowledge-based inputs in the transformation of farm productivity in India
abstract: Enhancing agricultural productivity is central to achieving sustainable development goals, particularly in rural economies characterized by smallholder farming. This study examines the role of financial inclusion, human capital, and technology adoption in shaping crop productivity among marginal farmers in India. Drawing on human capital and development perspectives, the research investigates how literacy and awareness interact with access to agricultural credit, farm size, and the adoption of modern technologies to influence productivity outcomes. Primary data were collected from 400 marginal farmers through a structured survey and analyzed using Structural Equation Modeling (SEM). The findings reveal that literacy and awareness significantly enhance crop productivity both directly and indirectly by strengthening the impact of technology adoption and access to credit. The results highlight a complementary relationship between knowledge-based inputs and technological resources in driving sustainable agricultural outcomes. In contrast, farm size shows a limited influence, reflecting structural constraints in smallholder contexts. By demonstrating the dual role of literacy as both an independent and moderating factor, the study contributes to the literature on sustainable agriculture and inclusive development. The findings underscore the need for integrated policy interventions that combine financial inclusion, capacity building, and technology dissemination to promote resilient and equitable agrarian systems. Such interventions can enhance food security, improve rural livelihoods, and support long-term sustainable development in emerging economies.

title: Sustainable biodiesel production from beef tallow and lard: A comparative study in Indonesia
abstract: The utilization of waste animal fats as biodiesel feedstock offers a sustainable alternative to conventional vegetable oils, particularly in regions where palm oil production competes with food resources. This study investigates the production and characterization of biodiesel synthesized from beef tallow and lard through alkali-catalyzed transesterification using methanol and sodium hydroxide. The produced fatty acid methyl esters (FAMEs) were purified through liquid–liquid extraction and subsequently characterized using FTIR and ¹H NMR spectroscopy, gas chromatography, and physicochemical analyses. Biodiesel conversion achieved 97.3% for beef tallow and >99% for lard with good-isolated yields 72% and 82%, respectively. The main fatty acids identified were palmitic, stearic, and oleic acids, while lard biodiesel contained a higher proportion of monounsaturated FAMEs. Key fuel characteristics such as viscosity, cetane number, density, and acid value, complied with ASTM D6751, EN 14214, and Indonesian National Standards, although cloud and pour points were slightly elevated due to saturated fat content. This study establishes that high-quality biodiesel can be efficiently produced from animal fats, offering a sustainable alternative to palm oil in Indonesia's renewable energy sector.

title: Políticas públicas productivas: Papel y desafíos en el empoderamiento de las mujeres en la agricultura en Aramango, Amazonas, Perú
abstract: Objective This study analyzes the relationship between productive public policies and women’s empowerment in agricultural activities in the district of Aramango, Amazonas, Peru. The aim was to identify which dimensions of public policies significantly influence the levels of intrinsic, instrumental, and collective agency among women farmers. Methodology The research adopted a quantitative, non-experimental, cross-sectional approach. A survey validated by experts was administered to 40 women belonging to active agricultural associations in El Porvenir. The variables—public policies and empowerment—were measured in five and three dimensions, respectively. Rating scales were used to establish perception levels, and Spearman’s coefficient was employed to analyze correlations between variables. Results The results reveal a positive and statistically significant correlation between productive public policies and women’s empowerment (ρ = 0.318; p < 0.05), with particularly strong effects in the dimensions of knowledge (ρ = 0.458; p = 0.003) and market access (ρ = 0.344; p = 0.030). The dimensions of infrastructure, access to resources, and institutional framework did not show significant correlations. Medium levels of empowerment predominated, although there were advances in autonomy and participation. Conclusions Women’s empowerment in rural agricultural contexts depends on targeted public policies that prioritize technical training and equitable market access. The evidence supports the need to redesign policies using a territorial and intersectional approach to overcome structural barriers and promote the economic, social, and political autonomy of rural women. Accordingly, it is recommended to redesign rural public policies by prioritizing technical training and access to information for women, as a central and more causally effective strategy for their empowerment.

title: Analyzing the Trends in Tobacco Industry Input Costs from the Lens of Leaf Tobacco Prices and Wholesale Price Index (WPI) of India
abstract: Abstract Background: India is among the world’s largest producers and consumers of tobacco, with Flue-Cured Virginia (FCV) leaf forming the backbone of cigarette production. Despite claims of supporting rural livelihoods, smallholder farmers of tobacco face low income, rising input costs, and environmental degradation. While the wholesale price index (WPI) of India has steadily risen over the years, farm-gate auction prices of tobacco have stagnated, widening disparities between manufacturers and growers. The introduction of the goods and services tax (GST) in 2017 further reshaped the fiscal landscape, but its implications for farmer incomes remain unclear. In this context, the study analyzes and compares the trends in leaf tobacco prices with those of WPI in India, drawing implications for farmers’ welfare and the sustainability of tobacco cultivation. Materials and Methods: Secondary data were obtained from the Tobacco Board of India; University of California, San Francisco Industry Documents Library; and International Monetary Fund databases. Average auction platform prices for FCV tobacco from 1984 to 2024 were compared with WPI (2010 = 100). Trends were analyzed across pre- and post-GST periods, with inflation-adjusted comparisons to assess real income implications for tobacco farmers. Results: The study findings reveal four decades of price stagnation, with FCV auction prices stuck between INR 50–70/kg until the early 2000s, rising modestly to INR 100/kg by 2010, and only recently reaching INR 257/kg in 2023–24. In contrast, WPI showed steady upward movement, reflecting broader inflation. Post-GST, farm-gate prices remained misaligned with WPI, offering no immediate relief. This prolonged disconnect suppressed farmer incomes while manufacturers benefited from relatively cheaper raw material costs. Conclusions: The study underscores structural inequities in tobacco leaf pricing in India for FCV tobacco growers, where farmers bear rising costs without proportional price gains. Urgent policy reforms are needed to ensure inflation-adjusted procurement, alongside sustainable crop diversification strategies, to protect the livelihoods and agricultural viability of tobacco.

title: Can Farmers’ Participation in E-Commerce Promote Common Prosperity? An Empirical Analysis Based on Survey Data of Farmers in 10 Chinese Provinces
abstract: Based on data from the 2020 China Rural Revitalization Comprehensive Survey, this study uses a sample of 2508 farm households from 10 provinces to empirically examine the effect of farmers’ e-commerce participation on common prosperity and its underlying mechanisms. The benchmark regression results indicate that farmers’ e-commerce participation significantly promotes common prosperity. The findings remain robust after a series of robustness checks, including propensity score matching (PSM), Tobit estimation, instrumental variable approaches, and alternative measures of the core explanatory variable. Heterogeneity analysis indicates that farmers’ engagement in e-commerce business has a significantly positive effect on common prosperity in the eastern, central, and western regions, with the largest estimated effect observed in the central region. Moreover, farmers’ engagement in e-commerce business significantly enhances common prosperity across groups with different income levels and average household educational attainment, with larger estimated effects among low-income households and those with lower average education levels, indicating greater benefits for relatively disadvantaged groups. Mechanism analysis results indicate that farmers’ participation in e-commerce operations mainly promotes common prosperity through two pathways: improving rural credit accessibility and enhancing information acquisition capabilities.

title: Optimization of protoplast cell division and microcallus formation toward somatic embryogenesis in oil palm
abstract: Background Efficient protoplast regeneration remains a major obstacle to the application of somatic hybridization, genome editing and precision breeding in oil palm ( Elaeis guineensis ); while early developmental stages, from cell wall regeneration and cell division to microcolony and microcallus formation, could be more important, which could be connected easily with the traditional tissue culture system for succeeding plant regeneration. This study aimed to optimize the protopalst culture conditions for cell division and microcallus formation by identifying the most effective combinations of culture systems, basal media and plant growth regulators. Methods Protoplasts isolated from different oil palm tissues (embryogenic callus, suspension cultures, and somatic embryos) were investigated by protoplast yield and viability; protoplasts from the embryogenic callus showed the most satisfactory response and was therefore used for subsequent optimization of culture conditions. The protoplasts were cultured using six culture systems (liquid, droplet, agarose pool, well-plate culture, feeder layer, and nurse culture) in combination with eight basal media (BH3, MS, WPM, Y3, KM, B5, N6, and KPR), and the culture effects were evaluated based on protoplast viability, plating efficiency, cell division, microcolony and microcallus formation. Microcallus emerged from the KPR solid medium were transferred to previously established traditional tissue culture system for further somatic embryogenesis and regeneration. Results BH3 liquid medium was particularly effective for early protoplast recovery and rapid cell wall regeneration, whereas KPR solid medium combined with the nurse culture system, provided the most favorable conditions for sustained cell division, plating efficiency, microcolony and microcallus formation. Cell division occurred within 3–7 days, followed by microcolony formation after approximately 7 days and visible microcallus formation after 60 days. Microcallus were transferred for further development, somatic embryos and bud regeneration was observed after 90 days and 120 days, respectively. Conclusions The present study focused on the early developmental stages of oil palm protoplast culture, and optimized a stage-specific culture strategy for quick microcallus formation; combined with previous oil palm tissue culture system, further somatic embryogenesis and bud regeneration were established successfully. This work not only promoted the protoplast regeneration of oil palm, but also provides a promising strategy for other tropical palm trees such as coconut and betel nut.

title: Long-term legacy effects of Eucalyptus plantation on soil properties, ant diversity, and ecosystem functioning in tropical montane ecosystems
abstract: Eucalyptus plantations are rapidly expanding across tropical mountains, where silvicultural practices modify soil properties and biodiversity. However, the long-term consequences of abandoned plantations remain poorly understood, particularly in biodiversity hotspots such as the Espinhaço Range, Brazil. Here, we evaluated the effects of active and abandoned Eucalyptus plantations on soil properties, ant community, and ant-mediated ecosystem services in tropical montane ecosystems. We compared reference vegetation ( Campo Sujo ), active Eucalyptus plantations (four years old), and abandoned plantations (approximately five years after harvesting) across three sites in the northern Espinhaço Range. Ant species were sampled using pitfall traps, while scavenging, granivory, and seed dispersal were assessed using bait arenas. Soil physical and chemical properties were also quantified. Mean values of soil organic matter, organic carbon, and potential cation exchange capacity were higher in abandoned and active Eucalyptus plantations than in Campo Sujo, indicating persistent differences in soil characteristics associated with previous silvicultural land use. Active and abandoned plantations exhibited higher nutrient availability compared to reference areas. Reference areas showed higher alpha and gamma diversity, whereas active and abandoned plantations exhibited increased beta diversity. Reference areas had 52% more ant species (61 species) than active plantations (40 species), with abandoned plantations showing intermediate richness (46 species). Ant species composition also differed significantly among treatments, suggesting strong anthropogenic filtering associated with Eucalyptus plantation and limited recovery after abandonment. Ecosystem services showed variable responses to land-use change. Scavenging was reduced in active plantations and was positively associated with ant richness only in reference areas. Granivory was higher in active plantations, while seed dispersal did not differ among treatments. Overall, our findings demonstrate that Eucalyptus plantation was associated with long-lasting changes in soil conditions and ant diversity and services in montane ecosystems. These persistent soil and biodiversity differences remain detectable after Eucalyptus plantation abandonment, highlighting the importance of incorporating post-harvest management and restoration strategies.Parte superior do formulário

title: Generative AI risk prediction capability and cross border agricultural trade resilience: a PLS-SEM empirical study of coastal Chinese enterprises
abstract: Introduction Maritime transport carries the predominant share of cross-border agricultural trade, and geopolitical conflicts, climate anomalies, port congestion, and proliferating trade barriers have intensified uncertainty for the coastal enterprises that depend on seaborne logistics. Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) offers new pathways for building resilient supply chains through multi-source data fusion and risk prediction capabilities. However, empirical evidence examining how GenAI risk prediction capability (GenAI-RPC) relates to cross-border agricultural trade resilience (CATR) remains scarce. Grounded in the resource-based view (RBV) and dynamic capability theory, this study develops a direct-effects model linking three GenAI-RPC dimensions---multi-source cross-border risk identification and scoring, prediction accuracy and anti-hallucination stability, and AI risk model calibration and decision empowerment---to CATR. Methods Using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM), we analyzed survey data from 300 agricultural enterprises engaged in cross-border trade across four coastal Chinese provinces (Shandong, Guangdong, Fujian, and Zhejiang). Results The measurement model demonstrated satisfactory reliability and validity: Cronbach's α ranged from 0.817 to 0.855, composite reliability from 0.880 to 0.902, and average variance extracted (AVE) from 0.623 to 0.697. All heterotrait-monotrait (HTMT) ratios were below 0.85, supporting discriminant validity. The structural model showed that all three GenAI-RPC dimensions were positively associated with CATR: multi-source risk identification ( β = 0.291, p < 0.001), prediction accuracy ( β = 0.251, p < 0.001), and model calibration ( β = 0.287, p < 0.001). The model explained 46.1% of the variance in CATR ( R 2 = 0.461; Stone--Geisser Q 2 = 0.112), with SRMR = 0.069 indicating acceptable fit. Among the control variables, enterprise digital transformation maturity showed a strong positive association with CATR ( β = 0.577, p < 0.001), and all three GenAI-RPC dimensions remained statistically significant after controlling for it. Discussion These findings contribute to the theoretical integration of GenAI capabilities with maritime supply chain resilience research and offer practical guidance for coastal agricultural enterprises and policymakers seeking to strengthen the resilience of seaborne food trade.

title: Sustainable energy for agricultural irrigation in Ethiopia: techno-economic and life cycle analysis of solar versus diesel pumps
abstract: Abstract This research presents a techno-economic and environmental life cycle assessment (LCA) comparison between diesel water pumps (DWP) and solar water pumps (SWP) for smallholder irrigation in Ethiopia.
