To evaluate long-term operational sustainability amid volatile fossil fuel markets, local hydrologic conditions, and rural decarbonization targets, the study uses an integrated three-stage simulation architecture of the CLIMWAT database, CROPWAT, and PVsyst. To deliver the required annual irrigation water volume for a 9-month double irrigation season, we use a 9.6 PV array with a 79% performance ratio. The dynamic 20-year projection period Net Present Cost (NPC) analysis indicates that the SWP system stands at $80,065, securing a net lifetime savings of a 38% reduction in cost compared to DWP. Financial feasibility metrics confirm SWP’s strong investment returns, effectively yielding an Internal Rate of Return (IRR) of 16%. From a 20-year environmental lifecycle perspective, the SWP system eliminates 9.90 t CO 2 per year, but its upstream embedded manufacturing debt is 9,144.10 kg CO 2 -e, which secures a net lifetime climate mitigation of a 95% footprint reduction. These empirical findings confirm that SWP systems offer a technically reliable, financially advantageous, and environmentally resilient framework for enhancing energy-water-food security and climate adaptation across Ethiopia.

title: Role of urban and peri-urban agriculture in nutritional diversity, cultural resilience and community-based food security in an Eastern Himalayan city
abstract: Urban food insecurity affects approximately 75% of the global food-insecure population, with nutritional diversity and accessibility increasingly constrained by climate change and rapid urbanization. This study examines urban and peri-urban agriculture (UPA) in Imphal, the capital of Manipur in Northeast India’s Eastern Himalayan region, as a community-based response to these interconnected challenges. Traditional Meitei homesteads featuring courtyards, ponds and kitchen gardens have been largely replaced by residential buildings due to population pressure, yet households continue to practice small-scale gardening using containers, terraces and rooftops. Health concerns over pesticide residues in market vegetables have driven a shift toward organic, chemical-free home cultivation. A mixed-methods survey ( n = 150 households) reveals that nearly all urban households engage in some form of food production, with women managing most gardens. Beyond immediate food needs, UPA in Imphal is deeply entwined with the region’s unique cultural heritage; diversified kitchen gardening has ensured food and nutrition security for centuries, contributing to a social resilience that makes farmer suicide unheard of in this region. UPA in Imphal contributes to nutritional security by diversifying household diets with fresh vegetables and herbs, enhances climate resilience through localized food systems and supports cultural continuity in a biodiversity-rich yet climate-vulnerable region.

title: Environmental Sustainability of Soybean Production in the Democratic Republic of Congo: Cases of Production Systems in the South‐Kivu and Kasaï‐Lomami Provinces
journal: Journal of Sustainable Agriculture and Environment
abstract: ABSTRACT Soybean is increasingly grown in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), produced mainly in small‐scale systems and supplied locally for human consumption. Prospects of large‐scale expansion and intensification, with potential environmental drawbacks, loom and call for a sustainability analysis of soybean agri‐food systems. We assessed the environmental impacts of different soybean production systems, and evaluated options for inputs reduction and yields improvement, in the east and centre of the DRC. We mapped soybean value chains of production in small and large‐scale systems, used the Life Cycle Assessment (LCA) method for inventory and assessment ecological impacts on climate change, acidification, fossil energy use, particulate matter formation, land use, biodiversity loss, and soil quality. We additionally examined the correlations between productivity and environmental sustainability. Results showed that small‐scale systems were mostly with less than 1 hectare, largely intercropped (> 80%) and had better land‐use efficiencies. Seed and compost inputs rates oscillated significantly across small‐scale farmers' systems, still their ecological footprints were similar. In contrast, large‐scale soybean productions were monocropped, with no amendment but relied on mineral fertilizers, and mechanized operations with fossil fuels. Large‑scale production delivered about four times more soybean yield but caused severe environmental impacts of tenfold higher than small‑scale production systems, in all the impact categories assessed except for land occupation. In small‐scale production systems, productivity and environmental sustainability indicators correlated positively with each other, but negatively with farm size, pinpointing the need to maintain and support the adoption of better farming practices even as the farm size increases. Our sensitivity analysis suggested that production in small‐scale with improved quantity and quality of seeds and compost inputs could achieve an economically viable yield with still much lower ecological impacts compared to the large‐scale production. Therefore, a system optimizing both productivity and environmental preservation is to be sought after. Our study and the LCA method implementation limitations are discussed and call for further investigation with larger samples sizes and adaptation of emissions modelling to the region for comprehensive LCA.

title: “My feet are no longer swollen”: Testing a co-designed podoconiosis protective footwear among rural female farmers in Rwanda
abstract: Podoconiosis is a disabling neglected tropical disease (NTD) caused by prolonged occupational exposure to alkaline red clay soil, disproportionately affecting female farmers in Rwanda. Although preventable through the consistent use of protective footwear, such as farming boots, high costs and limited availability at local markets impede rural farmers' access to appropriate footwear. Among female farmers, gender norms and cultural expectations further constrain their ability to access and wear farming boots. This qualitative community-based participatory project aimed to test a women-centered farming boot, co-designed by participants and the research team, to address previously identified barriers to protective footwear access among rural Rwandan farmers. Boots were distributed for testing, to male and female farmers, in four villages with the highest podoconiosis prevalence across Rwanda. This was paired with education campaigns and other informational materials. Sixteen audio-recorded focus group discussions were subsequently conducted to explore farmers' experiences with the boots. Farmers reported that receiving the footwear encouraged a more consistent use of farming boots, with female participants expressing feelings of pride and an emerging sense of empowerment associated with owning and wearing the boots. While community reactions to the boots varied, most female farmers noted that restrictive gender norms and expectations related to boot wearing persist but do not deter them from wearing the boots. Findings reiterate the importance of gender-sensitive, culturally tailored, and locally driven solutions in preventing podoconiosis and other skin NTDs. Future podoconiosis eradication strategies should strive to prioritize equitable access to protective footwear and address underlying social norms that limit women's access to preventive tools.

title: Digital Consumer Profile: Socioeconomic and Regional Determinants of E-Commerce Participation in Ecuador
journal: Journal of theoretical and applied electronic commerce research
abstract: This paper examines the socioeconomic characteristics associated with e-commerce use in a dollarized economy in Latin America—Ecuador—using a large, nationally representative household survey. Using a survey-weighted logistic model that accounts for the survey’s complex sampling design, it was found that education, income, frequency of internet use, and social media use are the strongest and most consistent predictors of e-commerce participation, while rural residence is associated with a lower likelihood of use. Participation also varies by region, and access to computers or tablets is positively associated with e-commerce use. Notably, gender, ethnicity, and age—commonly emphasized in the prior literature—are not statistically significant predictors once sampling weights are incorporated. This reflects reduced precision under the survey design rather than point estimates shifting toward no association, and it should not be read as evidence that these characteristics are unimportant. Documenting how survey weighting changes which associations reach statistical significance is itself a methodological contribution of this study. These results highlight the central role of digital and educational infrastructure over demographic targeting for enhancing e-commerce participation, and provide guidelines for effective, evidence-based marketing and public policy strategies that consider Ecuador’s social and economic reality.

title: A Suitable Groom: The Effect of Girl's Education on Dowry Payments
abstract: Abstract The social and economic costs of marriage for the bride represent a significant burden for low‐/middle‐income families, contributing to the disempowerment of women within their natal and marital households in multiple ways. This paper uses a large‐scale primary dataset from rural eastern India to investigate the association of dowry with women's education. We test two hypotheses: (a) the human capital effect, that is, the reduction in dowry because of an increase in the acquisition of human capital thereby improving her economic circumstances; (b) the hypergamy effect, that is, education can increase the incidence of dowry via the search for a potentially higher‐education attaining groom who will demand a higher dowry payment in the “marriage market.” Since the level of education of the women may itself be affected by dowry concerns and so is potentially endogenous, we use a state educational developmental policy as an intervention to understand the variegated impact of higher education attainment by women. Finally, the analysis shows an overall effect of the educational status of young women on the dowry payments made by their families, accounting for their distinction across two characteristics, higher human capital acquisition and greater potential to match a more educated groom in the marriage market.

title: Built, but not replaced: The policy failure behind the UK's ageing greenhouse sector
abstract: Societal Impact Statement Glass greenhouse horticulture is a highly productive but often overlooked component of UK agricultural, environmental and food policy, with significant potential to contribute to food security, public health and climate resilience. This paper argues that the ageing greenhouse estate reflects long‐term policy misalignment and the absence of conditions required for sustained investment and renewal. By reframing greenhouse production as infrastructure, it highlights opportunities to better align food production with energy systems, public procurement and spatial planning. Such integration could reduce import dependence, stabilise supply chains and strengthen links between domestic food production (incl. nursery plants) and public‐sector procurement, particularly within institutions such as the NHS and local authorities, supporting a more resilient and sustainable model of domestic production. Summary The United Kingdom's glass greenhouse horticulture sector is characterised by ageing infrastructure, with more than 70% of commercial greenhouse structures now over 40 years old and many constructed under technological and economic conditions that differ substantially from those of modern greenhouse production. This opinion piece argues that this is not simply the result of market conditions or technological change but the outcome of a long‐term policy trajectory in which food horticulture has been consistently included within agricultural frameworks without being recognised as a distinct, capital‐ and energy‐intensive system. A historical perspective is used to show how post‐war policy alignment enabled large‐scale infrastructure development, followed by a sustained period of underinvestment linked to policy frameworks that were poorly aligned with the capital, energy and infrastructure requirements of greenhouse production. Although recent policy developments signal renewed interest in controlled environment production, they remain insufficiently integrated. Reframing greenhouse horticulture as infrastructure provides a basis for aligning policy across energy, planning and procurement, and for addressing the risks associated with continued reliance on ageing systems and imported supply.

title: Men’s perceptions, experiences, and attitudes towards their involvement in contraceptive decision-making in suburban settings: a systematic review of qualitative evidence
abstract: Effective contraceptive decision-making is central to achieving positive family planning (FP) outcomes, yet men’s involvement remains underexplored, particularly in suburban settings worldwide. Understanding men’s views is essential for fostering shared decision-making and improving contraceptive effectiveness. This systematic review aims to synthesise qualitative evidence on men’s perceptions, experiences, and attitudes towards their involvement in contraceptive decision-making in suburban settings, including the barriers and facilitators influencing their involvement. Methods This systematic review was conducted in accordance with PRISMA guidelines and registered with PROSPERO (CRD42025642026). Studies published from 2015 to 2025 were eligible. Qualitative studies and qualitative components of mixed-methods studies exploring men’s perceptions, experiences, and attitudes towards contraceptive decision-making in suburban settings were included. Five databases (SCOPUS, PubMed, Web of Science, ProQuest, and EBSCOHost) were searched. The seven included studies were appraised using the Critical Appraisal Skills Programme (CASP) qualitative research checklist. Data were analysed using thematic synthesis, with identified themes mapped onto the Social Ecological Model (SEM). Results Seven studies were included and identified multilevel barriers and facilitators to men’s involvement in contraceptive decision-making. These included individual beliefs and misconceptions, partner communication and relationship dynamics, sociocultural and gender norms, healthcare interactions, and access to family planning information. Men reported feeling excluded from family planning programmes, while education, supportive healthcare interactions, and effective communication were identified as facilitators of involvement. Preferences for discreet contraceptive methods were also reported. Conclusion This review highlights the multilevel factors influencing men's involvement in contraceptive decision-making in suburban settings. The findings suggest that context-specific, gender-inclusive strategies that promote informed decision-making, shared responsibility, male-friendly services, and women's reproductive autonomy may strengthen FP programs. Further research is needed to better understand how suburban contexts influence men's involvement relative to rural and urban settings. Trial registration PROSPERO registration: CRD42025642026.

title: Rice farming resilience to climate variability: Impacts of adaptation strategies on food security and farm income in Thailand and Myanmar
abstract: With the increasing intensity of climate-induced threats, there is an urgent need for policy-level action to implement effective and timely adaptation strategies that sustain rural livelihoods and ensure food security. This study examines the adaptation of rice farm households to climate change, its determinants and economic impacts on food security and farm income in Thailand and Myanmar. Using cross-sectional data from 365 rice-farming households, the study employs logistic regression analysis to understand the adaptation determinants and a propensity score matching (PSM) method to evaluate the welfare impacts of adaptation on food security and net farm income. The results suggest that rice farmers were aware of climate change. Major climate adaptation strategies (CASs) include crop rotation, using high-yielding varieties, adjusting cropping calendars and changes in planting methods. Key determinants jointly influencing their adaptation decisions included access to education, farming experience, climate information, credit, and investments in road infrastructure. The findings from PSM method indicates that using CASs significantly improves food security by as much as 19.9% and increases net farm income by USD $242.22 per hectare. Greater benefits were realized by farmers who adopted a combination of adaptation strategies. These results suggest that promoting context-specific adaptation strategies that integrate formal technologies with farmer-led practices while also improving farmers' education, access to climate information and credit, and rural infrastructure can simultaneously enhance local food security and agricultural income and build climate resilience in rice-based farming systems.

title: Equity in Full Immunization Coverage Among Children Aged 12-23 Months in Urban and Rural Areas of Hyderabad, India: A Community-Based Cross-Sectional Study
abstract: Background: Persistently low and inequitable childhood immunization coverage remains an important public health concern, particularly among socially and economically disadvantaged populations.Fieldpractice-level data that align with the national surveys are needed to understand local drivers of immunization inequity.Objectives: This study aimed to determine the association between selected sociodemographic factors and full immunization status, to assess the extent and pattern of socioeconomic inequality in full immunization coverage, and to describe disparities by gender, geographic location, and urban-rural residence among children aged 12-23 months.Methods: A community-based cross-sectional study was conducted from August to October 2023 among 400 children aged 12-23 months (200 urban, 200 rural), selected by multistage random sampling from the fieldpractice areas of Osmania Medical College, Hyderabad, Telangana, India.Full immunization status was verified against Mother and Child Protection Cards and Anganwadi Centre records.Associations were assessed using the chi-squared test; socioeconomic inequality was quantified using the Erreygers Concentration Index, and Fairlie decomposition was used to identify contributors to the socioeconomic gap.Results: Among 400 children, 228 (57.0%) were fully immunized and 172 (43.0%) were non-fully immunized.Full immunization was significantly associated with socioeconomic status (SES), place of residence, sex, and birth order.Coverage was higher among children from the upper socioeconomic class (152/224, 67.86%) than the lower socioeconomic class (76/176, 43.18%; p<0.001), among urban (130/200, 65.0%) than rural children (98/200, 49.0%; p=0.002), and among males (140/226, 61.95%) than females (88/174, 50.57%; p=0.030).Maternal age, maternal education, and religion were not significantly associated with immunization status.A pro-rich distribution was evident (Concentration Index +0.1067; Erreygers Index +0.2432; Wagstaff Index +0.2481), with an absolute SES gap of 24.68 percentage points.Fairlie decomposition explained 1.96 percentage points (7.9%) of the observed gap; urban residence (+136.9%)and Hindu religion (+60.1%)widened the gap, whereas first birth order (-53.1%),male sex (-25.4%), and maternal literacy (-24.8%)narrowed it.The SES equity gap was wider among females (+34.15 percentage points) than males (+18.57) and among urban (+52.74)than rural children (-5.11).Closing the SES gap could increase overall coverage by 10.86 percentage points, corresponding to a population attributable fraction of 16.0%.Conclusion: Full immunization coverage in this population remains below global targets and shows a pattern by SES, residence, and gender, with disadvantage compounding among lower-SES girls and lower-SES urban households.Because measured sociodemographic factors explained less than one-tenth of the observed inequality, closing this gap will likely require health system and supply-side interventions alongside household-targeted approaches.

title: “We don’t know schistosomiasis can affect the female reproductive system and increase the risk of HIV”: A mixed-methods analysis reveals gaps in risk factor determinants and health consequences of female genital schistosomiasis in Southern Chad
abstract: BACKGROUND: Urogenital schistosomiasis caused by Schistosoma haematobium infection is a public health problem in Chad. Despite reports of urinary S. haematobium prevalence in endemic communities, research on the genital aspect of the disease, which disproportionately affects women, remains neglected especially given the contemporary geographical overlap with HIV/AIDS. This study was undertaken to establish baseline data on the awareness and perception of female genital schistosomiasis (FGS) among community inhabitants and healthcare professionals in southern Chad to inform effective policy decision-making. METHODS: A mixed-methods cross-sectional design was employed for data collection in communities within the Guelo district from June to July 2025. Structured questionnaires were applied to capture quantitative data, while qualitative information was obtained through eleven focus group discussions (FGDs) and fifteen key informant interviews (KIIs). Quantitative and qualitative data were analyzed using statistical tools and NVIVO software, respectively, and outcomes were organized according to thematic categories. RESULTS: A marked disparity characterized by sufficient knowledge about the urinary form of schistosomiasis [93.8% (CI: 91.5 - 96.2), 514/548] and minimal knowledge of FGS [3.1% (CI: 2.3 - 4.9), 17/548] was documented among the population. Moderate [63.2% (CI: 59.4 - 71.7), 325/514] and low [17.7% (CI: 11.3 - 21.8), 3/17] levels of awareness were respectively identified as predictors of urinary schistosomiasis and FGS, consistent with the perception that FGS is neither a risk factor for HIV nor cervical cancer. Additionally, verbal reports among informed community members and healthcare professionals revealed a shared belief that FGS is sexually transmitted and typically treated with antibiotics/antifungal medications. This belief was associated [χ2 = 13.7 (CI: 10.1 - 15. 6), p = 0.002] with negative consequences on hospital-treatment-seeking habits that arise from fear of identity-related stigma, particularly in cases involving recurrent genital symptoms. CONCLUSION: This study highlights the need for integrating FGS education and awareness initiatives within praziquantel delivery campaigns and sexual/reproductive preventive services at primary health care facilities in rural Chad. Furthermore, it underscores the urgency of providing comprehensive training for local healthcare professionals on the diagnosis and clinical management of FGS and the improvement of water, sanitation and hygiene (WaSH) services to minimize contact with freshwater bodies.

title: Urbanisation and the rural urban dietary diversity divide across districts in India
abstract: Food security depends on sustained access to nutritious and diverse diets during rapid structural transformation. Dietary diversity is widely used as an indicator of the utilization and quality dimensions of food security. This study examines how urbanisation shapes household food security through its effects on dietary diversity across rural and urban areas in India. Using district-level panel data from 2014 to 2020, we analyse rural–urban differences in dietary diversity and assess how economic, physical, and demographic dimensions of urbanisation influence dietary diversity over time. Urbanisation is measured using night-time lights, physical built-up area, and the share of urban population, while household dietary diversity is constructed from consumption expenditure data using Simpson’s Diversity Index. The results reveal significant and persistent rural–urban disparities in dietary diversity, indicating unequal access to diverse and nutritious diets. In the short run, urbanisation is associated with improvements in dietary diversity in both rural and urban households. However, in the long run, higher levels of urbanisation are linked to declining dietary diversity among urban households, pointing to emerging risks to diet quality and nutritional stability. Urbanisation initially widens rural–urban gaps in dietary diversity, but these gaps narrow over time. These findings highlight the non-linear and dynamic relationship between urbanisation and the nutritional dimension of food security in India. They underscore the need to view urbanisation not only as a driver of economic growth but also as a process that reshapes food environments and the stability of access to nutritious diets.

title: Who are you calling Mother Nature? Exploring metaphor resonance among young women farmers: A comparative study in the US and France
abstract: Background This study places the argumentative function of the Mother Nature metaphor at the heart of its analysis, aiming to map the understanding of the human–nature relationship by a group overlooked in environmental dialogues: farmers who work with “nature.” Among them, young women are increasingly entering agriculture by choice, moving beyond the traditional role of farmer’s wife to become farmers, and are recognized for their strong commitment to environmentally sustainable practices. This research examines how these young women define the Mother Nature metaphor, viewed as both empowering and ambivalent, and how these definitions reflect the values that guide their farming practices. Methods Data were gathered from 54 young women farmers in the USA and France through in-depth interviews. Participants shared their definitions and created imaginative illustrations of Mother Nature. Using qualitative thematic coding informed by argumentation theory, the study analyzed how the metaphor resonates with participants across three dimensions: verbal expression, meaning-making in farming careers, and visual representation, within a comparative cross-country framework. Results Findings indicate that resistance to the Mother Nature metaphor was primarily driven by its hierarchical framing and the medium through which it was presented, rather than its gendered aspects. French farmers more often rejected the metaphor’s sacred value, while American farmers focused on nature’s unpredictability instead of its divinity. Despite verbal resistance to hierarchical and personified views, visual and emotional responses revealed persistent, sometimes unconscious, associations with personification and interconnectedness. French farmers typically illustrated Mother Nature at the landscape or ecosystem scale, whereas Americans favored planetary or global scales. Conclusion Young women farmers’ narratives demonstrate a nuanced engagement with the Mother Nature metaphor, shaped by their environmental values, cultural backgrounds, and professional experiences. The study shows that the metaphor’s meaning depends on the interplay of cultural imagery, cross-cultural exposure, and the individual’s inner world.

title: A Study on Sources of Information Used by Kisan Credit Card Holders in Selected Cooperative-Bank Areas of Southern Rajasthan
journal: Journal of Scientific Research and Reports
abstract: The Kisan Credit Card (KCC) Scheme is an important institutional mechanism for providing agricultural credit in India, but the practical use of the scheme also depends on farmers’ access to clear and credible information. This descriptive survey examined the information sources used by KCC holders in selected cooperative-bank areas of Chittorgarh and Pratapgarh districts in Southern Rajasthan. Three District Central Cooperative Bank branches were purposively selected on the basis of KCC beneficiary concentration; two Primary Agricultural Credit Societies (PACS) were then selected from each branch, and 20 KCC holders were randomly selected from each PACS, giving a total sample of 120 respondents. Mean percent scores (MPS) and ranks were used for descriptive analysis. Overall, 66.67% of respondents had a medium level of information-source use, while 16.67% each were in the low and high categories. Individual contact was the most used broad method (MPS 65.63), followed by institutional contact (64.51), group contact (54.27), and mass contact (52.27). Local leaders (95.00), neighbours (94.58), and friends (93.75) were the leading individual sources; meetings (92.08) led group sources; television (94.17) led mass-media sources; and cooperative societies (98.33) led institutional sources. The findings indicate that trusted interpersonal networks and cooperative-credit institutions remain central to KCC information delivery, while television and social media provide complementary reach. Because the sites were purposively selected, the results should be interpreted as descriptive evidence from the sampled cooperative-bank areas rather than as population estimates for all of Southern Rajasthan.

title: Genetic-environment decomposition reveals geographical disparities in sunflower yield improvement across the Great Plains
abstract: Context While past decades have seen substantial gains in crop productivity, how much of this is due to genetic improvement versus changes in growing environment, including climate and management practices, remains unclear. Separating the roles of breeding improvements and environmental changes in crop improvement requires comprehensive data, including phenotypic data on plant varieties released over multiple years and environmental data that characterizes the variable growing conditions. Leveraging long-term variety field trial data is one way to evaluate the relative effects of crop genetic improvement and changes in environment to overall crop improvement over time. Methods Using a dataset of 46 years of commercial sunflower variety trial data from across the Great Plains of the US, we quantified the contributions of plant genotype (hybrid variety) and environment (including agronomy and climate) to overall productivity in these trials and compared them to long-term public farm-gate data. We determined the major meteorological drivers of sunflower yield improvements and projected how environmental quality for sunflower production in the Great Plains will change in the future. Results The rate of genetic improvement varied across the region, and environmental change was sometimes antagonistic to the goal of yield and quality improvements. The northern Great Plains experienced substantial increases in sunflower yield since the 1970s due to gains in both breeding and environmental quality, whereas the southern Great Plains had smaller genetic gains which were largely offset by a decrease in environmental quality. High yielding environments were associated with an optimal daily maximum temperature near 28°C at flowering time, low vapor pressure deficit, and high growing degree days. Under projected future climate scenarios, environmental quality for sunflower production, as defined by these parameters, will decrease across much of the growing region. As a result, sunflower production would be reduced in much of the Great Plains by mid-century, unless breeding and agronomy change to broaden environmental tolerances. Implications These insights inform strategies for breeders, agronomists, and farmers to optimize crop performance to local and regional climates, improve climate resilience, and maximize food security.

title: Cluster investigation report: a probable urine-associated transmission event of severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome—a case report
abstract: Introduction Severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome (SFTS) is an emerging tick-borne viral disease with a high case fatality rate. Human-to-human transmission has been increasingly documented, primarily through direct contact with blood or bloody secretions. On June 21, 2025, a case of SFTS was reported in Zhumadian City, Henan Province. On July 3, a second case—epidemiologically linked to the first—was reported to the local Centers for Disease Control (CDC) through the notifiable disease reporting system, following laboratory confirmation on July 1. Case presentation A 77-year-old female farmer with underlying comorbidities was hospitalized with fever, leukopenia, and thrombocytopenia, and subsequently died of SFTS. Her 31-year-old granddaughter, who had an open wound on her hand, cared for the patient and cleaned her urine. Eleven days later, she developed fever, nausea, vomiting, headache, fatigue, and myalgia. Laboratory tests confirmed SFTS virus infection by RT-PCR, with an initial cycle threshold (Ct) value of 38.85, which subsequently decreased to 31.48 over the following 2 days, indicating active viral replication. She recovered after antiviral therapy and was discharged on July 7. Comprehensive epidemiological investigation ruled out other potential transmission routes, including blood contact, tick bites, and environmental exposure. However, direct virological evidence from the index patient’s urine and genomic sequencing to confirm viral homology between the two cases were not available. Conclusion This report describes a probable human-to-human SFTS transmission event associated with urine exposure through an open wound. While the absence of direct virological and genomic evidence precludes definitive confirmation, the convergence of epidemiological, clinical, and temporal evidence strongly supports this transmission route. This case highlights the need for enhanced protective measures—particularly the use of gloves when handling any body fluids, including urine—during care of SFTS patients.

title: Food insecurity during a cost‑of‑living crisis: trends and housing‑related vulnerability in Portugal (2019–2023)
abstract: Background In high-income countries, food insecurity (FI) increasingly reflects economic pressures rather than food availability. Rising housing and food costs have intensified household budget constraints across Europe, especially among low-income families. Portugal is a notable example, having faced sharp post-pandemic food inflation and currently experiencing a severe housing affordability crisis. Using nationally representative EU‑SILC microdata, this study examines FI trends in Portugal (2019–2023) and assesses their relationship with socio-demographic factors, financial strain, and housing conditions, including housing tenure, a rarely analysed factor in high-income countries. Results FI increased from 13.8% in 2019 to 16.3% in 2023, with moderate or severe FI (MSFI) reaching 4.8% (using FIES probabilistic assignment). Item‑level responses suggest that households often reduce dietary diversity before reporting anxiety or shortages, indicating anticipatory coping and early nutritional compromise. Logistic regression analysis (based on FIES discrete assignment) shows higher odds of MSFI among young adults, lone‑parent households, individuals living alone, and non‑EU migrants, independent of income and other household characteristics. Indicators of financial strain (including difficulty making ends meet and inability to cover unexpected expenses) are strongly associated with MSFI. Housing emerges as a key vulnerability: tenants paying market rent have significantly higher odds of MSFI than homeowners, while tenants paying reduced rent face nearly three times the risk. Housing cost burden is strongly associated with MSFI, underscoring the close link between housing affordability and food access. Conclusions Rising living costs and housing pressures are linked to the prevalence and severity of FI in Portugal. Policy responses should therefore incorporate food, housing, and social protection measures, with targeted support for groups most at risk. These insights are broadly relevant to other high‑income countries experiencing similar cost‑of‑living and housing affordability crises.

title: Bridging the know-do gap in diabetes care: multi-level barriers to dietary adherence among adults with type 2 diabetes in Accra, Ghana—a cross-sectional study
abstract: In type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) management, high nutritional knowledge often fails to translate into appropriate dietary practices due to complex barriers. This study quantified the knowledge-practice gap and identified multi-level barriers influencing dietary non-adherence among adults with diabetes in Accra, Ghana, using a Socio-Ecological Model (SEM) framework. A hospital-based cross-sectional study was conducted among 392 patients with T2DM at the 37 Military Hospital in Accra between May and October 2024. Methodological reporting was aligned with STROBE guidelines. Participants were recruited via systematic random sampling (k = 5). Nutritional knowledge was assessed using the 24-item Diabetes Knowledge Questionnaire (DKQ-24), and dietary practice was measured using the Summary of Diabetes Self-Care Activities (SDSCA) scale. The knowledge-practice gap was defined as the percentage difference between patients achieving "Good Knowledge" (≥ 70%) and those achieving "Good Practice" (≥ 4 days/week, a pragmatically calibrated threshold for resource-constrained food environments). Multi-level perceived barriers were grouped using the SEM. Multivariable logistic regression was used to identify independent predictors of dietary practice, reporting both crude and adjusted odds ratios alongside model diagnostics. Of the 392 participants (mean age 55.4 years, SD = 10.9; 72.4% female), 74.4% exhibited "Good Knowledge" of diabetes nutrition, whereas 68.4% achieved "Good Practice", resulting in a population-level knowledge-practice gap of 6.0 percentage points. The individual-level "Failure to Translate" (FTT) rate was 21.9%, calculated as the proportion of knowledgeable patients who nonetheless exhibited poor practice (64/292). Main barriers spanned the SEM: structural food unavailability in local markets (84.6%), clinical diet unpalatability (65.9%), financial constraints (60.1%), long outpatient waiting times (54.8%), and inconsistent dietitian access (50.5%). Good nutritional knowledge was associated with a higher odds of dietary adherence (Adjusted Odds Ratio = 2.80, 95% Confidence Interval [CI]: 1.61–4.16), but this association was significantly attenuated by low daily household income (< 100 GHS/day; approximately US$6.70 at the time of the study; AOR = 0.54, 95% CI: 0.31–0.94) and the absence of family support (AOR = 0.48, 95% CI: 0.26–0.89, p = 0.019) was associated with approximately half the odds of dietary adherence compared to those with family support. Multivariable model diagnostics confirmed excellent fit (Hosmer–Lemeshow p = 0.554), minimal multicollinearity (mean VIF = 1.24), and strong discriminative capacity (Area Under the ROC Curve = 0.76). Theoretical knowledge is necessary but insufficient for dietary change when structural and socioeconomic barriers remain unaddressed. Structural food insecurity, low household purchasing power, and culinary mismatches with traditional Ghanaian cuisine prevent patients from translating knowledge into action. Public health policies must shift from generic patient education toward targeted nutritional safety nets and culinarily competent, culturally tailored dietary counselling.

title: Youth and the future of labor- and knowledge-intensive small-scale farming in West Africa under climate change and political instability
abstract: Debates on the future of smallholder farming in sub-Saharan Africa often interpret rural youth mobility and non-farm work as withdrawal from agriculture. This article examines how rural youth in coastal Guinea-Bissau engage with labour- and knowledge-intensive, climate-vulnerable mangrove swamp rice farming, and the conditions under which agriculture remains part of their imagined futures. We combine long-term ethnographic research, updated between 2020 and 2024, with a survey of 770 household heads in 13 villages, 98 biographical interviews, and conversations and group discussions involving 90 participants across 17 villages. Quantitative indicators were compared across household-head age groups, while qualitative material was analysed thematically and narratively. Results show that many young household heads remain engaged in agriculture while combining it with education, mobility and non-farm activities. Age differences in access to mangrove rice land are limited, although young household heads face higher dependency ratios and substantial rice deficits. Biographical evidence indicates that mobility and non-farm earnings often complement rather than replace agriculture. Nevertheless, climate-related risks, high labour costs, weak markets, political instability and inadequate rural services undermine its attractiveness. The study challenges binary portrayals of youth as either farmers or agricultural ‘exiters’ and shows that the future of mangrove rice farming depends on enabling diversified and mobile rural livelihoods.

title: Scaling paludiculture: stakeholder perspectives on adoption and enabling conditions in England
abstract: Paludiculture, the cultivation of wetland species on rewetted peatlands, is increasingly promoted as a nature-based solution for climate mitigation, biodiversity restoration and peat conservation; however, its adoption remains limited in the United Kingdom. This study examines stakeholder perspectives on the adoption of paludiculture and the enabling conditions required to support its scale-up. Drawing on 36 photo-elicitation interviews with farmers, land managers, conservation organisations, researchers, and policymakers, the study explores how stakeholders interpret the ecological, economic, and socio-cultural implications of transitioning from drained peatland agriculture to wetland-based systems. Results indicate widespread recognition of environmental benefits, including greenhouse gas mitigation, flood regulation, and habitat restoration. However, adoption is constrained by concerns related to food security, land valuation, regulatory complexity, and underdeveloped markets. Stakeholders also highlight gaps in policy frameworks, with existing financial mechanisms perceived as short-term and poorly adapted to peatland systems. Market development, long-term policy support, and a strengthened evidence base emerge as critical enabling conditions, requiring coordinated policy, sustained investment, and cross-sector collaboration to support viable supply chains and demand. Aligning policy design with locally grounded knowledge and stakeholder needs is essential to enable effective environmental management.

title: Sustainable ethyl levulinate production from oil palm empty fruit bunch: Integrated techno-economic analysis and life cycle assessment
abstract: Environmental concerns regarding non-renewable energy sources have driven a critical shift towards sustainable bio-based chemical production methods. Among these, the conversion of oil palm empty fruit bunch (EFB) to ethyl levulinate (EL) offers a low-toxic, biodegradable, high-performance fuel additive. This study established a multi-dimensional feasibility framework to evaluate the three conversion pathways using Aspen Plus simulation: a three-step conversion of cellulose-derived glucose via 5-hydroxymethylfurfural (5-HMF) and levulinic acid (LA) to EL (Route 1), and two furfural-based configurations valorising the hemicellulose fraction via furfuryl alcohol (Route 2) or intermediate LA production (Route 3). To determine the optimal design, a multi-criteria sustainability index (SI) was developed by integrating technical yield with economic profitability from techno-economic analysis (TEA) and environmental impact from life cycle assessment (LCA). Route 2 achieved an SI of 1 across the entire weighting space. This streamlined two-step furfural pathway achieved a technical yield of 23.5 wt% EL, an annual profit of RM 100.37 million, and a global warming potential (GWP) impact score of 4.98 tonnes of CO 2 -eq/tonne EL. Its dominance is driven by reduced complexity, lower capital investment, and decreased utility-related emissions. Although Route 3 yielded 23.0 wt% EL, its intensive energy requirements resulted in a higher GWP of 17.93 tonnes CO 2 -eq/tonne EL. Route 1 remained the least competitive overall, though it became more competitive than Route 3 only when environmental weighting exceeds approximately 32–88%. Process simplification effectively aligns technical, economic, and environmental objectives, thereby providing a robust model for the Malaysian circular bioeconomy.

title: Development of a farmer-centric UTAUT scale for measuring farmers’ behavioural intention towards the adoption of fluoride-safe practices
abstract: Background Fluoride contamination in groundwater is a serious problem in many parts of India and affects agriculture, livestock, and human health. Although the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT) has been widely used to explain technology adoption, no farmer-centric scale is available to measure farmers’ behavioural intention towards the adoption of fluoride-safe practices. Therefore, the present study was carried out to develop a farmer-centric UTAUT scale for this purpose. Methodology The initial statements were generated by reviewing UTAUT, UTAUT2, and other related technology adoption studies and were modified according to the agricultural context. Eighty-five statements were developed under seven constructs. After face validity, 66 statements were evaluated for content validity by a panel of 25 experts using Relevancy Weightage (RW), Mean Relevancy Score (MRS), and Overall Mean Relevancy Score (OMRS). Based on the predefined criteria, 49 statements were retained. A pilot survey was then conducted with 250 farmers from fluoride-affected areas using a five-point Likert scale. Exploratory Factor Analysis was performed using Principal Axis Factoring with Direct Oblimin rotation, followed by reliability analysis using Cronbach’s alpha. Results The KMO value (0.935) and Bartlett’s Test of Sphericity ( p < 0.001) confirmed the suitability of the data for factor analysis. Exploratory Factor Analysis supported a seven-factor structure consistent with the adapted UTAUT framework, explaining 77.23% of the total variance. Based on the factor loading criterion, seven statements were removed, resulting in a final scale consisting of 42 statements. Cronbach’s alpha values ranged from 0.882 to 0.979, indicating satisfactory internal consistency across all constructs. Discussion The developed scale can be used to measure farmers’ behavioural intention towards the adoption of fluoride-safe practices in fluoride-affected areas. It can also help researchers, extension professionals, and policymakers to understand the factors influencing farmers’ adoption decisions and to plan suitable extension programmes. Further validation of the developed scale through Confirmatory Factor Analysis using an independent sample is recommended.
keywords: Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology

title: Hybrid Artificial Neural Network-Genetic Algorithm modelling and optimization of multistage palm oil fractional crystallization
abstract: Abstract Fractional crystallization of refined, bleached, and deodorized palm oil (RBDPO) is highly sensitive to feedstock variability, particularly fluctuations in iodine value (IV), which influences nucleation, crystal growth, separation efficiency, and olein yield. This study developed and validated response surface methodology (RSM) and hybrid Artificial Neural Network-Genetic Algorithm (ANN-GA) framework for modeling and optimizing multistage palm oil fractional crystallization across RBDPO IV51–IV53. A structured three-stage experimental design encompassing supercooling, nucleation, and crystal growth generated 145 datasets. Stage-specific RSM models quantified process-variable effects and provided an interpretable benchmark, while a multilayer feedforward ANN (7-13-5 architecture) predicted olein yield, olein IV, cloud point (CP), slip melting point (SMP), and stearin IV, achieving R 2 values of 0.79–0.96. GA integration identified feed-specific optimum cooling conditions, predicting olein yields of 83.80%, 83.10%, and 87.98% for RBDPO IV51, IV52, and IV53, respectively. Experimental validation yielded overall prediction accuracies of 91.94%, 96.97%, and 97.75%, with corresponding mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) values of 8.06%, 3.03%, and 2.25%. RSM provided robust interpretability, whereas ANN–GA offered greater flexibility for nonlinear multistage interactions. Collectively, the framework supports feed-responsive optimization of yield and product quality and establishes a basis for adaptive crystallization control and future digitalized palm oil fractionation.

title: Options to reduce street market food waste in low-income urban communities: Perspectives from Zimbabwe
abstract: Street markets in developing countries provide low-income urban households access to affordable food, especially fresh fruits and vegetables; however, the food waste generated at these markets is a sustainability concern. This study examines the characteristics and quantities of food waste and explores the reasons behind it at a street market in Hatcliffe, Zimbabwe. A mixed-method approach combining Waste Composition Analysis, field observations, and face-to-face questionnaire surveys was used to collect data during the harvest and seasons. The results show that, on average, each stall generates an estimated 690 kg of food waste per year, of which 83% is avoidable food waste. Fresh vegetables, including tomatoes, cucumbers, bell peppers, and leafy greens, constituted 71% of the total food waste mass, and fresh fruits, such as bananas, lemons, and oranges, contributed 21%. Using the Social Practice Theory, the study identifies material -related factors such as poor stall infrastructure, limited storage space, and lack of refrigeration as the main reasons for food disposal. Vendor competences also influenced waste levels, with vendors who used purchasing and sales records generating a 60.6% decrease in food waste and those who repurposed “imperfect” products generating 45.9% less food waste than those who did not. Socio-cultural meanings shaping demand, consumer preferences for aesthetically perfect produce, and prioritising certain products contribute to food waste. To promote sustainable consumption, our recommendations include improving market infrastructure, such as wide-shaded stalls and low-cost cooling systems, raising consumer awareness about embracing “imperfect” produce and educating vendors to promote best food handling and preservation practices.

title: Articulations of poisoning: historicity, relationality, and contextuality of Chlordecone pollution in the French Antilles
abstract: Chlordecone, a highly persistent organochlorine insecticide, was widely applied to banana plantations in Martinique and Guadeloupe from 1972 until being banned in 1993. Decades later, its residues still permeate soil, waterways, food systems, and human bodies in the two islands. Classified as both a carcinogenic and an endocrine disruptor, the chemical compound has generated widespread protests, epidemiological debates, and political critique. Drawing on six months of non-consecutive ethnographic fieldwork conducted in Martinique between 2017 and 2022, this article examines how people interpret and navigate the chemical's enduring effects. We develop the concept of 'articulations of poisoning' to describe the ways in which Chlordecone is rendered meaningful, not simply as a biomedical or ecological risk, but as a lived, historically sedimented, and politically contested experience. These articulations unfold along three interconnected dimensions (i.e. historicity, relationality, and contextuality) that shape how poisoning is perceived, embodied, and contested in everyday life. Through the voices of activists, farmers, medical professionals, institutional actors, and community members, we explore how poisoning becomes entangled with colonial legacies, political debates, and the everyday struggle for environmental justice in the French Antilles.

title: Animal welfare in the world of digitalization: Computer Vision in the context of foundational structures
abstract: Abstract Computer Vision is an emerging technology within Precision Livestock Farming (PLF), combining camera systems with artificial intelligence to monitor animal welfare. While animal ethicists recognize its potential benefits, they also raise concerns about possible negative implications for animal welfare. This paper argues that addressing ethical concerns cannot rely on solutions targeting isolated ethical risks; rather, potential solutions must account for the technology’s embeddedness within society-wide structures. The focus in this paper will be on foundational structures, these structures concern how the world is experienced and understood, what is taken as self-evident. Over centuries, humans have increasingly delegated tasks to machines and standardized the world in doing so. This process has fostered growing trust in the outcomes of (digital) technologies. These developments have changed human experience and understanding of the world in various ways. Farmers, as members of society, are unlikely to be exempt from this trend. Therefore, reflection on Computer Vision must go beyond the farming practice and take into account these foundational structures that are currently reshaping society at large. Computer Vision examined as embedded within foundational structures demonstrates that ethical issues are also embedded within these structures, consequently, potential solutions must take account of them to increase their effectiveness.

title: Farm‐Level Greenhouse Gas Balance of Commercial Coffee Production in Minas Gerais, Brazil
abstract: ABSTRACT Coffee production is considered a potential contributor to climate change mitigation due to its perennial biomass and carbon storage capacity. However, empirical assessments of greenhouse gas (GHG) balances at the farm level remain limited for commercial coffee systems. This study quantified the carbon balance of 24 commercial coffee farms in Minas Gerais, Brazil, across two consecutive harvests (2020/21 and 2021/22). Farm‐level emissions of CO 2 , CH 4 , and N 2 O were estimated following IPCC guidelines (Scopes 1 and 2) using farm inventory data. Carbon removals were estimated using biomass increment coefficients for coffee plantations, Permanent Preservation Areas, and Legal Reserves. Estimated carbon removals exceeded on‐farm emissions in 16 (66.7%) and 19 (79.2%) of the evaluated farms in 2020/21 and 2021/22, respectively. Average carbon balances across farms were 104.5 Mg CO 2 e (0.59 Mg CO 2 e ha −1 ) in 2020/21 and 263.1 Mg CO 2 e (1.35 Mg CO 2 e ha −1 ) in 2021/22. Nitrogen fertilization represented the largest emission source, accounting for 66.7% and 54.2% of total emissions in each harvest. Higher productivity reduced emissions per unit of product but increased emissions per hectare due to greater input intensity. Coffee plantations accounted for 414.3 and 448.3 Mg CO 2 e of total removals in 2020/21 and 2021/22, respectively, corresponding to 70.9% of total removals across farms. These findings highlight the importance of considering both emissions and removals when evaluating the carbon balance of commercial coffee systems. Farm‐level carbon accounting provides useful information for understanding carbon dynamics in perennial cropping systems and supporting greenhouse gas assessments in coffee production. 2026 Society of Chemical Industry and John Wiley & Sons, Ltd.

title: Closing the opportunity gap: Exploring micro-enterprises' behavioral intention to integrate with digital platforms for a broader agri-food system
abstract: Digital agriculture platforms offer marginalized micro-enterprises a vital pathway to bridge the opportunity gap and overcome structural dependencies on focal companies. However, mainstream literature's focal-firm bias leaves the adoption logic of these grassroots operators underexplored. Addressing this gap, we operationalize an integrated Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and Theory of Planned Behavior (TPB) framework. Using PLS-SEM on data from 167 micro-enterprises, this study investigates their platform integration behaviors. Results reveal distinct adoption pathways: a platform's operational simplicity cannot trigger adoption without first cultivating a favorable organizational mindset (full mediation). Conversely, its tangible strategic benefits—unexpectedly anchored in macro-systemic food safety guarantees and ecological conservation rather than mere short-term profits—motivate integration both directly and indirectly (partial mediation). Socio-psychologically, although micro-enterprises clearly perceive external pressures like government mandates and peer emulation, these fail to translate into adoption intent—a recognition-action gap that leaves adoption strongly conditioned by financial affordability and technical readiness instead. Ultimately, these dynamics reframe the presumed myopic rationality of micro-enterprises: viewed through the lens of push-pull theory, the strategic draw of sustainable platform value is offset by baseline capability constraints, such that this value becomes actionable only when matched by sufficient capability. Theoretically, this demonstrates that cultivating truly inclusive digital ecosystems necessitates shifting the analytical focus from top-down focal designs to bottom-up grassroots decision-making. Practically, it advises policymakers and platform sponsors to move beyond normative persuasion toward tangible capability empowerment and value-driven platform architectures.

title: A socio-technical mechanism of the agricultural digital divide: Ecuador within a heterogeneous Latin American context
abstract: Digital agriculture can improve farm management, resource-use efficiency, and decision-making; however, access to technology alone does not guarantee equivalent economic benefits. This perspective article conceptualizes the agricultural digital divide as a socio-technical and economic inequality that can arise along a sequence linking structural conditions, resource accessibility, capability formation, technological appropriation, productive integration, economic value realization, and value capture and benefit distribution. This definition extends the analysis beyond connectivity and adoption by considering whether agricultural actors can integrate technologies into viable productive activities and retain a significant share of the value generated. Institutions, extension services, cooperatives, financing mechanisms, technology providers, business models, and data governance can shape the transitions between these stages. Ecuador is examined as a focal analytical case within a heterogeneous Latin America, without assuming regional representativeness. The framework redirects the evaluation of digitalization away from the number of technologies deployed and toward their productive appropriation, economic viability, and the distribution of their benefits, thereby reinforcing the relationship between digital transformation and agricultural economics.

title: Drivers of voluntary food safety standard adoption in developing value chains: Evidence from Cambodian fish processors
abstract: The traditional fish processing sector in Cambodia is vital for rural livelihoods but faces persistent food safety challenges. This study evaluates the socio-economic and institutional drivers of adopting the Cambodia Quality Seal (CQS), a voluntary national safety standard. Utilizing a survey of 165 processors across Phnom Penh, Siem Reap, and Battambang, we employ descriptive statistics and a binary probit regression model to isolate the key factors influencing compliance decisions. The descriptive profile reveals a heavily female-led industry (73.3%) dominated by middle-aged operators with primary education and low baseline CQS awareness (32.1%). Crucially, the probit model uncovers major structural paradoxes: while descriptive averages associate higher income with adoption, the regression reveals that wealthier firms exhibit a lower statistical propensity to adopt public food safety standards when holding other variables constant. Furthermore, registration with the Ministry of Commerce significantly deters adoption (β = -1.778, p < 0.01), whereas sector-specific registration with the Fisheries Administration strongly catalyzes compliance (β = 1.239, p < 0.05). Additionally, selling to supermarkets acts as a deterrent, indicating a substitution effect driven by private procurement standards. Conversely, firms processing high-risk, shelf-stable items like dried fish and fish sauce show a significantly higher likelihood of adoption. To enhance national food safety, policy interventions must prioritize reducing cross-agency bureaucratic friction, deploying gender-inclusive technical training, and aligning public certifications with commercial private standards.

title: The changing returns to physical exercise in China (2010–2023): a nine-wave repeated cross-sectional study
abstract: Background Since 2008, when China began to implement its strategy of building a sports power, the institutional context of physical exercise has changed substantially. Yet the temporal dynamics of the socioeconomic correlates of exercise remain underexplored. Objectives To examine whether and how physical exercise participation and its associations with income, self-rated health, and social trust changed over the 2010–2023 study period. Methods Using nine waves of the Chinese General Social Survey (CGSS 2010–2023, N = 78,467), we estimate annual marginal effects of exercise through ordinary least squares regression with exercise-by-year interactions. Three policy periods corresponding to phases of the Sports Power strategy are compared. Results Exercise participation rose from 31.68% in 2010 to 51.26% in 2023. The exercise–income association increased from 0.301 (Period 1, 2010–2012) to 0.367 (Period 3, 2018–2023, +21.9%), although formal cross-period tests did not reach statistical significance; the upward trend is therefore only weakly consistent with Hypothesis 1. The exercise–health association was negative and appeared to deepen across periods, but the cross-period differences lost statistical significance once the non-comparable 2011 wave was excluded, so this apparent change is interpreted cautiously. The exercise–trust association moved from a non-significant −0.013 to −0.101 (SE = 0.014). Subgroup analyses showed larger income associations for men than women (0.420 versus 0.279) and for rural than urban residents (0.449 versus 0.180). Conclusion Exercise participation rose markedly over the study period, and the exercise–trust association turned increasingly negative, but the exercise–income association did not strengthen to a statistically significant degree, and the health-selection pattern was sensitive to the exclusion of the 2011 wave. The observed changes are read as population-level associations rather than causal effects of the Sports Power strategy.

title: Home from school: University graduates become technology leaders in their smallholder communities
abstract: Every year, thousands of young Latin Americans leave their smallholder households to attend university, yet some aspire to return as technology leaders. To understand this overlooked segment of youth, we analyzed data from 3670 applicants to Ayllu AgTech, an FAO training program, including 67 autobiographical videos and 15 in-depth interviews. Our findings reveal that these youth remain rooted in their places of origin. Their farming experience and technical training equip them to combine scientific and local knowledge to address rural challenges like food insecurity and climate change. While some graduates do return to their home villages, others act as change agents from a nearby provincial city. Each young professional devises their own way to balance social service with professional growth. However, this group faces systemic barriers—a lack of capital, weak institutional support, and scarce job opportunities. We call for a rethinking of rural youth policy: just as governments support the return of internationally trained talent, they should invest in the development of educated youths as technology leaders for smallholder communities. This is an overlooked development strategy hiding in plain sight.

title: Overseas farmland investment for sustainable food systems: a systems analysis of long-term sustainability mechanisms of Chinese cross-border agribusiness
abstract: Introduction Overseas farmland investment has become an increasingly important but contested component of global food systems. Such investment can diversify food supplies, improve agricultural infrastructure, and support cross-border value-chain integration, but it also faces challenges concerning land governance, local livelihoods, ecological responsibility, and institutional legitimacy. This study examines, at the enterprise level, how institutional governance and supply-chain coordination support sustainable operations in overseas farmland investment. Methods Drawing on a systems perspective, it examines the investment of Xi’an Aiju Grain and Oil Industry Group in Kazakhstan using corporate reports, written interview records, and public sources. It develops an analytical framework comprising four interconnected subsystems: institutions and the external environment, organizational governance and capabilities, sustainable production, and supply chains and markets. Results The case analysis indicates that host-country institutions and local producer participation jointly shape investment and operating arrangements. Contract farming, technical cooperation, storage and logistics integration, and quality management further connect local agricultural production with enterprise processing and downstream markets. Actual processing and shipment volumes, changes in customs clearance costs for a specific shipment, and subsequent operating records provide evidence for examining the operating outcomes of these arrangements. Three complementary pathways, risk absorption, capability reconfiguration, and value creation, explain interdependencies across operating activities and responses to operating obstacles. Continued operations require both alignment between resources and markets and coordination of rights and responsibilities among participating actors. Discussion The study connects agricultural resource access with governance, production, and supply-chain organization, showing how cross-border coordination translates agricultural resources into operating capabilities. It provides an enterprise-level case explanation for research on overseas farmland investment and sustainable food systems, together with practical implications for agribusiness enterprises, policymakers, and financial institutions seeking to promote responsible agricultural investment.

title: Occurrence, load and transport-associated risk factors of Salmonella spp. in chickens sold in informal live bird markets in Centre-Nord Region, Burkina Faso
abstract: Informal poultry trade is central to live-bird value chains in sub-Saharan Africa, but transport and handling practices may facilitate the spread of zoonotic pathogens such as Salmonella spp. This regional study assessed the occurrence, bacterial load, and transport-related risk factors of Salmonella spp. in indigenous village chickens (Gallus gallus domesticus) marketed through the Kaya live-bird market in the Centre-Nord Region of Burkina Faso. A cross-sectional survey was conducted among 49 poultry collectors. Four clinically healthy indigenous chickens (Gallus gallus domesticus) were selected from each collector's transported batch using a stratified random sampling procedure based on spatial position (front, middle, rear) yielding a total of 196 birds. Birds originated from smallholder households in surrounding villages and were selected for live sale. Cecal contents were analyzed for Salmonella spp. using ISO 6579:2012 protocols, bacterial loads were quantified by the Most Probable Number method, and isolates were confirmed by MALDI-TOF MS. Structured interviews documented collector characteristics, sourcing, transport, hygiene, and biosecurity. Logistic regression identified factors associated with Salmonella occurrence, while linear regression assessed predictors of bacterial load. Salmonella spp. was detected in 41.3% of chickens, with 59.2% of collectors having at least one positive bird. Transporting 21-50 birds and collectors having verified the vaccination status of birds when collecting chickens were associated with higher odds of detection. Higher bacterial loads were linked to temporary stops during collection or transport and reuse of dedicated work clothing without proper cleaning. This regional survey highlights the collector and live-bird market stage as a critical interface for Salmonella circulation in village poultry systems. Practical recommendation include reducing overcrowding during transport, improving confinement and hygiene practices, and strengthening biosecurity measures among poultry collectors.

title: Conservation concessions or green grabbing? A critical perspective on mega conservation investments
abstract: Market-based mechanisms have gained traction in environmental governance during the Anthropocene. One such mechanism is conservation concessions, which are promoted in the Global South as a neoliberal strategy that aligns ecological protection with economic rationality. Yet empirical evidence on their actual conservation outcomes and community benefits remains scanty. In this perspective, we argue that within prevailing capitalist frameworks, conservation concessions risk functioning as a form of green grabbing. Anchored in a political economy approach and critical agrarian studies, we synthesize evidence from multi-country case studies, with particular attention to Sub-Saharan Africa, particularly in Malawi, to examine the interplay between state power, transnational capital, and local agrarian structures. Our analysis reveals that despite being discursively framed as apolitical and win-win, conservation concessions can lead to: (i) restructuring of property and access rights, alienating customary users from their subsistence means; (ii) creation of precarious labor relations that often fail to offer viable alternatives for displaced smallholders; and (iii) reconfiguration of rural class dynamics, empowering conservation-oriented elites while marginalizing the agrarian poor. We conclude that conservation concessions represent a symptomatic response by capitalism to its own ecological contradictions, commodifying and financializing nature as a new frontier of accumulation. The study advocates for a foundational shift toward radical land tenure security, community-led forest governance, and agroecological perspectives. We offer a critical framework for evaluating the socio-ecological viability of conservation investments and call for renewed debate on agrarian futures in the Anthropocene.

title: Encountering a conundrum: Agriculture and food system change and rural transformation in the Global South
abstract: Agriculture and food systems in the Global South are undergoing significant social and technological changes, forming a complex ecosystem of actors, commodities, practices, technologies, and institutions. These changes, primarily aimed at increasing agricultural production and modernizing food chains, are often deemed essential for food-system sustainability and urban food security. However, the ways in which these changes affect the economies and ecologies of rural spaces—the sites of food production where much of the Global South’s population lives—remain insufficiently studied. This paper revisits ongoing changes in India’s agriculture and food system in relation to broader trends across the Global South and conceptualizes them as three interconnected waves of change. The impacts of these waves on socio-economic life in villages are mixed, rendering rural transformation a complex and evolving process. The paper argues that, while these changes have increased food production and diversified livelihood opportunities, they have also reproduced the existing inequalities and climate vulnerabilities. They do so by exerting pressure on natural resources, creating a precariat through the casualization of labor, and accelerating capital accumulation within the village economy. Thus, the ongoing changes have produced a “conundrum” in the Global South: the pressure to ensure availability of affordable food for a growing population while preserving ecological resources and mitigating existing inequalities.

title: The dialectic of human-object relations in Chinese urban television drama: a reification-theoretical reading
abstract: Background Lukács’s theory of reification describes a social order in which relations among people appear as relations among things. It offers a productive way to read urban television narratives, where housing, consumption, professional performance, and intimate life regularly become measures of social worth. Objective This article examines how Chinese television dramas make reification visible through objects, space, and the body. It also asks how people-centered narration is constructed as a textual possibility for questioning those relations. Methods The study uses qualitative close reading of three urban dramas - Fake It Till You Make It, Nothing But Thirty, and Women in Beijing - and Meet Yourself, a contrastive case that begins with urban workplace pressure before relocating its protagonist to a rural community. Plot events, dialogue, character action, settings, and recurring motifs are examined through object alienation, reified space, the reified body, and dereifying practice. Results Across the urban cases, luxury goods, exclusive residences, professional schedules, and intimate calculations turn social value into visible and comparable signs. The contrastive case frames a partial interruption of that logic through care, shared activity, and a changed relation to work. These are narrative resolutions, not demonstrations of institutional transformation. Conclusion The article connects reification theory to the close analysis of Chinese television narrative. It argues that people-centered narration is most useful as an analytical term when it names concrete formal and relational practices rather than a general moral quality.

title: Maternal healthcare quality, continuity, and experiences among pregnant adolescents and adult women in Ethiopia, Kenya, and South Africa: A cohort study
abstract: The capacity of health systems to provide quality care for pregnant adolescents remains underexplored. This study examined the quality, continuity, and experiences of maternal healthcare among pregnant adolescents (<20 years) compared with adult women (20 + years) in Ethiopia, Kenya, and South Africa. It also explored factors associated with mistreatment and obstetric complications among adolescents using data from the Maternal and Newborn Health eCohort study. We followed 3,051 pregnant women from their first antenatal care (ANC) visit until six weeks postpartum. We used descriptive analyses to compare care quality and outcomes and logistic regression to identify factors among adolescents. The study included 380 adolescents and 2,671 adults. Adolescents had lower first-trimester ANC attendance (22% vs. 30%, p = 0.003), fewer follow-up ANC visits (mean 3.1 vs. 3.8, p < 0.001), and lower adherence to iron-folic acid supplementation (59.0% vs. 69.4%, p < 0.001). Continuity of care was also lower (53% vs. 59%, p < 0.001). Adolescents experienced more mistreatment during delivery (26.9% vs. 18.6%, p = 0.003). Obstetric complications occurred in 31% of adolescents compared with 25.9% of adults. Mistreatment was associated with rural residence (adjusted odds ratio (aOR): 2.61, 95% CI: 1.11-6.13, p = 0.028), public facility use (aOR: 4.33, 95% CI: 1.44-13.1, p = 0.009) and intimate partner violence (IPV) (aOR: 3.31, 95% CI: 1.16-9.39, p = 0.025). Protective factors included being in Kenya (aOR: 0.19, 95% CI: 0.05-0.75, p = 0.018), privacy during delivery (aOR: 0.44, 95% CI: 0.21-0.92, p = 0.030) and high perceptions of quality of care (aOR: 0.37, 95% CI: 0.18-0.76, p = 0.007). Obstetric complications were associated with rural residence (OR: 2.25, 95% CI: 1.09-4.63; p = 0.028) and antenatal depression (OR: 2.43, 95% CI: 1.19-5.00, p = 0.015). These findings highlight gaps in adolescent maternal healthcare. Strengthening adolescent-responsive and respectful care within primary healthcare, alongside integrated mental health and IPV support, may improve adolescents' maternal healthcare experiences and outcomes.

title: Multi-tissue resource characteristics and comprehensive utilization of medicinal and edible loquat (Eriobotrya japonica): a review
abstract: Loquat ( Eriobotrya japonica (Thunb.) Lindl.), a member of the Rosaceae family, exhibits pronounced tissue-specific metabolic specialization that underpins its nutritional value, pharmacological activities, and industrial potential. Contemporary research on loquat has largely focused on single tissues or individual bioactive compounds, whereas comprehensive cross-tissue comparative profiling and mechanistic analyses remain substantially underexplored. This fragmented research paradigm obscures both the tissue-specific distribution of secondary metabolites and the upstream regulatory networks governing their biosynthesis, resulting in the inefficient exploitation of by-products such as peels and seeds. In this review, we synthesize several decades of empirical and mechanistic studies on the phytochemical profiles, pharmacological functions, and resource-transformation mechanisms of the core bioactive constituents across five major loquat tissues—pulp, peel, seed, leaf, and flower. We clarify the core metabolites conserved across all tissues and the signature compounds specific to individual organs, and summarize their pleiotropic biological activities, including antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, antitumor, hypoglycemic, and multi-organ cytoprotective effects. Beyond phenotypic description, we further examine the evolutionary genomic origins and hierarchical regulatory networks underlying tissue-specific metabolism: lineage-specific whole-genome duplication is proposed to contribute to the heterogeneous accumulation of triterpenoids across tissues, whereas cold-adaptive signaling and developmental hormonal modulation cooperatively reshape organ-specific secondary metabolic reprogramming.
