Finally, we identify three pivotal industrial constraints on the sustainable valorization of loquat resources—fragmented processing layouts, low-efficiency recycling of agricultural residual biomass, and frost-induced instability of raw material supply—and propose targeted transformation strategies, including marker-assisted germplasm improvement, multi-omics dissection of tissue-specific metabolic regulatory networks, synthetic-biology-based green biosynthesis of high-value phytochemicals, and the development of a comprehensive circular industrial system. These strategies provide a theoretical basis for the integrated utilization of the medicinal and edible resources of loquat.

title: A semi-supervised multi-sensor remote sensing pipeline for mapping irrigation dynamics in ground-truth deficient conflict zones: a case study of the Kakhovka Dam failure
abstract: The ongoing war in Ukraine has drawn international attention to the impact of conflict on global agricultural production and food security. On 6 June 2023, the Kakhovka Dam was destroyed. The loss of this critical agricultural and energy infrastructure has left most farmers on the East bank of the Dnipro River without irrigation in Kherson and Zaporizhzhia oblasts. This study develops a multi-sensor Earth Observation framework combining high resolution satellite imagery (Sentinel-2, Landsat) with meteorological data (CHIRPS) and water productivity data (FAO WaPOR), using a semi-supervised machine learning pipeline. Using a rigorous stratified random-sampling approach with photointerpretation, we found pre-war irrigated areas between 2019 to 2021 to be on average 187.94 ± 14.43 kHa, approximately 4% of pre-war baseline cropland and 8% of summer season cropland in Kherson and Zaporizhzhia oblasts. In 2022, these numbers contracted to 140.04 ± 17.44 kHa with the expanded occupation of these territories by Russia, seeing an additional decline in 2023 to 74.97 ± 17.84 kHa. Fields in 2023 also exhibited variability in irrigation, ranging from interrupted irrigation owing to the destruction of the Kakhovka reservoir, to those that were sufficiently irrigated with water remaining in the channels. Irrigated areas diminished further in 2024 to 15.95 ± 9.97 kHa, a ∼91% decline from pre-war averages. Based on inspection, formerly irrigated fields before 2023 were either systematically abandoned or converted to winter cropland with lower input requirements by 2024–a pattern that continued into 2025 (total irrigated area 5.76 ± 0.87 kHa). This study demonstrates the power of advanced EO workflows to precisely quantify agricultural transformation and infrastructural failure in ground-truth deficient, high-risk environments.

title: Agro-residue forecasting for biogas-based green rural electrification in India: A Gaussian process regression-based decision framework
abstract: Reliable feedstock availability remains a critical challenge for biogas-based microgrids, particularly in agrarian economies where agro-residue supply is highly dynamic. Existing planning approaches often rely on static estimates, ignoring temporal variability. This work proposes a probabilistic forecasting-based decision framework to assess agro-residue availability and corresponding biogas-based electricity potential. The methodology integrates Lasso-based feature selection with Gaussian Process Regression using a novel composite kernel. The proposed model, named CK-GPR, is trained on four decades of historical agro-climatic, agronomic, and policy data. The composite kernel captures multiple underlying patterns, including long-term trends, nonlinear dependencies, and stochastic variations. Model validation using K-fold cross-validation shows that Gaussian Process Regression outperforms Support Vector Regression, Random Forest, and Long Short-Term Memory models even with a dot product kernel. Further improvement is achieved using the composite kernel (MAPE = 2.412%, R2 = 0.984). Rice being a major crop in India, forecasts for 2025–2027 indicate a biogas-based electricity potential of 152.9 - 155.36 * 102 GWhr and greenhouse gas reduction of 119.8 - 121.73 * 105 tonnes CO₂-equivalent and 5.24 - 4.85%, 11.81 - 10.59%, and 5.49 - 5.22% of national irrigation, rural household, and energy deficits, respectively. A sensitivity analysis and cross-crop validation using wheat further demonstrate the robustness and transferability of the proposed methodology. Bridging a critical gap between agricultural forecasting and biogas-based green energy system planning, a decision-support framework is proposed for microgrid operators, potential investors, and policymakers for planning capacity, deployment strategies, and feedstock supply chain logistics under biomass uncertainty.

title: Modes of action and emerging strategies in next-generation fungicide development against phytopathogenic fungi
abstract: Plant fungal diseases impose significant annual reductions of global crop yield and quality. Despite advances in our understanding of the etiology and molecular mechanisms of plant-fungus interactions, effective management of fungal diseases remains challenging due to climate-driven shifts in pathogen populations, the emergence of fungicide-resistant strains, globalization in agricultural supply chains, and postharvest vulnerabilities. To address these challenges, research in plant pathology has leveraged state-of-the-art technologies, with the development of novel fungicides serving as a major step forward in crop protection. This review highlights advances in fungicide development against pathogenic fungi, with an emphasis on the modes of action and regulatory mechanisms of commercial active ingredients that reflect current trends in efforts to secure global food resources. Furthermore, emerging technologies and innovative approaches for developing next-generation fungicides are discussed. By leveraging mechanistic insights and applied innovations, future research can be guided to enable the rational design of fungicides to mitigate both current and emerging agricultural challenges.

title: Influence of geographical origin on pistachio shell gasification: Experimental performance, supply chain feasibility, and sustainability assessment
abstract: Pistachio shell waste represents an abundant, underutilised lignocellulosic residue with potential for decentralised renewable energy production and waste valorisation. This study presents one of the first integrated assessments of pistachio shell waste sourced from major producing locations, combining feedstock characterisation, oxygen-limited gasification, supply-chain evaluation, life-cycle assessment (LCA), and techno-economic analysis (TEA). Gasification experiments demonstrate that feedstock origin and ash content vary producer gas quality. USA-derived shells achieved the highest H 2 selectivity 18.97%, compared to 10.86% when sourced from Semnan, Iran. Baseline analysis favoured pistachio shell waste sourced from the USA and Kerman, Iran, although USA–Greece blends proved optimal once geopolitical factors were included, specifically Aegina, as Megara shells contain high ash chlorine content meaning pre-processing (e.g. washing or leaching) is recommended to mitigate corrosion risks. LCA showed cultivation and harvesting dominated the environmental footprint, contributing >96% of cradle-to-gate greenhouse gas emissions under the base-case allocation approach, corresponding to a carbon intensity of 507 kg CO 2 -eq GJ −1 . Treating pistachio shells as an agricultural residue under a waste cut-off allocation approach reduced the carbon footprint, yielding an energy-normalised carbon intensity of approximately 16.7 kg CO 2 -eq GJ −1 , substantially lower than fossil energy pathways (natural gas and coal, ~56–95 kg CO 2 -eq GJ −1 ) ( IPCC, 2006 ). TEA indicated value in upgrading producer gas to H 2 production, yielding a preliminary levelised cost of USD 3.24 kg −1 H 2 . Integrating geographical sourcing and supply chain factors into the feedstock assessment, demonstrates that strategic feedstock selection can improve conversion performance, economic and sustainability viability.

title: A nationwide comparative analysis of household air pollution and anemia among women of reproductive age in Ghana by rural and urban residence and pregnancy status
abstract: Household air pollution remains a major public health risk in low- and middle-income countries and may contribute to anemia among women of reproductive age. Exposure to pollutants generated from solid fuel combustion can induce systemic inflammation, oxidative stress, and impaired iron metabolism, potentially increasing the risk of anemia . However, evidence on this relationship remains limited in many sub-Saharan African settings, including Ghana. This study examined the association between cooking fuel type and anemia in Ghana, assessing differences by pregnancy status and place of residence. We analysed secondary data from the nationally representative Ghana Demographic and Health Survey using survey-weighted regression models. Anemia was defined using World Health Organization hemoglobin thresholds, and cooking fuel type was classified as clean or unclean. Multivariable logistic models estimated adjusted odds ratios. Statistical significance was set at 0.05. Among 7,657 women, 41.1% were anaemic and 74.0% used unclean cooking fuels. Anaemia prevalence was higher among pregnant women (51.2%) than non-pregnant women (40.4%) and among rural women (43.4%) than urban women (39.4%). Pregnant women using unclean fuels had a higher prevalence of anaemia than those using clean fuels (57.4% vs. 32.5%). In adjusted analyses, unclean fuel use was not associated with anemia in the overall population (AOR = 1.00, 95% CI: 0.82–1.23), but was associated with elevated odds among pregnant women (AOR = 2.12, 95% CI: 0.95–4.74), although not statistically significant. The relationship between household air pollution and anemia appears to be concentrated among pregnant women in crude analysis, though the adjusted association did not reach statistical significance. Integrating clean cooking interventions into antenatal care and addressing structural determinants may reduce anemia burden in Ghana. Further research should explore causal pathways and longitudinal exposure assessment.

title: A copula-based geo-additive approach to childhood health outcomes in five West African nations
abstract: Background Anemia and malnutrition are major contributors to child morbidity and mortality in Sub-Saharan Africa, particularly in West Africa where their prevalence remains high due to multifaceted socio-economic and environmental factors. Malnutrition, as defined by WHO, includes both undernutrition and overnutrition and is linked to increased risk of non-communicable diseases. Anemia, characterized by low hemoglobin levels, impairs oxygen transport and is associated with developmental delays and increased mortality in children. Given their interrelated nature, a joint modeling approach is essential to understand shared risk factors and inform targeted interventions. Methods This study analyses pooled DHS data from Gabon, Gambia, Liberia, Mauritania, and Nigeria to identify determinants of anemia and malnutrition. Malnutrition is measured using the Composite Index of Anthropometric Failure (CIAF), which integrates stunting, underweight, and wasting for a comprehensive assessment. A copula-based geo-additive joint model is employed to simultaneously examine both conditions, accounting for spatial variation and interdependence. This approach offers a novel framework for informing policy and improving child health outcomes in West Africa. Results Key predictors of malnutrition and anemia were identified across five West African countries. Malnutrition risk was significantly associated with maternal education, water source, household wealth, child age, gender, and feeding practices. Notably, children from households using non-bottled water sources and those given milk were at higher risk. Several water-source categories were positively associated with malnutrition relative to bottled/sachet water; however, these associations may reflect socioeconomic and residential differences in the reference group and warrant cautious, non-causal interpretation. Anemia risk was significantly lower among urban children and those whose mothers had higher education. Fortified food and egg consumption were protective against anemia, while poverty and poor water sources increased risk. These findings highlight distinct and overlapping determinants of both conditions. Conclusion This study highlights the complex interplay of socioeconomic, environmental, and dietary factors influencing malnutrition and anemia among children in West Africa. Key predictors include maternal education, household wealth, water source, and feeding practices, with notable geographic variation. Addressing these challenges requires integrated, multisectoral strategies focused on improving maternal education, access to safe water, dietary diversity, and poverty reduction. Geographically targeted interventions and strengthened health systems are essential.

title: Assessing Nutritional Knowledge among Rural Women in Mulugu District of Telangana, India: Implications for Strengthening Nutrition-sensitive Agricultural Extension
journal: European Journal of Nutrition & Food Safety
abstract: Background: Nutritional knowledge plays an important role in enabling rural households to translate food availability into appropriate dietary practices. Rural women are particularly important in this process because of their involvement in agricultural production, food selection, preparation and household food management. However, gaps in practical nutrition knowledge may limit the effective utilisation of locally available nutrient-rich foods and reduce the nutritional benefits of agricultural production. Aims: To assess the nutritional knowledge of rural women in Mulugu district of Telangana and identify key knowledge gaps related to dietary diversity, nutrient sources and functions, food preparation, malnutrition and utilisation of locally available agricultural resources. Study Design: A descriptive study design was adopted among 120 rural women participating in agricultural activities in Mulugu district of Telangana. Methodology: Two mandals and eight villages were randomly selected. From each village, 15 rural women engaged in agricultural activities were purposively selected. Nutritional knowledge was assessed using a structured schedule covering balanced diet, macro- and micronutrients, food sources and functions, anaemia, fruits and vegetables, kitchen gardening, poultry, cooking practices and malnutrition. Responses were scored as 1 for “Yes” and 0 for “No”, with total knowledge scores ranging from 16 to 98. Results: The findings revealed that the majority of rural women (66.66%) had a medium level of nutritional knowledge, followed by 20.00% with high knowledge and 13.34% with low knowledge. Relatively higher knowledge was observed regarding nutrients required for body functioning (92.50%), protein-rich foods (85.00%), Vitamin A-rich foods (84.16%) and iron-rich foods (81.66%). However, considerable knowledge gaps were identified in relation to balanced diets (89.17%), dietary fibre (65.83%), functions of fats (67.00%), good cooking practices (81.67%), causes of undernutrition (62.50%), prevention of malnutrition (85.84%) and adverse health effects of malnutrition (91.67%). The findings also indicated a gap between the production or availability of nutrient-rich foods and their household utilisation, suggesting that nutritional awareness does not always translate into appropriate dietary practices. Conclusion: The findings indicate that rural women possess a basic foundation of nutritional knowledge, but substantial gaps remain in comprehensive and practical nutrition knowledge. Nutrition-sensitive extension should therefore move beyond awareness creation towards practical nutrition education, dietary diversification, kitchen gardening, poultry utilisation, appropriate cooking practices and behaviour-change communication. A farm-to-family nutrition approach can help strengthen the link between locally available agricultural resources, household food utilisation and improved nutritional practices.

title: Dietary diversity and healthy life expectancy among Chinese older adults: a multistate analysis of CLHLS, 2008–2018
abstract: Objective This study estimated healthy life expectancy (HLE) among Chinese older adults across varying levels of dietary diversity, and examined sex and urban-rural differences. Methods Drawing on the Chinese Longitudinal Healthy Longevity Survey (CLHLS) from 2008 to 2018, data on 9,953 older adults aged 65 years and older were included. Transition probabilities among health statuses were estimated. Further, a microsimulation model was used to calculate life expectancy (LE), HLE, and HLE/LE for older adults with varying levels of dietary diversity. Sex and urban-rural differences were also examined descriptively. Z -tests were applied to determine whether differences in HLE within subgroups were statistically significant ( p < 0.05). Results Compared with older adults with low dietary diversity, those with high dietary diversity exhibited a higher probability of transitioning from health to disability. However, they also exhibited a greater likelihood of recovering from disability and returning to health. Additionally, older adults with high dietary diversity exhibited lower transition probabilities to death from both health and disability. Across all age groups, older adults with high dietary diversity had higher LE and HLE values, albeit with lower HLE/LE ratios. At age 65, the difference in LE between the low- and high-dietary-diversity groups was 1.26 years [14.54 years (95% CI: 14.42–15.34) versus 15.80 years (95% CI: 15.55–16.17)]. Meanwhile, the corresponding difference in HLE was 0.90 years [13.32 years (95% CI: 13.25–13.95) versus 14.22 years (95% CI: 13.91–14.58)]. Stratified analyses further indicated that differences in HLE between dietary diversity groups were consistently observed across sex and urban-rural residence groups. Descriptively, the differences appeared larger among men and urban residents. Conclusion Higher dietary diversity was associated with a higher probability of transition from disability to health, lower probabilities of transition from either health or disability to death, and higher LE and HLE. These associations were observed across sex and urban-rural residence groups. Descriptively, larger differences in HLE between dietary diversity groups were observed among males and urban residents.

title: Rural industrial integration and household income in China: Mechanisms, distributional effects, and threshold dynamics
abstract: Achieving sustained growth in rural household income is a core challenge in agricultural and rural development. This study explores whether the integration of rural industries can promote farmers' income growth, and what the mechanism of this effect is. Based on seven waves of CFPS panel data of 2326 farmers in 30 provinces of China from 2010 to 2022, this paper uses the entropy weight method to construct the inter-provincial integration index, and analyzes its income effect, transmission path and distributional significance. The results consistently confirm that integration promotes sustained income growth. The study identifies two transmission mechanisms: the reallocation of labor to off-farm employment, which diversifies household income sources; and the easing of credit constraints, which improves smallholder access to productive resources and higher value supply chain activities. The analysis of regional heterogeneity shows that income growth is significant in highly urbanized areas and non-major grain producing areas, but weakens under the constraint of the staple grain value chain. The threshold regression finds a double threshold structure, suggesting that the income growth effect strengthens only after the degree of integration exceeds the critical level of intersectoral coordination. The quantile analysis further reveals distributional asymmetry: middle and high income farmers benefit substantially, while low income farmers have limited gains due to constrained access to value-added segments. The research results indicate that rural industrial integration can promote farmers' income growth by creating local non-agricultural employment opportunities and alleviating credit constraints. However, its benefits are influenced by regional conditions, family income status, and the stage of integration. These findings provide useful references for formulating rural industrial policies that are adapted to local development conditions.

title: Do Agriculture and Infrastructure Development Improve Life Satisfaction? Evidence from Rural Tanzania
abstract: Abstract Rural development in Sub-Saharan Africa is mostly measured by economic indicators, despite growing calls to broaden this narrow focus. Although wellbeing is used in discourse, it often repackages economic goals rather than capturing people’s subjective wellbeing. We address this gap by analysing how and why agricultural intensification, commercialisation and infrastructure interventions affect life satisfaction, a central component of subjective wellbeing, among Tanzanian smallholder farmers within the Southern Agricultural Growth Corridor of Tanzania (SAGCOT). Using longitudinal survey data from 2019 and 2023 ( N = 871) and focus groups, we show that life satisfaction has increased on average. Among the variables analysed in this study, access to electricity combined with Information and Communication Technologies (ICT) use is associated with higher life satisfaction. Despite development narratives, we do not find statistically significant evidence that agricultural intensification is associated with higher life satisfaction. Commercialisation is negatively associated with life satisfaction, which our qualitative findings link to perceived structural and market barriers. Infrastructure effects are heterogeneous and depend on household access: road improvements are associated with lower satisfaction among households without transport, while electricity is associated with higher satisfaction when used for ICT. These findings show that life satisfaction provides a valuable lens for understanding the intended and unintended impacts of development and can inform policies and practices by highlighting that these impacts are heterogeneous and vary across different groups.

title: Mobile internet connectivity and climate change literacy in Africa
abstract: Addressing climate change requires individual behavioral shifts and a deep understanding of its impacts, yet the role of information and communication technologies (ICT), a powerful driver of social movements and cultural shifts, in shaping climate change literacy remains underexplored. This study addresses a critical gap by exploring how ICT, particularly mobile Internet connectivity, influences climate change literacy in Africa. I provide the first causal evidence on the impact of mobile Internet connectivity on climate change literacy by exploiting variations in peer-based Internet connectivity in an instrumental variable strategy. Using newly georeferenced individual-level data on climate change literacy from over 42,000 respondents across 31 African countries, I show that climate change literacy increases among individuals connected to the Internet. The differential analysis indicates that Internet connectivity can help close climate-related information gaps, particularly for traditionally disadvantaged populations such as women, farmers, and those without formal education. Importantly, the impact is concentrated in climate-vulnerable arid and tropical regions. These findings suggest that closing the digital divide by addressing socioeconomic inequalities in Internet connectivity effectively enhances climate change knowledge. Although, Internet connectivity increases the frequency of using Internet and social media for news, there is no strong evidence that these platforms serve as channels linking Internet connectivity to climate literacy.

title: Biotechnological upgrading of palm kernel meal for poultry nutrition: Challenges and opportunities
abstract: In recent years, fluctuations in the cost of traditional feed ingredients for poultry farming have compelled producers to explore alternative raw materials to reduce costs. Palm kernel meal (PKM), a by-product of the palm oil extraction industry, is one such alternative. Although PKM is often deemed a low-quality ingredient for poultry feed due to its low energy density and high content of non-starch polysaccharides, particularly β-mannans, its availability and lower price relative to other meal products make it a viable option. This review highlights the nutritional challenges and demonstrates how biotechnology can convert a cumbersome waste product into a valuable feed ingredient. The data focuses on the use of exogenous enzymes, with an emphasis on the synergistic action of β-mannanases and multicarbohydrase cocktails. The use of solid-state fermentation (SSF) with fungal and bacterial strains was also discussed. These bioprocesses efficiently break down complex fibrous matrices, increase the content of crude protein through microbial biomass synthesis and release bioactive manno-oligosaccharides (MOS) in situ. In vivo studies demonstrate that incorporating processed PKM maintains and improves production performance. The released MOS act as prebiotics, stimulating the growth of beneficial gut bacteria, preventing the growth of pathogens, and improving intestinal mucosal architecture. Although biotechnological valorization offers a promising way to transform PKM into a high-value functional ingredient for poultry feed, this technology has certain limitations. These include substrate variability and high scaling costs. Further research is needed into industrial-scale SSF processes, as well as the optimization of eco-efficient enzyme combinations and sequential fermentations.

title: Ethnoveterinary medicine adoption and household food security among small ruminant farmers in Northern Ghana
abstract: Small ruminants’ production is critical to household food security in developing countries including Northern Ghana. Beyond serving as a source of food and income, small ruminants also act as a buffer or form of insurance against household shocks. As such, their health is pivotal to ensuring that these benefits are realised. Ethnoveterinary medicine (EVM), defined as the traditional or indigenous animal health practice which involves the use of plant extracts, serves as a potential pathway for increased household food security outcomes. These practices were promoted by the Association of Church-Based Development Projects (ACDEP) from 2019 to 2022 through their Ethnovet project. The study assesses the impact of ethnoveterinary medicine on food security outcomes using cross-sectional data from 400 small ruminant farmers in Northern Ghana. Employing the endogenous ordered probit with treatment effect model, the results show that household adoption decisions for EVM were influenced by sociodemographic and institutional factors including education, household size, off-farm income, distance to market, access to extension and access to credit. Awareness of EVM and perceived benefits also informed farmers’ choices for EVM. The treatment effect estimates show that adoption of EVM significantly influences household dietary quality, reduces the probability of falling into crises and exerts a moderate effect on household food access. Specifically, adoption increases the probability of household to fall in acceptable food consumption by 27 percentage points, reduces the probability of falling in severe coping strategies situation by 43 percentage points and increases the probability of falling into moderate food security situation by 14 percentage points. The study thus recommends the need for sustainable animal health practices such as the integration of EVM into the delivery of animal extension services. There should also be conscious scientific testing of these EVM practices and standardisation to ensure effective utilisation.

title: Soil and Water Conservation Mechanism in Oil Palm Plantations: A Review of Best Management Practices and Decision Support Strategies
journal: WSEAS TRANSACTIONS ON ENVIRONMENT AND DEVELOPMENT
abstract: Soil and water conservation on oil palm plantation is increasingly considered as a glimmer of hope for the future sustainability of land functionality and environment. Appropriate management practices and informed decision-making frameworks thus have a strong influence on conservation outcomes. This study aims to systematically identify, categorize, synthesize and quantitatively aggregate peer-reviewed evidence regarding soil and water conservation mechanisms in oil palm plantations, focusing on best management practice strategies and decision support. This study uses Systematic Litigation Review (SLR) the Scopus database is used as a reference in searching scientific publication. A keyword-based structured search was used to identify peer-reviewed articles published from 2020 to 2025 and subsequent screening in sequence based on relevance and language. Thirty-eight articles met all the selection criteria for analysis. Then we extracted data and analyzed it using thematic synthesis with descriptive quantitative aggregation of reported metrics (soil loss, SOC change, runoff reduction, or yield response). The results show six main interrelated themes: control of soil erosion; soil fertility and organic matter management; conservation of water and hydrological regulation; integrated land use and landscape management; agronomic best methods practices; and support for decision-making processes. Quantitative synthesis show that cover-based and structural BMPs decrease soil loss by 50–80%, organic amendments increase SOC by 10–35% and integrated water management decreases runoff by 20–60% across regions reported.

title: Urban Ecological Agriculture Versus Land Scarcity: A Tale of Two Realities Based on 6 Indonesian Cities
abstract: The discursive context of urban agriculture (UA) is the need to address urbanisation and ecological sustainability pressures through urban land-use policies. Most of the UA literature focuses on food security outcomes but undertheorises its effects on land scarcity. Land scarcity is, however, a structural factor shaping which UA models succeed or collapse. The objectives of this article are to investigate the following: (1) Which land scarcity types emerge from UA initiatives? and (2) Which governance structures influence the land constraints and contribute to the success of UA initiatives? Methodologically, the article critically compares UA projects across six Indonesian cities with documented evidence and statistical data. The results demonstrate that while UA projects are maturing and expanding across all cities, their operationalisation and the spatial distribution of benefits differ. Urbanisation consumes the very arable land urban farmers require, while UA attempts to integrate food production into dense, built-up environments. Community-led UA models are more resilient under land pressure than government-directed programs. The conclusions include: (1) policy recommendations recognising community agricultural land in urban zoning and coding, (2) advocating for urban farming in city-level ecosystem valuation, and (3) stimulating or creating hybrid governance approaches to enable these changes.

title: Breeding for productivity and quality: Evidence from Argentina’s INTA rice program
abstract: Sustained investment in agricultural research and development (R&D) is critical for productivity growth, food security, and competitiveness; yet, globally, public investment has stagnated relative to the size of the agricultural sector. This study evaluates the production, economic, and market impacts of Argentina’s INTA rice breeding program using variety trial data from 1991 to 2022, and production data from 2006 until 2023. We employ a multi-method approach combining econometric estimation of genetic gains, an economic surplus framework to quantify production benefits, and a spatial partial equilibrium model to assess market impacts. Using 446 observations from rice variety trials, we estimate annual yield gains of 0.775 %, equivalent to a cumulative increase of 29.45 % over the study period. Improvements in milling quality were significant but modest, while there were no significant changes in chalky rice, which indicates that yield gains were achieved without compromising grain quality. Adoption of INTA varieties expanded significantly across Argentina and neighboring countries, particularly Brazil, reflecting improved competitiveness relative to alternative varieties. The resulting production gains from adoption averaged 330 thousand metric tons annually, generating approximately US$115 million in added value per year and exceeding US$2 billion cumulatively. Market simulations indicate that, in the absence of these gains, rice production in Argentina and Brazil would be lower, prices higher, and export competitiveness reduced. Overall, the findings demonstrate that public rice breeding has delivered substantial and measurable benefits, reinforcing the importance of sustained investment in agricultural R&D to support productivity growth and market performance. Background Increasing rice productivity without compromising grain quality remains a significant challenge. Quality traits such as milled rice yield, head rice yield, and chalkiness are influenced by complex genetic and environmental factors, making simultaneous improvement difficult. As consumer demand for higher-quality rice grows, breeding programs must increasingly balance productivity gains with the maintenance of desirable grain characteristics. Objectives The objective of this study is to evaluate the genetic, production, economic, and market impacts of Argentina’s INTA rice breeding program, with particular emphasis on its ability to achieve sustained yield gains while maintaining grain quality. Methodology We used a multi-method approach to evaluate the impacts of the INTA rice breeding program. First, econometric models were applied to variety trial data from 1991 to 2022 to estimate genetic gains in yield and grain quality traits. Second, these estimated gains were combined with adoption data from 2006 to 2021 to quantify the additional rice production and economic benefits generated by INTA varieties. Finally, a spatial partial equilibrium model of the global rice market was used to assess the broader market effects of the productivity gains associated with the program. Results The INTA rice breeding program generated significant genetic gains in yield, averaging 0.775% per year and resulting in a cumulative increase of 29.45% between 1984 (the released year of the first variety) and 2022 (the released year of the last variety). Improvements in milling quality were positive but modest, while chalkiness remained unchanged, which indicates that yield gains were achieved without compromising grain quality. The widespread adoption of INTA varieties in Argentina, Brazil, and Uruguay generated an average of 330,000 additional metric tons of rice annually, valued at approximately US$115 million per year. Market simulations further showed that these productivity gains increased production, lowered prices, and strengthened export competitiveness in the region. Conclusion Overall, the INTA rice breeding program has generated significant productivity gains while maintaining grain quality, resulting in widespread adoption, higher rice production, and substantial economic benefits. The findings underscore the value of sustained public investment in plant breeding as a driver of agricultural competitiveness and productivity growth. Implications Breeding for higher yields and improved grain quality need not involve a tradeoff. The experience of the INTA rice breeding program shows that sustained gains in productivity can be achieved while maintaining key quality attributes valued by processors and consumers. One way to accomplish this is by explicitly incorporating both producer and consumer preferences into varietal development, ensuring that new rice varieties meet agronomic performance goals while satisfying market demand. Such an approach can strengthen adoption, profitability, and competitiveness across the rice value chain.

title: Beyond Income Level: Farmland Transfer, Organized Agricultural Operation, and Perceived Rural–Urban Income Inequality in Rural Hunan, China
abstract: China’s urban–rural income gap has narrowed in objective terms, yet rural households may continue to perceive substantial income inequality. Existing research often focuses on income levels; it remains unclear whether the source and institutional form of income shape perceived rural–urban income inequality among households at similar income levels. This study examines whether land transfer income, cooperative membership, enterprise cooperation, and non-farm employment stability are related to perceived rural–urban income inequality. Land transfer income is a binary indicator of whether household property income includes rental or other compensation income from transferring farmland management rights, and organized agricultural operation refers to cooperative membership or contractual enterprise cooperation. Using data from a 2025 survey of rural households in Hunan Province, this study estimates ordered logit models with county-clustered robust standard errors. Land transfer income, cooperative membership, and enterprise cooperation showed negative conditional relationships with perceived inequality, whereas having no fixed job showed the strongest positive relationship. The source-and-organization variables jointly improved explanatory performance beyond household income level (p < 0.001), and the core directions remained stable in robustness checks. Agricultural income change and agricultural subsidies are examined only as exploratory extensions. The findings offer potential implications for farmland transfer institutions, producer organizations, and rural employment policy, rather than causal policy prescriptions.

title: Exploring Factors Affecting the Performance of Water Users' Associations in the Mekong Delta of Vietnam
abstract: ABSTRACT Improving the performance of Water Users' Associations (WUAs) plays an important role in ensuring food security in countries with irrigation‐based agriculture, especially in climate‐sensitive deltas. This study investigates the factors affecting the performance of WUAs in the Quan Lo Phung Hiep area of the Vietnam Mekong Delta region, which is under great pressure from salinity intrusion and a decrease in upstream flows. The study adopts the two methods of exploratory factor analysis (EFA) and multiple linear regression analysis (OLS), with survey data collected from 225 managers across 102 WUAs (including cooperatives and collective groups) in the study area. The results indicate that internal factors, including technological modernization, financial capacity, human resources, and organizational structure, have a significant impact on performance. In contrast, external factors, including natural and environmental conditions, infrastructure and policy support, only have a more modest influence. Although social participation emerged as a construct from the EFA, it did not show a statistically significant association in the regression model. These findings suggest that the performance of WUAs can be substantially enhanced by promoting technological modernization, restructuring service pricing, and diversifying organizational services. Overall, this study offers valuable empirical lessons for improving decentralized irrigation management in regions facing similar socio‐ecological challenges.

title: Balancing Productivity, Ecology, and Social Well‐Being: Insights From Three Decades of Farmland Transformation in China
abstract: ABSTRACT Balancing food security, social equity, and ecological sustainability remains a persistent challenge in global agricultural systems. While economic and ecological aspects of land‐use transitions have been extensively studied, the long‐term dynamics of social functions and their interactions with other functions are less understood. This study investigates the decadal spatiotemporal patterns, functional relationships, and spatial association factors of farmland multifunctionality in China's major grain‐producing regions in 1990, 2000, 2010, and 2020. A multidimensional indicator system was developed to capture economic, social, and ecological functions across 185 prefecture‐level cities, and a CRITIC‐entropy hybrid weighting method was applied to construct multifunctionality indices. Correlation analysis with false discovery rate correction was used to examine trade‐offs and synergies, and the GeoDetector model was employed to identify the explanatory power of factor stratification and factor interactions. The results reveal a paradoxical trajectory across the four benchmark years: while economic and ecological functions improved substantially, the social function declined. Functional relationships were reconfigured, with economic‐ecological interactions changing from conflict to synergy, whereas social‐ecological interactions changed from synergy to trade‐off. Natural conditions were weakly associated with spatial heterogeneity, market and demographic variables exhibited stronger associations before 2010, and policy‐related variables, especially farmland protection policy indicators, showed the strongest statistical associations thereafter. These findings provide one of the most comprehensive large‐scale and long‐term assessments of farmland multifunctionality transitions in China's grain regions. They highlight the importance of institutional arrangements in explaining spatial variation in trade‐offs and synergies, and underscore the need for integrated governance strategies that simultaneously promote productivity, ecological integrity, and rural social well‐being.

title: IoT Adoption for Sustainable Agri-Food Logistics: Perceived Usefulness, Investment Intentions, and Implementation Barriers in Greece
abstract: Sustainability pressures in agri-food supply chains are creating growing interest in digital technologies that can improve the efficiency and responsiveness of logistics and supply chain operations. Within this context, the Internet of Things (IoT) is increasingly discussed as a tool with potential applications that extend beyond farm-level monitoring to broader agri-food logistics processes. This study examines perceptions of IoT and factors associated with its wider integration through the perspectives of key professional groups involved in the agri-food supply chain, moving beyond single-actor approaches. Based on survey data from 217 professionals in Greece, including 40.1% agronomists, 32.7% farmers, and 27.2% logistics professionals, the analysis explores IoT familiarity, practical exposure, perceived barriers, investment intentions, and factors associated with wider IoT integration across different positions in the agri-food system. The findings reveal moderate familiarity with IoT, while 61.3% of respondents reported practical exposure through use or observation. Perceived IoT usefulness did not differ significantly across professional groups, whereas several implementation barriers showed role-specific differences. Investment intention was positively associated with perceived usefulness (odds ratio = 3.56, p < 0.001) and positive expectations regarding the future role of IoT (odds ratio = 1.85, p = 0.016), while difficulty in converting IoT-generated data into useful information was negatively associated with investment intention (odds ratio = 0.71, p = 0.004). Perceived financial cost was not independently significant (p = 0.203). By linking broadly shared perceptions of IoT value with role-specific implementation conditions, the study provides implications for targeted support measures, capacity-building initiatives, and digitalization policies aimed at facilitating implementation and the wider practical integration of IoT into sustainable agri-food logistics.

title: Understanding Farmers’ Behavioral Intention to Adopt Digital Agricultural Technologies Under Climate Change: An Extended TPB Model from a Climate-Vulnerable Paddy Community in Sri Lanka
abstract: Digital Agricultural Technology (DAT) adoption remains poorly understood in climate-vulnerable tropical islands. To address this gap, this study examines how demand, supply, and environmental dimensions interact to shape farmers’ adoption decisions, applying the extended Theory of Planned Behavior. The data were collected from 400 farmers selected randomly in the Anuradhapura District, Sri Lanka, using a structured questionnaire. The analyses were conducted a Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Model. Four behavioral segments were identified: confident adopters (29.5%), utility-driven emerging adopters (42%), uncertain users (20.5%), and skeptical users (8%). Climate change awareness (β = 0.712), attitude (β = 0.297), social norms (β = 0.197), perceived behavioral control (β = 0.130), perceived usefulness (β = 0.162), access to infrastructure (β = 0.098), and risk aversion (β = 0.142) positively influenced farmers’ intention toward DAT. Climate change awareness strongly influenced attitudes, highlighting the central role of environmental dimensions. Institutional support had no significant effect. Behavioral intention and actual adoption (β = 0.575) influenced the willingness to continue DAT. Policymakers should move from ‘one-size-fits-all’ digital extensions to segment-specific interventions: peer-led networks for confident adopters, subsidies for utility-driven farmers, social learning for uncertain users, and in-person training for skeptical users. The study provides context-specific evidence that demonstrates how behavior shapes farmers’ adoption pathways under climate change, addressing SDGs 1, 2, 9, 12, 13, and 15.

title: Assessing the Adoption Level and Factors Influencing Circular Economy Adoption Among Adult Consumers in the Eastern Province of Saudi Arabia
abstract: Food-related circularity reduces food waste, enhances food security, and promotes sustainable food management. This study assessed the extent of food-related circularity adoption among adult consumers in the Eastern Province of Saudi Arabia and identified its associated socioeconomic, behavioral, and attitudinal factors. Primary data were collected from 384 Saudi adults (≥18 years) using a structured questionnaire in a cross-sectional survey. The data analysis included descriptive statistics and an ordinal logistic regression model (OLRM). The food-related circularity adoption index was constructed from 40 items that assessed individual practices related to recyclable or reusable food items, including bread, dates, cooked rice, cooked pasta, stewed vegetables, stewed meat, and fruit, with a Cronbach’s alpha of 0.931. Based on tertile classification, the food-related circularity adoption levels were distributed as follows: 3.1% low; 34.4% middle; and 62.5% high. The OLRM indicated that regular use of CE-related digital tools was positively associated with higher food-related circularity adoption. The respondents who disagreed that unwillingness to store leftovers contributes to food waste had significantly higher odds of high food-related circularity adoption (OR = 8.47, p < 0.01), and those who did not shop out of boredom had 4.87 times higher odds of high food-related circularity adoption (p < 0.01). The findings indicated that, given the use of convenience sampling and recruitment through social media, the reported prevalence of high food-related circularity adoption (62.5%) reflects the surveyed sample and should not be generalized to the broader population. Accordingly, CE-related digital platforms should clearly communicate the environmental, economic, and social benefits of food-related circularity practices; link individual and household actions to broader sustainability and food-security goals; and reinforce users’ sense of impact.

title: Market integration and value chain performance of head cabbage production in Southern Ethiopia
abstract: Despite its vital role in rural livelihoods, Southern Ethiopia’s horticultural sector faces systemic inefficiencies in agricultural value chain performance. Addressing the lack of research on the intersection of market participation, supply intensity, and structural logistical constraints, this study analyzes head cabbage market dynamics in Bonke District using primary cross-sectional data from 231 successfully completed producer questionnaires—administered via a multi-stage sampling technique across four kebeles—and 26 traders (categorized into licensed and unlicensed entities operating across formal and informal networks), analyzed via descriptive statistics and Cragg’s double-hurdle econometric model. The findings reveal a multi-tiered actor network constrained by an “infrastructure-perishability trap,” where poor roads and crop vulnerability cause severe post-harvest losses and erode bargaining power. Econometric results show that the probability of market participation (first hurdle) is significantly driven by education (dy/dx = 0.110), experience (dy/dx = 0.006), family size (dy/dx = 0.071), landholding (dy/dx = 0.116), and total production (dy/dx = 0.048), while being deterred by market distance (dy/dx = − 0.013). Conversely, supply intensity (second hurdle) is positively influenced by male household headship (dy/dx = 1.842), age (dy/dx = 0.025), landholding (dy/dx = 0.504), total production (dy/dx = 1.089), and market information access (dy/dx = 2.765), but negatively impacted by credit use (dy/dx = − 1.541) and distance (dy/dx = − 0.127). Ultimately, transforming cabbage production from a subsistence activity into a competitive, commercialized market requires integrated value chain management, prioritized rural infrastructure development, enhanced market information access, targeted credit utilization strategies, and regulatory frameworks that support both licensed and informal traders—thereby aligning local agricultural growth with Sustainable Development Goals (SDG) to foster sustainable agricultural development in Ethiopia.

title: Local Animal Genetic Resources for Biodiversity Conservation, Climate Resilience and Rural Bioeconomies in Ibero-America: A Scoping Review
abstract: Local animal genetic resources are a strategic component of agrobiodiversity and represent key assets for food security and sustainable development. The aim was to analyze the available evidence on the role of local animal genetic resources in biodiversity conservation, productive resilience, food security, and sustainable rural development in Ibero-America. The review was conducted in accordance with the PRISMA extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR). The literature and institutional documents published from January 2001 to June 2026 were searched in the Web of Science Core Collection, Scopus, CAB Abstracts, PubMed, SciELO, Redalyc, AGRIS/FAO, and relevant institutional repositories. The final search was completed on 15 June 2026. Eligibility was defined using the Population-Concept-Context framework, and evidence was synthesized thematically and comparatively. The scientific literature published was considered, with emphasis on local breeds, in situ and ex situ conservation, gene banks, phenotypic and genomic characterization, bioeconomy, public policies and rural production. The search identified 187 records. After removal of one duplicate, 186 records were screened by title and abstract, of which 77 were excluded. A total of 109 full-text reports were assessed and included in the scoping review. An additional 43 contextual or supporting references were cited outside the screened evidence set. Evidence indicates that creole and local breeds provide adaptive traits, heat tolerance, disease resistance or tolerance, cultural value and productive resilience. However, conservation initiatives remain fragmented and face limitations related to census data, funding, governance, genetic monitoring, traceability and economic valorization. Regional evidence indicates relevant progress in genetic characterization, germplasm banks, and research programs. The review concludes that animal genetic resources conservation will only be sustainable if it integrates living populations, representative germplasm banks, reproductive biotechnologies, genomic information, public policies, economic incentives, differentiated markets, and active producer participation. Local animal genetic resources must be considered as biological infrastructure for climate adaptation, food security, and inclusive rural bioeconomies.
keywords: in situ and ex situ conservation

title: Mapping climate change adaptation policy instruments in European agriculture: a qualitative analysis of National Adaptation Strategy and National Adaptation Plan
abstract: Abstract Climate change poses an increasing threat to agricultural production and food security. While many European countries have developed National Adaptation Strategies (NASs) and National Adaptation Plans (NAPs), the alignment between proposed policies and their supporting mechanisms remains under-explored. This study maps adaptation frameworks across ten European countries—Finland, Austria, Switzerland, Belgium, the Netherlands, Denmark, Estonia, Spain, Latvia, and Lithuania—to clarify diverse national policies and identify how specific instruments are prioritized to address adaptation goals. Drawing upon 20 official documents available on the Climate-ADAPT platform and using ATLAS.ti for qualitative analysis, 131 climate adaptation policies in agriculture were extracted to form a thematic synthesis. Then, we determined which policy instruments (categorized into four groups: information-based, legal and regulatory, economic, and infrastructural and physical instruments) were associated with each policy. The findings indicate that while these frameworks provide strategic guidance, they place significant emphasis on information-based and awareness-raising measures. This suggests a distinct pattern in European climate governance: a preference for farmer engagement and voluntary action over more direct regulatory or economic interventions.

title: A comparative analysis of organic, inorganic manures, and integrated nutrient management in carrot growth and yield in the global south
abstract: Abstract Amid global fertilizer supply chain disruptions and the emerging dual-market demand for carrot ( Daucus carota ) taproots and leafy biomass, optimizing nutrient management is now essential for sustainability. This study investigated the comparative efficacy of organic manure (OM), inorganic manure (IM), and integrated nutrient management (INM) on carrot growth and yield to determine the most viable approaches for farmers in the global South. Using a completely randomized design with three replicates over a 12-week experimental period, the Kuroda variety was subjected to four treatments: an unamended control ( C 0 ), poultry manure ( T 1 ), NPK 15:15:15 ( T 2 ), and a combination of poultry manure and NPK for INM ( T 3 ) . Data were analyzed using means. ANOVA was used to test the null hypotheses at the 0.05 significance level. Findings revealed that carrots planted in T 3 (at 34.39 mm) were taller than those planted in soil treated with IM (28.54 mm), OM (32.35 mm), or C (26.39 mm). Also, carrots planted in T 3 had higher leaf biomass (12.23) than those in T 2 (9.10), T 1 (11.37), and C 0 (8.44). Findings further revealed that carrots in T 2 had longer tubers (17.86 mm) and greater weight (59.52 g) than those in T 3 (14.84 mm, 54.15 g), IM (13.35 mm, 42.48 g), and C 0 (11.55 mm, 31.25 g). Indicating that, while INM ( T 3 ) maximized above-ground vegetative parameters, suggesting it could be the optimal strategy for cultivating carrots for the leafy biomass for livestock feed, the OM application ( T 1 ) had a higher optimum harvestable root yield. Although numerically higher values were observed under INM, there was no statistical significance for leaf biomass. There was a statistically significant difference in root tuber performance. Adopting targeted OM and INM practices could provide sustainable, goal-oriented pathways to optimize agricultural production while buffering domestic farming in the global south against global challenges in food production.

title: TED-FinRisk: a hybrid topic-enhanced framework for typologizing illegal fundraising risk from multi-source case texts
abstract: Illegal fundraising is increasingly conducted through dispersed digital channels, cross-regional operations, and rapidly changing promotional narratives, which makes static rule lists and purely expert-driven typologies difficult to maintain. This paper presents TED-FinRisk, a hybrid framework for constructing an interpretable risk taxonomy from multi-source case texts. The framework combines term frequency–inverse document frequency (TF-IDF) feature construction, topic exploration assisted by t-distributed stochastic neighbor embedding (t-SNE), latent Dirichlet allocation (LDA)-based topic extraction, and Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP)-based expert priority calibration under the Financial Action Task Force (FATF) threat–vulnerability–consequence perspective. After the taxonomy is finalized, FinBERT is used for a reclassification consistency check aligned with the final expert labels, examining whether the taxonomy corresponds to recognizable text-semantic patterns within the study corpus. The study is based on a corpus of more than 1,000 illegal fundraising cases and nearly 6,000 associated risk-related records covering scenarios such as elder care, virtual currencies, supply-chain finance, agricultural ventures, film investment, social e-commerce, and overseas investment. The resulting taxonomy contains six primary categories and a set of secondary labels linked to operational indicators for downstream monitoring. These results suggest that combining data-driven topic discovery with expert calibration can produce a risk taxonomy with regulatory semantics and monitoring relevance. The paper contributes a methodology-oriented case study, a reusable taxonomy design process, and a structured basis for future benchmarking and early-warning applications.

title: The Future of Agricultural Extension and Economics: Integrating Artificial Intelligence, Behavioural Science, Climate Resilience and Inclusive Markets
journal: Journal of Scientific Research and Reports
abstract: Agricultural extension is being reshaped by four simultaneous pressures: the arrival of low-cost digital and artificial-intelligence-based advisory tools, the reframing of farmer decision-making by behavioural economics, the intensification of climate risk and the restructuring of agri-food markets. These developments are usually reviewed in separate literatures, which obscures how they interact in determining whether advice changes practice and whether practice change raises and protects smallholder incomes. This critical narrative review examines that interaction. Peer-reviewed economics, agricultural, computer-science and climate-services literature published from 2004 to July 2026 was identified through multidisciplinary scholarly indexes, economics repositories, institutional sources and citation tracking, and was appraised with particular attention to identification strategy, external validity, field validation and distributional analysis. The evidence indicates that digitally delivered advice produces modest but cost-effective improvements in adoption, whereas effects on yields, prices and incomes are inconsistent. Image-based diagnostic models achieve high accuracy on curated datasets but lose performance under field conditions, and large language models remain supported mainly by design studies, benchmark tests and surveys of extension staff rather than by evaluations of farm outcomes. Behavioural mechanisms, particularly limited attention, present bias and social learning through well-chosen messengers, are well documented, yet generic nudges and behavioural framings frequently show small or null effects. Climate information services and risk-reducing technologies can crowd in investment, but uptake is strongly conditioned by farmers' resources, gender and trust. Market information alone rarely improves farm-gate prices where intermediaries hold bargaining power, and gains appear larger when market access rewards quality or relaxes liquidity constraints. The review proposes an integrated framework in which advisory technology is necessary but insufficient, and in which risk, liquidity, market structure and social position determine the returns to information. Priorities include field trials of generative advisory systems with safety outcomes, bundled designs that address several binding constraints, evaluation at scale and governance arrangements for agricultural data. The central conclusion is that the future of extension depends less on the sophistication of advisory algorithms than on their integration with institutions that manage risk and distribute market gains.

summary_id.tujuan: Mengkaji secara kritis interaksi antara penyuluhan berbasis AI dan digital, ekonomi perilaku, ketahanan iklim, dan struktur pasar agri-pangan dalam menentukan apakah nasihat mengubah praktik dan melindungi pendapatan petani kecil.
summary_id.metode: Tinjauan naratif kritis terhadap literatur peer-reviewed di bidang ekonomi, pertanian, ilmu komputer, dan layanan iklim yang terbit 2004 hingga Juli 2026, dicari melalui indeks akademik multidisiplin, repositori, sumber kelembagaan, dan pelacakan sitasi. Kualitas studi dinilai pada strategi identifikasi, validitas eksternal, validasi lapangan, dan analisis distribusi; jumlah studi dan lokasi spesifik tidak disebutkan.
summary_id.temuan: Layanan penyuluhan digital meningkatkan adopsi secara sederhana namun hemat biaya, sementara dampak pada hasil panen, harga, dan pendapatan tidak konsisten. Model diagnosis berbasis citra akurat pada data terkurasi tetapi menurun di lapangan, nudge generik sering berdampak kecil atau nol, dan informasi pasar saja jarang menaikkan harga di tingkat petani bila perantara memegang daya tawar. Ini merupakan sintesis bukti dari berbagai studi, bukan estimasi kausal baru.
summary_id.relevansi: Sangat relevan dengan agenda penyuluhan digital, akses pasar petani kecil, dan kelembagaan petani; kerangka bahwa nasihat perlu dipadukan dengan lembaga pengelola risiko dan likuiditas dapat diuji pada rantai nilai sawit maupun pangan pedesaan di Kalimantan Tengah. Agenda uji lapangan dan tata kelola data pertanian yang diusulkan juga dapat dibawa ke konteks Indonesia.

title: Multidimensional sustainability assessment of Indonesia's emerging konjac agrifood system: A case study in Sidenreng Rappang
abstract: Konjac ( Amorphophallus muelleri ), locally known as porang, is an emerging bio-based commodity with the potential to support rural livelihoods, export diversification, and domestic value addition in Indonesia. However, production expansion may not generate sustainable outcomes unless ecological suitability is supported by technological capacity, resilient markets, inclusive social arrangements, and effective institutional coordination. This study assessed the multidimensional sustainability and transition readiness of the konjac agrifood system in Sidenreng Rappang Regency, South Sulawesi. Transition readiness was diagnosed from dimensional performance, disparities among dimensions, root mean square leverage scores, and policy priorities. An adapted RAPFISH multidimensional scaling approach termed RAP-Konjac assessed 27 attributes across economic, social, environmental, technological, and institutional dimensions using 32 purposively selected key informants. The system was moderately sustainable overall (mean index 57.41), but varied substantially across dimensions. Environmental sustainability achieved the highest index (67.73), whereas technology was the lowest (48.80) and was the only less sustainable dimension. Monte Carlo analysis confirmed classification stability. Leverage analysis identified supply chain efficiency, export market dependence, industrial processing, agricultural extension, partnership effectiveness, seed variety conservation, and pest and disease management as priority intervention points. The findings demonstrate that ecological potential alone is insufficient for sustainable transformation. Policy should prioritize post-harvest and processing technologies, domestic value addition, market diversification, extension, inclusive partnerships, and ecological safeguards. Nevertheless, the assessment is limited by its case study scope, purposive informant selection, stakeholder scoring, and cross-sectional design; thus, findings are context-specific and require validation through longitudinal research and applications in other konjac-producing regions.

title: Soil Health Under Climate Change: A Review of Climate Impacts, Sustainable Management Strategies, and Future Directions
abstract: Soil health is fundamental to sustainable agriculture, crop productivity, and vital ecosystem services. However, climate change increasingly threatens the functional integrity of soil due to rising temperatures, altered precipitation patterns, elevated atmospheric carbon dioxide levels, and extreme weather events. These factors accelerate soil degradation and disrupt the physical, chemical, and biological processes essential for maintaining soil health. This review synthesizes recent evidence regarding the impacts of climate change on soil health and crop production, while also evaluating sustainable management strategies designed to enhance agricultural resilience. Techniques such as conservation agriculture, organic matter management, diversified cropping systems, and integrated nutrient management can improve soil structure, nutrient cycling, water retention, carbon sequestration, and overall crop productivity. Furthermore, emerging technologies offer new opportunities for real-time, site-specific, and data-driven soil management. These technologies include remote sensing, geographic information systems, artificial intelligence, digital agriculture, and advanced soil monitoring tools. Additionally, policy and socioeconomic factors—particularly financial incentives, extension services, and institutional support—are critical in encouraging farmers to adopt these practices. Despite recent advancements, challenges such as economic barriers, technological limitations, regional variability, and a lack of long-term evidence hinder the widespread implementation of sustainable soil health practices. This review provides an integrated perspective that links climate-driven changes in soil’s physical, chemical, and biological properties with sustainable management practices, emerging technologies, and policy support. It highlights the interactions and trade-offs among these components to promote climate-resilient and sustainable agricultural systems.

title: Different seeds, same pest? Exploring smallholder farmers’ lived experiences of fall armyworm impacts on hybrid and local maize in Kenya
abstract: Fall Armyworm (FAW) is a persistent threat to maize-based food systems in sub-Saharan Africa, but less is known about how farmers experience its effects across seed types and household livelihoods. This exploratory qualitative study examined smallholder farmers’ lived experiences of FAW damage in hybrid and local maize in Siaya County, Kenya. Face-to-face semi-structured interviews lasting 30–45 min were conducted with 88 purposively selected farmers, and responses were analyzed thematically by two independent researchers. Farmers described FAW as recurrent and difficult to control; 43.2% reported infestation every season. Most participants (77.3%) perceived hybrid maize as more severely affected than local maize, whereas 9.1% perceived local maize as more affected and 9.1% reported similar effects. Participants associated infestation with reduced yields, impaired crop growth, lower-quality harvests, lost income, pesticide and labour costs, depleted maize stocks, food purchases, and stress related to financial and food uncertainty. Reported responses included pesticide use, repeated spraying, purchasing food, crop diversification, and reconsidering maize varieties. Because the study relied on farmers’ accounts rather than controlled varietal comparisons, the perceived differences cannot be attributed to seed characteristics independently of management and growing conditions. The findings indicate that farmers evaluate FAW damage through interconnected production, livelihood, food-security, and seed-choice concerns, supporting locally tested pest-management and seed advisory services.

title: International research partnerships and cross-cultural project management: a Vietnamese beef cattle agribusiness autoethnographic case study
abstract: Introduction This case study explores enablers and barriers that contribute to the successful implementation of a complex official development assistance (ODA) research project, focusing on a multiyear research project aimed at integrating smallholder households and farm production systems into commercial beef supply chains in Vietnam. Researchers from diverse institutions in two countries have worked together over time to implement project activities that have involved local governments and private stakeholders. Methods This qualitative research uses an autoethnographic case study approach to explore the enablers, barriers and collaborative dynamics of an international research partnership. Through collective sense-making, our international and multicultural research group collaboratively interpreted our experiences of working together on a multi-year project that aims to investigate new collaborative approaches between smallholder farming households and commercial intensive agricultural systems with a focus on beef supply chains in northern Vietnam. Results Transdisciplinary research conducted by a multicultural research team required engagement across sociocultural, institutional and relational layers or boundaries. Key factors contributing to success included long-term relationship building and trust, distributed and culturally sensitive leadership, multi-level communication systems, methodological pluralism and shared problem framing. Discussion A design and evaluation framework is presented to assist researchers to plan, design, modify and evaluate their international projects. Lessons from this case study provide insights into managing interdisciplinary and intercultural collaborations and improving the effectiveness of international research partnerships.

title: Sustainability governance, assessment, and assurance frameworks in Australian agriculture
abstract: Australian agriculture increasingly needs to demonstrate sustainability performance to governments, consumers, export markets, investors, and downstream food businesses. The sector has responded through various sustainability governance instruments. This paper reviews the architecture of sustainability governance instruments in Australian agriculture. The review used documentary analysis of national, commodity, and cross-cutting frameworks. The analysis identifies four layers: (i) national overarching frameworks for common language and disclosure expectations; (ii) commodity frameworks that translate sustainability into sector-relevant themes, indicators and reporting cycles; (iii) regulatory and assurance systems that operationalise claims through compliance, certification, traceability and market access; and (iv) data, traceability and disclosure mechanisms. The review finds that Australian frameworks are aligned around environmental stewardship, animal welfare, social responsibility, and economic resilience, but vary in indicator specificity, reporting arrangements, assurance mechanisms, implementation maturity, and administrative requirements. Emerging climate disclosure, nature positive and digital traceability expectations are likely to increase demand for consistent, verifiable farm and supply chain data. We argue that the framework development should prioritise interoperability, proportionality for small and medium farms, clearer links between farm practice and outcome indicators, and stronger integration of social, cultural and governance dimensions. These improvements would support coherent sustainability evidence, credible market claims, and policy alignment.

title: Low-Carbon Transition Performance of Cropland Use in the Principal Grain-Producing Counties of Sichuan Province: Spatiotemporal Evolution, Spatial Spillovers, and Driving Factors
abstract: The low-carbon transition of cropland use must reconcile emission reduction with food security in major grain-producing areas. Using panel data for 89 major grain-producing counties in Sichuan Province, China, from 2010 to 2022, this study measures the low-carbon transition performance of cropland use (LCTP-CLU) with a global-benchmark undesirable-output super-efficiency slacks-based measure (GB-US-S-SBM) model. Spatial autocorrelation analysis and a spatial Durbin model are then used to examine spatiotemporal patterns, driving factors, and spillover effects. LCTP-CLU increased overall, with the sample mean rising from 0.558 in 2010 to 0.618 in 2022. Performance was higher in northeastern Sichuan and lower in southwestern Sichuan, and high-value counties became increasingly contiguous by 2022. The cropland area per agricultural worker, multiple-cropping index, and rural economic development significantly improved LCTP-CLU, whereas the agricultural industrial structure reduced it. LCTP-CLU also exhibited significant positive spatial spillovers; cropland area per agricultural worker, multiple-cropping index, and rural economic development generated positive effects in neighboring counties. These findings support differentiated county-level policies and cross-regional coordination to advance low-carbon cropland use while safeguarding grain production.

title: Livelihood benefits, ecosystem services, and food security trade-offs of khat cultivation in eastern Ethiopia
abstract: Abstract Khat (Catha edulis) cultivation and consumption are deeply embedded in the socio-economic and cultural systems of Habro Woreda, Ethiopia, shaping livelihood strategies and land-use decisions. This study examined the socio-economic significance, cultural drivers, environmental perceptions, and health-related attitudes associated with khat using a mixed-methods approach involving household surveys of 111 respondents, key informant interviews, focus group discussions, and field observations. Khat chewing was highly prevalent (96.9%), with age significantly associated with chewing behavior (χ² = 9.683, p = 0.046), whereas sex showed no significant association (χ² = 0.020, p = 0.886). More than half of respondents recognized potential cardiovascular risks, although education level was not significantly associated with health-risk perception (χ² = 11.048, p = 0.354). Most farmers (81.1%) perceived khat as beneficial for soil and water conservation, and this perception significantly varied with cultivation intensity (χ² = 7.907, p = 0.019). Economically, khat was identified as the dominant livelihood activity, with 96.9% of respondents reporting it as a reliable income source. Qualitative findings revealed extensive indigenous knowledge systems, including moisture-conserving practices such as basin construction around khat plants, alongside concerns regarding declining food-crop areas, market dependency, and excessive youth consumption. Overall, the findings highlight the dual role of khat as a livelihood asset and perceived land-management strategy while emphasizing trade-offs related to food security, agricultural diversification, and long-term sustainability. The study underscores the need for integrated land-use policies that balance rural income generation with ecosystem resilience and sustainable agricultural development.

title: An Explainable, Privacy-Preserving AI Framework for Credit Risk in Nepalese Cooperative Banks: A Federated Survival Graph Bayesian Approach
abstract: Nepal’s cooperative banking sector is in serious trouble. By mid-July 2025, non-performing loans across the country’s banking and financial institutions had climbed to Rs 258.19 billion, and the cooperative sector accounts for a large share of this problem. Forty cooperatives alone embezzled Rs 87.89 billion from over 60,000 depositors, many of them farmers, housewives, retirees, and daily wage laborers. The National Cooperative Bank Limited reported a capital adequacy ratio of just 0.82 percent, which points to technical insolvency rather than mere distress. The International Monetary Fund has warned that further cooperative failures could threaten the stability of Nepal’s entire banking system. The paper proposes a new theoretical architecture for credit risk management in Nepalese cooperative banks, which we call the Federated Survival Graph Bayesian Framework (FSGBF). Conventional binary classification approaches predict whether a borrower will default, but they cannot tell us when. Our framework addresses this through Cox proportional hazards survival analysis. It captures network contagion effects using Graph Neural Networks that map borrower interdependencies within cooperative communities. Cross-institutional learning is enabled through Federated Learning with Differential Privacy, so that 31,450 primary cooperatives can collectively strengthen their models without sharing sensitive member data. Epistemic uncertainty is quantified through Bayesian Neural Networks with Monte Carlo Dropout, which helps distinguish between data noise and genuine model ignorance. Causal explanations come through interventional Shapley values, which identify which features correlate with default and which features actually cause changes in default risk when manipulated. The paper proves the consistency of the Cox partial likelihood estimator, derives the Breslow baseline hazard estimator, and establishes the convergence of GraphSAGE under neighborhood sampling. We also prove the FedAvg convergence theorem under convexity and bounded gradient assumptions, derive the Renyi differential privacy composition rule, and show that Monte Carlo Dropout approximates variational inference with a Bernoulli variational posterior. The four Shapley axioms for the interventional (causal) Shapley value are verified, and the bias-variance decomposition for the composite FSGBF predictor is established. Drawing on Nepal Rastra Bank’s Financial Stability Report FY 2024/25, the National Cooperative Federation of Nepal’s 2025 sectoral snapshot, parliamentary investigation findings, and the IMF’s July 2024 country report, we situate this mathematical framework within Nepal’s institutional reality. The sector has 7.4 million members, 56 percent of them women, holding Rs 847 billion in deposits.
