Yet it operates under split oversight, where 25,000 of 32,000 cooperatives are financial intermediaries with minimal real-time supervision. The paper argues that without predictive, network-aware, privacy-preserving, uncertainty-quantified, and causally explainable credit risk management, Nepal’s cooperative movement will collapse under the weight of its own opacity, and millions of livelihoods will go with it.

title: Wheat Rust Diseases: Global Impact, Integrated Disease Management, and Emerging Biotechnological Innovations for Sustainable Crop Protection
abstract: Wheat (Triticum aestivum L.) remains one of the most important staple crops worldwide and serves as a primary source of calories and protein for billions of people. Global wheat production, however, continues to be threatened by rust diseases caused by Puccinia triticina, Puccinia striiformis f. sp. tritici and Puccinia graminis f. sp. tritici. These pathogens are highly adaptive and frequently give rise to new virulent races, causing resistance in wheat cultivars to breakdown. Under favorable environmental conditions, severe epidemics can develop and substantial yield losses may occur. In response to these challenges, traditional management approaches such as resistant cultivars, crop rotation, sanitation and fungicide application have long been employed in wheat production systems. Yet these strategies have increasingly been constrained by resistance breakdown, genetic uniformity in modern cultivars, and climate-driven changes in pathogen distribution. Conventional management practices are evaluated alongside emerging technological solutions including genomic-assisted breeding, gene pyramiding, CRISPR-based genome editing, biological control agents and precision agriculture tools. In addition, nanotechnology has emerged as a promising tool in plant disease management, where nanoparticles such as silver, copper and zinc oxide exhibit strong antifungal activity and enable targeted delivery of agrochemicals. Nano-enabled formulations can enhance fungicide efficiency, reduce chemical inputs and improve plant defense responses, offering a sustainable complement to existing wheat rust management strategies. Particular attention is given to integrated disease management strategies, which combine traditional agronomic practices with modern surveillance technologies such as remote sensing, artificial intelligence-based forecasting models, and pathogen genomics. These combined approaches can improve resistance durability and build more resilient wheat production systems. Future directions emphasize climate adaptation, global surveillance and collaborative breeding. In an era of increasing climatic uncertainty and evolving pathogen populations, durable rust management will depend on coordinated global efforts that align scientific innovation, farmer adoption, and policy support to safeguard wheat productivity and global food security.

title: A theoretical interpretation of the interaction between formal and illegal institutions in migrant labour recruitment in Italian agriculture
abstract: Labour exploitation is widespread in Italian agriculture. Although a substantial body of research has sought to explain these trends, further scientific investigation is still needed to understand how formal and illegal institutions interact. Institutional analysis could provide an original contribution to the study of this issue. This study adopts this perspective and seeks to address the following research question: what kinds of interactions take place among these institutions that may be associated with the emergence of the observed working and exploitative conditions? The manuscript examines migrant labour in Italian agriculture and investigates how migration regulations, migrants’ legal status, labour market dependency, and illegal recruitment practices interact in producing vulnerability and exploitation. In particular, this study contributes to the debate by shedding light on the interaction between formal and illegal institutions and by integrating them into a unified theoretical framework. Following Helmke and Levitsky (2004), this article classifies these illegal institutions and their interactions as competing in nature. The existing literature provides considerable evidence that supports this theoretical framework. However, the study has two main limitations. First, the analysis relies on a non-systematic narrative literature review. A more structured analysis could enrich the interpretation of the phenomenon. Second, the study lacks empirical research specifically designed to test the proposed theory. Future research should therefore focus on this task and further enrich the theoretical interpretation by examining, above all, the impact of institutional interactions on enterprises and agri-food value chains.

title: Bridging theory and practice in just energy transitions: A multi-method analysis integrating AI-driven computational frameworks and qualitative field research in post-lignite Greek regions
abstract: The European Union's just transition framework allocates over €150 billion to ensure that decarbonization does not disproportionately burden fossil-fuel-dependent communities, with Greece receiving approximately €1.6 billion for its post-lignite regions of Western Macedonia and Peloponnese. The stakes are considerable: these regions face cascading socio-economic disruption, mass displacement of lignite workers, youth out-migration rates exceeding 10% per decade, and agricultural decline driven by aging workforces, structural constraints and the impacts of extreme weather events. Compounding these challenges is a collective crisis of belief among populations subjected to successive economic shocks since 2009. Existing research has examined just transition financing, governance design, and stakeholder perceptions in isolation, and has established that place-based approaches, inclusive participation, and capacity building are essential to equitable outcomes. However, no study has systematically diagnosed why transitions that appear to possess all conventionally recognized success factors, including strong political commitment, substantial funding, and technically available solutions, nonetheless struggle to deliver results at the community level. The mechanisms linking policy ambition to implementation shortfall remain poorly understood. This study addresses that gap through a convergent multi-method design integrating rule-based and machine-learning computational text analysis with independent qualitative field research. The evidence base comprises two independent studies conducted in 2025: a computational study of 20 semi-structured stakeholder interviews and two focus groups in Western Macedonia and Megalopolis (22 sessions, approximately 55,000 words, collected February to May 2025), and a qualitative field study of 25 interviews, two focus groups, and site observations across Western Macedonia, the Peloponnese, Laconia, and Athens (June to August 2025). The computational component applies 13 analytical frameworks simultaneously, using NLP and ML techniques including TF-IDF vectorization, Latent Dirichlet Allocation topic modeling, VADER sentiment analysis, K-Means clustering, spaCy named entity recognition, and network centrality algorithms, producing quantified diagnostics across multiple dimensions that single-framework approaches cannot capture. The qualitative fieldwork comprises 25 interviews, two farmers groups (farmers; national-level decision makers focus groups, and makers), with site observations across four Greek regions including the non-lignite agricultural district of Laconia as a within-region contrast case, providing the environmental, cultural, and experiential depth that computational methods alone cannot reach. All reported scores are researcher-defined, discourse-based indicators; their construction, decision rules, and uncertainty are documented in the supplementary materials, and they should be read as exploratory diagnostics rather than validated measurements. The converging results indicate a paradox of plenty: expressed leadership commitment and resource-related discourse register high (8.0/10 and 10.0/10 on framework-specific indices), yet corpus-level awareness (1.7/10), demonstrated capability (1.3/10), and expressed will (1.0–1.9/10 across categories) register critically low; because these indices derive from different frameworks and analytical units, they are reported side by side rather than combined into a single validated scale. This gap coexists with strikingly low discourse presence of affected populations (workers 4.8% of coded discourse, women 0.5%), a concentration of resource-related discourse on technology (53% of resource-related segments; 48.6% normalized) despite critically low readiness, a generational sentiment divide (75.6% positive among youth-focused passages versus 50.0% in aging-population passages) that plausibly accelerates the demographic erosion necessary for adoption, and unaddressed water scarcity that undermines the agricultural modernization upon which diversification strategies depend. These findings are formalized as Implementation Gap Theory, which identifies four interacting gap types (vertical, horizontal, temporal, and cognitive) proposed as testable mechanisms of implementation shortfall despite favorable preconditions. The framework is offered as a candidate diagnostic for coal-dependent transition regions across the European Union, pending independent validation, and demonstrates that funding adequacy and policy commitment are necessary but insufficient conditions for just outcomes.

title: The water–energy nexus in Saudi Arabia’s agriculture sector: Water demand forecasts and policy implications
abstract: Agriculture in semi-arid Saudi Arabia relies heavily on non-renewable groundwater resources to support food security. This study estimates agricultural water demand using the Autoregressive Distributed Lag (ARDL) model with annual data for 1992–2024 and projects alternative demand scenarios through 2050. Fully Modified Least Squares, Dynamic Ordinary Least Squares, and Autometrics general-to-specific modeling approach are employed as robustness checks. Agricultural income, groundwater pumping costs (proxied by agricultural electricity tariffs), and rainfall are identified as the primary determinants of agricultural water demand in Saudi Arabia. The estimation results indicate that, in the absence of additional policy interventions, agricultural water demand is projected to increase by 54%, reaching 17.8 billion cubic meters (bcm) by 2050 under a median precipitation scenario. This growth reflects both baseline trends and additional water requirements associated with the Saudi Green Initiative (SGI). Under the median precipitation scenario, the associated energy demand for groundwater extraction would increase by 37%, reaching 19.5 TWh by 2050. The results indicate that the long-run elasticity of water demand with respect to groundwater pumping costs is −0.22, whereas the estimated impact of policy measures, such as banning water-intensive crops, is larger. The findings suggest that bans on water-intensive crops have produced substantial and persistent reductions in agricultural water demand, highlighting the effectiveness of direct regulatory measures when duly enforced. The results further suggest that higher agricultural electricity tariffs could complement existing regulatory measures by encouraging farmers to adopt more water-efficient production practices, thereby slowing groundwater depletion without significantly affecting agricultural output.

title: Microbial Biostimulants for Drought Resilience in Plants: Mechanisms, Plant–Microbiome Interactions, and Sustainable Agricultural Applications
abstract: Drought stress is one of the most significant challenges for global agriculture, adversely affecting crop yields and food security. In recent years, microbial biostimulants have emerged as a promising solution to enhance plant resilience against such abiotic stresses. This review explores the mechanisms by which microbial biostimulants, including beneficial bacteria and fungi, confer drought tolerance in plants. Key interactions between plants and their associated microbiomes are highlighted, emphasizing the roles of root-associated microbes in promoting plant growth, nutrient uptake, and stress mitigation. We examine microbial-induced plant responses, including improved water relations, photosynthetic performance, and osmotic adjustment. Additionally, the review examines the sustainability of microbial biostimulant use in agricultural practices, addressing their potential to reduce reliance on chemical inputs and improve soil health. Evidence from field studies across diverse crops is also discussed, highlighting the potential of microbial biostimulants to improve plant performance and yield stability under water-limited conditions while emphasizing the context-dependent nature of their efficacy. Furthermore, we underscore the importance of microbial diversity and community composition in maximizing the benefits of biostimulants. By integrating microbial biostimulants into conventional agricultural practices, farmers can enhance drought resilience, thereby contributing to sustainable food production systems. This review aims to provide a comprehensive understanding of the interactions between microbial biostimulants and plants under drought stress, and to highlight future research directions for optimizing their use in sustainable agriculture.

title: Co-Designing Local Water Security: A Participatory Comparative Case Study of Perceived Climate Risks in Northeastern Thailand
abstract: Khon Kaen Province in Northeastern Thailand is repeatedly exposed to both floods and droughts, undermining agricultural livelihoods. This study examines perceived climate risks and adaptive governance through a participatory action research (PAR) approach at four reservoir communities of the Khon Kaen Irrigation Project—Huai Sai, Huai Toei, Huai Yang, and Laloeng Wai. Using a mixed-methods design, the study combined semi-structured interviews with 12 irrigation officials, focus group discussions with Joint Management Committees, community workshops with 240 residents, and a household survey (N = 400). Perceived risk levels, evaluated using a study-specific composite index based on the IPCC AR6 framework, were moderate at Huai Sai (11.02) and low at Huai Toei (8.81), Huai Yang (7.90), and Laloeng Wai (7.68). Because perceived hazard, exposure and vulnerability showed substantially overlapping 95% confidence intervals across sites, collective response capacity was the dimension that varied most widely across sites and the dimension to which the index is structurally most sensitive. Through participatory STEEP prioritization workshops, all four communities identified economic drivers as their primary concern, reflecting seasonal income fragility alongside strong social capital. To address these economic priorities within local water constraints, a pilot agricultural prototype—cultivating Hom Thong banana under localized drip irrigation—was co-designed with provincial agricultural and irrigation agencies. The prototype was installed to specification, and the stand had established and reached full vegetative growth approximately two months after planting; no participant feedback, satisfaction or yield data were collected during the reporting period. This comparative case study documents the process of co-designing a localized, risk-informed adaptive strategy with communities and public agencies, and the feasibility of implementing it at one site; whether such strategies build community resilience remains to be tested.

title: Analysis of the maize and groundnut seed value chains in central and northern Tanzania
abstract: Abstract Background Maize and groundnut are important crops in Tanzania; therefore, understanding their seed value chains (VCs) is critical for improving the seed systems. The study aimed at establishing key components for model maize and groundnut seed VCs by understanding the formal and informal seed VCs to provide relevant recommendations for; improving these value chains, propose interventions that would encourage more investment by seed companies, and improve access to quality seed by farmers. The study used data collected through survey, with a sample size of 252 and 162 seed producing households for maize and groundnut, respectively, conducted using structured questionnaire. VC actors including; seed companies, agricultural research institutions, agrodealers, seed regulatory authority, public seed production agency, extension staff and Ministry of Agriculture, were also interviewed. Porter’s value chain approach was applied to analyse the various components of the VC and identify the links between the key nodes and understand their operational functions. Results The maize seed producing households were dominated by men (71%) while for groundnut, women (69%) were engaged in seed production. Government agricultural extension services are the main source of information; 30% and 58%, for maize and groundnut, respectively. Seed companies were the main producers of maize seed (51.7%) while for groundnut, public research institutions were the main seed producers. Most of business enterprises were owned by men (83.3%). Compared to maize, the formal seed sector is weak for groundnut in Tanzania, with very few private seed companies being engaged in seed production and supply. Most groundnut seeds are accessed through agrodealers and seed associations that produce quality declared seed (QDS). Community seed banks were recognized as an efficient option for providing improved groundnut varieties to smallholder farmers. There are no prominent seed companies aggressively operating for both crops in central Tanzania. Excessive reliance on farm-saved seed by farmers was identified as one of the major factors negatively affecting the demand for certified seed. Stakeholder analysis of the seed production and supply chain showed that there was poor coordination between key stakeholders involved in the seed VC. Conclusion This study provides recommendations for strengthening the seed value chains in Tanzania by addressing identified gaps along the VC components. Future studies can build from the outcomes of this study and generate more information, especially on market and different seed systems, as these have great influence on demand and supply of seed.

title: Small millets in India: a review of nutritional security, climate resilience and sustainable livelihoods
abstract: Small millets ( Setaria italica, Panicum sumatrense, Paspalum scrobiculatum, Echinochloa frumentacea, Panicum miliaceum and Brachiaria ramosa ) are emerging as climate-resilient, nutrient-dense crops with considerable potential to address food insecurity, malnutrition, environmental degradation and livelihood vulnerabilities. Although these crops have long been cultivated under diverse agroecological conditions, their production and consumption declined following the dominance of rice and wheat-based production systems during the Green Revolution. This systematic literature review synthesizes current evidence on the nutritional composition, climate resilience, socio-economic importance, value addition, market opportunities, institutional support and policy interventions related to small millets in India. The review followed the PRISMA 2020 guidelines for systematic literature identification, screening and study selection. Literature published up to June 2026 was systematically retrieved from Scopus, Web of Science Core Collection, ScienceDirect, SpringerLink, CAB Abstracts, AGRICOLA and Google Scholar, together with relevant reports from national and international organizations. After applying predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria, 150 studies were included in the qualitative synthesis. The evidence indicates that small millets are rich sources of dietary fibre, quality protein, essential minerals, vitamins and bioactive compounds such as polyphenols and flavonoids, contributing to nutritional security and reducing the risk of non-communicable diseases. Their tolerance to drought, heat stress, poor soil fertility and low-input production systems makes them highly suitable for climate-smart and sustainable agriculture. Beyond their agronomic and nutritional advantages, small millets support the livelihoods of tribal and marginal farming communities, strengthen indigenous knowledge systems and enhance household food security. The review further highlights the significant role of women in millet cultivation, processing, value addition and marketing, as well as the contributions of self-help groups and farmer organizations to rural development and income generation. Advances in processing technologies, product diversification, entrepreneurship and export opportunities have enhanced the economic potential of the millet sector. National and international initiatives, including the International Year of Millets 2023, millet missions, nutrition-sensitive programmes and institutional interventions, have further accelerated millet promotion. However, challenges such as low productivity, inadequate processing infrastructure, weak market linkages, limited consumer awareness and policy implementation gaps continue to constrain wider adoption. Addressing these challenges through increased research, value chain strengthening, gender-inclusive interventions, market expansion and supportive policy frameworks will be essential for integrating small millets into sustainable food systems and advancing the Sustainable Development Goals related to food and nutritional security, climate resilience, environmental sustainability and inclusive rural livelihoods.

title: Integrated microbiome and green technologies for sustainable rice production: Current advances, challenges and future perspectives
journal: Journal of Agriculture and Food Research
abstract: Rice cultivation faces severe threats from climate change, resource depletion, and the ecological damages of conventional high-input farming. This review evaluates the deployment of microbial and non-microbial green technologies to foster sustainable, low-carbon rice intensification. By utilizing a systems-based framework, it examines technological synergies, climate resilience, socioeconomic barriers, and smallholder accessibility across biological and digital dimensions. Microbial innovations, such as synthetic microbial communities (SynComs), genome-edited microorganisms (GEMs), and nano-encapsulated biocontrol agents, optimize rhizosphere functionality, nutrient cycling, and stress adaptation. Concurrently, non-microbial technologies including UAV-based remote sensing, AI-driven decision-support systems, smart irrigation, and renewable energy integration provide the physical infrastructure necessary to scale up these biological processes. However, widespread field adoption is hindered by high implementation costs, inconsistent field survival of bioinoculants, genotype–microbe incompatibilities, and restrictive regulatory frameworks. The distinct novelty of this study lies in its holistic integration framework. While existing literature independently reviews biological interventions or engineering approaches, this review integrates microbial and non-microbial technologies within a common framework while considering their synergies, trade-offs, and implementation challenges. Ultimately, this review shifts the focus from isolated interventions to a unified, climate-smart framework, offering critical pathways for future multi-disciplinary research, targeted policy creation, and equitable technology deployment for global food security.

title: Biomass potential and sustainability assessment of bioenergy in Indonesia
abstract: This systematic literature review uses a narrative thematic synthesis to examine existing studies on biomass potential and the sustainability assessment of bioenergy in Indonesia, highlighting the role of bioenergy in achieving national climate goals and government bioenergy targets. The analysis of the literature reveals that palm oil remains the dominant feedstock in Indonesia’s current bioenergy pathway, while agricultural and forest residues also offer significant opportunities for renewable energy production. The reviewed literature further highlights the importance of biomass resource modelling for understanding biomass availability and utilisation pathways. However, most existing studies focus primarily on technical biomass potential while providing limited consideration of practical constraints such as competing biomass uses, supply chain limitations, land-use pressures, and international trade dynamics. More integrated biomass resource assessments are therefore needed to support economically viable and environmentally sustainable bioenergy development. This review also evaluates sustainability assessment frameworks, particularly through comparison between the Global Bioenergy Partnership (GBEP) indicators and Indonesia Bioenergy Sustainability Indicators (IBSI). Although IBSI incorporates environmental, social, and economic dimensions, several important sustainability indicators, such as land-use change, biodiversity impacts, and food system interactions, are not addressed within the framework. These omissions are particularly relevant given Indonesia’s strong dependence on palm oil-based bioenergy pathways. Additionally, existing bioenergy regulations remain heavily concentrated on palm oil-based pathways. In contrast, policy support for a broader range of feedstocks, particularly agricultural, forestry, and other residual biomass resources, remains relatively limited. Addressing these challenges through more integrated policy frameworks will be crucial for maximising biomass potential in Indonesia’s energy transition. Overall, this literature review underscores both the significant potential of bioenergy in Indonesia and the key policy, sustainability, and governance challenges that must be addressed to support its long-term sustainable development.

title: How Governance Interactions Across Multiple Levels Shape Strategies for Sustainable Private Forest Management: A Case Study of Bulukumba Regency, Indonesia
abstract: The sustainability of private forest management has become increasingly important in response to natural forest degradation, market uncertainty, climate change, and institutional transformation. However, previous studies have mainly examined private forests from economic, ecological, social, or institutional perspectives, with limited attention to governance interactions across multiple governance levels. The study examines how governance interactions shape private forest management in Bulukumba Regency, Indonesia. A qualitative case study was conducted using in-depth interviews with 28 key informants, field observations, and document analysis. The results show that private forest management is shaped by interactions among economic, institutional, market, environmental, and social factors operating across micro, meso, and macro governance levels. At the micro level, farmers' economic rationality influences harvesting decisions while encouraging the retention of trees standing as long-term household assets. At the meso level, institutional restructuring following changes in forestry authority has reshaped coordination mechanisms. At the macro level, market dynamics and climate variability generate external pressures requiring adaptive governance responses. Across these levels, local social capital (assamaturu) strengthens coordination, collective action, and adaptive capacity. The study advances multilevel governance literature by demonstrating that governance interactions, rather than individual governance factors, provide the basis for developing strategies toward sustainable private forest management. The findings highlight the importance of strengthening institutional coordination, integrating formal governance with local social capital, and promoting adaptive governance to support long-term sustainability.

title: An intersectionality-based policy analysis of COVID-19 measures and women informal food vendors in Kisumu, Kenya
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Women working as informal food vendors in Kisumu faced precarious work conditions that worsened during the COVID-19 pandemic. Despite playing a vital role in urban household food security, they were excluded from policy decisions, which were largely confined to technical experts and national government officials. METHODS: Using the Intersectionality-Based Policy Analysis (IBPA) framework, this study examined the engagement of women informal food vendors and the disparities in COVID-19 control policies. Between July 10, 2024, and October 15, 2024, we conducted a qualitative study using key informant interviews (n = 20), in-depth interviews (n = 20), four focus group discussions (n = 40; 10 participants each), and a purposive review of four policy documents. Participants were recruited via purposive sampling in collaboration with Pamoja Community Based Organisation, and data were analyzed thematically guided by the IBPA principles. RESULTS: The findings indicate that excluding women vendors from decision-making led to gender-insensitive policies that worsened existing inequalities by overlooking the vendors' diverse social identities. Furthermore, inconsistent policy implementation increased gender-based vulnerabilities, leaving these women exposed to harassment, extortion, and physical assault. DISCUSSION: To prepare for future emergencies, governments must establish inclusive, gender-responsive policy frameworks that prioritize the perspectives of informal food vendors, thereby safeguarding sustainable urban food systems. Specifically, municipal, county, and national authorities should create consultative mechanisms to ensure women informal food vendors actively participate in decision-making processes. Such integration will foster gender-sensitive policy development and keep vendors' lived experiences central to urban food governance. Ultimately, this research demonstrates the value of applying an intersectional policy analysis framework to health research, advancing equity and social justice by strengthening the participation of marginalized groups in emergency response and regulatory planning.

title: Do varietal preferences reflect livelihood orientations? Evidence from sorghum farmers in Kenya
abstract: Existing studies in sub-Saharan Africa on farmers' varietal preferences have paid limited attention to how these preferences relate to different livelihood orientations. This study investigates whether variations in farmers' preferences for sorghum traits are linked to differences in their livelihood orientations. Using data from a discrete choice experiment involving 362 farmers in Homa Bay County, preferences for six attributes: end use (household and industrial), yield potential, maturity, grain price, seed price, and bird tolerance were analyzed through a latent class model. The findings identify two distinct preference classes: Class 1 values higher yields, early maturity, higher grain prices, and multi-end use, whereas Class 2 strongly prefers improved bird tolerance. Farm size and cultivation of both local and improved varieties were significantly associated with class membership, while farmer-group membership was marginally significant. Post-hoc profiling further showed significant differences between the classes in farm size, household size, sorghum yield, quantity sold, and variety type. The preferences and class profiles may point to a productivity orientation in Class 1 and greater sensitivity to production risk in Class 2. These findings highlight the importance of targeted, inclusive breeding programs that address smallholder farmers' varied needs and challenges.

title: Economic performance and profitability drivers of women Bambara nut farmers in Nigeria: Implications for women's economic development
abstract: Women play a significant role in food production in Nigeria, yet many remain concentrated in small-scale farming with limited economic returns. Despite growing interest in underutilized crops, empirical evidence on the profitability of Bambara nut production among women farmers and the factors influencing their economic performance remains limited. This study examines the economic performance of women Bambara nut farmers in Nigeria using profitability indicators and beta regression analysis. The findings indicate that Bambara nut production is economically viable, with variable costs accounting for the largest share of production expenses, particularly labor, agrochemicals, and seeds. The enterprise generated positive returns, indicating favorable profitability and economic performance among women farmers. The results further reveal that formal education, annual income, access to credit, extension services, fertilizer use, cooperative membership, farm size, and household size are positively associated with profitability, while high input costs are negatively associated. The study contributes to the literature on women’s agribusiness participation and underutilized crops by providing evidence on the profitability drivers of Bambara nut farming in Nigeria. The findings suggest that improving women farmers’ access to productive resources and institutional support could enhance the economic outcomes of Bambara nut production.

title: Early Evidence on Household Food Security and Livelihood Changes Associated with an In-Kind Agricultural Microcredit Programme in Rural Uganda
abstract: Food insecurity remains a major global development challenge across sub-Saharan Africa. While conventional cash microcredit yields mixed socio-economic outcomes, this study evaluates an innovative, progressive in-kind agricultural microcredit programme as a sustainable development tool in rural Uganda. Employing an observational design, we compare agribusiness microcredit recipients with a training-phase cohort across 2022 baseline and 2025 follow-up rounds. The evaluation integrates the Months of Adequate Household Food Provisioning (MAHFP) indicator with qualitative livelihood assessments to examine self-reported changes perceived by participants in relation to economic, food-related, and personal or social dimensions. Cross-sectionally, microcredit recipients exhibited significantly higher MAHFP scores (8.17 vs. 6.86) and experienced less severe seasonal food stress. Longitudinally, the intervention is associated with a potential buffering pattern against deteriorating food security rather than driving rapid income growth. Although direct financial returns were modest and largely absorbed by rigid expenses like school fees, beneficiaries reported marked improvements in dietary quality, reduced reliance on purchased food, and enhanced socio-economic empowerment. These findings highlight that while this integrated credit-plus approach is not a quick fix for chronic food insecurity, it provides preliminary evidence on how integrated credit-plus approaches may support livelihood resilience and food security in vulnerable smallholder settings.

title: The impact of rural population shrinkage on cultivated land non-grain conversion—dual causal inference based on machine learning
abstract: Against the backdrop of rapid advances in new urbanization and continued rural population contraction, the expansion of cropland non-grain use poses a potential challenge to national food security. Based on 3,598 observations from 257 prefecture-level cities in China over the 2011–2024 period, this study introduces a double machine learning approach and combines two-way fixed-effects models, threshold models, and spatial Durbin models to systematically examine the mechanisms through which rural population contraction affects cropland non-grain use. The results show: (1) rural population contraction significantly raises the degree of cropland non-grain use: for every one-unit increase in rural population contraction, cropland non-grain use rises by 0.089 units. (2) The relationship exhibits nonlinear characteristics, with per-mu grain returns serving as the threshold variable. As per-mu grain returns increase, the effect follows a pattern of “strong promotion–weak promotion–significant inhibition.” (3) Heterogeneity results show that the promoting effect of rural population decline on cropland non-grainization is more pronounced in eastern regions and major grain-marketing areas. (4) Spatial econometric analysis confirms that rural population decline exhibits significant positive spatial spillover effects, with the magnitude of the indirect spillover effect substantially exceeding that of the local direct effect. These findings are expected to provide empirical evidence and decision-making references for advancing differentiated and tiered governance of cropland non-grainization and strengthening food security.

title: Enabling the circular bioeconomy: institutional mechanism design for sustainable development of bio-breeding in China
abstract: The circular bioeconomy provides an opportunity for aligning agricultural innovation with sustainable development goals. Biotechnology breeding (bio-breeding) represents a transformative pathway for improving seed quality, reducing chemical inputs, and building a resource-efficient and circular agricultural system. However, its industrializing transition remains constrained by fragmented regulations, weak intellectual property protection, and limited public acceptance. Existing studies mainly focus on technological development or administrative planning, with limited systematic attention to the institutional mechanisms required to support a sustainable bio-breeding ecosystem. This study employs a qualitative policy analysis approach grounded in the New Haven School of law and policy studies and its “Five Intellectual Tasks.” It develops an analytical framework based on the cyclical and collaborative evolution of “technological innovation—efficiency leap—institutional adaptation—consumer feedback—technological revolution.” The analysis examines China’s bio-breeding value chain and, where relevant, compares regulatory models and industrial pathways in China with those in the United States and the European Union. The analysis identifies four key institutional bottlenecks in the bio-breeding value chain: R&D collaboration, biosafety approval, intellectual property governance, and market acceptance. Lengthy approval processes, misaligned governance structures, insufficient mechanisms for technology transfer and intellectual property protection, and consumer mistrust constrain the effective integration of bio-breeding into a circular economy model. To address these constraints, this study proposes an institutional reform pathway that strengthens technology transfer mechanisms, optimizes the biosafety regulatory system, enhances product regulatory efficiency, and increases consumer participation through labeling systems and public awareness strategies. These findings deepen the theoretical understanding of the institutional transformation required for a circular bioeconomy and provide actionable policy recommendations for supporting sustainable bio-breeding development in China and other emerging economies.

title: Influence of seed sources and seeding rates on bread wheat (Triticum aestivum L.) productivity in Banja District, Northwestern Ethiopia
abstract: Abstract Bread wheat productivity in Northwestern Ethiopia is extremely low due to poor-quality seeds and inappropriate seed rates. To address these problems, field and laboratory experiments were conducted during the 2024 cropping season in Banja District to evaluate the effects of seed sources and rates. Seed quality was evaluated in the laboratory using a Completely Randomized Design with three replications. The field experiment employed a factorial randomized complete block design with three replications, including four seed rates (125, 150, 175, and 200 kg ha⁻¹) and three seed sources: Adet Research Center, Ediget Bandnet Cooperative, and farmer-saved seeds of the Danda’a variety. Laboratory results indicated that seed sources significantly influenced by initial seed quality of bread wheat. Seeds from Adet Research Center showed the highest physical purity (99.97%), standard germination (98.33%), thousand kernel weights (41.20 g), seedling vigor index I (27.18), and seedling vigor index II (0.02). In the field experiment, grain yield was highly significantly affected by both seed sources and rates. The highest grain yield of 5.39 t ha⁻¹ was achieved with Adet Research Center seeds, while 200 kg ha⁻¹ seed rate produced 5.37 t ha⁻¹. The combination of Adet Research Center seed with 200 kg ha⁻¹ contributed the maximum net benefit of 103,480.30 Ethiopian Birr ha⁻¹ and a marginal rate of return of 582.9%. These results suggest that using 200 kg ha⁻¹ of Danda’a variety seeds from Adet Research Center can substantially improve wheat productivity. Further verification across multiple varieties, locations, and years is recommended to confirm these findings.

title: Trade-offs in the environmental and social sustainability of conventional and alternative pig production systems
abstract: Sustainability assessments of livestock systems have largely prioritized environmental and economic outcomes, with comparatively limited attention to social performance or the trade-offs that emerge when multiple objectives interact. We advance a more holistic perspective by jointly evaluating environmental and social sustainability across conventional indoor and alternative pig production systems on the island of Ireland, the latter encompassing outdoor and agroforestry-based systems. Environmental life cycle assessment (E-LCA; cradle-to-farm-gate) and social life cycle assessment (S-LCA; pork value chain) were implemented in parallel to characterize the systems contrasting sustainability profiles. The alternative system increased global warming potential, land use and water consumption by 36.2%, 129.7% and 29.7%, respectively, but reduced terrestrial acidification, freshwater eutrophication and marine eutrophication by 75.7%, 72.0% and 52.5%, respectively. Higher resource-use impacts reflected greater production efficiency in conventional systems, whereas lower acidification and eutrophication resulted from more diffuse manure dispersion. Social performance showed similarly divergent patterns. Conventional systems exhibited lower social risks associated with policy intervention and socio-economic contribution but higher risks concerning farm working conditions and pig welfare. The converse was the case for the alternative systems. Social risk hotspots were identified among farmers, local communities and pigs stakeholder groups in the conventional system, and among farmers in the alternative system. Overall, neither production system achieved comprehensive sustainability. Instead, clear trade-offs emerged, underscoring that different production models deliver distinct environmental and social benefits and burdens. These findings highlight the need for more holistic, multi-dimensional assessment frameworks when evaluating the sustainability of livestock production systems.

title: Inequitable nutritional impact of India’s first COVID-19 lockdown: a national cross-sectional analysis
abstract: BACKGROUND: India's first nationwide COVID-19 lockdown in March 2020 disrupted food systems, healthcare access, and livelihoods, raising concerns about its impact on nutritional outcomes. While the effects of the pandemic on food security have been widely documented, national-level evidence on nutritional status, particularly across economic strata, remains limited. METHODS: We analyzed data from India's fifth National Family Health Survey (NFHS-5), a national household survey conducted between 2019 and 2021, during which the COVID-19 lockdown occurred. We assessed underweight status (Body Mass Index (BMI) < 18.5 kg/m²) in adults, wasting (weight-for-height z-score < -2) in children under five, and anemia in men, women, and children under five. Outcomes were analyzed by wealth quintile (Q1-Q5). Adjusted prevalences were estimated by marginal standardization. Survey-weighted multivariable logistic regression models were used to examine associations between lockdown period and outcome prevalence, and concentration indices and curves were applied to assess changes in economic disparities. RESULTS: After adjustment, underweight prevalence among men increased only in the near-poor second quintile (adjusted Odds Ratio (aOR) 1.25, 95% Confidence Interval (CI) 1.12-1.40) and declined in the wealthiest, while among women it declined in the wealthier quintiles and overall and was largely unchanged among the poorest. Wasting declined across all wealth quintiles in children, with smaller reductions among the poorest. Anemia declined across all groups. All outcomes remained concentrated in the poorest quintiles in both periods. Concentration indices and curves confirmed widening disparities in underweight and wasting, with smaller or less consistent shifts for anemia. CONCLUSIONS: Following India's first COVID-19 lockdown, undernutrition improved for most groups, but these gains were inequitably distributed: improvements were concentrated among wealthier households while the poorest improved least, and near-poor men experienced a rise in underweight. Anemia declined across all groups but remained highest in the lower wealth quintiles. These estimates should be interpreted with caution, as the cross-sectional design precludes causal inference and higher mortality among the most vulnerable during the lockdown may have rendered post-lockdown estimates conservative. These findings point to the need for equity-focused interventions and resilient nutrition systems to protect at-risk populations during and after crises.

title: Valorization of pumpkin-derived residues and waste: An analysis
abstract: The global agricultural sector faces increasing pressure to manage the substantial volumes of waste generated throughout pumpkin production, processing, and utilization, which traditionally represents both an economic burden and an environmental liability. This paper explores the valorization of pumpkin waste within a circular bioeconomy framework, evaluating the conversion of heterogeneous pumpkin-derived biomass into value-added food, nutraceutical, environmental, material, and energy products. Through a comprehensive synthesis of contemporary research, this paper demonstrates that pumpkin residues contain diverse recoverable compounds and structural fractions that can serve as feedstock for multiple valorization pathways, including nutraceuticals, advanced environmental remediation media, and industrial composite materials. Quantitative evidence from recent studies reveals a range of reported performance metrics, including polysaccharide extraction yields, improvements in protein solubility, and recovery or enrichment of phenolic compounds. In the realm of environmental engineering, pumpkin-derived adsorbents have been reported to achieve substantial contaminant removal efficiencies and adsorption capacities, while the incorporation of pumpkin-based fillers has been shown to modify and, in some formulations, improve the mechanical properties of composite and construction materials. Furthermore, energy conversion pathways for biogas and biodiesel production have demonstrated variable reported conversion and yield values depending on feedstock characteristics and process conditions. Despite these reported technical advances, the transition from laboratory-scale demonstrations to technically, economically, and environmentally viable larger-scale implementation remains a primary hurdle. Key future research imperatives include the standardization of feedstock characterization, harmonization of performance metrics and experimental protocols, rigorous long-term ecological safety assessments, and the adoption of predictive digital frameworks to address the challenges posed by inherent biomass heterogeneity. The integration of hierarchical and cascaded biorefinery architectures could facilitate the sequential recovery and utilization of multiple pumpkin waste fractions, thereby providing opportunities to improve overall resource utilization relative to isolated valorization routes, where supported by integrated technical, economic, and environmental assessments. This systemic approach provides a basis for advancing pumpkin waste valorization from individual laboratory-scale applications toward integrated and scalable biorefinery systems, with potential contributions to resource efficiency, reduced reliance on fossil-derived materials, and the development of more sustainable agro-industrial value chains.

title: Rules versus reality in agricultural subsidies: entitlements, capture, and inequality
abstract: Agricultural subsidies are commonly regarded as an important policy instrument for stabilizing agricultural production, raising farm household income, and safeguarding food security. Yet the conversion of policy rules into payments actually received by rural households, and further into real economic benefits and distributional improvements, is not automatic. Focusing on implementation deviations between rules and reality, this paper uses an unbalanced household-county panel for rural China from 2010 to 2022, together with county-year subsidy policy documents, fiscal final accounts, land-transfer records, and household survey data, to construct rule-based agricultural subsidy entitlements, actual agricultural subsidies, and the subsidy take-up rate. It then systematically examines the determinants of subsidy conversion and further investigates the effects of actual agricultural subsidies on rural income and the underlying mechanisms. The results are as follows. First, conditional on rule-based entitlements, actual operated land area and household asset endowments significantly increase the household subsidy take-up rate. Second, land-market activity and land-finance dependence amplify these conversion gaps, suggesting that land-factor marketization and local fiscal incentives alter the economic incidence of subsidy rules in grassroots implementation. Third, actual agricultural subsidies have a significantly positive effect on per capita household income after subsidies are excluded, but this income-stimulating effect is stronger at middle and upper income quantiles; the average subsidy intensity at the county level also significantly increases the Gini coefficient and Theil index, indicating that subsidies may raise average income while widening within-rural income inequality. Fourth, mechanism tests show that increases in the county-year per-mu subsidy standard promote land-rent capitalization, while increases in actual agricultural subsidies foster land inflow, agricultural material inputs, agricultural service inputs, and non-farm investment, thus generating a subsidy-land-input-investment transmission process. The contribution of this paper is to move agricultural subsidy research from nominal payment amounts to a full-process analysis of rule-based entitlements, actual receipt, economic benefit, and income distribution. It reveals the key roles of implementation deviations and land-market conditions in shaping the distributional incidence of subsidies. The findings suggest that improving the performance of agricultural subsidies requires attention not only to aggregate subsidy amounts and standards, but also to subsidy registries, payment verification, the assignment of subsidy rights in land transfers, and the take-up capacity of resource-constrained households, so as to reduce hidden distributional biases in policy implementation.

title: BeLFG-Net: A Lightweight Betel Leaf Freshness Grading Network via Hybrid Depthwise Separable Convolutions
abstract: Post-harvest quality grading of betel leaves ( Piper betle L.) is critical to supply chain efficiency across South and Southeast Asia, yet assessment remains an entirely manual process susceptible to inter-rater inconsistency and throughput bottlenecks. Visual freshness cues—saturated green pigmentation, surface desiccation, and brown discoloration—form a continuous rather than discrete progression, making threshold-based color analysis insufficient. We propose BeLFG-Net, a Betel Leaf Freshness Grading Network, that addresses this challenge through a hybrid four-block encoder combining standard convolutions for initial feature establishment with depthwise separable pairs for parameter-efficient cross-channel mixing, followed by global average pooling and a compact classification head. The key efficiency gain arises from the depthwise separable factorization, which decouples spatial filtering from channel-wise integration and reduces computation approximately 8–9 × relative to equivalent standard convolutions, yielding a total of only 979,651 parameters. We further introduce a progressive dropout schedule ( p ∈ {0.25, 0.25, 0.25, 0.50}) that imposes strongest regularization at the bottleneck transition, effectively curbing overfitting on the 766-image field dataset augmented to 6,262 samples. On the three-class freshness discrimination task—fresh, moderate, and stale—BeLFG-Net achieves 95.72% test accuracy with per-class F1-scores of 0.96, 0.96, and 0.95, outperforming ResNet-50 (93.77%) and MobileNetV2 (91.65%) while using 26 × and 3.5 × fewer parameters, respectively. Ablation experiments confirm that the hybrid depthwise separable block design, progressive dropout, and global average pooling each contribute independently to generalization, with combined improvements of + 6.76 % over a standard CNN baseline. These results establish that domain-specific lightweight architectures can deliver high-accuracy post-harvest classification under the resource constraints common to agricultural edge deployments.

title: Towards a Sustainable Food Supply Chain: Digital Transformation via Blockchain, IoT and AI
abstract: Supply chain management (SCM) plays a pivotal role in achieving competitive advantage, enhancing customer value, and ensuring efficient transformation of raw materials into finished food products. However, the increasing complexity and globalization of agri-food supply chains (AFSCs) have intensified challenges related to food safety, waste management, traceability, and sustainability. In response, digital transformation driven by Industry 4.0 technologies, particularly Blockchain, Internet of Things (IoT), and Artificial Intelligence (AI), has emerged as a critical enabler of sustainable food systems. This review critically examines the role of these technologies in enhancing transparency, efficiency, and resilience across food supply chains. Blockchain ensures secure, immutable, and transparent data sharing, thereby improving traceability and trust among stakeholders. IoT facilitates real-time monitoring of environmental and logistical parameters, reducing post-harvest losses and ensuring product quality. AI-driven analytics enable predictive decision-making, demand forecasting, and resource optimization, contributing to reduced food waste and improved operational performance. Collectively, these technologies support precision agriculture, smart logistics, and data-driven supply chain integration, thereby advancing sustainability goals. Despite these benefits, the adoption of digital technologies faces significant barriers, including high implementation costs, interoperability challenges, data privacy concerns, and limited technological infrastructure. This study highlights current advancements, identifies research gaps, and proposes future directions for scalable and secure digital integration to achieve sustainable and resilient food supply chains.

title: The Upgrading and Transformation of Farmer Professional Cooperative in the Digital Age: Insights from China Digital Village Policy
abstract: Farmer professional cooperatives are important vehicles for agricultural modernisation. In the digital age, the development of cooperatives has followed two typical pathways: upgrading in scale and transformation in business operations. Existing research has focused on the impact of digitalisation on the former, while paying less attention to the issue of structural transformation within cooperatives. To investigate this issue, this study constructs a difference-in-differences model based on a sample of data from Chinese farmer professional cooperatives. By leveraging the quasi-natural experiment of the digital village policy to construct variables, this study examines the impact of rural digitalisation on cooperative upgrading and transformation and analyses the mechanisms driving the divergence of cooperative development pathways. The study indicates that: (1) The China Digital Village Policy has had a significant positive impact on both the transformation and upgrading of farmer professional cooperatives. (2) Conditional on observable variables, the China Digital Village Policy is positively associated with cooperative upgrading and transformation, with patterns consistent with potential pathways through information channel capability and technological innovation capability. (3) Under the same observable-variable constraints, market expansion capability and capital acquisition capability show conditional association patterns that are significantly positively associated with cooperative upgrading. For cooperative transformation, however, they show conditional suppression patterns. This indicates that agricultural digitalisation is closely linked to cooperative upgrading and transformation. The differentiated empirical patterns of digitalisation along the dimensions of information channels, technological innovation, market expansion and capital acquisition provide empirical evidence for understanding the pathways of cooperative differentiation.

title: GLP-1 Revolution and Future of Food Systems: Current Evidence, Emerging Trends, & Projected Impacts
abstract: Background The rapid adoption of glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) and dual incretin therapies, particularly semaglutide and tirzepatide, represents a transformative development in obesity management with implications extending beyond clinical practice. Originally developed for type 2 diabetes, these therapies induce substantial and sustained weight loss by suppressing appetite, enhancing satiety, and altering food preferences, with the potential to reshape population-level food consumption. Despite extensive evidence of their clinical efficacy, their broader implications for food systems remain largely unexplored. Scope and approach This narrative review synthesises peer-reviewed clinical, nutritional, consumer-behaviour, and food-system evidence alongside industry and market intelligence. To address the limitations of the current data landscape, evidence was classified into three distinct tiers established, emerging, or scenario-based according to the methodology and empirical strength of the supporting data. Drawing on literature from nutrition, consumer behaviour, agricultural economics, and food systems science, the review evaluates potential impacts across agricultural production, food manufacturing, retail, food service, and global supply chains. Key findings and conclusions Increasing GLP-1 adoption may contribute to changes in food purchasing, product reformulation, marketing and retail strategies, and demand for nutrient-dense and protein-rich foods. However, empirical evidence for population-level food-system effects remains limited and heterogeneous. Much of the available data is derived from short-term clinical trials, localized observational analyses, household purchasing data, and commercial industry reports rather than long-term, population-scale systems studies. The review identifies key knowledge gaps, including the critical need to quantify long-term dietary transitions, treatment persistence, and their subsequent consequences for global food production, resource use, and environmental sustainability. By integrating evidence across health, nutrition, and food systems disciplines, this review provides an interdisciplinary framework for examining how sustained GLP-1 use could hypothetically influence food demand and the wider food economy, while highlighting priorities for future empirical research and policy preparedness.

title: Traditional Knowledge of Edible Non-Timber Forest Products in Africa: Research Trends and Contributions to Food Security, Human Health, and Livelihoods
abstract: Traditional knowledge related to edible non-timber forest products (NTFPs) plays a crucial role in supporting food security, nutrition, and livelihoods in forest-dependent communities across Africa. While global syntheses have examined research on edible NTFPs, the continent-wide patterns and research orientations within Africa remain insufficiently understood. To address this gap, this study analyzes research trends concerning traditional knowledge related to edible NTFPs using the African subset ( N = 162) of a global dataset. The dataset was developed through a Scopus-based search targeting studies at the intersection of traditional knowledge, edible resources, and NTFPs. The analysis examined geographic and temporal distributions, NTFP categories, reported impacts, research methods, and keyword occurrence patterns in Africa. The results reveal a pronounced geographic concentration of research, with studies clustered in a limited number of countries, particularly Ethiopia, South Africa, and Uganda, while Central Africa remains substantially underrepresented. Methodologically, African studies of traditional knowledge related to NTFPs rely predominantly on interview-based ethnobotanical approaches, whereas laboratory-based nutritional or biochemical analyses remain rare. Medicinal plants constitute the dominant focus of research, reflecting a broader emphasis on health-related applications. Although descriptive studies documenting the use of medicinal herbs are widespread, relatively little attention has been given to commercialization, value-chain development, and industrial applications. Traditional knowledge contributes to biodiversity conservation and sustainable resource management through locally embedded knowledge systems and management practices. These findings suggest that future research on traditional knowledge related to edible NTFPs should adopt a more strategic perspective that incorporates value addition, market development, and livelihood enhancement. Expanding thematic coverage, geographic representation, and methodological diversity would strengthen the contribution of traditional knowledge to food security, nutrition, and sustainable rural development across Africa.

title: Lippia alba essential oil as a botanical biopesticide: From chemotype diversity, crop protection potential, and value chain challenges
abstract: Growing concerns regarding the environmental and health impacts of synthetic pesticides have intensified the search for sustainable crop protection alternatives. Among plant-derived bioproducts, essential oils (EOs) have attracted increasing attention due to their broad-spectrum biological activities and favourable environmental profile. In this context, Lippia alba (Mill.) N.E.Br. ex Britton & P. Wilson ( L. alba , Verbenaceae), a chemically diverse and agronomically adaptable aromatic species, has emerged as a promising source of botanical biopesticides. This review synthesizes current knowledge on the geographical distribution, agronomic characteristics, EO yield, and chemotype variability of L. alba . Particular attention is given to the relationship between chemical composition and biological activity, highlighting the insecticidal, fungicidal, nematicidal, bactericidal, and acaricidal properties reported against major agricultural pests and pathogens. Available evidence indicates that citral-, carvone-, and linalool-rich chemotypes are among the most promising profiles for crop protection applications. Beyond biological efficacy, this review examines the opportunities and limitations associated with the valorization of L. alba EO as a commercial biopesticide. The species benefits from broad ecological adaptability, ease of propagation, and growing demand for bio-based crop protection products. However, large-scale deployment remains constrained by chemotype variability, standardization challenges, formulation limitations, insufficient field validation, and regulatory barriers. By integrating agronomic, chemical, biological, technological, and socio-economic perspectives, this review identifies key knowledge gaps and highlights strategic priorities to support the development of L. alba EO as a sustainable biopesticide within agroecological and bioeconomy-oriented production systems.

title: Deep learning-based multi-view perception and adaptive grasp pose correction for cooperative dual-arm fruit harvesting under occlusion
abstract: This study presents a failure-recovery cooperative harvesting pipeline for a dual-arm agricultural robot, where each arm harvests independently and switches to cooperative manipulation only when a single-view grasp on an occluded fruit fails. Such cooperation is necessary because accurate grasp pose inference degrades substantially when target fruits are heavily occluded by surrounding foliage or branches; existing approaches, including explicit 6D pose estimation and shape-completion-based methods, depend on reconstructing geometric information that is often unavailable under heavy occlusion. To address this limitation, the proposed framework, referred to as the Cooperative Active Harvesting Robot Scheme (Co-AHRS), integrates direct grasp pose inference from incomplete point clouds, active multi-view perception, and closed-loop visual servoing. Instead of reconstructing hidden geometry, the framework leverages Contact-GraspNet to generate feasible grasp candidates directly from partial observations. When the initial grasp attempt fails—due to either inaccurate pose inference under heavy occlusion or physical displacement of the target fruit during approach—the opposite arm is reassigned as an auxiliary observer whose upward-facing viewpoint enables closed-loop visual servoing, continuously estimating the 3D positional error between the gripper and the target fruit for real-time pose correction. The Co-AHRS was evaluated through a laboratory implementation and achieved harvest success rates of 89.2% and 78.5% under unoccluded and occluded conditions, respectively. The proposed framework also substantially outperformed frustum-based localization (75.0% and 55.2%) and explicit 6D pose estimation (57.1% and 7.7%). A further evaluation on a second configuration built from two same-model manipulators verified that the two arms harvest in parallel and quantified the occluded condition by a visible surface ratio of 0.549 ± 0.101. These results demonstrate that direct grasp inference combined with cooperative multi-view visual feedback is an effective strategy for autonomous fruit harvesting in occlusion-prone orchard environments.

title: Modeling Incentive‐Driven Cooperation in Agricultural Water Use Under Unequal Withdrawal Condition
abstract: Abstract Water allocation has long been framed as a general optimization problem in which users compete for a finite resource, leading much of the existing literature to adopt a top‐down perspective on how water should be distributed among users. However, in practice, water withdrawals may also be influenced by physical access and operational arrangements, such as direct abstraction from river channels through intake facilities for agricultural and industrial use. In such systems, disparities may arise between institutional allocation principles and effective access to water during shortage conditions, potentially creating asymmetric impacts among upstream, midstream, and downstream stakeholders. This study quantifies these impact asymmetries across river locations and evaluates stage‐based intake restriction strategies designed to mitigate inequitable outcomes during droughts. The proposed framework is applied to the Yeongsan River Basin in southwestern Korea through computational experiments to demonstrate how drought‐stage‐based intake regulations can improve both net profit and equity among stakeholders. A game‐theoretic approach is further employed to assess the potential for compensation across Pareto‐optimal solutions by examining whether the additional gains generated under cooperation are sufficient to offset stakeholder losses relative to the non‐cooperative baseline. The analysis is extended to projected scenarios of intensified climatic and socio‐economic droughts to assess the robustness of the proposed policies under future stress conditions. Through this approach, the study introduces a generalized framework for identifying water allocation policies that reconcile efficiency, equity, and sustainability under institutional and hydrologic constraints.

title: Discrimination and material-need insecurities intersect in association with poor mental health among youth and young adults with type 1 diabetes
abstract: OBJECTIVE: Little is known about how perceived discrimination and material-need insecurities jointly contribute to poor mental health among youth and young adults (YYA) with diabetes. We examined how these factors intersect to influence mental health among YYA with type 1 diabetes. METHOD: Analyses included 829 YYA with type 1 diabetes from the SEARCH Food Security Cohort study. Classification tree analysis identified patterns among perceived discrimination, material-need insecurities, demographic, and socioeconomic characteristics that distinguish between moderate-to-severe and minimal-to-mild depressive and anxiety symptoms assessed using the Center for Epidemiological Studies-Depression and the 7-item Generalized Anxiety Disorder scales. Material-need insecurities included household food insecurity, housing, and transportation insecurity. RESULTS: Overall, 35.6% of participants reported moderate-to-severe depressive symptoms and 27.6% reported moderate-to-severe anxiety symptoms. Discrimination intersected with food insecurity among YYA with type 1 diabetes such that 86% of those experiencing greater discrimination and food insecurity reported moderate-to-severe depressive symptoms compared to 47% among the food secure group. In those reporting less discrimination, 56% of those with food insecurity reported moderate to severe depressive symptoms compared to 17% among the food secure group. For anxiety, 56% of those with food insecurity reported moderate-to-severe symptoms among those who were food secure, 40.4% of those with greater discrimination and 16.8% of those with less discrimination reported moderate-to-severe anxiety symptoms. Adding discrimination to models which included food insecurity and demographic measures improved prediction accuracy (AUC=0.71 versus AUC=0.64 for depressive and AUC=0.68 versus AUC=0.64 for anxiety symptoms). CONCLUSIONS: Addressing household food insecurity and discrimination may help to decrease mental health problems among YYA with type 1 diabetes.

title: Climate-driven agricultural migration improves livelihoods but risks nationalizing deforestation and climate vulnerability: evidence from Kafinda game management area in Zambia
abstract: Climate variability, worsened by extensive deforestation from traditional animal-drawn farming involving complete clearing and stump burning, is exacerbating drought in Zambia's Southern Province. This is driving local Tonga-speaking farming communities to permanently migrate to higher-rainfall regions. However, the livelihood and environmental consequences of this movement remain poorly quantified. From 2020 to 2025, we used a mixed-methods approach combining structured surveys, interviews, transect walks and satellite imagery analysis to establish the consequences of this migration. We evaluated crop yields, livelihoods, farming practices and forest cover change among 87 migrant households across six villages in Kafinda Game Management Area (KGMA), Chitambo District. Among migrant households, maize yields increased dramatically from about 10 to 72 tons and revenue from ZMW 70,000 to 464,100 per household. This resulted in marked improvements in food security (53% to 87%) and in households' ability to afford quality health services (43% to 84%), decent shelter (38% to 77%), quality clothing (48% to 96%) and education (49% to 93%). However, 85% of these households continued with deforestation-prone animal-drawn farming in KGMA, with only 15% adopting climate-smart practices. As a result, mean farm size expanded from 4.48 ha to 30.9 ha, causing a 32.7% forest cover loss (42,549 ha to 26,026 ha) within Community Forest Management Areas. As the first assessment in KGMA buffering Kasanka National Park, our results show permanent climate-driven migration improves livelihoods but transfers climate vulnerability via deforestation. Continued unsustainable farming risks nationalizing localized degradation. Culturally compatible climate-smart farming practices are urgently needed to ensure sustainable livelihood gains and foster genuine national climate resilience.

title: Determinants of acute malnutrition among children aged 6-59 months in public hospitals of the Eastern zone Tigray, Ethiopia
abstract: Background Malnutrition is a global public health concern. While Africa and Ethiopia face significant nutritional challenges, the Tigray region faces a disproportionately high burden of child under nutrition, with a recent 2024 Global acute malnutrition (GAM) rates of 44.3%. This crisis is severely exacerbated by recent conflict, mass displacement, and the collapse of health infrastructure. Consequently, the rate of acute malnutrition in Tigray following the recent armed conflict is substantially higher than prior to the armed conflict. However, while a few studies highlight the prevalence of acute malnutrition in Tigray following the conflict, no study has yet been conducted to identify the determinant factors of acute malnutrition in the study area. Objective To identify the determinants of acute malnutrition among children aged6 to 59 month s in public hospitals of the Eastern zone Tigray, Ethiopia,2025. Methodology An institutional-based unmatched case control study was carried out among 402 study participants with a 1:2 case to control ratio(134 cases and 268 controls)in public hospitals of the Eastern zone Tigray from March 1 to June 30, 2025.A systematic sampling method was used, and Data were collected via Kobo Toolbox and exported to Microsoft Excel for data cleaning, then imported into SPSS version 25 for analysis. Multivariable logistic regression identified determinants using Adjusted odds ratio (AOR) with 95 % confidence interval (CI) at p- value< 0.05.To assess the model fitness, Hosmer-Lemeshow goodness-of-fit test was applied. Result A 100% response rate was achieved. Female child (AOR=3.2, 95% CI:1.792-5.641), poor dietary diversity (AOR= 5.64, 95% CI:3.004-10.576), household food insecurity (AOR= 3.32, 95% CI: 1.772-6.213 ),acute respiratory tract infection (AOR= 2.24, 95% CI:1.222-4.094), incomplete vaccination (AOR=3.14, 95% CI: 1.132-8.692 ), and lack of infant and young child feeding (IYCF) counseling (AOR=2.64, 95% CI:1.152-6.049) were the determinants of acute malnutrition. The Hosmer-Lemeshow test indicated good model fit (p-value=.691). Conclusion This study identified that being female, poor dietary diversity, household food insecurity, acute respiratory infection, incomplete vaccination, and lack of IYCF counseling are the determinant factors for acute malnutrition. Targeted interventions are urgently needed to improving household food security, promoting dietary diversity, optimizing routine immunization and healthcare services, and expanding community-based IYCF counseling for mothers.

title: Fractional condensation of pyrolysis vapors from Eucalyptus globulus biomass residues in an auger reactor prototype: a comparative study
journal: Journal of Analytical and Applied Pyrolysis
abstract: The study evaluates the influence of condensation stages (2–4) and set-point temperatures on the fractional condensation of pyrolysis vapors from residual Eucalyptus globulus biomass using a prototype-scale continuous auger reactor. Fractional condensation with two or three stages effectively recovered bio-oil fractions with low water content and selective enrichment of compound groups. During E. globulus branches pyrolysis, heavy phenolic compounds and anhydrosugars concentrated above 110 ºC, while light phenolic compounds, furans, and organic acids predominated above 60 ºC, and terpenic compounds were preferentially collected bellow 60 ºC. Stage 1 at 110 ºC yielded the largest organic fraction (34-46%wt.), low water content (< 8%wt.), high heating value (> 29 MJ/kg), high carbon (> 65%wt.) and low oxygen content (< 20%wt.), indicating potential for energy applications, refinery co-processing, biofuels upgrading, and chemicals production. Light fractions (<110 ºC), although water-rich (> 75%wt.), exhibited chemical profiles suitable for anaerobic digestion and agricultural use. Biomass type influenced bio-oil properties and fractionation behavior. Branches pyrolysis produced heavy fractions richer in carbon, aliphatic, and terpenic compounds, with lower oxygen content, while sawdust showed greater recovery of organic compounds from the light fraction into the heavy fraction, but with less improvement in bio-oil quality after fractionation. ¹H NMR revealed a high abundance of aliphatic compounds in all HFs, especially from branches, contrasting with GC-MS results and highlighting the importance of using complementary characterization techniques. Future research should assess the long-term stability of bio-oil fractions to support their integration into chemical and energy value chains.

title: Low self-reported awareness of and participation in school food programs among Canadian youth: Trends from secondary analysis of cross-sectional surveys from 2019 to 2023
journal: Journal of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics
abstract: BACKGROUND: School food programs (SFPs) provide access to nutritious food, particularly for youth from food-insecure households. There is limited population-level data on participation in Canadian SFPs over time. OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to examine trends in self-reported awareness of and participation in SFPs among Canadian youth, including differences across sociodemographic and food insecurity groups. DESIGN: This study was a secondary analysis of repeat cross-sectional data from national surveys conducted annually from 2019 to 2023. Data were not collected from Northwest Territories, Yukon, and Nunavut. PARTICIPANTS/SETTING: A total of 16173 youth aged 10 to 17 years residing in Canada participated in the study. MAIN OUTCOME MEASURES: The main outcome measures observed were youth self-reported school breakfast and lunch program awareness and participation. STATISTICAL ANALYSES: Weighted logistic regression models examined changes in breakfast or lunch program self-reported awareness and self-reported participation across survey years and by sex, age, province, and household food insecurity.
