RESULTS: Across all years, less than 30% of youth reported awareness of a breakfast program and approximately 7.5-13.9% of youth reported participation in a breakfast program. In the same period, 16.2% or fewer youth reported awareness of a lunch program and 4.5-9.1% reported participation in a lunch program. Decreases in self-reported participation coinciding with the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic were observed in 2020 for both breakfast (OR=0.59; 95% CI: 0.50, 0.71; p< 0.001) and lunch programs (OR=0.73; 95% CI: 0.58, 0.92; p=0.009), followed by a return to pre-pandemic levels by 2023. Self-reported participation in SFPs was associated with household food insecurity, race, and province of residence (all contrasts p<0.001). Less than one-third of youth from food-insecure households reported participation. CONCLUSION: Despite decreases in participation in 2020, no statistically significant change in self-reported participation was observed between 2019 and 2023, with self-reported participation highest among youth experiencing food insecurity.

title: Sustainable agriculture intensification: An MCE model analysis of yam farmland suitability in Ghana
abstract: Yam production is important in West Africa due to its contribution to food security, the economy, and increasing demand in international markets. Thus, recent statistics show that about 94% of global yam production is in the sub-region. However, current yam farming approaches are unsustainable and result in land degradation and deforestation. This study employs Multi-Criteria Evaluation (MCE) model in GIS to identify suitable sites for sustainable yam farming in Ghana, needed to minimize the environmental impacts of intensive production while maximizing yields to achieve food security. The model results showed mixed site suitability within the yam growing belt in Ghana. About 52.51% of the total suitable lands are located within the Guinea Savannah, while 98% of the evaluated area in the Transitional Forest Belt could support sustainable intensification. However, there is a need to target specific areas for intensification even within these climate zones. The result further showed a higher likelihood of farmers encroaching into protected environmental areas (e.g., 70.49% overlap), highlighting the need for policies to prevent such practices. These findings provide useful information for local and national efforts towards promoting sustainable yam production in Ghana and other parts of Africa. By applying an MCE model, we provide a foundation for collaborative regional and national strategies to maintain or restore farmlands for yam production through multicriteria assessment.

title: Migration Role in Proactive and Reactive Adaptation to Perceived Climate Risks in Ethiopia
abstract: Climate change threatens agricultural sustainability and food security, particularly in developing countries like Ethiopia. This study examined household adaptation types to climate risk perception in Oromia and the former Southern Nations, Nationalities, and Peoples’ (SNNP) regions. A cross-sectional design collected data through interviews with 1,024 households between September and December 2022. Using Bayesian multilevel multinomial logistic regression, key determinants of adaptation choices were identified. Households with social network support were 7.33 times more likely to adopt reactive adaptation compared to no adaptation, and 4.08 times more likely to adopt combined reactive and proactive strategies. Wealthier households were 5.07 times more likely to adopt proactive adaptation and 3.43 times more likely to adopt both strategies compared to the poorest households. Household heads with secondary or higher education were 5.43 times more likely to adopt reactive adaptation than those who could not read or write, while primary education was associated with a 2.48-fold increase in proactive adaptation. Perceptions of flood risk and erratic rainfall increased the likelihood of adopting reactive, proactive, and combined strategies, with relative risk ratios (RRRs) ranging from 1.08 to 1.19. Larger household size and higher adaptive capacity were positively associated with proactive and combined adaptations. In contrast, higher psychosocial well-being was linked to a lower likelihood of reactive adaptation (RRR = 0.86) but a slightly higher likelihood of proactive adaptation (RRR = 1.08). At the community level, households in low-poverty areas were 4.05 times more likely to adopt combined strategies than those in high-poverty areas. Migration history also influenced adaptation, with non-migrant households being less likely to adopt proactive strategies (RRR = 0.33). These findings highlight the multifaceted social, economic, educational, and perceptual factors shaping climate adaptation, underscoring the need for targeted interventions to strengthen resilience in vulnerable communities.

title: The social acceptance of agrivoltaics: Exploring the cognitive and affective outcomes of technological, contextual, and personal beliefs
abstract: Agrivoltaics -the co-siting of photovoltaic energy and agronomic production- has been promoted as a win-win solution to reconcile renewables expansion with food security, yet its deployment has raised ambivalence and public opposition. Existing studies have largely focused on farmers and experts, leaving lay citizens’ views underexplored. This paper addresses that gap by examining the determinants of agrivoltaics’ acceptance among non-experts. Acceptance was assessed through the integrated Sustainable Energy Technology Acceptance framework, further extended by introducing outcome evaluation as both a cognitive (perceived efficacy) and an affective (positive emotions) pathway to acceptability, and by incorporating anticipatory solastalgia, understood as present distress over anticipated landscape change. A convenience sample of Italian citizens (N = 849), mostly residing in urban or semi‑urban areas, completed an online questionnaire during the early phase of APV implementation in Italy, thus providing anticipatory evaluations. Hierarchical regressions and path analyses show that technological beliefs, especially perceptions of global and local sustainability, are the strongest predictors of agrivoltaics’ acceptability. Contextual beliefs, notably legitimacy, fairness, and trust in agrivoltaics’ technical-scientific actors, further enhance acceptability. Personal beliefs contribute as well: injunctive norms encourage acceptability, whereas anticipatory solastalgia significantly hinders it. The findings provide a quantitative baseline against which context-specific case studies can be interpreted as installations spread across the territory in the future. Findings suggest that policy and communication should highlight agrivoltaics’ environmental and socio-economic benefits and engage local experts rather than political actors; implications concerning landscape framing are advanced as hypotheses to be tested with affected populations.

title: Home and wild food procurement interacts with local food purchasing to improve dietary quality among food-insecure households: Evidence from a cross-sectional study in two rural U.S. States
abstract: This study uses cross-sectional survey data (n = 1,438) from Maine and Vermont, USA, to examine how home and wild food procurement (HWFP, including fishing, foraging, gardening, hunting, and raising backyard animals) and direct-to-consumer (DTC) purchasing correlate with dietary quality, measured using the Prime Diet Quality Score. Food-insecure respondents relied more on HWFP, while food-secure respondents relied more on DTC outlets. Both were associated with higher dietary quality, especially among food-insecure individuals, though combining both strategies was associated with diminishing returns. These findings suggest the potential value of policies promoting access to these food procurement strategies.

title: Hegemonic sustainability: Examining narratives and imbalanced power dynamics in supply chain governance
abstract: This study examines how sustainability narratives are constructed, legitimised, and contested within power-imbalanced supply chains. Drawing on the concept of cultural hegemony, the study offers insights into how dominant sustainability meanings become accepted as legitimate and taken-for-granted, even when they generate uneven outcomes for weaker actors. The research is conducted in the UK dairy supply chain, a highly regulated business-to-business context. Drawing on semi-structured interviews with retailers, processors, farmers, and industry representatives, we develop a qualitative, theory-building account of hegemonic sustainability governance. Findings identify four mechanisms through which sustainability narratives are stabilised and challenged: (1) narrative framing around measurability and auditability, (2) legitimisation through consent and voluntariness, (3) marginalisation of alternative sustainability concerns grounded in lived producer constraints, and (4) incipient counter-hegemonic mobilisation through horizontal collaboration and alternative legitimacy-building. The study contributes to sustainable supply chain governance research by conceptualising sustainability narratives as a hegemonic governance mechanism and helping explain the persistence of dominant sustainability arrangements beyond coercive power. Regarding social implications, findings suggest that industry frameworks can marginalise weaker actors under the guise of sustainability compliance. The study calls on managers and policymakers to recognise narrative dominance, move beyond molecular changes, and adopt inclusive governance that protects vulnerable actors.

title: Promising Practices to Promote Snap at Schools: A Quantitative Analysis of Snap Outreach Efforts
abstract: BACKGROUND: In 2023, 17.9% of US households with children experienced food insecurity. While the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) aims to reduce food insecurity, persistent under-enrollment, labeled the "SNAP Gap," limits its impact. Schools represent a strategic yet underutilized setting to reach eligible families. This study examined school-based strategies to increase caregivers' awareness and knowledge of SNAP. METHODS: Twelve diverse school districts implemented stigma-free SNAP outreach initiatives, reaching 8601 participants across 37 outreach events statewide. Caregiver knowledge and perceptions about SNAP were then assessed via online retrospective post-then-pre surveys and analyzed using descriptive statistics and chi-square tests. RESULTS: Among caregivers (n = 1144), SNAP outreach was associated with statistically significant increases in knowledge (p < 0.001), including awareness of benefits, eligibility, application sites, and available assistance. IMPLICATIONS FOR SCHOOL HEALTH POLICY, PRACTICE, AND EQUITY: Tailored, school-based outreach can reduce stigma, normalize use, and increase knowledge of SNAP. Partnerships with community organizations enhance support while minimizing school staff burden. CONCLUSIONS: Schools are effective access points for narrowing the SNAP Gap through outreach, education, and stigma reduction. Future research should examine student perspectives on SNAP and school meal program participation.

title: Prevalence and determinants of food insecurity among displaced and vulnerable adolescents in accommodation centers in Metuge (Cabo Delgado) and KaMavota (Maputo City), Mozambique
abstract: Food insecurity constitutes a major public health problem, particularly in the contexts of forced displacement, poverty, and socioeconomic vulnerability, and significantly affects adolescents’ health, nutrition, and development. However, evidence on the magnitude and factors associated with food insecurity among adolescents remains limited. The present study aimed to determine the prevalence and factors associated with food insecurity among adolescents aged 15 to 19 years living in situations of displacement and vulnerability in the districts of Metuge, Cabo Delgado Province, and KaMavota, Maputo city. This cross-sectional study involved 341 adolescents aged 15–19 years who were selected through stratified probabilistic sampling in the districts of Metuge and KaMavota. Data collection was carried out through semistructured interviews via the Household Food Insecurity Access Scale (HFIAS), adapted to the local context. Descriptive statistics were used to summarize participant characteristics. Associations between independent variables and food insecurity were initially assessed using Pearson’s chi-square test. Variables with p < 0.20 were included in a multivariable logistic regression model. Adjusted odds ratios (AORs) and 95% confidence intervals (95% CI) were estimated, and statistical significance was set at p < 0.05. Model fit and multicollinearity were assessed. All analyses were conducted using SPSS version 28. The results revealed that more than 9 out of every 10 adolescents experienced food insecurity, with a prevalence of severe food insecurity of 96.6%, which was higher in Metuge (97.8%) than in KaMavota (92%). Adolescents reported consuming, on average, two meals per day, whereas a considerable proportion of those in Metuge consumed only one meal daily. Significant associations were observed between food insecurity and factors such as weight, height, body mass index, BMI classification, educational level, type of household occupation, and monthly household income. The dietary diversity was lower in Metuge, whereas KaMavota presented greater consumption of processed foods. Food insecurity is highly prevalent among adolescents living in accommodation centers in Metuge and KaMavota, affecting a substantial proportion of the study population. These findings indicate that food insecurity remains a severe, persistent, and multidimensional challenge in these settings and may adversely affect adolescent health, growth, and development. The results underscore the urgent need for integrated and multisectoral interventions that extend beyond immediate food assistance, including strengthened social protection, improved livelihood opportunities, enhanced access to education, greater dietary diversity, and targeted health, nutrition, and income-generation programs for adolescents and their parents/caregivers in contexts of displacement and social vulnerability.

title: Impact of cluster-farm participation on wheat efficiency and commercialization: practices from Northwest Ethiopia
abstract: Introduction Cluster farming has increasingly been promoted as a collective agricultural approach to improve smallholder productivity, market integration, and rural livelihoods in Ethiopia. Using Collective Action Theory, this study examines the factors influencing farmers’ participation in wheat cluster farming and its impact on production efficiency, and household wheat commercialization. Methods A multi-stage sampling procedure was used to collect cross-sectional data from 384 wheat-producing households in Northwest Ethiopia. The association between cluster farming participation and wheat efficiency and commercialization level was estimated using an endogenous switching regression model. Results The probit results show that sex, family size, land size, livestock holding, cooperative membership, extension contact, cluster farming-specific training and awareness are positively associated with participation in cluster farming, while distance from the cluster farming site is negatively associated with participation. The ESR estimates further suggest that participation in cluster farming has a significant positive impact on production efficiency and commercialization. The estimated ATT shows that participation increases technical efficiency (0.383), allocative efficiency (0.252), economic efficiency (0.105), and commercialization level (0.252). Similarly, the ATU estimates indicate significant potential benefits for non-participating households if they participate, with increases of 0.398, 0.291, 0.152, and 0.274 in TE, AE, EE, and HCI, respectively. The robustness propensity score matching result also confirms the ESR findings. Conclusion The results imply that collective farming is associated with farm performance through better access to productive resources, improved institutional support, reduced transaction costs, and enhanced market integration. The results highlight the need for fostering inclusive cluster farming through specific extension services, support to cooperatives, and better access to cluster sites, which is associated with the efficiency and commercialization level of farmers.

title: From income diversification to market vulnerability: the risk–reward dynamics in Tanzanian horticultural value chains
abstract: Introduction Export-oriented horticulture can generate substantial income and create market opportunities for smallholders, yet the governance of exchange may simultaneously create, redistribute or intensify risks. This study examines how governance arrangements shape risk–reward dynamics in orange, avocado and snow peas export value chains in Tanga Region, Tanzania. The cases represent informal, semi-formal and formal coordination, respectively. Methods Drawing from Social Exchange Theory, the study analyses how trust, dependency, power asymmetry and commitment operate through pricing, grading, payment, technical support and market access. Evidence was generated from 20 focus group discussions involving 179 participants, 23 in-depth interviews and nine key informant interviews, and analysed through deductive and inductive qualitative content analysis. Results Findings show that governance does not merely determine access to rewards; it conditions where risks emerge, how they are transmitted, and who ultimately bears them. Informal orange exchange sustained flexible market participation but exposed farmers to opaque pricing, selection and counting practices. Semi-formal avocado arrangements facilitated export access while concentrating grading, information and purchasing power among intermediaries. Formal coordination of snow peas reduced production and market-entry constraints through bundled services, but dependence on a dominant buyer concentrated systemic exposure, magnifying losses following the buyer withdrawal. Discussion Across cases, governance also mediated economic consequences of production and climatic shocks. The study demonstrates that greater coordination does not inherently reduce vulnerability, rather, it reconfigures risk. Effective governance therefore requires transparency, accountability, enforceable safeguards, diversified market access and mechanisms for sharing concentrated risks, while preserving the benefits generated by coordination.

title: Personality traits, nutritional knowledge, and social capital as determinants of livelihood diversification under disaster risk: Evidence from livestock households in rural Indonesia
abstract: Building resilience in rural livelihoods against disasters and climate change is a major global challenge. Most existing models of livelihood diversification and disaster adaptation focus mainly on structural and economic factors, with less attention to the household behavioral and psychological characteristics that shape adaptive decision making under repeated shocks. This study examines how personality traits mediate the relationships between nutritional knowledge, market integration, and social capital, and the livelihood diversification strategies of livestock-raising households. In doing so, it addresses a gap in disaster risk and rural development research, which rarely incorporates psychological traits into diversification models. The research focuses on livestock households in disaster-prone regions of Indonesia: Aceh, Nusa Tenggara Timur, and South Sulawesi. Using data from a cross-sectional survey of 602 such households (response rate ≈ 94%), the study applied Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) to examine mediation and moderation relationships among structural, cognitive, and behavioral factors. The measurement model showed reliability and validity (CR ≥ 0.70; AVE ≥ 0.50 with all indicator loadings above 0.70). The results indicate that nutritional knowledge and social capital are positively associated with livelihood diversification, both directly and indirectly through personality traits. Market integration, by contrast, had no significant direct association with diversification but did operate indirectly through personality traits, showing the importance of behavioral pathways that connect structural opportunities to livelihood strategies. Among the structural model factors, personality traits showed the strongest direct association with diversification, which suggests that behavioral dispositions are important determinants of livelihood diversification. Farm size significantly moderated the relationship between personality traits and diversification, meaning that resilience strategies differ by operational scale. By incorporating psychological factors into diversification models, this study offers new empirical evidence that livelihood resilience arises from the interaction between external resources and internal behavioral capacities. These findings suggest the potential value of combined interventions that pair nutrition education with behavioral skill building, strengthen market participation alongside entrepreneurial and risk management skills, and tailor social capital efforts to differences in farm scale. This research contributes to disaster risk and rural development scholarship by proposing a behavioral structural framework that integrates psychological traits with nutrition knowledge, market integration, and social capital to explain livelihood diversification among climate-vulnerable agricultural households.

title: Determinants of farmers’ willingness to adopt technologies for the agroecological and precision management of potato pests and diseases in Rwanda
abstract: Introduction Potato ( Solanum tuberosum L. ) production in Rwanda is limited by pests and diseases, resulting in significant yield losses and increased use of synthetic pesticides. Despite growing interest in sustainable agriculture, few studies provide empirical evidence on farmers’ knowledge of agroecological pest management practices and precision agriculture in Rwanda. This study assessed farmers’ management practices, awareness and perceptions of agroecological practices and precision agriculture technologies, as well as factors that may influence the willingness to adopt precision agriculture tools in smallholder potato systems. Methods A farm household survey using a semi-structured questionnaire was conducted among 223 potato farmers in three districts of Rwanda (i.e., Rubavu, Gicumbi, and Nyamagabe) in July 2025. Descriptive statistics, Chi square tests, and Fisher’s exact tests were used to analyze farmers’ practices and perceptions. A Firth-penalized logistic regression model, constructed based on a purposeful selection of covariates strategy, was used to identify factors associated with farmers’ willingness to adopt precision agriculture technologies. Results Findings revealed that pests and diseases were the main production constraints, with bacterial wilt, viruses, late blight, and whiteflies being the most frequently cited. Farmers primarily used synthetic pesticides to manage aerial pests and foliar diseases, while preventive agronomic practices were used to manage soil-borne pests and diseases. The use of biopesticides remained extremely limited and farmers were aware of the negative impacts of pesticide misuse and expressed a strong willingness to adopt better pest management practices. Knowledge of precision agriculture technologies was mainly limited (79%). Farmers associated precision agriculture primarily with mechanization, whereas awareness of drones, sensors and digital decision-support tools was limited. They demonstrated highly positive perceptions toward precision agriculture (90%) and a strong willingness to learn more (87%). The results of the logistic regression showed that mobile phone usage (OR = 20.58, p < 0.01) and the willingness to adopt agroecological practices (OR = 67.73, p < 0.001) were associated with a higher likelihood of expressing willingness to adopt precision agriculture technologies. Discussion These results highlight the opportunity to integrate precision agroecology approaches in Rwanda. Mobile-based advisory systems and low-cost digital technologies could serve as effective entry points for promoting sustainable potato production systems among smallholder farmers.

title: Does rural digitalization improve food production security? Evidence from China’s digital village construction policy
abstract: Introduction Food production security (FPS) remains a core challenge for developing economies. Although rural digitalization serves as a fundamental strategy to reshape agricultural systems in developing countries, its impact on food supply resilience remains underexplored. Methods This study investigates the impact of rural digitalization on regional FPS by exploiting China’s Digital Village Construction policy as a quasi-natural experiment. We employ the DID model on a panel dataset comprising 334 prefecture-level cities from 2015 to 2024. Results The empirical results demonstrate that rural digitalization significantly improves regional FPS. Specifically, the digital intervention increases the FPS of treated cities by an average of 8.2 percent. Regarding the mechanisms, we find that rural digitalization enhances FPS by facilitating smallholders’ food production viability and promoting food-oriented land reallocation. Furthermore, heterogeneity analyses reveal that the impact is more pronounced in regions equipped with superior agricultural socialized services, advanced agricultural industry structures, and major food producing area designations. Discussion These findings demonstrate that comprehensive rural digitalization strengthens the resilience of food production systems in developing economies and offer guidance for other Global South countries pursuing similar rural development paradigms.

title: Mapping long-term fractional forest cover dynamics in the Leuser Ecosystem, Indonesia by integrating historical imagery and Landsat observations spanning the 1960s to 2020
abstract: A B S T R A C T The Leuser Ecosystem (LE), Indonesia, is one of the most important tropical forest landscapes, yet its long-term fractional forest cover (FFC) dynamics remain poorly documented because observations extending into the pre-Landsat era are limited. We integrated Corona imagery from 1965, Landsat MSS observations from 1972–1974, and multi-sensor Landsat data from 1988–2020 to reconstruct long-term FFC dynamics. Object-based image analysis (OBIA) was applied to Corona imagery to derive a 30 m historical FFC baseline, while PlanetScope-3B reference FFC was used to train a random forest (RF) model for Landsat-based FFC estimation, generating isolated FFC snapshots from the available MSS observations for 1972–1974. An adapted continuous change detection and classification (CCDC) framework subsequently reconstructed vegetation-index (VI) trajectories and generated date-specific daily FFC estimates from 10 January 1988 to 17 November 2020. Independent validation showed good agreement with PS-3B reference FFC (R 2 = 0.71, RMSE = 0.16), while complementary cross-product assessments using GFW-FFC for 2000 and 2010 (R 2 = 0.55 and 0.49, respectively) and three non-Landsat FFC products for 2020 revealed substantial product-dependent differences in cross-product agreement. Trend analysis for 1988–2020 identified significant positive FFC trends over 77.39% of the analyzed area, negative trends over 6.40%, and no significant trend over 16.21%. However, positive FFC did not necessarily represent natural forest recovery; selected trajectories in documented oil-palm and plantation landscapes showed post-disturbance FFC increases consistent with plantation establishment and canopy maturation. This study extends the temporal perspective of tropical FFC monitoring and provides a transferable framework for interpreting long-term forest-cover dynamics and supporting conservation and land-management planning.

title: Perceptions and Adaptive Responses to Soil Salinity in Irrigated Systems of the Abaya–Chamo Lakes Basin, Ethiopia
abstract: Soil salinization threatens agricultural sustainability, food security, and essential soil functions in arid and semi-arid regions, including Ethiopia's Abaya–Chamo Lakes Basin. This study assessed smallholder farmers' perceptions of soil salinity and their adaptive strategies within irrigated farming systems. A mixed-methods design was employed, drawing on household survey data from 380 farmers selected through multistage stratified random sampling across five purposively selected kebeles, complemented by key informant interviews, focus group discussions, and field observations. Data were analyzed using both descriptive and inferential statistical techniques: descriptive statistics summarized household profiles, farm-level attributes, and socioeconomic conditions, while multinomial logistic regression identified the determinants of adaptation choices. Most farmers rated salinity severity as severe (98.9%) and chronic (50.5%), while technical awareness of salinity dynamics remained moderate (51.3%). Salinity moderately affected cultivated land for 53.9% of respondents and caused severe yield losses for 65.0% of farmers, particularly in banana (43.2%) and maize (33.9%) production systems. Farmers' vulnerability was compounded by heavy dependence on on-farm income (47.9%) and limited livelihood diversification (81.6%). Dissatisfaction with institutional support for salinity management was widespread (91.9%), reflected in a low mean satisfaction score of 1.45. Farming experience, landholding size, labor availability, and income diversification significantly influenced adaptation and coping decisions. The findings reveal a capacity–vulnerability paradox, whereby better-resourced farmers adopt more advanced adaptation measures yet may still incur larger absolute income losses. Strengthening resilience in the study area therefore requires integrated interventions that combine technical salinity management, enhanced institutional support, and livelihood diversification.

title: First Report of Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. cubense Tropical Race 4 Causing Fusarium Wilt to Bananas in Ecuador
abstract: Banana (Musa spp.) is one of Ecuador's most important export commodities, valued at USD 3.6 billion in 2024, equating to nearly 3% of the national gross domestic product (GDP). The industry notably contributes to the advancement of the socio-economy of the country by employing around 2 million people throughout the supply chain (Sistema de Información Pública Agropecuaria 2026). In August 2025, typical vascular wilt symptoms were observed in three Cavendish banana plants on a 7-ha farm located in the Santa Rosa canton in El Oro province, Ecuador (3°27′12.22″ S, 79°55′55.86″ W). Affected plants displayed wilting and progressive leaf yellowing. Upon internal examination of the pseudostem, a distinct dark red to brown vascular discoloration was observed (Figure 1). Pseudostem samples were collected from two diseased plants, from which fungal isolations were made. Small pseudostem pieces where healthy and diseased tissue met were surface sterilized with a 70% ethanol solution for 30 s, plated onto potato dextrose agar (PDA) amended with 0.04 g/L streptomycin, and incubated for 7 days at 25°C. The two fungal colonies that developed, one from each diseased plant, were then purified, single-spored and deposited in the culture collection at Stellenbosch University (CAV 6135 and CAV 6136). Cultural and morphological characteristics of the two isolates were studied by growing the cultures on PDA and carnation leaf agar (CLA). White colonies with purple centers developed on PDA, while falcate macroconidia with two to five septa, abundant microconidia borne in false heads on short monophialides, and globose chlamydospores were observed on CLA after 10 days. Observed characteristics were typical of those of the Fusarium oxysporum species complex (Leslie and Summerell 2006). Molecular identification was then performed using a F. oxysporum f. sp. cubense tropical race 4 (Foc TR4)-specific polymerase chain reaction (PCR; Li et al. 2013) and two qPCR assays (Aguayo et al. 2017; Matthews et al. 2020). DNA extracted from the two Ecuadorian isolates was positively identified with amplification similar to that of the positive control. Vegetative compatibility (VCG) testing was also conducted by pairing nit mutants generated from the two Ecuadorian isolates with universal VCG testers of VCG 01213/16, and heterokaryon formation confirmed complementation (Leslie and Summerell 2006) (Figure 2). To confirm pathogenicity, the two Ecuadorian isolates and a reference strain of Foc TR4 (CAV 789, from Australia) were infected on 2-month-old Cavendish banana plants. Three plants were inoculated per isolate, and the experiment was repeated. During inoculation, roots were immersed in a conidial suspension (1 × 106 conidia/mL) for 2 h, while the negative control plants were treated with sterile water. Plants were planted in a 1:1:1 soil:sand:peat substrate and kept under controlled environmental conditions (27°C, 60% relative humidity). Within 4 weeks, the Foc TR4-inoculated plants developed typical Fusarium wilt symptoms, including foliar yellowing and internal rhizome necrosis. Negative control plants remained symptomless (Figure 3). The pathogen was re-isolated from symptomatic tissues and identified as Foc TR4 with a loop-mediated isothermal amplification assay (Ordóñez et al. 2019), thus fulfilling Koch's postulates and confirming the presence of the pathogen in Ecuador. The detection of Foc TR4 represents a significant threat to banana production in Ecuador and highlights the importance of continued surveillance and containment efforts.

title: Retail-driven variations in heavy metal contamination of commercial fruits and associated health risks in Bangladesh
journal: Journal of Food Composition and Analysis
abstract: Increasing fruit consumption requires effective monitoring of heavy metal contamination; however, supply chain-specific data remain limited. Therefore, this study quantified As, Pb, Cd, Cr, and Hg in five commercially important fruits (banana, guava, mango, papaya, and pineapple) collected from production sites, local markets, and supermarkets in Chattogram, Bangladesh, to assess contamination risks across the supply chain. Quantification via ICP-MS revealed that Cr was the most prevalent contaminant, peaking in mangoes (1.958 mg/kg). Hg concentrations in guavas (0.691 mg/kg) and bananas (0.478 mg/kg) exceeded the FAO/WHO limit. As no certified reference value for Hg was available, these results are considered preliminary and require independent confirmation. A strong correlation between As and Hg (r = 0.69) suggested a possible common source, whereas Pb exhibited a distinct pattern in the principal component analysis. The Hazard Index (HI) reached 24.60, with Hg accounting for 65.7% of the non-carcinogenic risk. The cumulative carcinogenic risk exceeded the acceptable threshold (1.0 × 10⁻⁴), primarily due to Cr, although these estimates are conservative because ICP-MS measured total Cr rather than Cr (VI). This study provides the first baseline data on heavy metal contamination in commercial fruits across the Chattogram supply chain, highlighting the need for targeted regulatory monitoring despite the study's cross-sectional design and limited sample size.

title: Oil palm fiber extract as a fermentable functional ingredient: in vitro gastrointestinal carbohydrate hydrolysis, feline fecal fermentation, and microbiota-associated metabolite production
journal: Frontiers in Food Science and Technology
abstract: Obesity-associated gastrointestinal disturbances in companion animals have increased interest in dietary ingredients that may modulate intestinal fermentation and microbial metabolism. This study evaluated the in vitro gastrointestinal digestion, fecal fermentation, microbiota responses, and metabolite production associated with oil palm fiber extract (OPF) in a feline gastrointestinal model. OPF, commercial feline diet (CFD), OPF-supplemented CFD (OPF+CFD), and commercial weight-control diet (WCD) were subjected to simulated gastrointestinal digestion followed by 24 h of anaerobic fecal fermentation. Fecal samples from nine cats were pooled to prepare a common inoculum. Carbohydrate hydrolysis of OPF following simulated gastrointestinal digestion was 4.01% ± 0.54%, indicating limited hydrolysis under the experimental conditions. Phenolic and flavonoid-equivalent responses were retained after digestion, although values exceeding 100% were interpreted as increased assay responses rather than recovery above the initial values. During fermentation, OPF was associated with increased concentrations of acetate, propionate, and butyrate, together with changes in branched-chain fatty acids. Microbiome profiling indicated treatment-associated changes in bacterial community composition and diversity patterns. LC-QTOF-MS analysis detected several phenolic-related metabolites in OPF-containing treatments after fermentation, including hydroxyphenylpropionic acid- and coumarin-related compounds. However, these metabolites were tentatively annotated, and their formation from specific OPF precursors was not directly demonstrated. Because each treatment was represented by a single fermentation vessel using the pooled fecal inoculum, analytical replicates were not considered independent biological replicates; consequently, microbiome and fermentation findings were interpreted descriptively. Overall, the results provide preliminary in vitro evidence that OPF can undergo gastrointestinal processing and subsequent fecal fermentation, with associated changes in fermentation metabolites and microbial community profiles. Further studies using independent donors, biological fermentation replicates, quantitative metabolite validation, and controlled feeding trials are required to establish the physiological relevance, efficacy, and safety of OPF in cats.

title: Groove angle and quenching medium in shielded metal arc welding of mild steel: Multi-criteria decision analysis, machine learning and energy absorption
abstract: Weld groove geometry and post-weld cooling regime are among the least systematically investigated factors influencing the performance of arc-welded joints, and even when they have been studied, the analysis has almost always been limited to a single optimisation criterion. This paper re-examines shielded metal arc welding of AISI/SAE 1020 mild steel across a 55–60° single-V groove range and three quenching media (air, water, palm oil), using six mechanical responses, and advances the analysis in four directions. First, a normalised Type III effect-share analysis establishes the practical rather than merely statistical weight of each factor: the quenching medium accounts for 70.3–94.6% of the estimated effect across the six responses, while groove angle accounts for 4.4–25.7%, and the factor interaction never exceeds 3.2%. Second, the tensile records are reconciled against the reported applied loads, recovering the specimen cross-sections actually used and permitting two derived responses that the original analysis did not report: the modulus of toughness, which orders the media 8.68, 5.96 and 3.66 MJ m⁻³ for air, water and palm oil, and the Hollomon strain-hardening exponent, obtained on true stress and true plastic strain axes, which falls from 0.528 for air-cooled weldments to 0.292 and 0.253 for water- and oil-quenched material. Third, four independent multi-criteria schemes, namely Shannon-entropy-weighted grey relational analysis, equal-weight grey relational analysis, the technique for order of preference by similarity to ideal solution, and Derringer–Suich desirability, are applied to the same candidate set, and all four return the same ordering. Fourth, machine-learning surrogates of the recovered stress–strain records locate where the medium acts: over the strain interval common to all three media a functional analysis of variance attributes only 1.16% of the stress variance to the medium, and truncating the comparison at that strain reverses the ordering, so the advantage of air cooling is one of extensibility rather than strength. Gaussian-process sampling returns credible intervals near ±9% on the toughness values and preserves the ranking in every draw. The convergence of four aggregation philosophies, combined with the independent evidence of the energy-absorption analysis, establishes a 60° single-V groove with unforced air cooling as a weight-robust rather than merely method-dependent optimum for structural weldments in thin-section low-carbon steel.

title: Comparative Study on Growth Performance, Carcass Yield, and Gut Morphology of Broilers Fed Soy Oil, Poultry Fat, Acidulated Fat, or Palm Oil
journal: The Journal of Applied Poultry Research
abstract: This study evaluated four dietary fat sources on growth performance, carcass yield, and intestinal morphometry in broiler chickens. A total of 1,152 male YPM × Ross 708 chicks were randomly assigned to 48 pens and fed diets containing soybean oil (SO), poultry fat (PF), acidulated fat (AF), or palm oil (PO). Body weight and feed intake were recorded weekly to calculate weight gain, feed intake, and feed conversion ratio (FCR). Intestinal development was assessed on day 42 by measuring villus height, crypt depth, and villus-to-crypt ratio. On day 43, nine birds per pen were processed to determine yields of breast fillet, thigh, drumstick, wing, and carcass yield. Data were analyzed using PROC ANOVA in SAS with significance at P ≤ 0.05. No differences were observed among treatments for final body weight or FCR. However, transient effects occurred during production. On day 28, SO had greater body weight gain (736 ± 13.7 g) than PF (675 ± 27 g). On day 35, PO showed higher feed intake (1,394.1 ± 42.3 g) than PF (1,288.7 ± 13.9 g). By day 42, PO had lower feed intake (1,461.1 ± 55.8 g) than SO (1,593.4 ± 31.2 g). No differences were detected in carcass yield, parts yield, or intestinal morphometry (P > 0.05). Breast yield ranged from 28.29–28.71%, wings 9.84–10.07%, thighs 13.29–13.55%, drumsticks 12.25–12.44%, and carcass yield 76.78–77.79%. These findings indicate that these fat sources can be used interchangeably in broiler diets without affecting performance or carcass traits.

title: Functional, nutritional, and sensory enhancement of emmer wheat bread using lupine and indigenous plant ingredients
abstract: Underutilized plant resources can enhance bread’s nutritional and functional quality while valorizing local crops and agro-industrial by-products. However, combining cereals, legumes, fruit by-products, and indigenous leafy vegetables involves trade-offs among nutritional quality, digestibility, technological properties, and sensory acceptability. Their limited utilization, particularly in low-income countries such as Ethiopia, highlights the need for systematic formulation optimization. This study developed and optimized composite bread from emmer wheat flour, white lupine flour, banana peel powder, Urtica simensis leaf powder, and Amaranthus caudatus leaf powder using a constrained D-optimal mixture design, with clove powder fixed at 1%. Eight composite formulations and a control were evaluated for proximate composition, functional properties, bread quality, in vitro starch digestibility, predicted glycemic index (pGI), and sensory characteristics. Scheffé mixture models and multi-response desirability optimization were applied to identify the optimum formulation. Increasing incorporation of the plant ingredients significantly ( p < 0.05) increased protein, dietary fiber, resistant starch, water absorption capacity, oil absorption capacity, and swelling power, while reducing pGI. The optimum formulation (M5; 50% emmer wheat, 10% white lupine, 15% banana peel, 15% U. simensis , and 10% A. caudatus ) had predicted values of 14.6% protein, 6.8% dietary fiber, 15.0% resistant starch, pGI of 67.1, loaf volume of 388 cm 3 , specific volume of 1.50 cm 3 /g, and sensory score of 7.6. Although ingredient incorporation reduced loaf volume and specific volume, M5 maintained acceptable sensory and technological performance. Overall, the findings demonstrate the potential of combining locally available plant resources and agro-industrial by-products to develop nutritionally improved and sustainable functional bread.

title: Synthesis of slow-release nano-fertilizer from plasma nitrogen and banana peel cellulose
abstract: The increasing demand for affordable nitrogen fertilizers could promote the use of low-cost non-thermal plasma nitrogen (PN) harvesting from the atmosphere and from water sources. Similar to urea, PN faces challenges in the controlled release of nitrogen. In this study, PN was electrocatalyzed to form an N-rich ammonium chloride salt, which was graft-polymerized with banana peel cellulose nanofibrils (BPCNF) to develop a nano-plasma N (NPN) compound for slow nitrogen release. For comparison, urea was also encapsulated in BPCNF to produce nano-urea (NU). To evaluate agronomic performance, a screenhouse experiment was conducted to assess the fertilizing effect of NPN on maize. Structural and chemical characterizations of NPN and NU provided evidence for semi-interpenetrating polymer networks (semi-IPNs) and component interactions that help control moisture diffusion, thereby improving nutrient retention in the soil. The produced nano-fertilizers demonstrated excellent water absorption, with swelling values of 235% for NPN and 226% for NU. They also enhanced the soil's water retention capacity by extending the time to reach 50% field capacity by two days from nine days. These responses enable efficient water use and reduce irrigation frequency. Moreover, the nano-fertilizers exhibited controlled nitrogen release, with 93% and 76.2% released for NU and NPN, respectively, after 29 days, indicating the need to meet European standards. Similar to NU, NPN application in maize increased growth, biomass, and grain yield by up to 37, 36, and 30%, compared to urea and PN. The Nitrogen Recovery Efficiency increased up to 60% and 83% for NU and NPN, respectively, improving the economic yield per fertilizer nutrient. These benefits combined with an eco-friendly production process that leverages plasma and nanotechnology, strengthen the potential of NPN to address fertilizer challenges in sustainable agriculture.

title: Encapsulation of a vitamin E- and carotene-rich lipophilic extract by β-cyclodextrin inclusion complexes
abstract: Lipophilic extracts rich in vitamin E and carotenes contain compounds of nutritional interest for food applications, but their low water solubility and sensitivity to storage conditions can limit their direct incorporation. Therefore, this study evaluated the effect of the β-cyclodextrin (β-CD): extract ratio and stirring time on encapsulating a vitamin E- and carotene-rich high-oleic palm oil extract through inclusion complexes. The complexes were prepared using three β-CD: extract ratios (1:1, 1.3:1, and 1.6:1, w/w) and three stirring times (1, 3, and 5 h). The resulting powders were evaluated for process yield, encapsulation efficiency, moisture content, color, morphology, FT-IR spectra, thermal behavior by DSC and TGA, and refrigerated storage stability. The best balance between powder recovery and bioactive compound retention was obtained with a β-CD: extract ratio of 1.6:1 and 1 h of stirring, yielding 72.61% powder recovery and encapsulation efficiencies of 53.53% for vitamin E and 59.10% for carotenes. The selected powder contained 968.88 mg/kg vitamin E and 125.90 mg/kg carotenes, with reduced moisture content and extract-associated color changes. SEM, FT-IR, DSC, and TGA showed modified particle morphology, spectral changes consistent with β-CD–extract interactions, reduced water-loss events, and a shift of the main degradation event toward higher temperatures. After 60 days at 4 °C, the encapsulated extract retained more vitamin E (91.42%) and carotenes (86.27%) than the free extract (82.74% and 74.00%, respectively). These results show that inclusion complexation with β-CD can effectively protect and stabilize lipophilic extracts rich in vitamin E and carotenes for future food applications.

title: Mapping sustainability research, education and training in agriculture and horticulture
abstract: Agriculture and horticulture education are increasingly recognised as essential for promoting sustainable farming practices, climate resilience, and environmental stewardship. Despite growing scholarly interest, the literature remains fragmented, limiting a comprehensive understanding of its intellectual development, emerging research priorities, and contributions to sustainable agricultural systems. This study presents a bibliometric analysis of 1476 publications (articles, reviews, book chapters, books, and short surveys) indexed in the Scopus database between 2000 and 2024. Publications were retrieved using a structured search strategy, and bibliometric mapping was conducted using VOSviewer to analyse citation, co-authorship, co-citation, and keyword co-occurrence networks, complemented by thematic synthesis to develop a conceptual framework. The analysis identified van der Hoek [ 76 ] and Jallow [ 27 ] as the most influential authors within the co-citation network, while Sustainability (Switzerland) emerged as the leading publication outlet and Science of the Total Environment demonstrated the highest citation impact. Keyword co-occurrence analysis revealed five dominant thematic clusters: (i) sustainability, (ii) climate change and adaptation, (iii) education and capacity building, (iv) farmers’ behaviour and technology adoption, and (v) pesticides, food safety, and agricultural policy. The findings demonstrate a marked shift towards interdisciplinary, sustainability-oriented research integrating environmental stewardship, climate resilience, technology adoption, and educational innovation. By mapping influential contributors, thematic developments, and emerging research directions, this study advances understanding of the intellectual structure of agriculture and horticulture education and provides a theoretical and evidence-based foundation for future research, educational practice, and policy development.

title: Compositionally Distinct Fertilization Regimes Produce Divergent Responses Across Soil Properties, Fresh-Shoot Chemistry and the Shoot Metabolome in a Mature Tea Plantation
abstract: Fertilization regimes in tea plantations must be evaluated across soil conditions, harvested-shoot chemistry and practical input requirements. We compared an unfertilized control with five compositionally distinct regimes in a randomized complete block field experiment. The field plot was the experimental unit, with three independent plots per treatment, and the first observation occurred after the first fertilizer application. At the autumn-2024 sampling, 12 of 15 soil and conventional fresh-shoot traits showed a treatment effect after Benjamini–Hochberg correction, but the direction and statistical support of pairwise differences varied among endpoints. Of 4609 metabolic features, 4069 passed pooled-QC criteria and 3845 were fully detected across the 18 biological samples. A total of 495 unique quantitative-event features contributed 988 feature–contrast events and were summarized in seven empirical modules. Only M1 alkaloid overrepresentation remained significant after correction within the preselected responsive subset; M1 contained 32 selected features, including seven putatively annotated alkaloids, and its unadjusted plot-level association with conventionally measured caffeine was weak. This is limited exploratory compositional evidence, not a confirmed biological mechanism. A total of 9 of 105 correlations among conventional indicators retained correction, whereas none of 35 candidate-metabolite-to-shoot-trait correlations did. Fertilizer material costs ranged from 187.5 to 7500 CNY mu−1 among the five fertilized regimes under the stated price assumptions. These costs and an owner-reported farm-operation scenario provide practical context but are not treatment-specific profitability estimates. The results support regime-specific evaluation under the tested formulations, rates, site and observation period, without establishing fertilizer-source superiority, an organic–mineral interaction or a causal soil-to-metabolite mechanism.

title: Drought effects across seasonal temperature regimes on root morphology, growth, electrical impedance traits and fungal community of Pinus sylvestris var. mongolica seedlings
abstract: Water stress is considered to be the main factor causing the decline of Mongolian Scots pine ( Pinus sylvestris var. mongolica ) seedling plantations. Most previous studies have examined seasonal drought under fluctuating ambient temperatures. However, how drought occurring at successive growth stage temperatures regulates root growth, physiological traits, fungal communities and their internal interactions remain poorly understood. In this experiment, two-year-old seedlings were subjected to drought treatments at different growth stages, which were regulated by exposing them to sequential temperatures of 5/2 ℃, 15/10 ℃, 25/20 ℃, and 35/30 ℃ for 20 days each. Well-watered seedlings served as the control. Multiple root and soil parameters were analyzed after each drought period and at final harvest. Drought at 5/2 ℃ stage induced osmotic adjustment via starch hydrolysis, and root tips recovered at final harvest. At 15/10 ℃ stage, seedlings changed to conservative carbon allocation by enhancing starch accumulation. The most severe and irreversible damage occurred at 25/20 ℃ (optimal growth temperature) stage, causing persistent carbon deficit and impaired recovery. In contrast, seedlings at 35/30 ℃ stage exhibited heat-drought acclimation, maintaining stable non-structural carbohydrate levels, preserving antioxidant activities, and enriching stress-tolerant ectomycorrhizal fungi. Electrical impedance spectroscopy parameters effectively tracked root physiological and morphological changes throughout the experiment. These findings highlight the critical role of growth-stage temperature in seedling drought recovery, providing a scientific basis for forest water management in semi-arid regions.

title: From water to plate: stakeholders drawing the tilapia supply chain in family-based fish farming
abstract: Introduction Research on aquaculture value chains has expanded in recent years, yet limited attention has been given to how local stakeholders visually perceive and represent these systems. This study investigated how local actors conceptualized the Oreochromis niloticus (tilapia) value chain in the Itamarati Rural Settlement, Ponta Porã, Brazil, through participatory co-design activities focused on the “water-to-plate” journey. Methods More than 150 participants, including family farmers, rural youth, extension workers, researchers, and community members, participated in the workshops. Although the participatory process extended beyond the production of handmade drawings, the analytical dataset consisted of 31 voluntarily produced drawings. These drawings were analyzed using an inductive mixed-methods approach combining qualitative coding and descriptive quantitative analysis. Independent coding by multiple analysts was used to identify recurring variables represented in the drawings. Results Eleven recurring variables were identified. The most frequently represented elements were local and regional markets (77.4%), presence of people (77.4%), subsistence fish farming (48.4%), and school meals (38.7%). In contrast, cooperatives, public policies, technical assistance, water reuse, and technological innovation were less frequently represented. Discussion The findings suggest that participants primarily perceived the tilapia value chain through community-oriented and socially embedded relationships, whereas institutional and technological dimensions had lower visual visibility. The study highlights the potential of participatory visual methodologies to support territorial diagnosis, institutional learning, participatory governance, and sustainable rural development in family-based aquaculture systems.

title: Farmers’ Perceptions of the Advantages, Risks and Farmer-Centred Targeting of Sustainable Intensification Innovations in the Mtunthama EPA, Central Malawi
abstract: Smallholder farming systems in sub-Saharan Africa are highly heterogeneous, resulting in differences in farmers’ capacities, priorities, and responses to sustainable intensification (SI) innovations. This study assessed farmers’ perceptions of six SI innovations and evaluated their suitability across four farm typologies in the Mtunthama Extension Planning Area, Central Malawi. A mixed-methods participatory approach involving focus group discussions and farmer-led innovation ranking was used across 44 trial farmers. Qualitative data were analysed using thematic content analysis, while preference rankings were converted into weighted standardised scores for comparison across farm types. Kruskal–Wallis tests were applied to assess whether maize grain yield differed significantly across farm typologies by treatment. Farmers generally perceived SI innovations positively, identifying improved yields, soil fertility, food security, dietary diversity, and climate resilience as major benefits. Labour requirements, input constraints, management complexity, and limited training were identified as key barriers. Innovation preferences differed across farm typologies, reflecting variations in household resource endowment and livelihood strategies. Although conventional ridging with continuous sole maize received the highest proportion of first-choice rankings, conservation agriculture incorporating legumes, particularly maize-cowpea double-row strip cropping, achieved the highest overall preference scores across farm types. Yield analysis revealed significant differences across farm typologies for CA Maize-Lablab Rotation (H = 9.823, p = 0.020) and Conventional Maize (H = 12.834, p = 0.005), with resource-constrained farmers consistently recording lower yields. Field days attended by 253 independent observers confirmed community-level preference for cowpea-based CA innovations, with maize-cowpea strip cropping receiving the highest vote share at both sites. Post-project follow-up revealed that 68 out of 253 field day observers (26.9%) independently adopted cowpea-based conservation agriculture in the following season, of whom 58.8% were women. Adoption was driven by the early maturity of the cowpea variety under climate variability and access to a ready vendor market. These findings demonstrate that integrating farm typology analysis with participatory innovation assessment and post-project tracking improves the targeting of SI interventions and supports the design of context-specific innovation packages more likely to achieve sustained adoption than blanket technology recommendations.

title: Does varietal performance information drive better seed choices? Experimental evidence from Kenya
journal: Journal of Agriculture and Food Research
abstract: Context Despite substantial gains in hybrid maize performance in Kenya, many farmers continue to plant varieties released over two decades ago. Slow varietal turnover limits productivity gains and resilience, particularly under increasing climate stress. While multiple demand- and supply-side constraints contribute to this pattern, a key and underexplored constraint is farmers’ limited access to independent, credible, and up-to-date information on the performance of currently available hybrids. Objective To assess whether providing contextually relevant and product-specific performance information influences farmers’ maize seed choice, with a focus on selection of top-performing hybrids. Methods We implemented a randomized controlled trial in Kenya in which farmers in the treatment group received farmer-reported yield information for ten commercially available maize hybrids grown in their county in the previous season. Farmers in the comparison group received placebo information unrelated to seed selection. We measured effects on stated purchase intentions and actual seed purchases. Results and conclusion s: Providing performance information tripled farmers’ intent to purchase top-performing hybrids (from 7% to 25%) and more than doubled actual purchases (from 5% to 11%). Although stockouts constrained some intended purchases, treated farmers remained significantly more likely to select these hybrids. The results indicate that lack of credible performance information is a binding constraint on improved seed choice and contributes to slow varietal turnover. Significance The findings underscore the importance of generating and disseminating independent, farmer-relevant varietal performance data. Investing in rigorous testing of commercially available hybrids and improving how results are shared with farmers can strengthen seed systems, accelerate varietal turnover, and support more informed decision making in Kenya and similar smallholder contexts. Realizing the full potential of these investments, however, requires parallel efforts to strengthen seed supply chains and support farmer experimentation."

title: How Is Farmer Cooperation Possible? Interaction, Identity, and Community Capacity in a Chinese Rural Community
abstract: ABSTRACT How can cooperation emerge in communities where institutional enforcement is weak and social relations are fragmented? Drawing on a longitudinal case study of Village L in rural China (2017–2021), this paper develops a five‐stage process model that explains the endogenous emergence of cooperation. Moving beyond incentive‐ and institution‐centered accounts, the analysis shows how cooperation is dynamically generated through a sequence of interactional mechanisms: initiated by exemplary action, expanded through observational learning and symbolic reinforcement, deepened through deliberative coordination that activates a collective identity, and stabilized through ritualization into a cooperative cultural structure. The study demonstrates that farmers' agency is not a pregiven individual capacity but an emergent, relational outcome of interactional processes unfolding over time. By examining how interaction, identity formation, and cultural stabilization are linked in practice, this article treats cooperation as an emergent social accomplishment rather than a fixed equilibrium or a problem of institutional design. It develops a process‐based explanation of how community capacity and collective agency are gradually built in rural settings marked by weak institutions and fragmented social relations. In doing so, the study speaks to ongoing debates in rural sociology about how cooperation is generated and sustained in everyday social life.

title: Investigating smallholder farmers’ willingness to adopt and pay for agricultural insurance policies in Osun State, Nigeria: a cragg’s double hurdle approach
abstract: Abstract Agricultural production is highly vulnerable to risks arising from climate variability, pests, diseases, and market uncertainties. Agricultural insurance serves as an important risk-management instrument; however, its uptake among smallholder farmers in Nigeria remains low. This study examined smallholder farmers’ willingness to adopt and pay for agricultural insurance policies in Osun State, Nigeria. A multistage sampling technique was used to select 240 respondents, and data were analysed using descriptive statistics and Cragg’s double hurdle model. The results showed that the average farmer was 50 years old, had 32 years of farming experience, and cultivated 1.65 hectares of farmland. While only 34% of respondents were aware of agricultural insurance, 31% belonged to cooperative societies. The first hurdle estimates revealed that age ( p < 0.05), education ( p < 0.01), marital status ( p < 0.10), farm size ( p < 0.01), and access to credit ( p < 0.05) significantly influenced farmers’ willingness to adopt agricultural insurance. The second hurdle results indicated that education ( p < 0.01), farm size ( p < 0.05), cooperative society membership ( p < 0.05), risk perception ( p < 0.01), and insurance awareness ( p < 0.01) significantly increased the intensity of willingness to pay. The study recommends strengthening awareness campaigns, cooperative-based extension services, and farmers’ access to education and credit to enhance agricultural insurance demand.

title: Machine learning classification techniques for smart agriculture: a review of disease detection and crop recommendation
abstract: The adoption of Internet of Things (IoT) and Machine Learning (ML) in agriculture presents a revolutionary step toward efficient agricultural practices using data to address global issues surrounding food security. This review conducted a systematic search of the Scopus, IEEE Xplore, ScienceDirect, and SpringerLink databases for articles published between January 2023 and January 2026. It used keyword combinations like “IoT and machine learning and agriculture”, “crop recommendation”, “plant disease detection”, and “precision farming”. From the initial pool of articles found, 30 articles met the criteria for empirical methodology, quantitative performance reporting, and clear dataset descriptions. These were chosen for detailed analysis. It was discovered that the ensemble, as well as the traditional machine learning methods, such as Random Forest, Support Vector Machine (SVM), and Decision Trees, produce highly accurate predictions of the crop yields with an accuracy of 99.9%. Meanwhile, Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) and ResNet-based deep learning models detect diseases with an accuracy above 98% while Gated Recurrent Units (GRU) and Long-Short Term Memory (LSTM) time-series models provide forecasts of weather conditions with an accuracy ranging from 94 to 98%, due to the complex nature of the environment dynamics. The application of IoT systems for precision agriculture produced a significant improvement in terms of resource utilization, resulting in 60–96% of water savings, 25% increased yield, and 36–38% reduced herbicide use. Although these advancements have been made, wider application is still hindered by high costs of implementation, lack of technological skills among farmers, data privacy concerns, issues of scalability within different agricultural settings, and consistent internet connection in rural areas. The current paper evaluates the use of IoT and ML in the agriculture sector from diverse data sources and studies to reveal the immense benefits offered by the two systems in enhancing farming activities.

title: Weather and health shocks in rural Uganda: heterogeneous consumption effects and coping strategies
abstract: Abstract Background Compound and cascading shocks are common in rural areas and pose significant threats to food security and household welfare. While the importance of these combined shocks for rural communities is gaining attention, there is still very limited empirical research on the topic. This paper aims to assess the combined effects of weather and health shocks on the food, non-food, and total consumption of rural households in Uganda. Our analysis uses customized high-frequency panel household survey data collected across six waves, employing fixed effects quantile regression methods. Results The findings indicate that a short-term increase in temperature leads to a reduction in total consumption by 12–16%, with a more pronounced lagging effect on food consumption, which can be as high as 30%. Similarly, excessive rainfall adversely affects food consumption and diet diversity. The combined effects of health and weather shocks on consumption are negative and significant for lagged interaction terms, exhibiting varied effects across different household categories. Notably, the poorest quartile experiences the most substantial negative effects. Additionally, the findings reveal considerable consumption mobility among rural households over a 12-month period. Even households in the richest quartile may find themselves in the lowest consumption categories at certain times of the year. To manage these fluctuations in consumption, the poorest quartiles tend to rely on group networks and loans, while wealthier quartiles more frequently utilize remittances. Conclusion and policy implications Recognizing Uganda's vulnerability to extreme weather events and epidemics, this paper suggests key policy measures. Enhancing social protection through access to credit, social networks, safety nets, and health insurance can help households cope with climate challenges. These strategies will strengthen food system resilience and promote sustainable development.

title: Household Food Consumption in Kazakhstan 2001–2025: National Observations and Recent Regional and Socioeconomic Contrasts
journal: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health
abstract: Published household statistics describe food quantities and budget allocation but do not directly measure individual dietary intake. This study examined food-group-specific socioeconomic and household-composition contrasts and food-purchase expenditure distributions in Kazakhstan in 2025. An ecological repeated cross-sectional study used official household survey aggregates. Regional maps reproduced published fruit and fish indicators for 2025. Recent regional urban–rural comparisons covered 2022–2025, with the principal interpretation restricted to 11 oblasts not involved in the 2022 regional splits; six oblasts with estimated 2022 values were displayed separately. The national annual series for 2001–2025 was retained as historical context rather than a fully harmonised estimate of dietary change. In 2025, the highest population decile of per capita income used for consumption had a fish indicator 3.9 times that of the lowest decile; corresponding ratios were approximately 3.3 for meat, milk/dairy products and fruit and 1.5 for bread/cereal products. Per capita indicators were lower across all ten food groups in households with five or more members than in one-person households. Food purchases exceeded 50% of consumer expenditure in 64.0% of households and 71.7% of households with five or more children. Recent regional changes differed by food group and urban–rural category. These descriptive findings identify contrasts in household apparent consumption and expenditure allocation. They do not establish individual dietary adequacy, food-insecurity prevalence, household-level associations between separately tabulated indicators, or independent causal effects.

title: Integrated fisheries and limno-ecological assessment of a medium reservoir in Central India: Implications for sustainability and the inland blue economy
abstract: Reservoirs play an important role in inland fisheries, biodiversity conservation and rural livelihoods in India. This study presents an integrated assessment of the limno-chemical characteristics, fish diversity, fishery production, management practices and livelihood contribution of Kodar Reservoir, a medium reservoir in Chhattisgarh, Central India. The study recorded 52 fish species, increasing the cumulative checklist to 60 species across 10 orders and 21 families, including 11 species not reported in earlier inventories and four exotic species. The reservoir exhibited marked seasonal variation in limno-chemical characteristics, with principal component analysis showing that the first three components explained 85.4% of the total variance. Fishery production during 2019–20 was 40.9 t, corresponding to a yield of 19.95 kg ha⁻¹ yr⁻¹, with variations in catch composition and fishing activity. The fishery was supported by cooperative-based management involving stocking, mesh-size regulation and seasonal fishing restrictions. An exponential decay survival model estimated a stocking requirement of 600 Indian major carp fingerlings ha⁻¹ yr⁻¹. Fishing contributed approximately 40% of household income, complementing agriculture and other livelihood activities. The findings highlight the relationships between environmental conditions, fish assemblage and fishery performance within a cooperative management framework and provide a baseline for adaptive management of medium reservoir fisheries. Continued ecological and fishery monitoring, species specific stocking, protection of potential breeding habitats, surveillance of exotic fishes and strengthening of cooperative management could support sustainable fisheries and livelihood security. Keywords: Cooperative management, Exponential decay survival model, Exotic species, Kodar Reservoir; Reservoir fisheries

title: From Breast to Bowl: A quasi-experimental, mixed-methods evaluation of peer learning to improve complementary feeding in rural northeastern Ghana
abstract: Background In rural Ghana, the transition from breastfeeding to complementary feeding is critical; however, gaps in maternal and child nutrition services contribute to low dietary diversity, inadequate feeding frequency, limited maternal knowledge, and poor child growth. This study evaluates the impact of peer-learning approaches on improving these practices. Methods A quasi-experimental mixed-methods design was conducted in Ghana’s North East Region, comparing intervention (n=4) and comparison (n=4) communities. Intervention sites implemented peer-learning groups with counseling and caregiver discussions, while comparison sites continued routine practices. A probability sample of 420 caregivers participated. Household surveys assessed dietary diversity, feeding frequency, and maternal knowledge of recommended practices. Facility records documented counseling sessions and staff training. Focus group discussions and key informant interviews were conducted with caregivers and health workers. Results Dietary diversity increased by 24 percentage points (pp) in intervention communities versus 3 pp in comparison sites (p=.001). Feeding ≥3 meals/day rose by 23 pp in intervention areas compared to 4 pp (p<.001). Appropriate knowledge scores improved by 38 pp in intervention sites versus 8 pp in comparison areas (p<.001). Facility counseling use rose from 2.1 to 3.4 sessions/month in intervention areas (t(28)=4.80, p<.001) and from 2.0 to 2.2 in comparison sites. Qualitative narratives confirmed dietary changes, e.g., “We used to give only maize porridge, but now we add groundnut and beans” (32-year-old mother, FGD). Conclusions Peer-led education, male caregiver engagement, and strengthened facility support improved complementary feeding. These findings highlight scalable nutrition interventions in Ghana and provide transferable lessons for other low-resource settings. Keywords:complementary feeding, caregiver practices, northeastern Ghana

title: Aflatoxin Contamination in the Maize Supply Chain: A Case of Nampula Province, Mozambique
abstract: Aflatoxin contamination in maize remains a major food safety and public health concern in Nampula Province, Mozambique. Maize samples obtained from farmers, traders, and milling units across the districts of Malema, Mossuril, Mecuburi, Monapo, and Nampula in 2024 and 2025 were analysed using UPLC-ESI-MS/MS. In 2024, aflatoxins were detected in samples from Mecuburi (43%), Mossuril (17%), Monapo (17%), and traders (13%), with some exceeding the regulatory limit of 15 µg/kg. AFB1 was the predominant aflatoxin, followed by AFB2. At the farmer level, Mecuburi recorded the highest contamination, with AFB1 and AFB2 detected in 43% of samples and AFG1 and AFG2 in 29%, while Mossuril had 20% contamination with AFB1 and AFG1. The maximum concentration was 4221.33 µg/kg of AFB1 in Mecuburi, whereas the minimum detected concentration was 2.82 µg/kg of AFB2. Aflatoxins were not detected above the limit of detection in milling samples or in samples collected in 2025. Despite the relatively low prevalence, the occurrence of extremely high aflatoxin concentrations highlights persistent contamination risks and the need for integrated mitigation strategies throughout the maize supply chain.

title: Food access, purchasing habits and dietary diversity of peri-urban households in Hanoi, Vietnam
abstract: Background: Urban and peri-urban areas increasingly concentrate food insecurity, making food access a key urban equity issue. In rapidly urbanising Asian cities, formal and informal food vendors coexist, so households can choose among food sources with different characteristics. Yet studies often analyse food access using income or residential location alone, overlooking the role of everyday purchasing behaviours. Objective of the study: This study examines how food purchasing patterns and vendor choice relate to dietary diversity among peri-urban households in Hanoi. Methods: We use cross-sectional survey data, collected from 157 households in 11 geographically and socioeconomically diverse wards in a peri-urban area of Hanoi. Using k-means clustering, we group households by food-purchasing frequency and their reasons for choosing specific vendors. We compare clusters (“frequent buyers” and “low-frequency buyers”) across socioeconomic characteristics, food expenditure, transport modes, spatial access to vendors, urban agricultural activity, and their household dietary diversity score (HDDS). Results: Low‑frequency buyers had higher mean income per capita, while frequent‑buyers had a slightly higher mean HDDS. This difference was driven primarily by greater consumption of processed food groups (oils, fats and sweets) rather than increased intake of fresh or nutrient-dense foods. Both groups prioritised proximity, affordability, and product assortment when choosing where to shop. Although proximity was the primary consideration, we found no significant differences in distance-based access to food vendors, though transport modes differed between clusters. Conclusions: Our results show how purchasing habits mediate between upstream drivers and dietary diversity. The association between frequent purchasing and higher processed food consumption may reflect time constraints, which lead households to favour convenience items, even when shopping at traditional markets. The ongoing expansion of supermarkets could further accelerate this trend of increased processed food consumption. Behaviour-based segmentation complements income- or location-based approaches for studying urban food policy, nutrition and food accessibility in rapidly growing cities by recognising the important role of traditional food sources.

title: Community radio as a catalyst for social learning, knowledge co-production, and adaptive capacity: a sequential explanatory mixed-methods study in Northern Ghana
abstract: Introduction Community radio has increasingly been recognised as an important platform for climate communication in sub-Saharan Africa.
