Nature-inclusive architecture sometimes prioritizes human preferences and excludes species that are "less appealing" but ecologically vital, such as spiders or snakes, which may trigger negative emotional responses. A survey of 600 residents in Greece found that likeability was the strongest predictor of whether people wanted more encounters with a wildlife taxon, with butterflies and songbirds among the most preferred species (Hu & Lima, 2024). This human-centered filtering forms the gap between the perceived "nature" and the actual needs of a functioning ecosystem.Marginalizing species that lack visual appeal may exclude groups with different values, hindering the ecological functions necessary to support broader urban biodiversity. Designs incorporating ecological interpretation hold the potential to enhance the acceptance of "undesirable" species and other ecologically valuable elements.The benefits people derive from nature-integrated architecture are often unevenly distributed.Wealthier neighborhoods typically feature more diverse vegetation and better-maintained green spaces, reflecting a "luxury effect" (Eyster et al., 2024;Hazbei et al., 2025). Improved greening may increase land and property values, but it can lead to green gentrification and the displacement of low-income residents, especially where green spaces are scarce and housing protections are weak (Ceballos & Jatoespino, 2026). The social performance of building-integrated greenery should therefore be assessed through affordability, shared access, and the distribution of benefits across neighborhoods.Nature-inclusive architecture encompasses various types of green spaces that differ in their potential contributions to health and biodiversity. The preceding discussion indicates that synergies emerge when green spaces provide habitats, environmental comfort, perceptible nature experiences, and opportunities for physical activity and shared stewardship. These spaces may also introduce safety risks, ecological disturbance, high maintenance demands, and unequal access. Understanding the strengths and challenges of different types of green spaces can inform design decisions that enhance synergies and manage trade-offs. Taking three-dimensional green spaces as an example, they can be classified into nine types based on the openness and verticality of spaces (Table 1).Table 1 Strengths and challenges of various spatial types of three-dimensional green spaces in buildings. This typology translates the preceding synergies and trade-offs into a context-sensitive and performance-oriented framework. Context-sensitive design responds to spatial position, microclimate, access, and surrounding ecology; performance-oriented design considers factors such as health experience, habitat quality, environmental comfort, maintenance demand, risk exposure, and accessibility.Nature-inclusive architecture, particularly through three-dimensional green spaces, offers a promising yet complex pathway for aligning dense urban development with ecological and health goals. Its contributions to human health and urban biodiversity depend on how synergies and trade-offs are addressed. It can support stress reduction, cognitive performance, positive emotions, physical activity and social cohesion, while creating challenges related to hygiene and safety, wildlife disturbance, maintenance, ecological function, accessibility, and social equity. Hence, the effectiveness of natureinclusive architecture relies more on the configuration, perception, and experience of the biodiverse environment than on the mere presence of greenery. Different spatial types present distinct benefits and limitations, highlighting the need for tailored design rather than a one-size-fits-all approach. The proposed typology can guide the selection and combination of three-dimensional green spaces according to site conditions and intended health and biodiversity outcomes. When design decisions address trade-offs and accommodate both human and non-human needs, nature-inclusive architecture can function as socio-ecological infrastructure in dense urban environments.

title: How Does E-Commerce Participation Promote Farmers’ Green Production Behavior? Evidence from the China Rural Revitalization Survey
abstract: Promoting farmers’ green production behavior is essential for ensuring the quality and safety of agricultural products and advancing sustainable agricultural development. As information and communication technologies become increasingly integrated into agriculture, rural e-commerce has emerged as an important means of reshaping agricultural product marketing and farmers’ production decisions, while providing new impetus for green agricultural transformation. Based on 1950 crop-growing farm households from the 2020 China Rural Revitalization Survey (CRRS), this study estimates the effect of e-commerce participation on farmers’ green production behavior using ordinary least squares (OLS), two-stage least squares (2SLS), and mechanism analysis. The empirical results show that e-commerce participation significantly promotes farmers’ green production behavior, and this effect is stronger in areas with higher logistics accessibility. The mechanism analysis further suggests that farmland transfer-in and credit access may serve as potential pathways through which e-commerce participation influences farmers’ green production behavior. These findings highlight the need to improve rural e-commerce services and logistics infrastructure and strengthen farmland transfer and rural financial services to reinforce the role of e-commerce participation in promoting farmers’ green production behavior.

title: A stocktake of opportunities and knowledge gaps in advancing digital agriculture in Quebec
abstract: Abstract Sustainable development has become a key priority for the agricultural sector, both globally and in Quebec. Digital agriculture, as an important component of sustainable agricultural systems, represents a promising pathway toward achieving sustainable development goals. However, despite the recognized benefits of digital agriculture, the opportunities, limitations, and research gaps associated with its contribution to sustainable development in Quebec remain insufficiently understood. This study applies a systematic tracking approach to identify applications of digital technologies in Quebec’s agricultural sector and evaluate their potential contributions to provincial sustainable development objectives while highlighting gaps and opportunities for their enhanced deployment. A total of 59 peer-reviewed publications and grey literature reports were identified and analyzed. Overall, 14 categories of digital technologies were documented within Quebec’s agricultural sector. Their representation in the scientific literature was primarily concentrated in three dominant categories: web/mobile applications and software (31%), machine learning and sensors (14%), and satellite technologies (13%). The identified digital technologies have significant potential to support sustainable development objectives in Quebec agriculture through improved pesticide monitoring, soil health assessment and conservation, fertilizer management optimization, water-use efficiency, and biodiversity conservation. Collectively, these technologies could be combined in 65 distinct ways to support sustainable development goals; however, only 54% of this potential is currently being exploited in Quebec. This highlights substantial opportunities for expanding the role of digital agriculture in addressing sustainability challenges. The study also reveals important knowledge gaps, particularly regarding the social dimensions influencing the diffusion and adoption of digital technologies in agriculture. A limited understanding of the factors affecting Quebec farmers’ adoption decisions remains a major barrier to maximizing the benefits of digital agriculture. Addressing these social and behavioral dimensions will be essential for accelerating the transition toward more sustainable, digitally enabled agricultural systems in Quebec.

title: Epistemological Friction: Embodied Expertise and the ‘Last Mile’ of Agricultural Automation in the US Tree‐Fruit Industry
abstract: ABSTRACT Autonomous and AI‐driven agricultural technology is often framed as a panacea for labour dependency. While proponents envision autonomous technologies seamlessly optimising farming, this rationalised model misunderstands the reality of on‐farm integration. Based on an ethnographic and comparative study of 16 operations in the US West Coast Tree Fruit Industry (California and Washington), this article examines the ‘last mile’ of agricultural automation. The study reveals that integrating AI and robotics is a contested negotiation shaped by epistemological friction—the tension between the algorithmic logic of developers and the embodied, site‐specific expertise of farmers and farm workers. Rather than resulting in seamless labour replacement, we find that agricultural automation reconfigures work, creating an invisible reliance on ‘human middleware’ to navigate the biological recalcitrance of the orchard. Demonstrating how regional contexts and participatory implementation shape technological trajectories, this study extends Labour Process Theory. We argue for the need for a relational approach recognising the essential cognitive labour of farmers and farm workers that is demanded by digital agriculture. Ultimately, this study shows the ‘farm of the future’ depends on reconciling rigid systems with the situated expertise of the farm workforce.

title: Determinants of climate-resilient irrigation practices uptake among smallholder onion farmers in Laikipia Central Subcounty, Kenya
abstract: Climate-resilient irrigation practices (CRIPs) defined here as drip, sprinkler, and rain hose irrigation are essential for sustaining smallholder agricultural productivity in semi-arid regions of Kenya, where water scarcity limits crop output. Despite their benefits, uptake of CRIPs among smallholder onion farmers in Laikipia Central Subcounty remains low, with 56.05% still relying on traditional furrow irrigation. Sprinkler irrigation had the highest uptake (12.63%), followed by rain hose (11.84%) and drip irrigation (5.53%); combined adoption of CRIPs accounted for the remaining 13.95%. Data were collected from 380 smallholder onion farmers selected through multistage sampling, using a pre-tested semi-structured questionnaire. The Multivariate Probit model revealed that determinants of uptake varied across the three irrigation practices. Climate change awareness, extension visits, and onion income were positively associated with all three practices. Education and group membership were positively associated with drip and rain hose adoption; off-farm income was positively associated with sprinkler and rain hose; while farm size was negatively associated with both. Technology-specific effects included household size and credit amount being positively associated with drip; sex and distance to farm being negatively associated with sprinkler; and years of Water Resource Users Association membership was positively associated with rain hose, while age and distance to market were negatively associated with rain hose irrigation. The study recommends targeted subsidies and harvest-aligned credit channelled through farmer groups to promote drip irrigation uptake; pay-as-you-go solar pump financing to address energy and liquidity constraints for sprinkler irrigation and for rain hose irrigation, strengthened agro-dealer stock support, spare-parts distribution, and local technician training, complemented by Water Resource Users Association linked water scheduling and Village Savings and Loan Associations based purchase plans to improve affordability and accessibility.

title: Soybean Expansion in the MATOPIBA Region of Piauí, Brazil (1985–2024): Native-Vegetation Conversion, Overlap with Legally Protected Areas, and Implications for Sustainable Land Governance
abstract: Monitoring whether agricultural expansion advances over native vegetation and legally protected land is central to assessing the sustainability of commodity frontiers. This study reconstructs four decades (1985–2024) of soybean expansion in the MATOPIBA region of Piauí, Brazil, from annual 30 m land-cover maps, and quantifies its overlap with the protection instruments of the Rural Environmental Registry (CAR) and with strictly protected conservation units. The region holds 32.6% of the state’s territory but accounts for 41.1% of the gross loss of native vegetation recorded in Piauí. Only 23.7% of the 2024 soybean area was converted directly from native vegetation in a single annual step, yet 98.9% of it carried native vegetation in 1985, and the median interval between clearing and the first soybean season is three years: expansion over previously cleared land is largely expansion over land cleared in the preceding seasons. Resolving overlaps between declarations reduces the area under protection instruments from an apparent 40.2% of the region to a unique 34.5%. Soybean overlaps were declared Legal Reserves and Permanent Preservation Areas, unregistered land, and the Uruçuí-Una Ecological Station, where a 6001 ha complex occupies 4.6% of the unit and was confirmed against 10 m imagery. These indicate potential non-compliance to be verified, not adjudicated violations, and support anchoring deforestation-free supply-chain screening on the date of native vegetation loss.

title: Inflation and Agricultural Commodity Price Volatility in India: An Empirical Analysis
journal: Journal of Scientific Research and Reports
abstract: Agricultural commodity prices occupy an unusually important position in India’s inflation process because food has a large household-budget share, production is exposed to weather and biological lags, and farm-to-retail supply chains remain heterogeneous in storage, transport, market integration and competitive structure. This critical narrative review synthesises empirical evidence on the relationship between agricultural commodity price volatility and inflation in India, with emphasis on the modern commodity-market era from 2003 to 10 July 2026 while retaining earlier evidence where conceptually necessary. The literature indicates that neither “food inflation” nor “commodity volatility” is a single process. Cereals have generally displayed stronger insulation from world-price volatility because procurement, public stocks and trade policy buffer domestic markets, whereas vegetables, pulses and oilseeds exhibit larger short-run variability linked to production shocks, seasonality, market arrivals, storage constraints and import dependence. Evidence on market power and vertical price transmission shows that retail and wholesale mark-ups can amplify shocks, especially in perishables, although the magnitude is commodity- and market-specific. Global food and oil prices matter, but pass-through is episodic and conditioned by domestic policy. Commodity futures often contribute to price discovery, yet studies disagree on whether spot or futures markets lead and on hedging effectiveness, cautioning against general claims that futures trading either causes or cures volatility. Monetary tightening can limit persistence and second-round effects, but recent quantile evidence suggests that direct control of urban food inflation through monetary policy is weak when shocks are supply-driven. The strongest policy implication is therefore a layered response: commodity-specific supply and logistics measures for first-round shocks, predictable trade and stock policies, better market integration and competition, and monetary policy focused on preventing propagation rather than suppressing relative-price adjustment. Major research gaps concern causal identification, spatially granular consumer prices, climate extremes, market concentration, policy endogeneity and real-time integration of wholesale, retail and futures data.

title: Effect of the formal milk market participation on the gross margin of dairy producers in Nyandarua County
abstract: Dairy production is a critical value chain for Kenya's rural employment and household income. However, the sector experiences low production and informal marketing. As a result, the government has established several interventions to support farmers in rural areas, including encouraging the formation of formal markets. However, it is not clear whether farmers have utilised and benefited from joining the formal markets (dairy cooperative and processors). This study, therefore, estimates the effect of the formal milk market on the gross margin of dairy producers using an endogenous switching regression model. The data was collected using a semi-structured questionnaire from 384 households drawn from Nyandarua County. The finding indicates that formal milk market participation increased the gross margin by about 38%. Moreover, the results revealed that risk-taking, proactiveness, autonomy, education, experience, land size, herd size, and milk yield significantly influence the choice of the formal milk market. This study recommends initiatives that increase formal market participation for enhanced welfare among dairy farmers.

title: Transforming food chains for a sustainable future in Sub-saharan Africa: Roles of consumers, industry, and government
abstract: ABSTRACT Food chain sustainability is a pressing global concern, especially in sub-Saharan Africa (SSA), where weak infrastructure, limited public awareness, and fragmented policies obstruct environmentally sound practices. The region experiences up to 30–50% post-harvest losses for perishable commodities, while food waste contributes to an estimated 1.3 billion tonnes of global carbon dioxide equivalent emissions annually. This highlights the urgency for systemic change. Agriculture in SSA is dominated by smallholder systems, yet livestock and other animal-based food production account for approximately 57% of global food-related greenhouse gas emissions, which also emphasizes the importance of sustainable production and dietary shifts. This paper, therefore, analyses how consumers, the food industry, and government bodies can each contribute to more sustainable systems in the region through targeted interventions in policy, sustainable behaviour, technology adoption, and production practices. Major identified obstacles include consumer distrust, limited awareness of sustainability standards, weak policies, and inadequate institutional support. The integration of digital technologies like artificial intelligence, blockchain, and ICT can further transparency, efficiency, and coordination across the food chain. Governments, food producers, and consumers can jointly build more sustainable and resilient food systems by taking a coordinated, holistic approach, one that addresses specific barriers such as inadequate infrastructure, poor policy enforcement, and unsustainable consumer behaviour while aligning efforts across economic, environmental, and social domains.

title: Racial Bifurcation of Benefit and Burden: A Bioethical Analysis of Petrochemical Development in Louisiana's Cancer Alley
abstract: Photo ID 57449093 © Tomas1111 | Dreamstime.com Introduction In Louisiana's Cancer Alley, an eighty-five-mile stretch of industry along the Mississippi River between Baton Rouge and New Orleans, the petrochemical sector has long defended its development on economic grounds.[1] Industry representatives and state officials frequently credit petrochemical plants with creating jobs, generating tax revenue, and contributing to the economic viability of the regions where they operate. Yet conversations and research conducted with residents reveal a more complicated story: the wages, security, and mobility that people expect from such employment rarely materialize as promised.[2] This narrative is not unique. It reflects a broader idealism that circulates in community gatherings and local government meetings, where proponents widely credit the petrochemical industry with sustaining the region's economic viability. Notably, white residents are the main proponents of this narrative, while being a demographic that is largely absent from the frontline communities most affected by risk factors caused by petrochemical pollution.[3] One explanation lies at the intersection of racial discrimination and a broader ideological commitment to industrialization as an economic necessity, a commitment so entrenched that it precludes scrutiny.[4] In this framework, industrialization is self-evidently beneficial, while the testimony of residents living in its shadow is merely anecdotal.[5] The “Jobs Equal Wealth” Narrative and Its Limits The assertion that petrochemical investment constitutes an economic boon for Cancer Alley communities relies heavily on Louisiana's Industrial Tax Exemption Program (ITEP), established in 1936. Under the ITEP, manufacturers are eligible for property tax exemptions of up to eighty percent for up to ten years, without requiring approval from the local government.[6] Since 1998, the ITEP has granted more than twenty billion dollars in business tax incentives.[7] Recently, in a single fiscal year alone, the program cost state and local governments an estimated 1.5 billion dollars in forgone property tax revenue, much of it drawn from public school funding.[8] A twenty-year examination of the program found that it had funneled twenty-three billion dollars in public funds to industry while, over that same period, net employment among companies receiving these credits declined by twenty-six thousand jobs.[9] The claim that ITEP-subsidized industries deliver economic benefits to local populations is empirically unsupported. One study, in line with local residents’ complaints, found no statistically significant relationship between the scale of a parish's ITEP exemptions and its growth in household income.[10] This situation reflects a failure of distribution, not merely one of inefficiency. The GDP contributed by petrochemical industries does not translate into a definite value for local employees, since a substantial share of that generated wealth is transferred out of state, while much of the employment generated during a facility's construction phase goes to temporary workers brought in from elsewhere.[11] Nor are these arrangements' costs shared equally among Cancer Alley's residents. The parishes where petrochemical facilities are concentrated are disproportionately Black and Brown, even as the ITEP diverts tax revenue that would otherwise have funded the schools and municipal services on which these same residents depend.[12] Ironically, industry defenders cite these services as justification for offering tax exemptions in the first place, since supporters credit the ITEP with sustaining the very jobs residents rely on. The literature does not suggest that the petrochemical industry has created no jobs, or that no resident of the affected areas has benefited. It suggests, rather, that the industry's broader economic argument does not hold up to scrutiny and disproportionately impacts communities. Historical and Structural Roots The current geography of Cancer Alley is not accidental. Before acquiring its moniker, the eighty-five-mile stretch between Baton Rouge and New Orleans was referred to as Plantation Country.[13] Many of the petrochemical plants built along this corridor since the 1960s occupy land that was once sugar plantations toiled by enslaved laborers, a legacy so entrenched that a number of these facilities still bear the names of the plantations on which they stand.[14] After emancipation, newly freed Black residents established Free Towns on land they purchased or were granted, communities that also included Union soldiers and formerly self-liberated people who had escaped bondage before the war's end. Yet as industry expanded into the corridor in the twentieth century, many of these Free Towns faced encroachment, and their residents were displaced or pushed out entirely.[15] This history carries ethical and descriptive significance. It reframes the corridor's industrial geography not as a neutral outcome of infrastructure or resource logic, but as the continuation of a much older pattern of dispossession. Quantitative environmental justice research also suggests that race, not zoning considerations, remains the strongest predictor of where hazardous industry is sited in this region.[16] Cancer Alley serves as a classic example of this phenomenon. It conflates, within a single geography, two stages of land exploitation that remain, in most other contexts, comparatively diffuse and difficult to trace to one another. The descendants of those who built the land's initial wealth under slavery remain excluded from the industrial wealth generated by that same land today. Cumulative Health The conventional method of assessing environmental pollution considers only one pollutant, one facility, and one exposure route at a time. This approach ignores the cumulative burden borne by populations experiencing multiple sources of pollution, as well as additional forms of socioeconomic or environmental pressure.[17] In recent years, the US Environmental Protection Agency has advocated for cumulative impact assessment as an alternative framework.[18] The case of Reserve, Louisiana, illustrates the considerable cost of adhering to the standard model. A federal inquiry found that residents living near a plant that manufactures chloroprene, a chemical used in the production of synthetic rubber, face one of the highest lifetime cancer risks in the country due to airborne chemical contamination.[19] The plant exposes residents of this predominantly Black neighborhood, many of them children from low-income families attending an elementary school located less than half a mile from the plant, to cancer risks that substantially exceed levels deemed acceptable by the agency's own standards.[20] High-precision mobile air quality monitoring has since confirmed that concentrations of volatile organic compounds in the surrounding air correspond to cancer risk levels well above federal thresholds, corroborating what residents themselves had reported for decades.[21] The Bioethical Problem: A False Symmetry The argument surrounding Cancer Alley is typically framed as an ordinary bioethical trade-off between economic development and public health, where one value must be weighed against another. This framing presupposes that the same parties bear both the costs and the benefits. However, in Cancer Alley, those who benefit, namely shareholders, senior management, and tax authorities, are indifferent to where their revenue originates. Conversely, those who bear the highest costs and environmental harm are disproportionately Black residents living along the fence line. This is not a trade-off in the traditional sense, since a trade-off describes a single party weighing costs and benefits for itself. It is instead a transfer: one group absorbs harm so that another group can capture the resulting gain. This situation also has an evidentiary dimension that constitutes a case of epistemic injustice: the unfair treatment of individuals, specifically in their capacity as knowers or sources of information.[22] In the context of Cancer Alley's public hearings, this injustice operates through two related mechanisms. The first is testimonial injustice, by which the system dismisses or recasts residents’ accounts of their exposure, their illnesses, and their uncompensated labor as mere anecdote, a discrediting rooted in their identity as low-income Black residents of a working-class industrial corridor. The second is representational injustice, by which the frameworks used to evaluate industrial expansion (chiefly, aggregate job counts and projected tax revenue) are structurally incapable of registering accumulated lived experience as a form of harm. When a resident recounts a father's decades of uncompensated labor, or when a mother describes her child's chronic lung disease, this is not merely testimony; it is a lifetime's evidentiary record of harm that regulatory frameworks have only recently begun to measure. It is not neutral to disregard this evidence while treating a company's self-reported revenue projections as self-evident fact. The Department of Justice brought into sharp relief the question of whose knowledge counts in 2025, when it dismissed its civil rights case against the operators of a petrochemical plant in Cancer Alley despite a substantial body of resident testimony documenting the harm at issue.[23] Dismissing this case did not resolve the underlying dispute over harm. Rather, it eliminated the institutional mechanism through which resident testimony could be treated as legally cognizable evidence, instead of as an anecdote. The bioethical question this paper raises, then, is not whether economic development and public health can be balanced against one another, but who holds the authority to define knowledge within that balancing process. title: Policy coordination of public data openness and supercomputing center for agricultural chain resilience
abstract: Strengthening agricultural supply chain resilience is critical for safeguarding food security and promoting high-quality agricultural development in the face of escalating external shocks, including climate extremes, market volatility, and geopolitical uncertainties. Although public data openness and supercomputing infrastructure represent critical pillars of digital transformation, how their coordinated deployment enhances agricultural resilience remains both theoretically underdeveloped and empirically underexamined. Using provincial panel data from 31 Chinese provinces over 2011–2024, we exploit the staggered rollout of public data platforms and supercomputing centers as quasi-natural experiments, constructing a synergistic difference-in-differences (DID) model to isolate their coordinated policy effects. The causal identification is further fortified using event-study parallel trend tests, placebo simulations, propensity score matching (PSM-DID), and double/debiased machine learning (DDML). Our baseline estimates demonstrate that policy synergy between public data openness and supercomputing infrastructure substantially enhances agricultural supply chain resilience, with effects remaining robust across multiple specifications and economically significant. Mechanistic analysis reveals two primary transmission channels through which policy synergy strengthens resilience: (i) industrial structure rationalization, and (ii) agricultural electrification enhancement. Specifically, policy coordination (1) reduces informational barriers between agricultural and related industries, (2) facilitates optimal factor reallocation across sectors, and (3) accelerates the adoption of electricity-intensive precision agriculture technologies. Heterogeneity analysis reveals that policy effectiveness is substantially greater in central and western regions (coefficient ~0.089) compared to eastern regions (coefficient ~0.036), suggesting a ‘technology compensation effect’ whereby digital infrastructure offsets traditional regional disparities. Policy effects remain robustly positive across both major grain-producing and grain-consuming zones, indicating broad applicability. By unpacking the complementary and sequential dynamics between data factors and computing capacity, this study moves beyond the traditional “black box” treatment of the digital economy, providing critical policy insights for the coordinated deployment of digital public goods to secure modern food systems.

title: Nature's minor plants: a multi-dimensional analysis of their integration into European value chains
abstract: Addressing the challenges of climate change, economic instability and sustainability in food production requires a shift toward more diversified and resilient agricultural systems. The integration of minor crops, underutilized, neglected, and climate-resilient species, presents a viable strategy for enhancing food security, biodiversity, and sustainability while reducing the environmental footprint of food production. This conceptual study integrates a literature review, policy analysis, and evidence from EU-funded projects to evaluate pathways for integrating minor crops into sustainable food systems. This study applies the 6Ms framework (Methods, Machines, Materials, Manpower, Measurements, and Milieu) to support the adoption of minor crops into European food value chains. The framework addresses barriers related to processing, product innovation, scalability, regulation, and market uptake. It also emphasizes the role of minor crops in enhancing food security, biodiversity, and resilience to climate change. The findings highlight the need to improve crop productivity and advance food processing technologies, while promoting stakeholder collaboration to address supply chain gaps, regulatory constraints, and financial barriers. By aligning with evolving dietary trends and consumer preferences, minor crops can contribute to more resilient food systems. Our study identifies key trade-offs and synergies across the 6Ms and provides evidence-based recommendations, from crop selection and processing to awareness and policy measures, to improve adoption, nutrition, and sustainability of minor crops. Overall, this work provides a roadmap for advancing minor crops as sustainable food sources through innovation in processing, policy support, and consumer-oriented strategies, contributing to climate-resilient food systems and the achievement of Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).

title: From field to pouch: Life cycle-based external costs of pineapple puree from Costa Rica to Italy
abstract: Global food systems are responsible for one-third of anthropogenic emissions, yet traditional market prices rarely reflect the full societal costs of this production. This study applies Life Cycle Assessment and external cost monetization to quantify resource use, environmental impacts, and price distortions along the pineapple puree value chain from Costa Rica to Italy. Primary data cover agricultural production, processing, logistics, and packaging end-of-life. The impact assessment uses ReCiPe 2016 Midpoint, and environmental results are weighted using monetization factors from the Environmental Prices Handbook. Results per 1 tonne of pineapple puree show that the total external cost of production amounts to €3,002.94, with human toxicity, particulate matter formation, and climate change as dominant impact categories. Processing stages are the main contributors to external costs, while agricultural production plays a secondary role. Internalizing these costs increases the producer price by 58%. Two mitigation scenarios in the production phase—waste sorting and packaging substitution—demonstrate a potential reduction of external costs of 8.9% and 18.6%, respectively. Monetization of environmental impacts emerges as a promising approach to analyse the unfair distribution of costs-impacts along value chains. Findings support decision-making and highlight the need for policy frameworks to integrate external costs into pricing.

title: Contract Farming and Technical Efficiency: Evidence From a Stochastic Frontier Analysis of Greek Durum Wheat Farms
abstract: ABSTRACT This study investigates whether participation in contract farming improves the technical efficiency of durum wheat producers in Greece. Drawing on farm‐level survey data for 338 contract and non‐contract farmers in Central Greece, it examines the extent to which vertical coordination contributes to improved farm performance in the production of a high‐value staple crop. Technical efficiency is estimated with a translog stochastic frontier model, while propensity score matching is used to reduce the association between observable selection bias and participation in contract farming. The results indicate that both contract and non‐contract farmers operate at relatively high levels of technical efficiency. Nevertheless, contract farmers achieve a significant efficiency increase of 0.89 percentage points (93.39% vs. 92.50%). Although this difference is modest in absolute terms, it represents a consistent improvement in efficiency within an already highly productive farming environment. The findings suggest that the benefits of contract farming stem primarily from better input coordination, enhanced managerial discipline, and lower levels of technical inefficiency, rather than from major changes in production technology. By providing evidence from a developed European agricultural setting, this study extends the existing literature on contract farming to strengthen farm performance and improve the functioning of agri‐food value chains.

title: Extreme climate shocks and agricultural net carbon sinks: the moderating role of supply chain resilience in China
abstract: Introduction Extreme climate shocks increasingly challenge the ability of agricultural systems to sustain crop carbon fixation while controlling production-related emissions. Methods Using panel data for 240 Chinese cities from 2002 to 2023, this study examines the relationships between four climate shocks—extreme high temperature (HTD), extreme low temperature (LTD), extreme rainfall (ERD), and extreme drought (EED)—and agricultural net carbon sinks (NCS), together with the moderating role of agricultural supply chain resilience. NCS is measured as annual crop-biomass carbon fixation net of selected agricultural production emissions, thereby providing an integrated, production-based indicator of agricultural carbon performance. Results Two-way fixed-effects estimates show that all four climate shocks are negatively associated with NCS, and the direction of these relationships remains stable across alternative accounting boundaries, sample adjustments, leave-one-province-out tests, and double machine learning specifications. Agricultural supply chain resilience significantly conditions the climate–carbon relationship. Its resistance, recovery, and reorientation capacities attenuate the adverse associations of high-temperature, extreme-rainfall, and drought shocks with NCS. The low-temperature result further indicates that the effectiveness of resilience depends on matching supply chain functions with the biological mechanisms and intervention windows of specific climate hazards. Heterogeneity analyses confirm that climate sensitivity and resilience requirements vary with regional location, agricultural productivity, modernization, and irrigation conditions. Complementary machine-learning analysis identifies nonlinear predictive patterns and reinforces the importance of differentiated adaptation. Discussion These findings extend agricultural climate research from production and emissions to an integrated carbon-balance perspective and demonstrate that hazard-specific supply chain resilience can support both climate adaptation and low-carbon agricultural development.

title: Social structural factors outperform economic assumptions in explaining global municipal waste generation
abstract: Municipal solid waste generation depends on a complex mix of economic, social, environmental, and governance factors, yet the drivers behind it remain poorly understood. Here we show that waste generation across countries is linked to socioeconomic inequality, gender gaps in employment, and resource-intensive economic models, as well as to health indicators such as mental health, drug-related mortality, and life expectancy. Broader measures of human development, the balance between rural and urban populations, marriage equality, education levels, carbon emissions, and birth rates also shape how much waste a country produces. Agricultural land area is tied to waste levels, reflecting food supply chains and agro-industrial activity, while freedom of expression is associated with consumption-driven waste in open, economically advanced societies. These results show that waste generation reflects a country’s overall social development and institutions, not just its wealth or degree of urbanization, pointing to targeted levers for waste-reduction policy. The Human Development Index, CO2 emissions per capita, disease prevalence, and life expectancy are key predictors of municipal waste generation across countries, according to a machine learning analysis of 239 indicators from 195 countries.

title: The 2024 Lebanon conflict: a multidimensional assessment of syndemic impacts on public health and sustainable development goals
abstract: Lebanon entered the 2024 armed conflict with health, environmental, and social systems already weakened by successive crises, including the COVID-19 pandemic, prolonged economic collapse, and the 2020 Beirut Port explosion. This narrative review aimed to synthesize evidence on the documented and anticipated effects of the conflict on public health, healthcare services, the environment, food security, education, and progress toward the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). Evidence was drawn from peer-reviewed studies and reports issued by governmental institutions and international organizations. Documented damage to hospitals and primary healthcare facilities, together with disruptions to medical supply chains, affected routine and emergency care and complicated the management of chronic diseases. Population displacement, overcrowding, and interruptions to essential services also increased the risk of infectious disease transmission and created conditions that may facilitate the spread and emergence of antimicrobial resistance, particularly in displaced and otherwise vulnerable populations. Concurrently, explosive weapons, fires, and infrastructure damage affected air, water, soil, agricultural land, and ecosystems. These environmental and agricultural impacts created plausible pathways linking conflict-related damage to food security, livelihoods, and long-term population health, although direct epidemiological evidence remains limited. Overall, the conflict generated interconnected pressures across health, environmental, and social systems and compounded pre-existing vulnerabilities. Coordinated recovery efforts should restore healthcare capacity, protect environmental and agricultural resources, strengthen surveillance, and support essential social services to reduce long-term harm and promote sustainable recovery.

title: Timing of psychrotrophic cellulolytic bacterial inoculation affects humification and heavy metal immobilization during low-temperature chicken manure composting
abstract: The relatively low ambient temperatures during spring in northeastern China can severely limit the self-heating capacity of aerobic composting, resulting in insufficient compost maturity before agricultural application. In this study, psychrotrophic cellulolytic bacteria were inoculated at different phases of the composting process. The results showed that, except for the control, all composting treatments reached temperatures that met the sanitation standards of the United States Department of Agriculture. The initial stage (D0) treatment outperformed the control, with pile temperatures rapidly reaching 65 °C and remaining above 45 °C for 10 d. Additionally, D0 treatment substantially enhanced humification, increasing the humification index by 125% and humic acid content by 226% relative to the control. This treatment enhanced heavy metal immobilization, with the most pronounced reduction observed for EXC-Pb (87.14%). Microbial analysis revealed the preferential enrichment of cellulose-degrading bacteria ( Pseudoxanthomonas and Cellvibrio ) and taxa potentially involved in heavy metal immobilization ( Devosia ) in the D0 treatment. Compared with the control, D0 increased microbial network complexity, with cooperative interactions rising from 76.08% to 86.71%. Structural equation modeling suggested that microbial communities were associated with HMs bioavailability through physicochemical property- and humification-related pathways (β = 0.342, P < 0.05). In saline-alkali soil pot trials, treatment with organic fertilizer modified by D0 produced the highest pakchoi ( Brassica rapa subsp. chinensis) biomass while simultaneously enhancing soil fertility. This study provides evidence that initial inoculation with a psychrotrophic cellulolytic consortium improves humification and heavy metal immobilization during low-temperature composting, with potential implications for cold-region composting.

title: Knowledge Level of Farmer Producer Organization Members about FPOs in Manipur, India
journal: Journal of Scientific Research and Reports
abstract: Farmer Producer Organisations play an important role in collectivising small and marginal farmers and improving their access to inputs, services, markets and institutional support. The present study was conducted to assess the knowledge level of FPO members about Farmer Producer Organisations in Manipur during 2025–2026. The study covered four FPOs promoted by Central Agricultural University, Imphal, and the Small Farmers’ Agribusiness Consortium in four purposively selected districts of Manipur. A total of 115 respondents were selected through random sampling, and data were collected using a structured interview schedule. An ex-post facto research design was followed, and the data were analysed using frequency, percentage, mean and standard deviation. Knowledge was assessed through 15 multiple-choice questions covering the activities, objectives, structure, functioning and facilities of FPOs. The findings revealed that 60.87% of respondents had a medium level of knowledge, followed by 25.21% with a high level and 13.91% with a low level of knowledge. Respondents demonstrated comparatively better knowledge of the meaning and benefits of FPOs, while considerable gaps were observed regarding governance, leadership, registration procedures, record maintenance and organisational structure. The study suggests strengthening training, awareness and capacity-building programmes to improve members’ knowledge and effective participation in FPO activities.

title: When the neediest are the least ready: Open business models in Indonesian banana value chains
journal: Journal of Open Innovation Technology Market and Complexity
abstract: This study challenges the narrative that open business models drive inclusive agricultural development. A comparative case study of Indonesian banana value chains confirms that an open, cooperative-mediated export model is associated with lower transaction costs, reduced information asymmetry, and greater financial inclusion than a closed, middleman-dominated domestic model. However, four critical complications have emerged. First, the transparency of the open model is superficial; cooperative management remains obscure to members, revealing that outward openness masks inward closures. Second, farmers do not commit to one model but maintain portfolio strategies, retaining ties to the closed system as insurance against open-system risks. Third, a break-even analysis shows that the closed system's credit terms dominate formal options when the harvest failure probability exceeds approximately 37% under the median-rate and full-waiver assumptions—an illustrative scenario rather than a general empirical threshold, because the threshold ranges from 26% to above 100% across the observed rate and waiver combinations, indicating that closed models persist through competitiveness, not merely exploitation. Fourth, the wide interest rate dispersion within the closed model (48–150%) reveals an internal spectrum from extractive to relational intermediaries. This study makes three contributions: nested closure, portfolio rather than binary adoption, and a Capability–Need Inversion Paradox advanced as a theory-generating proposition supported by preliminary researcher-rated evidence and by the captured-openness, dominance-region, and intermediary-gradient findings. These findings challenge simplistic openness-development narratives and provide a framework for understanding business model dynamics in asymmetric institutional contexts, where relational complexity, risk management, and local adaptation fundamentally shape the outcomes.

title: Can information increase farmers’ willingness to pay for digital agricultural technologies? A survey experiment on agricultural drones in rural China
abstract: Can information interventions increase farmers’ willingness to pay (WTP) for digital agricultural technologies, and do their effects vary by mode of access? We conduct a large-scale survey experiment across eight provinces in China, providing farmers with technical and market information about agricultural drones. The intervention significantly increases WTP by approximately 29% for drone services and 37% for direct investment, relative to their baseline levels. Mechanism analysis suggests that farmers’ improved cognition of technical characteristics exhibits an inverted-U relationship with service WTP but a positive relationship with investment WTP, whereas cognition of market conditions is positively associated with WTP for both modes. Using a saturation design, we identify a positive spillover effect on service WTP and a treatment-saturation effect consistent with social interaction: treated farmers in partially treated villages exhibit lower gains in service WTP than those in fully treated villages, with this pattern moderated by local adoption status. Importantly, while advantaged farmers exhibit larger WTP gains for direct investment, disadvantaged farmers (smallholders, elderly, less educated) respond more on the service margin, suggesting a potential pathway to address the digital divide. Illustrative projections based on stated WTP suggest possible increases in investment rates. These findings imply that extension programs should be tailored to local adoption conditions and facilitate service-based access for inclusive agricultural digitalization.

title: Behavioral decision-making and marketing institution preferences in coconut agroindustry development: evidence from SWOT-AHP and value-added analysis in Indonesia
abstract: Introduction Coconut agroindustry supports rural livelihoods and economic resilience in Indonesia, yet many producers remain dependent on inefficient marketing systems characterized by intermediary dominance, weak bargaining power, and limited value-added diversification. This study examines how behavioral decision-making influences marketing institution preferences and strategic agroindustry development in Buton Regency, Indonesia. Methods A field-based mixed-method study involved 489 copra processors, 182 coconut shell charcoal processors, marketing actors, and 10 institutional experts. Economic performance was evaluated through Hayami value-added analysis, farmer’s share, marketing margins, and a price-spread efficiency index. The archived expert-consensus ordering of five marketing-institution criteria was converted into normalized rank-order centroid weights. The retained four-group priority vector was analyzed through a transparent group-level SWOT-AHP synthesis and one-at-a-time sensitivity analysis. Results Coconut shell charcoal processing generated an average value added of IDR 1,002.52/kg and a value-added ratio of 54.87%. The shorter marketing channel increased farmer's share from 75.00% to 85.71% and reduced the price-spread index from 25.00% to 14.29%. Selling price (0.4567), demand stability (0.2567), and accessibility (0.1567) were the leading preference criteria. SWOT weights were 0.4658 for strengths, 0.2771 for opportunities, 0.1611 for weaknesses, and 0.0960 for threats. The normalized strategy scores ranked SO first (0.3715), followed by ST (0.2809), WO (0.2191), and WT (0.1286); no rank reversals occurred under ±10% and ±20% weight perturbations. Discussion Coconut-agroindustry decisions reflect both economic incentives and institutional constraints. Higher-value processing and shorter marketing channels improve economic outcomes, but liquidity certainty, transaction security, accessibility, and institutional familiarity continue to shape producer preferences. The behavioral interpretation is therefore preference-based and conceptual rather than a psychometric validation of bounded rationality or institutional trust.

title: Nitric Oxide Signaling in Photosynthetic Resilience: Linking Photoprotection and Carbon Gain in Tropical Crops
abstract: Tropical crops are increasingly exposed to climate-driven, recurrent combinations of heat, excessive irradiance, high vapor pressure deficit (VPD), drought, flooding, salinity, and pathogen pressure that collectively impair photosynthesis and reduce crop productivity. Unlike individual stress events, these interacting stresses simultaneously disrupt photoprotection, electron transport, carbon assimilation, stomatal regulation, and chloroplast redox homeostasis, ultimately limiting whole-plant carbon gain under fluctuating environments. Nitric oxide (NO) has emerged as a central signaling molecule coordinating these adaptive responses, yet its roles in photosynthetic regulation remain dispersed across molecular, physiological, and crop-specific studies. This review presents an integrated framework linking chloroplast-level NO signaling with whole-plant photosynthetic performance in major tropical crops, including maize, sugarcane, banana, cassava, and oil palm. We propose that NO regulates photosynthetic resilience through three interconnected axes: (i) reversible protein S-nitrosylation that modulates photosynthetic complexes and Calvin–Benson cycle enzymes; (ii) maintenance of chloroplast redox homeostasis through coordinated reactive oxygen species (ROS) and reactive nitrogen species (RNS) signaling, antioxidant networks, and S-nitrosothiol metabolism; and (iii) ABA-mediated stomatal regulation that optimizes the trade-off between carbon assimilation, stomatal conductance, and water-use efficiency under environmental stress. We further discuss the emerging roles of S-nitrosothiols (SNOs) and S-nitrosoglutathione (GSNO) as central regulators of NO homeostasis and potential biochemical indicators linking chloroplast signaling with whole-plant carbon performance. By synthesizing current evidence across climate-relevant stress combinations, including heat + high light, drought + high VPD, flooding + hypoxia, salinity + pathogen interactions, this review provides a conceptual framework for understanding NO-mediated photosynthetic resilience and identifies key research priorities for developing NO-based strategies to enhance productivity and climate resilience in tropical cropping systems.

title: AI-assisted smartphone-based prompt fluorescence imaging for adulteration monitoring of extra virgin olive oil
abstract: Detection of adulteration in extra-virgin olive oil (EVOO) and tracing possible sources remain critical challenges for food authenticity, consumer safety, and regulatory enforcement, particularly in resource-limited settings where the application of high-accuracy analytical tools is impractical. In this work, a practical integration of a machine learning system with a compact, ultra-low-cost smartphone-based prompt fluorescence imaging platform is presented for on-site detection of EVOO adulteration, where prompt fluorescence refers to fluorescence recorded during excitation without time-delayed detection. The proposed platform employs a λ= 405 nm laser excitation source and orthogonal fluorescence imaging geometry, customized with a smartphone CMOS camera. The smartphone runs as a two-stage analytical framework, comprising adulterant classification followed by concentration estimation. The performance of machine-learning approaches (LightGBM, SVM, KNN, RF, Logistic Regression, Naive Bayes, Gradient Boosting, Decision Tree, Lasso Regression, SVR) has been evaluated using EVOO adulterated with common sources of adulteration such as refined olive oil, soybean oil, and palm oil over a wide concentration range. Machine learning models attain strong discrimination ability and high predictive accuracy by utilizing non-linear relationships within the fluorescence-derived RGB features. Independent validation using real samples confirms reliable adulterant identification and accurate EVOO purity estimation, with an average error of 3.1%. The present framework has been developed and validated using binary mixtures containing EVOO and a single adulterant, with the minimum operational detection threshold being 2% adulterant concentration. The proposed approach overcomes key limitations of conventional methods by enabling simultaneous detection of adulterant type and quantification without prior knowledge of the adulterant type, and therefore allowing users to predict the possible source of adulteration.

title: Unraveling the catalytic potential of a heterometallic Zn-Ca metal-organic framework for intensified green biodiesel synthesis from waste palm oil
abstract: The diminution of fossil fuel reserves and the escalating environmental concerns have triggered a worldwide search for sustainable energy solutions. In this light, the present study explores the use of a heterometallic structured zinc-calcium metal-organic framework (Zn-Ca MOF) as a heterogeneous catalyst to address this problem. The novelty of this work lies in integrating this heterometallic Zn-Ca MOF catalyst with statistical process optimization and economic assessment for the conversion of waste palm oil into biodiesel. To optimize the transesterification process, Response Surface Methodology (RSM) based on a Central Composite Design (CCD) was employed to assess the interactive impact of key process variables, specifically methanol-to-oil molar ratio, catalyst loading, reaction temperature, and time, to maximize the production of fatty acid methyl esters (FAME). Under the optimized conditions of a methanol-to-oil ratio of 6:1, a catalyst loading of 5 wt %, a temperature of 75 °C, and a reaction time of 180 min, a remarkable biodiesel productivity of 97.34% was achieved. Catalyst reusability tests demonstrated sustained catalytic activity without decay over seven consecutive reaction cycles, while life cycle cost analysis (LCCA) confirmed the economic feasibility of the process. These findings validate that the Zn-Ca MOF is a robust, efficient, and cost-effective hetero-catalyst for sustainable biodiesel production.

title: Judicial Interpretation and Employee Compensation in Corporate Insolvency: A Comparative Analysis of Malaysia and Australia
abstract: When a company is wound up, employee compensation is recognised, but it usually occupies a vulnerable position. Although most insolvency systems grant priority to unpaid wages, termination benefits, and accrued employment entitlements, substantive recovery often remains uncertain due to asset insufficiency and interactions with secured creditor claims. This article examines how judicial interpretation mediates the relationship between formal priority and actual recovery in corporate insolvency. The study adopts a doctrinal and comparative case law approach based on the analysis of leading insolvency decisions in Malaysia and Australia. The findings indicate that courts in both jurisdictions consistently uphold statutory hierarchy but differ in their interpretive engagement with employee vulnerability and asset characterisation. Australian cases more often involve questions of circulating assets, receivership, and estate scope, and operate within a framework supplemented by the Fair Entitlements Guarantee (FEG) scheme. Malaysian courts generally adopt a more formalist interpretive posture within insolvency distribution law, where employee recovery remains more directly dependent on statutory priority and the sufficiency of the insolvent estate. The article contributes to comparative insolvency scholarship by clarifying how interpretive choices and structural constraints shape employee protection in practice.

title: The hidden wealth of forests: quantifying shadow protection value via a revealed-preference Hartman-Faustmann extension
abstract: This paper introduces a revealed-preference application of the Hartman-Faustmann forestry valuation to construct a one-sided, benchmark-relative opportunity-cost measure for privately owned forests, combining population-wide administrative data on forest owners with forest characteristics. Using stand-level data for over 690,000 privately owned forest stands in Finland, I compare observed stand ages with Faustmann-optimal rotation ages calculated under the benchmark model. Stands left unharvested beyond the Faustmann-optimal rotation age are assigned a shadow protection value (SPV), defined as the foregone timber value associated with observed harvest postponement relative to that benchmark. I examine how owner characteristics are associated with extended rotations and foregone timber revenue. The results imply an aggregate SPV of €196–323 million (€423–724 per hectare of delayed-rotation forest) across discount rates of 3% to 1%. Around 36.8% of identifiable private forest owners have stands with extended rotations, covering 3.6% of privately owned forests. Among delayed-rotation stands, SPV and extension length are higher for rural residents and owners with larger forest holdings, while the associations with owner age and heir-estate status are sensitive to model specification. The observed heterogeneity may inform targeting of forest policy instruments by indicating for whom liquidity constraints and ownership-transfer frictions may be most relevant.

title: The perceptions and attitudes of small-scale farmers toward climate change in eThekwini Municipality, KwaZulu-Natal
abstract: Climate change poses substantial risks to small-scale agricultural production and rural livelihoods, yet evidence on how farmers perceive and respond to these risks remains limited in South Africa’s rural–urban–per-urban agricultural settings. This study examined small-scale farmers’ perceptions and attitudes toward climate change in withering Municipality, KwaZulu-Natal, and assessed the socioeconomic and institutional factors associated with these outcomes. Using a cross-sectional quantitative design, primary data were collected through structured interviews with 296 small-scale farmers. Descriptive statistics, composite perception and attitude indices, independent-samples t-tests, and Tobit regression models were employed. Most farmers reported substantial climate-related challenges: 93% perceived negative effects of climate change on crop yields, 97% reported that changing rainfall patterns had made farming more difficult, and 87% identified water shortages as a major production challenge. Although 69.7% of farmers reported awareness of climate change and 70.3% had access to climate information, only 15.8% reported access to agricultural credit. Perceptions did not differ significantly between farmers who reported being aware of climate change and those who did not ( p = 0.603), nor did attitudes ( p = 0.186). In the Tobit model, marital status (β = 0.045; p = 0.049) and access to climate information (β = 0.060; p = 0.046) were positively associated with perception scores at the 5% significance level. Attitude scores were positively associated with farmer-organization membership (β = 0.060; p = 0.018) and access to climate information (β = 0.066; p = 0.022) at the 5% level, while gender (β = 0.058; p = 0.080), farming experience (β = 0.003; p = 0.087), and agricultural training (β = 0.021; p = 0.100) were associated at the 10% level; extension visits were negatively associated with attitudes (β = −0.003; p = 0.083). These findings suggest that climate-risk recognition is widespread, but awareness alone may be insufficient to support effective adaptation. Policy should therefore priorities accessible, location-specific climate information, strengthened extension and farmer-organization platforms, targeted agricultural training, and improved access to adaptation finance and climate-resilient technologies.

title: Mapping of digital transformation in the African agri-food trade system
abstract: Background Digital trade is an important component of modern food systems as it enhances efficiency, business transactions, traceability and regulatory compliance. In the African continent, digital transformation of agri-food systems is needed, as reflected in the continental initiatives to advance digital trade. Agriculture is a key driver for economic development for the continent. However, there is currently no coherent synthesis of literature on the state of digitalisation supporting agri-food trade in Africa. Scope and approach This study systematically reviews scientific and grey literature to examine how Africa’s digital landscape aligns with agri-food digital trade requirements. It maps trends, drivers, and barriers to digitalisation in the African agri-food sector, digital solutions, and technologies. Key findings and conclusions The analysis reveals steady growth, but several imbalances between countries, value chains, and actors. The study identifies five categories: digital extension services, fintech, supply chain management, digital farm management and digital marketing, and the underlying technologies. Existing studies do not provide a coherent digital trade framework based on compliance with trade and digital standards, which is consistent with the fact that Africa’s paperless and streamlined trade processes, the goal the continent is aspiring to, are far from being realised. Digital transformation in Africa is occurring in a fragmented manner across different domains rather than as part of an integrated digital ecosystem aligned with trade requirements and is therefore insufficient to address fundamental barriers in Africa’s agri-food trade systems. The findings suggest that unlocking Africa’s agri-food trade potential requires a systematic digital trade ecosystem approach.

title: A secure federated learning framework with blockchain-based authentication for anomaly detection in cooperative smart farming
abstract: Agriculture is still a crucial global pillar of the world economy, ensuring food security and livelihood. But changing climate conditions and increasing reliance on the Internet of Things (IoT) based precision agriculture have brought new challenges, mainly cybersecurity. Cooperative Smart Farming (CSF) schemes promote resource pooling among small farmers and thus, the adoption of cutting-edge technologies. Although democratizing precision farming also makes it more accessible to cyber threats. To sort out all these problems, the proposed method introduces a secure federated learning framework along with blockchain-based authentication for anomaly detection in CSFs. The proposed method employs a federated transfer learning-based shadow attention mechanism, in conjunction with the Zeiler and Fergus network, to amplify the performance of the anomaly detection technique. This allows farms to detect threats in premises while protecting data privacy, as only model updates that are encrypted are transmitted. A blockchain-backed decentralized authentication scheme based on the proof of authentication consensus protocol is built to provide trust and resistance to tampering. Moreover, the random k-sparsification technique with changing rank adjustment has a positive impact on communication efficiency, which results in the same level of accuracy but with less communication overhead. The proposed method is executed on four datasets, CSE-CIS-IDS2018, MQTTset, ToN-IoT, and Edge IoT, achieving classification accuracies of 99.99%,99.93%,99.94%, and 99.91%, respectively, and it performs better than the current techniques. This comprehensive framework provides a scalable and trusted method for anomaly detection in CSFs, enabling resilient, privacy-preserving, and intelligent smart farming ecosystems.

title: Terrain–Infrastructure Interactions and Modeled Freight Trip Attraction in a Mountainous City: Evidence from Chongqing, China
abstract: Mountainous terrain fragments urban land, constrains network design, and raises the cost of linking firms across supply chains. This study examines how terrain and the built environment are associated with modeled freight trip attraction (FTA) in Chongqing, China. A route-level dataset for large and medium-sized enterprises is combined with measures of water and mountain obstacles, elevation variation, road and building density, and industrial-park configuration. XGBoost models and SHAP values are used to identify nonlinear relationships and interactions. The results show that water barriers, mountain obstacles, and elevation variation are generally associated with lower FTA. Road and building density can moderate these constraints, but the relationships are threshold-dependent and show diminishing or reversing contributions at high levels. Industrial-park configuration also matters: the same infrastructure characteristic has different associations depending on whether origin and destination firms are located inside or outside a park. Sector-specific models further indicate that agriculture-related chains respond more strongly to improved connectivity, whereas coal and other extractive activities remain sensitive to elevation. Our findings support terrain-sensitive land-use and freight planning that coordinates industrial location, road investment, and cross-barrier connections rather than relying on uniform infrastructure expansion.

title: Designing climate-adaptable agricultural supply chain networks with heterogeneous regions for perishable food systems in Turkey: A sustainable multi-echelon optimization approach
abstract: This study develops a drought-aware agricultural supply chain network (AGSCN) for perishable crops at risk of drought, explicitly incorporating spatial zoning across heterogeneous farming regions with distinct production characteristics, including low- and high-risk zones. A bi-objective mixed-integer linear programming (BOMILP) model is formulated to simultaneously minimize total system cost and carbon emissions, thereby capturing economic efficiency and environmental sustainability considerations in perishable agricultural supply chain (AGSC) operations. The key contributions of this study are: (i) explicit integration of spatially heterogeneous production zones, enabling region-dependent production and allocation decisions under drought conditions; (ii) incorporation of region-specific drought disruption rates and yield factors to represent heterogeneous climate impacts on agricultural production capacity and supply chain performance; (iii) development of a unified BOMILP framework that jointly optimizes economic and environmental objectives in perishable AGSCNs; and (iv) a sequential multi-echelon distribution structure linking (iv) a sequential multi-echelon distribution structure linking farmers, local markets, wholesale markets, processing/export facilities, and consumers while accounting for capacity limitations and the operational characteristics of perishable agricultural products. A real-world case study of the Turkish tomato supply chain demonstrates the applicability of the proposed framework. The results show that increasing drought severity substantially changes regional sourcing patterns: the contribution of the high-risk Zone B to total supply decreases from approximately 45% under mild drought conditions to 22% under severe drought. In contrast, the model increases reliance on the more reliable Zone A, whose contribution reaches approximately 78% of the total network supply. These results demonstrate the model's ability to dynamically reallocate production and distribution flows in response to heterogeneous drought impacts while maintaining supply continuity. Overall, the findings highlight the importance of spatial diversification and adaptive sourcing strategies for improving the resilience and sustainability of perishable AGSCs under climate-induced disruptions.

title: Mixed‐Methods Insights on Trade Efficiency and Sustainability in Indonesia's Palm Oil Sector
abstract: ABSTRACT This study combines quantitative trade modelling with qualitative stakeholder perspectives. The quantitative analysis integrates gravity modelling and stochastic frontier analysis to evaluate trade efficiency across destination markets, revealing generally low export efficiency with considerable variation across markets and product groups. While tariffs exhibit a more consistent negative relationship with trade performance, the relationship between regulatory distance in non‐tariff measures and trade performance is less robust across model specifications. Qualitative insights from government, industry, smallholders, and non‐governmental organizations (NGOs) provide important context for these findings. Stakeholders consistently identify sustainability requirements, particularly certification, traceability, and land legality, as central to market access. Government actors emphasize trade diplomacy and market diversification, industry representatives highlight compliance costs and technical adaptation, smallholders stress price volatility and the risk of exclusion from formal supply chains, while the limited NGO responses identify sustainability as an important consideration for market legitimacy. Across stakeholder groups, sustainability emerges as a key link between trade barriers, market opportunities, and export competitiveness. Integrating both strands of evidence reveals convergence between the negative association of regulatory distance with trade performance and stakeholder concerns about sustainability‐related market barriers, particularly in the European Union (EU), while also highlighting firm‐level and implementation frictions that are not captured by macro‐level trade models. The findings suggest that access to the EU market is becoming increasingly dependent on compliance with stringent sustainability requirements. The study concludes that strengthening Indonesia's export performance requires a coordinated strategy combining efficiency improvements, sustainability compliance, trade diplomacy, and targeted support for smallholders.

summary_id.tujuan: Studi ini menganalisis efisiensi perdagangan dan dampak hambatan non-tarif, khususnya persyaratan keberlanjutan, terhadap ekspor minyak sawit Indonesia, dengan memadukan pemodelan perdagangan kuantitatif dan perspektif pemangku kepentingan kualitatif.
summary_id.metode: Desain campuran (mixed-methods) yang menggabungkan model gravitasi perdagangan dan stochastic frontier analysis untuk mengukur efisiensi ekspor lintas pasar tujuan, serta analisis kualitatif terhadap perspektif pemerintah, industri, petani kecil, dan LSM. Abstrak tidak menyebutkan periode data, sumber data, jumlah sampel, jumlah informan, maupun lokasi penelitian secara rinci.
summary_id.temuan: Efisiensi ekspor sawit Indonesia umumnya rendah dengan variasi besar antarpasar dan kelompok produk. Tarif menunjukkan hubungan negatif yang lebih konsisten dengan kinerja perdagangan, sedangkan hubungan jarak regulasi (non-tariff measures) dengan kinerja perdagangan kurang robust antarspesifikasi model. Temuan ini bersifat asosiatif, bukan kausal, dan keterkaitan dengan persyaratan keberlanjutan di Uni Eropa hanya diperkuat melalui konvergensi dengan persepsi pemangku kepentingan.
summary_id.relevansi: Studi ini langsung berkaitan dengan agenda riset mengenai kelapa sawit, akses pasar petani kecil, dan rantai nilai, terutama terkait sertifikasi, ketelusuran, dan legalitas lahan sebagai syarat akses pasar UE. Temuan tentang kerentanan petani kecil terhadap volatilitas harga dan risiko keluar dari rantai pasok formal dapat diuji ulang dengan data petani sawit swadaya di Kalimantan Tengah, termasuk kelembagaan petani dan kesiapan adopsi sistem ketelusuran digital.

title: Mapping climate resilience and food security outcomes in smallholder agricultural systems research in low- and middle-income countries
abstract: Climate change threatens agricultural systems and food security in low- and middle-income countries. Seven agricultural interventions have been identified for their potential to improve both food security (FS) and climate resilience (CR) in smallholder systems. This review examines how FS and CR outcomes are measured across these interventions, where research has concentrated, and where gaps remain. We focus on simultaneous measurement of both outcomes in contrast to previous reviews that examined one or the other. We conducted searches in six databases. Using a combination of manual screening and ML classification we identified a subset of 127 studies reporting at least one FS and one CR outcome. Based on this subset, literature is concentrated on biophysical interventions; soil conservation, improved water management, and crop diversification, while enabling interventions such as improved market access, access to climate information and extension services, and post-harvest management and storage are sparsely represented. Most studies assess short-term outcomes at community or household level, providing highly context-specific insights. The focus on biophysical indicators restricts understanding of how smallholder resilience is shaped with enabling interventions beyond the farm gate. Similarly, emphasis on short-term impacts, and small study scales, limits development of systemic insights. Addressing these constraints requires a shift toward multi-level, longitudinal research and adoption of harmonized FS and CR indicators enabling comparability and scaling. Collaborative efforts among research networks, donors, and international organizations promoting standardized indicators and impact-evaluation frameworks will be essential to build coherent evidence base capable of guiding resilient food-system transformation under increasing climate stress.

title: From plantation to secondary market: A mesoeconomic thematic analysis on labour demand–supply coordination and food waste reduction in the Australian banana industry
journal: Journal of Agriculture and Food Research
abstract: ABSTRACT Food waste in fresh produce supply chains is often attributed to logistics, retail standards, or consumer preferences, yet the role of labour demand–supply coordination in labour-intensive horticulture remains under-examined. This study investigates how labour coordination, market structures, organisational capacity, and value-recovery pathways jointly shape food-waste generation and the recovery of off-spec bananas through secondary markets and circular-economy pathways in the Australian banana industry. Using a mesoeconomic perspective, four in-depth semi-structured interviews were conducted across four Queensland banana farms of different operational scales, involving three growers/decision-makers and one central packing-shed manager. Thematic analysis examined how labour pipelines, training systems, technology, market access, and organisational practices interact to influence food-waste outcomes. The findings show that food waste is not primarily a technical failure but an outcome of interrelated coordination processes involving labour systems, market structures, organisational practices, and recovery mechanisms.
