Family-based farms rely on tacit labour and short marketing circuits to minimise waste, whereas medium- and large-scale operations use institutionalised migration schemes, structured training, and data-driven packing systems to stabilise labour supply and manage quality losses. Supermarket grading standards and transport distances contribute to structurally embedded waste, while secondary processing, animal feed, and other value-recovery pathways partially offset these losses. Across the cases, workforce continuity, training, and organisational coordination were associated with lower preventable waste and greater recovery of off-spec fruit. By positioning food waste within the mesoeconomic organisation of production, labour, markets, and recovery pathways, this study contributes to agricultural economics by demonstrating how interconnected organisational and market mechanisms shape waste generation and value recovery. The findings provide practical implications for labour policy, migration schemes, secondary-market development, and circular-economy strategies in perishable agricultural supply chains.

title: Beyond awareness: accounting for information exposure bias in adoption and income effects of Orange-Fleshed Sweet Potato technology among smallholder farming households in Nigeria
abstract: This study examined the role of information exposure in the adoption of Orange-Fleshed Sweet Potato (OFSP) technology and its effect on the income of smallholder sweet potato farming households in Nigeria. Using cross-sectional primary data collected from 320 smallholder sweet potato farming households in Osun and Kwara States through a two-stage sampling procedure, the study accounted for heterogeneous awareness exposure and actual adoption behavior. The Heckman probit selection model was employed to distinguish between awareness exposure and adoption conditional on awareness, while the Endogenous Treatment Effect (ETE) and Inverse-Probability-Weighted Regression Adjustment (IPWRA) models were used to estimate the income effects of OFSP adoption while correcting for potential endogeneity and selection bias. The findings showed that awareness exposure was significantly influenced by age, marital status, household size, and membership in farmer associations, whereas adoption conditional on awareness was significantly associated with education, farming experience, and access to credit. Descriptively, OFSP adopters reported more favorable perceptions of the technology’s productivity, climate resilience, and nutritional benefits than non-adopters. Both ETE and IPWRA estimates further indicated that OFSP adoption had a positive and significant effect on household income. The study concludes that awareness and adoption are distinct stages influenced by different factors. Policies aimed at promoting OFSP adoption should therefore strengthen targeted information dissemination, extension support, farmer education, and access to credit to enhance adoption, household income, food security, nutrition, and rural livelihoods.

title: From Farm to Global Markets: Enhancing Rural Livelihoods Through Sustainable Superfood Supply Chains
abstract: ABSTRACT This research examines the cultivation and distribution business strategies of rural superfoods aimed at sustainable development. Superfoods have the potential to sustainably improve rural livelihoods, promote healthy consumption and enable integration into global markets as health consciousness rises. Accordingly, the study has explored the Sustainable Business Development Factors (SBDFs) that could contribute to the attainment of the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) including poverty alleviation (SDG 1), health awareness and sustainable wellness (SDG 3), business modernization and structural development (SDG 9), sustainable harvesting and dietary habits (SDG 12) and collaboration for collective success (SDG 17). The research uses Fuzzy Analytical Hierarchy Process (FAHP), Pareto analysis, and Fuzzy DEMATEL to identify, rank and analyse causal relationships among the SBDFs. Analysis shows that social motivation, sustainability‐driven behaviours and government support lead to success. The prominent causal SBDFs identified were local and regional food systems, rural development and infrastructure, information governance and digital infrastructure and institutional support and capacity building. They influence social responsibility and ethical standards, supply chain transparency and traceability, sustainable packaging and transportation, health and safety standards and carbon footprint reduction. This analysis enables superfoods to integrate environmental, social and governance (ESG) sustainability, providing smallholders with actionable knowledge to develop sustainable, digitally enabled business models.

title: The Prospects and Challenges of Community Seed/Field Banking of Bananas, Roots and Tubers: Insights from the Literature and a Pilot Initiative in Ghana
abstract: Neglected and underutilized species, also known as minor or orphan crops, are a core component of local food systems in Africa. Roots, tubers, and bananas (RTB) are a particular group of these crops characterized by vegetative propagation. This reproductive system poses challenges for their conservation. Community seed banks commonly conserve seeds of grains, oil crops, pulses, and vegetables. However, little is known about whether and how community seed banks around the world include roots, tubers, and bananas, which cannot be easily stored in conventional seed-bank facilities. The objective of this review was to contribute to the design of a method that can be effectively used by community seed banks to conserve RTB while complementing the conservation method already used for other crops. We conducted a systematic literature review and assessed the initial results of a pilot study involving a new community-based conservation mechanism introduced in Ghana: the community field bank. The strengths and challenges of the two methods were compared. Field bank and seed bank can become complementary components, both conceptually and practically, of a dynamic conservation system that farmers can master through learning by doing. Initial observations from the field in Ghana suggest that farmers have grasped the concept and are now monitoring the practicalities of RTB field-bank plots, with the distribution of the first vegetatively propagated planting materials taking place toward the end of 2026. Further research, both within and beyond the pilot study sites, is warranted to refine the field-bank method.

title: Performance of millet intercrops under Casuarina junghuhniana Miq.-based agroforestry system and consequent changes in soil fertility
abstract: An intercropping experiment was made through three consecutive crop cycles with Casuarina junghuhniana Miq. Plantations of (Casuarinaceae) established between 3–18 months after tree planting to determine the most suitable millet species and to determine the effect of intercropping on soil fertility. Six millet intercrops-kodo millet (Paspalum scrobiculatum L.), foxtail millet (Setaria italica (L.) P.Beauv.), finger millet (Eleusine coracana (L.) Gaertn.). Invading species include Gaertn., barnyard millet (Echinochloa frumentacea Link) and three crop species including little millet (Panicum sumatrense Roth) and proso millet (Panicum miliaceum L.) were tested in a randomised block design (RBD) with 3 blocks at the tree spacing of 2 m × 2 m. Evaluation was done for growth attributes, dry matter production (DMP), grain yield, crop equivalent yield (CEY), tree growth parameters, soil fertility and economics. Little millet always had the highest DMP (2560–2650 kg ha-1) and grain yield (770–1890 kg ha-1) under intercropping and added the highest value for tree height (5.63 m at 18 months) and wood production (29.84 t ha-1). C. junghuhniana + little millet produced the highest total land equivalent ratio (land equivalent ratio (LER) = 2.92) followed by C. junghuhniana + barnyard millet (LER = 2.51). Maximum net income (₹26000) and benefit to cost ratio (B : C = 3.16) was also obtained for little millet. The post-harvest soil analysis showed that the soil under all intercropping treatment was better in terms of soil electrical conductivity, soil organic carbon and available soil nutrients, namely nitrogen (N), phosphorus (P) and potassium (K) than in the tree-alone treatment. Kodo millet was least compatible intercrop in the study. Little millet is suggested as the best intercrop for C. junghuhniana-based short rotation plantation agroforestry, providing a viable option to the smallholder farmers to obtain short-term food and income and to promote the growth of trees and regeneration of soil fertility, thus emphasising the importance of selecting the appropriate species for agroforestry intercrop systems for better ecological and economic returns.

title: Perceptions of forest certification among key audiences in a mediterranean landscape dominated by forestry plantations
abstract: Forest certification (FC) was created to promote responsible forestry by requiring compliance with defined environmental, social, and economic standards. Across Europe, interest in FC has grown in response to climate change mitigation and increasing societal demand for sustainable production. In Portugal, however, uptake remains low. Although small landowners hold most forested land, most certified areas are managed by two major pulp and paper companies, highlighting long-standing challenges in Portuguese forest management. Promoting sustainable forestry requires understanding how stakeholders who depend on and use forest products perceive forests and FC. To explore this, we conducted an anonymous semi-structured survey of forest managers, technicians, workers, landowners, and residents/users of plantations in Central Portugal. Respondents widely recognised forests as key providers of ecosystem services and consistently distinguished between native forests and eucalypt plantations, rating native forests more positively overall; however, perceptions varied across groups, particularly between forestry professionals and the general public. Knowledge of FC also differed, with forestry-related respondents showing greater familiarity and more positive assessments of its benefits, while others reported limited awareness. Nonetheless, most participants considered FC a valuable management tool, noting that uncertified plantations often lack active management. Among landowners, economic gain was the primary motivation for pursuing certification, while non-certified landowners cited small property size and lack of awareness as barriers. Our findings highlight the need for locally-adapted strategies that address the economic, administrative, and social concerns identified by stakeholders, and strengthen cooperative management structures (e.g., forest owners’ associations) to support broader adoption of FC across Portugal.

title: How does agribusiness-led contract farming affect the rural common prosperity: empirical evidence from China
abstract: Agribusiness-led contract farming is widely recognized as an institutional arrangement that reduces transaction costs and stabilizes smallholder incomes, yet its macro-level implications for rural common prosperity remain insufficiently understood. Using prefecture-level panel data from 272 Chinese cities over 2015–2023, this study empirically examines how agribusiness-led contract farming affects rural common prosperity through the dual lenses of affluence and sharing. Baseline estimates show that agribusiness-led contract farming significantly raises rural disposable income while narrowing both inter-city rural income gap and urban–rural income disparities. These effects operate through enhancing agricultural labor productivity and facilitating non-agricultural employment. Heterogeneity analyses reveal stronger impacts in industrially weak, remote, and economically lagging regions. Spatial econometric estimates further indicate that the positive spillover effects of agribusiness-led contract farming depend more on economic connectivity than on geographic proximity alone. Policy implications include scaling up agribusiness-led contract farming in underdeveloped areas, strengthening rural vocational training, and fostering inter-regional value-chain linkages.

title: Beyond administrative boundaries: how agricultural socialized services drive grain-oriented cropping transformation in China
abstract: China’s grain security rests on a smallholder sector in which the average household cultivates 0.6 hectares, a scale that constrains mechanization and limits gains in production efficiency. Since 2013 the government has responded through agricultural socialized service (ASS) pilots, which deliver mechanized and technical services to fragmented producers without altering land ownership. Causal evidence on how such policies reshape land allocation remains scarce, and their reach beyond implementing jurisdictions has been largely overlooked. Drawing on a panel of 30 Chinese provinces from 2006 to 2022, this study combines a multi-period difference-in-differences design with a spatial Durbin model to estimate the effect of the ASS pilots on grain-oriented cropping structure. The policy raises the grain share of sown area by 2.8 percentage points, an effect concentrated almost entirely in wheat, the most mechanization-compatible of the major grains. Four transmission channels register significant responses: land transfer consolidation, agricultural mechanization, cooperative development, and a widening rather than a narrowing of the grain portfolio. The last of these runs counter to the conventional specialization account and is consistent with service provision relaxing the timing constraint on multiple cropping, so that grain expansion and crop diversity advance together rather than trading off. Heterogeneity tracks physical conditions more closely than administrative geography: the estimated effect in plains provinces is roughly twice that in hilly provinces, whereas differences across the eastern, central and western belts are not statistically distinguishable. Spillovers are substantial. Indirect effects are 1.8 times direct effects and account for close to two thirds of the total, so non-spatial estimation understates the total policy effect by approximately 41% while overstating its purely local component by approximately 40%. Three implications follow: target service expansion by mechanization compatibility rather than by administrative region; sequence implementation outward from high-capacity provinces so that spillovers are harvested deliberately rather than incidentally; and evaluate service-oriented policies at a supra-provincial scale, since province-by-province assessment misstates both their magnitude and their geographic incidence.

title: Decarbonizing Rice cultivation through residue management: Technologies, trade-offs and future perspectives
abstract: Rice cultivation is vital for India's food security. It produces about 137–150 million tonnes of grain annually from ~46 million hectares. However, it also generates 160–225 million tonnes (MT) of straw. About 40–50 MT remains surplus, mainly in the Indo-Gangetic Plains. The short rice–wheat turnaround period promotes open-field burning, particularly in Punjab, Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh. In 2017, crop-residue burning in India released an estimated 211 Tg CO₂-equivalent greenhouse gases and 824 Gg of PM₂.₅. Rice straw was a major contributor. Burning therefore worsens air quality, threatens public health and causes soil nutrient losses. Several studies have explored alternatives to burning. These include thermochemical routes such as pyrolysis, gasification and combustion. Biochemical routes include anaerobic digestion, bioethanol and biohydrogen production. Electrochemical systems and construction-material applications have also been investigated. Life Cycle Assessment (LCA) studies show that many pathways can reduce greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions compared with open burning. Electricity generation, for example, can achieve savings of up to 1471 kg CO₂-eq per tonne of residue. Rice straw can also generate biochar, bioenergy and industrial feedstocks. These pathways support a circular bioeconomy. However, large-scale adoption remains limited. Key barriers include high capital costs, fragmented supply chains, poor logistics, weak market linkages, limited policy enforcement and farmer dependence on burning. These challenges are greater for smallholders with limited access to machinery and markets. Therefore, technology alone cannot solve the residue problem. This review integrates technological, environmental, economic and policy perspectives on rice-residue management in India. It harmonises reported GHG savings using a common functional unit. It also examines why LCA results differ and compares major pathways based on carbon and economic performance. A region-specific technology-selection framework is proposed. The review also explores how artificial intelligence can support residue assessment, prediction, logistics, technology selection and decision-making. It highlights the importance of decentralized biorefineries, market-based incentives, better logistics and climate-smart practices such as Direct Seeded Rice and Alternate Wetting and Drying. Together, these approaches can help reduce residue burning and turn rice straw from an environmental burden into a valuable resource for a circular bioeconomy.

title: A framework for AI-integrated models to assess agricultural resilience
abstract: Agricultural supply chains are vulnerable to disruptions through linked biophysical and economic systems. We develop a novel AI-powered tool that integrates economic models (GTAP) with biophysical models (APSIM) to analyze supply chain shocks, enabling policymakers and market participants to assess cross-disciplinary impacts through queries and responses written in natural language. We present a conceptual vulnerability framework that categorizes the agricultural supply chain as a social-ecological system with biophysical and economic exposures and a working prototype that couples domain models through a lightweight AI orchestration layer. Our framework is an important first step in orchestrating existing domain models to illustrate the power of model coordination. An empirical example illustrates both the power of the tool and remaining gaps.

title: Towards robust agroecological market-gardening systems: lessons from a system experiment in crop diversification
abstract: Abstract Farming systems are facing strong disturbances due to climate change, mounting pressure from pests and diseases, and economic and market crises. Increasing crop diversification promises to improve system robustness by reducing and spreading out crops’ exposure to hazards, mitigating their vulnerability if exposed, and thus preserving their performance. Vegetable crops face severe biotic and abiotic stresses. In southern France, most medium-sized market-gardening farms still rely on specialized and lettuce-centered winter cropping systems, compromising long-term field potential and robustness. Many other species are agronomically feasible, but farmers face numerous impediments to significantly diversifying their winter systems. Providing results from agronomic field trials of contrasted diversification options can help overcome these obstacles. Few system experiments target market-gardening cropping systems, and even fewer evaluate strategies of crop diversification combined with other agroecological levers. This article presents the system experiment DIVEGFOOD, implemented in the French Mediterranean region to assess three agroecological diversified cropping systems and a poorly diversified baseline. DIVEGFOOD provided an original assessment of connection between diversification levels and robustness of agroecological market-gardening systems. Diversified systems still tend to be exposed to biotic pressure and injuries to harvests, but less so than the baseline, and to be less exposed to non-optimal conditions. Their production was preserved or improved on average, although some trade-offs had to be accepted for agroeconomic outputs. As it involved complex agroecological systems, DIVEGFOOD illustrated how crop diversification design and assessment require time, trade-offs and a systemic approach. We discuss why this pluriannual system experiment is emblematic of agroecologists’ methodological challenge to design and test promising systems in consistent farming conditions, using relevant assessment and analysis methods. Systems design and outcomes are discussed beyond the single technical field level, highlighting the leeway that could be opened by better dialogue between production and supply chain stakeholders, to support the agroecological transition.

title: "The New Era of Tech-Enabled Traceability": Tensions between the FDA’s Data Governance Vision and the Lived Realities of Food Producers
journal: Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction
abstract: The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA)’s Food Traceability Rule, promulgated as part of the Food Safety Modernization Act (FSMA), requires agri-food supply chain stakeholders (stakeholders) —including farmers, fishers, retail workers, and others—to maintain detailed tracking records beginning in January 2026. Through this Rule, the FDA envisions a “New Era of Tech-Enabled Traceability,” in which standardized, harmonized tracking data serve as a foundational public health infrastructure, enabling more rapid identification and removal of potentially contaminated food and ultimately reducing the risk of foodborne illness. Despite this promising vision, we observe that the Rule reconfigures agri-food stakeholders into data laborers by mandating stringent data-collection, formatting, and reporting requirements. In this paper, we examine the tensions and burdens that arise from such reconfiguration. Leveraging Data Feminism as an orientation to attend to how data-driven policy implementation disproportionately burdens smaller, under-resourced stakeholders who lack the infrastructural and financial capacity to comply, we analyze 1,198 public comments submitted to Regulations.gov in response to the proposed Rule. Our qualitative document analysis reveals three key tensions: (1) the individual labor, financial, and educational burdens stakeholders experience as they are reconfigured into data workers; (2) moments where data tracking becomes infeasible due to infrastructural limitations, cultural contexts, and situated production practices; and (3) instances where the Rule’s intended flexibility instead introduces confusion and burden due to its ambiguity. This work contributes to CSCW by providing an empirical account of how data-driven policy reconfigures stakeholders as data producers. We demonstrate that those reconfigured as data workers under data-driven governance must be recognized as meaningful policy partners rather than merely as actors subjected to compliance obligations. We further suggest that CSCW can play a critical role in uncovering their yet invisible burdens, supporting their capacity to voice concerns through participatory democratic mechanisms, and aiding their ability to “make-do” under imposed data works.

title: Multifaceted dynamics in variety and seed choices: the case of pumpkin farmers in northern Vietnam
abstract: Abstract Smallholder farmers’ crop variety and seed choices shape agro-biodiversity and livelihood sustainability. However, existing studies often overlook the dynamic, context-specific nature of these choices. We explored how introductions of hybrid pumpkin affected farmers’ pumpkin variety choices, seed sourcing, and seed management strategies across spatial and temporal contexts. We interviewed 72 stakeholders and 178 households from 3 ethnic groups in 15 villages at 2 altitudes in northern Vietnam. We assessed farmers’ encounters and experimentation with introduced pumpkin types, and why they grew different types, defined by fruit shape and seed origin (self-saved or purchased), using thematic analysis. Farmers were grouped according to the dynamics of their choices. In Mai Son (700 m above sea level), four groups emerged: (i) farmers abandoning traditional types and only growing introduced types, (ii) farmers growing traditional and introduced types, (iii) farmers only growing traditional types after experimenting with introduced types, and (iv) farmers exclusively growing traditional types without trying introduced types. In Sa Pa (1600 m above sea level), the first group was absent. Farmers encountered and experimented with introduced types, resulting in adoption or eventual dis-adoption based on agronomic performance, market opportunities, and how introduced varieties fitted within broader livelihood systems co-influenced by market access, land and labor allocation, and food and feed needs. These factors operated differently across the two agro-ecologies. Traditional types were maintained if serving farmers’ needs, not for conservation. We showed for the first time how the dynamics of variety use were shaped by a range of changes, not static decisions. Simple adoption models are not useful for designing interventions that enhance the use of introduced pumpkins or the conservation of traditional pumpkins: variety choice proved to be an ongoing, dynamic, contextualized process. Interventions need to align with farmers’ shifting priorities and constraints to support innovation and in situ conservation.

title: "We Belong to the Land": Centering Aesthetic Experience in CSCW Research on Urban Farming
journal: Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction
abstract: Urban farming is increasingly recognized as a response to sustainability challenges caused by industrial agriculture. However, CSCW research has largely examined farming through optimization and coordination in large-scale and rural agricultural settings. This paper shifts the focus from achieving sustainability as a predefined goal to examining the ongoing process of sustaining, through which cooperative work is maintained over time, using aesthetic experience as an analytical lens. Drawing on an empirical study of small-scale urban farmers, we show that sustaining unfolds through four interrelated qualities of aesthetic experience, including attunement, rhythm, expressive form, and consummation. Through these qualities, farmers’ efforts to nourish neighbors, balance access with livelihood, and repair communities take form in everyday practice. At the same time, these experiences are continually shaped, and frequently disrupted, by material, social, ecological, and organizational constraints. We call for designing for sustaining to support continuity under constraint by deepening attunement, aligning rhythms, and supporting expressive forms that foster mutual appreciation. This study advances CSCW research by foregrounding the aesthetic dimensions of urban farming and opens up new directions for future digital technologies that foster sustainable community food systems.

title: A study on entertainment farm education television programs in rainfed areas of the North-Western Himalayas, India
abstract: Introduction Entertainment–education (E–E) integrates educational messages with engaging narrative and entertainment formats and can complement conventional agricultural extension by improving the accessibility and practical salience of technical information. Evidence on farmer preferences for agricultural E–E television in rainfed Himalayan farming systems remains limited. Methods This study assessed farmers’ preferred agricultural technology themes, ranked selected agricultural television programs, and identified priority program contents among 150 television owning farmers in Reasi district, Jammu and Kashmir, India. Four Community Development blocks were randomly selected from the district’s 12 blocks, followed by random selection of Gram Panchayats, villages, and respondents. We collected data using a structured interview schedule and analyzed them descriptively using frequencies, percentages, and preference rankings. Results and discussion Methods of using insecticides and pesticides were the most preferred technology theme for E–E presentation (56.66%), followed by dairy production (25.33%), poultry production (10.66%), and soil-improvement techniques (7.33%). Krishi Darshan was the most preferred agricultural television program (72.66%), followed by agricultural and allied-sector programs on DD Kisan (18.00%) and Sadi Dharti Sade Lok (9.33%). Among program contents, insecticide and pesticide-use information ranked first (87.00%), followed by dairy guidance (79.00%), animal husbandry (75.00%), and monthly crop-management schedules (69.00%). The findings indicate a strong demand for practical, problem-oriented agricultural information and support the potential of E–E television as a complementary extension channel. From a sustainable food-systems perspective, future E–E programming should integrate integrated pest management, pesticide safety, soil health, climate resilience, and crop–livestock integration. Future research should test effects on knowledge, adoption, farm economics, and environmental outcomes using larger samples and experimental or longitudinal designs.

title: Radial growth resilience assessment and management implications for major planted forests in the west loess plateau based on improved parameters
abstract: Under the background of global climate change, frequent and severe drought have led to forest decline and tree mortality, ultimately threatening the structure, function, and stability of forest ecosystems. However, forest ecosystems and individual trees exhibit a certain degree of growth resilience to the impacts of drought. A profound understanding of the growth resilience of forest ecosystems and individual trees to drought is of great significance for maintaining the stability of forest ecosystems, particularly for plantation ecosystems. Based on an improved resilience assessment framework (maximum averaged growth reduction and recovery rate with the flexible time window), this study compared the radial growth resilience of major tree and shrub species between planted forests across different sub-climatic zones of the west Loess Plateau and corresponding natural forest species in adjacent area. The results indicate that: 1) Compared to plantations, natural forest tree species exhibit higher growth resilience. 2) Platycladus orientalis , Hippophae rhamnoides , and Caragana korshinskii possess high growth resilience, rendering them highly suitable for afforestation across the arid regions of the Loess Plateau. In contrast, Picea crassifolia and Pinus tabulaeformis showed lower resilience and should be confined to high altitude, semi-arid zones with higher precipitation. 3) In terms of plantation management in areas with insufficient precipitation, appropriate silvicultural interventions, such as rainwater harvesting, soil moisture conservation, and stand tending, must be supplemented to maintain the healthy and sustainable development of planted forests. These findings provide a scientific basis for species selection and adaptive plantation management on the Loess Plateau.

title: Scale-appropriate mechanization as a pathway to sustainable family farming: farm-level evidence from Northeast Brazil
abstract: Family farming is central to sustainable food systems, rural livelihoods, and food security in Brazil, but many family farms in the Northeast still face labor constraints and limited access to machinery suited to small, fragmented, and diversified production systems. Scale-appropriate mechanization may offer a targeted pathway to address labor bottlenecks, improve operational timeliness, lower operational costs, and support locally adapted mechanization services. This study examined farm-level changes associated with the adoption of small- to medium-scale agricultural machinery in family-farming systems of Northeast Brazil, focusing on labor use, machine-use intensity, mechanization-related operational cost, and the practical conditions shaping mechanization outcomes. The analysis combined a purposively selected balanced before-and-after panel of 59 regular pilot-project machinery-using family farm cases, giving 118 observations. The before period represented farmers’ regular production practices, while the after period represented regular use of machinery introduced through the pilot project, complemented by operation-level field and qualitative evidence from Apodi, Russas MST, and Maranhão. Farmer fixed-effects models were used to estimate within-farmer before-and-after changes associated with machinery adoption. The results showed that labor use declined from 14.42 to 3.21 h/ha, a reduction of 11.21 h/ha or 77.72%, while machine use increased from 1.06 to 2.95 h/ha, an increase of 1.89 h/ha or 178.35%. Total mechanization-related operational cost declined from R$574.44 to R$184.77/ha, a reduction of R$389.67/ha or 67.83%. Operation-level evidence showed that the largest observed changes were concentrated in rice land preparation, vegetable bed preparation, inter-row weeding, forage harvesting, sowing, and rice harvesting. In Apodi, targeted mechanized operations reduced time by 50.0–96.3% and cost by 45.3–86.0%. In Russas, cooperative machinery use reduced selected operation costs by 61.7–88.5% while in Maranhão, mini combine harvesters sharply reduced rice harvesting time. These findings suggest that scale-appropriate mechanization can improve labor allocation and cost efficiency among machinery-using family-farm cases. However, the before-and-after design does not establish a full causal treatment effect, and sustained benefits depend on machine-agronomy fit, collective access, and localized mechanization support services.

title: Power dynamics in community-led landscape restoration: a social network analysis of the Farmer Managed Natural Regeneration project in Humbo, Ethiopia
abstract: Community based forest management has emerged as a prominent approach for landscape restoration. However, formal policy frameworks often overlook the complex power relationships among stakeholders that ultimately determine project outcomes. This study examines how information, resource, and coercive power dynamics influence restoration activities through a case study of the Farmer Managed Natural Regeneration project in Humbo, Ethiopia. By integrating Actor-Centered Power theory with Social Network Analysis, we mapped nine distinct power networks across 78 stakeholders. The findings reveal that international non-governmental organizations orchestrate project governance through the centralized provision of information and financial resources, forming a highly centralized network. Government agencies exercise coercive power through a division of roles across administrative levels, where national entities establish enabling legal frameworks and local authorities manage operational permissions. Within this structure, local cooperatives function as highly embedded implementers who adapt external protocols to local contexts, successfully generating environmental and livelihood benefits. Ultimately, sustainable carbon forestry governance depends on partnerships that align external technical and financial resources with secure local land tenure and explicit administrative roles.

title: Application and Enhancement of Design for the Maintenance of Sociotechnical Networks (DFMSN): A Case Study of Agricultural Equipment in Burkina Faso
journal: Current Journal of Applied Science and Technology
abstract: Background: Agricultural mechanisation in resource-constrained environments depends not only on machinery performance but also on the capacity of local maintenance networks to sustain equipment operation. Conventional maintainability approaches largely emphasise product-related characteristics, while the influence of local technical skills, spare-parts availability, repair capabilities, costs, and procurement constraints is less explicitly incorporated into design decisions. The DFMSN approach addresses this gap, although its empirical validation and operational application to agricultural equipment remain limited. Aims: This study evaluates and extends the Design for the Maintenance of Sociotechnical Networks (DFMSN) approach to redesigning a two-wheel tractor suited to resource-constrained operating and maintenance conditions in Burkina Faso. Study Design: A field-based case study was conducted to characterise the local sociotechnical maintenance network and translate its technical, economic and logistical constraints into design requirements. Place and Duration of Study: The study was conducted in the Soum agricultural area, Nando Region, Burkina Faso, involving actors engaged in two-wheel-tractor operation, maintenance, repair and component supply. Methodology: A survey of 39 stakeholders was undertaken, comprising 27 users, two maintenance technicians, two welders, three spare-parts suppliers, three non-governmental organisations (NGOs)/cooperatives and two raw-material suppliers. Data on failures, maintenance practices, component availability, procurement lead times, costs and local repair capabilities were analysed. The findings guided the application of the eight original DFMSN rules to the redesign of a two-wheel tractor. Results: The user occupied a central position within an open maintenance network connecting repairers, suppliers and support organisations. Maintainability was strongly influenced by component availability, procurement lead times and ease of intervention. The application of DFMSN favoured a standardised power unit, simplified transmission, locally available components, a welded frame and a reduced range of fasteners. These findings supported the development of DFMSN+, incorporating operational rules for functional simplification, local procurement, manufacturability, autonomous maintenance and technical documentation. Conclusion: DFMSN+ provides a practical framework for translating local sociotechnical maintenance constraints into actionable design rules for agricultural equipment in resource-constrained environments. The findings constitute preliminary field validation; further assessment of prototype reliability, maintainability, performance and durability over several agricultural seasons is required.

title: Exploring Revenue-Sharing Strategies as a Pathway to Inclusive Growth and Sustainability in Sri Lanka’s Tea Value Chain
abstract: Purpose The tea industry, a cornerstone of agricultural economies across Asia and Africa, faces persistent challenges related to unequal value distribution, rising production costs, labour shortages, and climate uncertainty. This study systematically examines revenue-sharing (RS) strategies as a mechanism for promoting inclusive growth, equitable value distribution, and long-term sustainability within the tea value chain, with particular emphasis on the Sri Lankan context. Design/methodology/approach A Structured Literature Review (SLR) was conducted following a PRISMA-based review protocol. A total of 186 records were identified from five major academic databases, of which 32 studies published between 2000 and 2024 met the inclusion criteria. Bibliometric analysis using VOSviewer, together with thematic content analysis, was employed to identify the intellectual structure, research trends, and emerging themes within the literature. Findings The review identified four major research clusters: (1) smallholder empowerment through revenue-sharing incentives, (2) digital traceability and blockchain-enabled revenue-sharing systems, (3) cooperative governance and risk-sharing mechanisms, and (4) policy frameworks and institutional barriers. The findings indicate that revenue-sharing mechanisms have considerable potential to improve producer incentives, strengthen transparency, enhance stakeholder trust, and promote sustainable value-chain governance. Based on these findings, the study proposes an integrated conceptual framework linking revenue-sharing mechanisms, digital technologies, cooperative governance, and sustainability outcomes. Research limitations/implications The study is based on secondary literature and therefore highlights the need for future empirical validation of revenue-sharing models, particularly blockchain-enabled contracts, digital payment systems, and gender-inclusive governance frameworks within plantation economies. Practical implications The findings provide evidence-based recommendations for policymakers, tea boards, cooperatives, exporters, and plantation companies, including regulatory reforms, tax incentives, mandatory revenue-sharing disclosure, digital traceability, and cooperative digitisation to facilitate equitable and sustainable value-chain development. Originality/value This study represents the first structured literature review dedicated to revenue-sharing in the tea value chain. It develops the first integrated conceptual framework connecting revenue sharing, digital technologies, governance, and sustainability while proposing the first comprehensive future research agenda for tea-sector revenue-sharing. The study advances both theory and practice by providing an evidence-based roadmap for achieving inclusive growth and sustainable transformation in plantation-based value chains.

title: Integrating agrarian differentiation and labor mobility into TAPE-based assessments of agroecology. A methodological exploration in the Cambodian rice sector
abstract: Agroecology is increasingly considered to be a promising pathway to more sustainable agriculture. The Tool for Agroecology Performance Evaluation (TAPE) is a multiscale interdisciplinary assessment framework that helps tackle the complexity of such transitions. We critically engaged with TAPE and explored ways to enhance the approach based on empirical case studies conducted in Cambodia, in two rice-based agricultural landscapes with contrasted degrees of agricultural intensification. We complemented the TAPE framework by clarifying and operationalizing perspectives on the political-economic dynamics of agrarian change, including the reconstruction of agrarian history, a farming-system typology based on the distribution of land, and other assets and explicit consideration of off-farm work and migration. We then assessed TAPE at the local level, using focus group discussions with farmers’ collectives, in-depth household surveys, and interviews with village authorities and public administration at the local and provincial levels. The study helped frame agroecological performance from the perspective of the recent agrarian dynamics that have emerged in each area and have largely favored conventional agriculture models that rely on synthetic agro-chemicals and mechanization to achieve higher production and exports. This modernization pathway has unfolded in both landscapes and has resulted in rapid differentiation between smallholder farming households in terms of asset structure and labor processes. Our approach provides a basis for understanding why farmers’ production logic, constraints, and opportunities to engage time and resources in more sustainable farming practices vary considerably between and within landscapes. We argue that enriching the TAPE approach with such political-economic questions of agrarian changes makes it possible to link scales and to understand how agrarian modernization intersects with transition to agroecology. We see it as an important component for tailoring meaningful policies and practices that embrace the daily labor realities of smallholder farming households.

title: Communication channels for promoting regenerative agricultural practices among maize farmers: preferences and predictors in Ghana’s transitional belt
abstract: Agricultural extension, knowledge exchange, behavioural change, and smallholder innovation are fundamental to accelerating sustainable agricultural transformation and strengthening climate-resilient food systems in Africa. Effective knowledge exchange enables farmers to adopt environmentally sustainable practices that improve soil health, enhance productivity, and contribute to food and nutrition security. However, limited evidence exists on how farmers’ communication preferences influence the adoption of regenerative agricultural practices (RAPs). This study examined determinants of maize farmers’ preferred communication channels for receiving RAP information in Ghana’s transitional belt. A cross-sectional survey was conducted among 385 maize farmers selected through a multistage sampling procedure. Data were collected using a structured interview schedule administered to the selected respondents. Data were analysed using descriptive statistics, one-way analysis of variance, chi-square tests, and multinomial logistic regression. Mass communication emerged as the most preferred channel (38.7%), followed by individual (37.1%) and group communication (24.2%). Despite being the least preferred, group communication was associated with significantly higher adoption of RAPs than mass and individual channels. Communication preferences were significantly influenced by education, sex, farming experience, land ownership, market incentives, location, and farm fragmentation. The findings demonstrate that communication effectiveness depends not only on information access but also on opportunities for interaction, peer learning, and contextualised advisory support. The study recommends integrating mass communication with participatory group-based and targeted interpersonal extension approaches to enhance RAPs adoption. This supports SDG 2 (Zero Hunger), SDG 12 (Responsible Consumption and Production), SDG 13 (Climate Action and SDG 15 [Life on Land]). By linking communication preferences with regenerative agriculture adoption, this study extends agricultural communication theory and provides evidence for designing farmer-centred extension systems that strengthen resilient agricultural and food systems across sub-Saharan Africa.

title: Farmland Transfer Contract Stability and Green Production Technology Adoption: Evidence from Guizhou, China
abstract: Agricultural green transformation is essential for high-quality agricultural development and rural modernization, and farmers’ adoption of green production technologies is central to this process. Although many studies have examined such adoption, limited attention has been paid to farmland transfer contract stability. Using survey data from 1211 farm households in Guizhou Province, China, this study examines how farmland transfer contract stability affects farmers’ adoption of green production technologies. Logit and negative binomial models estimate adoption decisions and adoption intensity, while the control function approach and propensity score matching address endogeneity and selection bias. The results show that contract stability significantly increases both the likelihood and intensity of green production technology adoption, with renewal intention exerting the strongest effect. Mechanism analysis indicates that contract stability works mainly by enhancing farmers’ perceived stability of long-term green returns and promoting mechanization investment/service use. Partly substitute for the effect of contract stability on adoption intensity. The effect on adoption intensity is strongest among medium-scale farmers. Cooperatives weaken the effect of transfer duration but strengthen that of renewal intention, while science and technology commissioners complement contract stability, particularly for written contracts and renewal intention. These findings suggest that improving farmland transfer contract systems and coordinating land institutions with green incentive policies can advance agricultural green transformation.

title: Perceptual and sociocultural determinants of agricultural entrepreneurship in developing countries: a GEM data analysis
journal: Journal of Agribusiness in Developing and Emerging Economies
abstract: Purpose Responding to calls for greater understanding of the behavioural drivers of agricultural entrepreneurship, this study examines how perceptual and sociocultural factors, together with key demographic characteristics, influence individuals' engagement in early-stage agricultural entrepreneurship in developing economies. Design/methodology/approach This study uses data from the Global Entrepreneurship Monitor (GEM) Adult Population Survey (2020). Logistic regression analysis is applied to examine the influence of perceptual factors (opportunity perception, fear of failure and entrepreneurial self-efficacy), sociocultural factors (entrepreneurial role models, social status of entrepreneurs, media coverage and entrepreneurship as a desirable career choice) and demographic characteristics (age, gender and household income) on individuals' engagement in early-stage agricultural entrepreneurship across 20 developing countries. Findings Findings indicate that entrepreneurial self-efficacy is the only perceptual factor with an independent effect on engagement in agricultural entrepreneurship. When the variables were aggregated into broader perceptual and sociocultural constructs, both constructs were significantly associated with engagement in agricultural entrepreneurship, indicating the relevance of both individual perceptions and the broader sociocultural environment. Analysis also reveals a significant gender difference, with women less likely than men to engage in early-stage agricultural entrepreneurial activity. Research limitations/implications Findings indicate that entrepreneurial self-efficacy is the only perceptual factor with an independent effect on engagement in agricultural entrepreneurship. When the variables were aggregated into broader perceptual and sociocultural constructs, both constructs were significantly associated with engagement in agricultural entrepreneurship, indicating the relevance of both individual perceptions and the broader sociocultural environment. Analysis also reveals a significant gender difference, with women less likely than men to engage in early-stage agricultural entrepreneurial activity. Social implications Fostering agricultural entrepreneurship could help address poverty, unemployment, and gender disparities in developing countries, as the vast majority are associated with agriculture. Originality/value This study contributes to the agricultural entrepreneurship literature by providing empirical evidence on the behavioural drivers of engagement in agricultural entrepreneurship in developing economies. By examining perceptual, sociocultural and demographic determinants using cross-country GEM data, the study advances understanding of the respective roles of individual capabilities and sociocultural environments in agricultural entrepreneurial engagement in agricultural systems where agriculture remains central to rural livelihoods and economic development.

title: Factors associated with farmers’ multidimensional participation in e-commerce
abstract: Introduction As an important ICT-enabled business model, rural e-commerce has attracted growing attention, yet existing studies predominantly focus on binary adoption while overlooking heterogeneity in farmers’ participation depth, participation breadth, and platform choice. This study examines the multidimensional characteristics of farmers’ e-commerce participation. Methods Using data from 2,508 farm households in the 2020 China Rural Revitalization Survey, this study examines factors associated with four dimensions of e-commerce participation and uses ISM to identify the hierarchy of factors associated with participation decisions. Results (1) E-commerce training is positively associated with participation decision, depth, and breadth and with the probabilities of choosing social and traditional e-commerce. The household head’s education is positively associated with participation decision, depth, and breadth and negatively associated with the probability of remaining offline. In contrast, age is negatively associated with participation decision and depth and with the probabilities of choosing social and traditional e-commerce. (2) Cultivated land area is positively associated with participation decision and depth and with the probabilities of choosing social and traditional e-commerce. Organizational participation is positively associated with participation decision and depth, while average household education is positively associated with participation decision, depth, and breadth. Village e-commerce service stations are positively associated with participation decision and depth and with the probability of choosing social e-commerce. Local non-farm industrial development is positively associated only with participation breadth. (3) Within the ISM hierarchy of factors associated with participation decisions, e-commerce training is identified as a surface direct factor; organizational participation and village e-commerce service stations as shallow indirect factors; cultivated land area and average household education as middle-level indirect factors; and the household head’s age and education as deep-seated root factors. Discussion These findings demonstrate the multidimensional nature of farmers’ e-commerce participation and show that the same factor may have differentiated associations across dimensions. Policies should therefore shift from general encouragement to dimension-specific support through targeted training, organizational services, village e-commerce facilities, resource matching, and locally adapted industrial support.

title: Drivers of advisory chatbot adoption in smallholder agriculture: A MICMAC analysis of farmer intermediary perceptions in the Sundarbans, India
abstract: In low-literacy, climate-vulnerable agricultural settings, smallholder farmers rarely evaluate new technologies independently; adoption is mediated through trusted institutional intermediaries. However, the systemic factors driving intermediary-perceived adoption of AI advisory tools remain unmapped. This study applies the Matrice d'Impacts Croisés-Multiplication Appliquée à un Classement (MICMAC) method to examine the systemic drivers of the adoption of generative AI-based agricultural chatbot s , namely, Krishi Dishari, based on the responses of thirty Gram Unnayan Karmi (GUK) intermediaries in the Sundarbans, India, a region facing salinity intrusion and extreme climate challenges. Using a structured bilingual influence matrix survey, the study mapped and classified twelve socio-technical variables by their driving and dependence power. The results indicate that institutional trust is a critical systemic linkage variable, with smartphone access serving as the primary technical driver and social learning emerging as the dominant diffusion mechanism. Furthermore, native language comfort (Bengali) emerged as a key transmission driver, confirming that linguistic accessibility is a prerequisite rather than an enhancement for technology adoption in low digital-literacy contexts. Consequently, this study offers a framework, although transferability warrants exhaustive validation, indicating that AI-based advisory services in vulnerable agricultural settings depend on institutional trust and social learning, not only on technological innovation.

title: Low‐Carbon Transition in China's Agrifood System: Potential, Pathways and Global Implications
abstract: ABSTRACT Global agrifood systems must undergo a low‐carbon transition to achieve Paris Agreement temperature goals. Accounting for 13% of global agrifood systems emissions, China has a critical role to play; yet without further action, China's agrifood emissions will continue to rise, jeopardising its carbon neutrality commitment. This study employs a mixed‐methods approach combining a narrative literature review and integrated modelling to: (1) characterise the emissions of China's agrifood system, (2) project carbon emission reduction and carbon sequestration potential under multiple domestic policy scenarios, and (3) provide wider implications for developing countries. Under the baseline scenario, holding current trends and policies constant, annual emissions are projected to rise slowly from a baseline of 1.6 billion tons in 2021 to 1.83 billion tons of CO 2 eq by 2060, driven primarily by the expansion of the livestock sector and growing energy use. However, our modelling results suggest that a combination of measures, including productivity improvements, the adoption of low‐carbon technologies, food loss and waste reduction, production structure adjustment, and a low‐carbon energy transition, could reduce emissions by over 60% or 1.1 billion tons CO 2 eq by 2060 relative to the baseline. At the same time, carbon sequestration alone could ensure carbon neutrality, with potential reductions of 1.8 billion tons CO 2 eq annually, thereby contributing to the national carbon neutrality goal. These results underscore that synergistic, system‐wide interventions substantially outperform isolated measures. China's experience offers a valuable reference for other countries in formulating sustainable agricultural policies and pursuing low‐carbon transitions.

title: Adaptive management of human–elephant conflict in the anthropocene: An importance–performance analysis in Dong Nai Biosphere Reserve, Vietnam
abstract: The Anthropocene has intensified human–wildlife interactions, making Human–Elephant Conflict (HEC) a major challenge for biodiversity conservation and rural livelihoods across Southeast Asia. This study assessed community adaptive capacity for sustainable human–elephant coexistence in the Dong Nai Biosphere Reserve (DNBR), Vietnam, using an integrated analytical framework that combined Importance–Performance Analysis (IPA), Exploratory Factor Analysis (EFA), and Hierarchical Cluster Analysis (HCA). Data were collected from 430 residents living in HEC-prone areas. The IPA results revealed persistent gaps between the perceived importance and performance of several adaptive management measures, particularly in communities lacking electric fencing. EFA identified three dimensions of perceived adaptive capacity: Resource-based Adaptation (F1), Inclusive Governance Mechanisms (F2), and Local Collective Action (F3). These dimensions corresponded closely with the clusters identified by HCA, which grouped adaptive management indicators into coherent strategic clusters and highlighted the interconnected roles of material resources, institutional arrangements, and community participation in managing HEC. The findings suggest that preventive infrastructure, institutional enhancement, livelihood diversification, agro-ecological adaptation, ecological knowledge integration, and participatory governance constitute key foundations for long-term human–elephant coexistence. Policy interventions should therefore adopt an integrated approach that strengthens resource-based adaptation, promotes inclusive governance, and supports collective learning and action. By linking community perceptions with the adaptive capacity framework, this study provides a practical framework for enhancing socio-ecological resilience and advancing human–wildlife coexistence in protected landscapes in the Anthropocene.

title: Two-Stage Pre-Sale Financing Strategy for Agricultural Products Supply Chain Considering Capital Constraints
abstract: In the agricultural production cycle, farmers face financial constraints both before planting and before harvesting, which can substantially restrict production decisions and operational efficiency. With the rapid development of agricultural e-commerce and supply chain finance, platform loans and pre-sale financing have become important channels through which farmers can obtain the funds needed for agricultural production. This study develops a two-stage financing portfolio decision model for an agricultural product supply chain and examines the farmer’s optimal financing strategy, planting quantity, and pricing decisions under exogenously given platform loan and pre-sale financing conditions. The results show that the loan interest rate and commission rate significantly influence the farmer’s choice of financing strategy. Specifically, holding other conditions constant, a higher loan interest rate increases the farmer’s incentive to adopt pre-sale financing, whereas a higher commission rate reduces the incentive to adopt it. Numerical simulations further identify the decision boundaries of the two-stage financing portfolio strategies under different parameter conditions. This study provides theoretical insights into farmers’ financing decisions and the selection of multi-stage financing strategies in agricultural product supply chains.

title: Measurement of interest linkage level between land trusteeship enterprises and farmers in China: based on TOPSIS method with comprehensive weighting
abstract: The cooperative outcomes between land trusteeship enterprises and farmers have fallen substantially short of expectations due to trust deficits, factor mismatches, and imbalances in benefit distribution. The root cause of this paradox lies in the absence or weakness of interest linkage mechanisms. Measuring the interest linkage level and optimizing the interest linkage mechanism are therefore key to resolving this issue, yet existing research has paid insufficient attention to this problem. Accordingly, first, this study innovatively constructs an indicator system for measuring the interest linkage level in land trusteeship based on the interest linkage theory. Second, the AHP and Entropy method was used to determine the subjective and objective weights. Finally, we use the TOPSIS method to measure the interest linkage level, analyze its spatio-temporal characteristics and heterogeneity. The results show that: (1) Overall, the interest linkage level between land trusteeship enterprises and farmers stands at 0.516, representing a moderate level. Among the three sub-dimensions, resource sharing is relatively high, mutual benefit is moderate, and cooperative trust is comparatively low, indicating that weak trust constitutes the most prominent shortcoming of the current interest linkage mechanism. (2) In terms of temporal changes, between 2021 and 2022, the levels of interest linkage, cooperative trust, resource sharing, and mutual benefit all exhibited an upward trend, with resource sharing recording the fastest rate of increase. In terms of regional disparities, Jining city of China exhibits the highest level of interest linkage, whereas Weifang city records the lowest. (3) Regarding heterogeneity, the interest linkage level is highest for small-scale pure farmers, followed in descending order by part-time farmers and large-scale specialized farmers. The interest linkage level increases as the number of trusteeship service links expands. Among the three principal trusteeship models, differences in interest linkage levels exist but are not pronounced. The findings contribute to the theoretical development of interest linkage mechanisms and offer actionable policy implications for improving enterprise–farmer cooperative arrangements.

title: Factors influencing the adoption of climate-smart agriculture practices among smallholder farmers in Melani and Msobomvu villages, Eastern Cape Province
abstract: Climate-Smart Agriculture (CSA) is widely recognised as an effective approach for improving agricultural productivity, strengthening resilience to climate change, and enhancing food security among small-scale farmers. However, the adoption of CSA practices remains uneven in many rural communities, including Melani and Msobomvu villages in the Raymond Mhlaba Local Municipality, Eastern Cape Province, South Africa. This study investigated farmers’ awareness and understanding of climate-smart agriculture practices, identified the barriers limiting CSA adoption, and examined the socio-economic and institutional factors influencing adoption decisions. A descriptive research design within a quantitative research approach was employed. Data were collected from 158 randomly selected small-scale farmers using a structured questionnaire and analysed using descriptive statistics, including frequencies, percentages, means, and standard deviations. One-Way Analysis of Variance (ANOVA) was used to determine the significance of selected socio-economic and institutional factors influencing CSA adoption. The findings revealed that respondents generally possessed a good awareness and understanding of climate-smart agriculture practices, although awareness differed across technologies. Rainwater harvesting (80%), crop diversification (71%), conservation agriculture (68%), and soil conservation (68%) recorded the highest levels of awareness, whereas awareness was comparatively lower for drought-tolerant crop varieties (57%), climate information services (55%), and improved livestock management (49%). The study further identified farmer resistance to change, inadequate financial resources, and limited extension materials as the major barriers limiting CSA adoption. One-Way ANOVA indicated that financial constraints, market access, knowledge of climate-smart agriculture technologies, and extension support were statistically significant factors influencing adoption decisions ( p < 0.05).

title: The impact of digital technology adoption on farm profitability for smallholder sunflower farmers: empirical evidence from Singida, Tanzania
abstract: This study examined the impact of digital technology adoption on farm profitability among smallholder sunflower farmers in Iramba District, Singida Region, Tanzania. Using cross-sectional data from 174 farmers collected through structured questionnaires, the study employed an Endogenous Switching Regression (ESR) model and complementary OLS, conventional 2SLS, and heteroskedasticity-generated instrumental-variable robustness checks. The ESR estimates indicate a positive Average Treatment Effect on the Treated, suggesting higher predicted profitability among current adopters, while the negative Average Treatment Effect on the Untreated indicates that current non-adopters may not obtain similar gains under adoption. However, although the OLS adoption coefficient is positive and statistically significant, the conventional 2SLS and Lewbel-IV adoption coefficients are substantially smaller and statistically insignificant. These results indicate that the estimated profitability effect is sensitive to identification assumptions. Digital skills and education emerge as more consistent determinants of profitability. The study concludes that digital technologies can support farm profitability, but benefits depend on farmer readiness and complementary capabilities rather than adoption alone.

title: Advancing community-based disaster risk reduction in volcanic landscape: A spatially integrated approach for resilient tourism villages
abstract: Global disaster risk reduction initiatives prioritize resilience. Indonesian tourism villages emphasize appeal and community empowerment, however they have specific disaster risks. Mount Semeru's eruptions–pyroclastics flows, lava flows, ashfall, and lahars–together with landslides and the susceptibility of rural livelihoods, render Pronojiwo a volcanic hazard-prone area. This study develops a disaster-resilient tourism village strategy, geographically integrated mixed-method study employs literature review, field observation, Focus Group Discussion (FGD), participatory mapping, GIS-based disaster risk assessment, thematic analysis, and Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities, and Threats (SWOT) analysis. The results show Pronojiwo as a multi-hazard tourist system, contains almost 80% of its territory among moderate-to-high hazard zones, with specific vulnerabilities in Sumberurip and Supiturang. Tourism management must enhance the incorporation of catastrophe risk due to capacity constraints. The model delineates a distinct village system with Sidomulyo as the tourism nucleus, Sumberurip as the diversification and transition zone, and Supiturang as the resilient and educative catastrophe tourism village. This study is distinctive as it employs Geographic Information System (GIS)-based risk assessment for accurate spatial comprehension, community mapping for local insights, and Community-Based Disaster Risk Reduction (CBDRR) principles for implementable and locally governed solutions. This comprehensive framework enhances geographical zoning, tourism product creation, institutional functions, and safety regulations, rendering it a more cohesive and actionable Disaster Risk Reduction (DRR) strategy by integrating community participation and local knowledge into risk mapping, preparedness training, early-warning dissemination, evacuation planning, and coordinated responsibilities among village institutions, tourism actors, and local communities according to each village's risk profile and tourism function.

title: From motivation to action: Exploring the triggering mechanism of digital transformation in farmer cooperatives
abstract: As a pivotal vehicle for upgrading the agricultural industry, farmer cooperatives play both a foundational and strategic role in advancing rural industrial revitalization through digital transformation. Drawing on the perspective of network embeddedness, this study analyzes the triggering mechanisms and operational logic underlying the digital transformation of 35 farmer cooperatives in Zhejiang Province, China. The findings reveal that digital transformation among farmer cooperatives follows a processual triggering logic of “motivation—conditions—path—performance.” Alleviating labor shortages and meeting market demand serve as key motivations for farmer cooperatives to embark on digital transformation. Under conditions of strong dynamic capabilities of responsible personnel and government support, these motivations translate into action. The pathway of gradual adaptive restructuring facilitates the effective application of digital technologies. Positive feedback on economic performance further strengthens the momentum for continuous transformation, while feedback on environmental and social performance improves the conditions for continuous transformation. This study not only elucidates the internal logic of digital transformation among farmer cooperatives but also offers theoretical and practical insights for optimizing policy design and accelerating agricultural digitalization.

title: Dual valorization of oil palm empty fruit bunches: acetyl-modified lignin and lignin-derived graphene quantum dots for sustainable photothermal conversion
abstract: Lignin derived from oil palm empty fruit bunches (EFB) represents an abundant renewable aromatic resource but remains underutilized in advanced solar-energy materials. Herein, a dual-valorization strategy was developed by converting EFB lignin into two complementary photothermal components, namely acetylated lignin (Ace-L) and palm lignin-derived graphene quantum dots (PL-GQDs). Ace-L served as the primary photothermal matrix, whereas PL-GQDs functioned as broadband light absorbers and nanoscale heat-generating domains. Structural characterization confirmed successful lignin acetylation while preserving the aromatic framework, and PL-GQDs with graphitic characteristics and particle sizes of approximately 2–5 nm were successfully synthesized. The resulting materials were integrated into a photothermoelectric film and a solar-driven aerogel. The optimized film (F-GLa50%) achieved an apparent photothermal conversion efficiency of 23.2% under one-sun irradiation and the optimized aerogel (SDLA-AceG) exhibited an evaporation rate of 944.7 g m −2 h −1 with a solar steam generation efficiency of 59.2%, while maintaining stable performance over six consecutive cycles and sustained steam generation under saline conditions up to 10 wt% NaCl. Mechanistic investigation revealed that the synergistic interaction between Ace-L and PL-GQDs simultaneously improves light harvesting, interfacial heat utilization, and structural compatibility, resulting in enhanced photothermal conversion in both material platforms. This work demonstrates an effective approach for simultaneously upgrading EFB lignin into two high-value photothermal materials for renewable electricity generation and solar-driven water purification.

title: Postharvest Management of Fruits: Navigating the Affordability, Efficacy, and Non-Destructive Quality Evaluation of Thermal Versus Non-Thermal Interventions
abstract: Postharvest losses (PHLs) present a critical bottleneck to global food security, with fresh fruit losses reaching 23-40% due to rapid physiological deterioration, mechanical stress, and microbial decay. This review evaluates the metabolic cascades, including respiration kinetics, transpiration, and hormone-mediated factors, that govern fruit degradation. We reviewed thermal and non-thermal treatments for affordability, including thermal interventions such as hot water treatment (HWT), microwave treatment, and radio frequency treatment, alongside emerging non-thermal preservation modalities such as edible coatings, cold plasma atmospheric treatments, and ultrasound processing. The review places particular emphasis on climacteric tropical fruits such as mango, papaya, banana, and citrus, for which postharvest losses and preservation challenges are especially acute due to their climacteric nature. To address the quality tracking highlighted by modern commercial chains, this review integrates an assessment of non-destructive quality evaluation technologies, focusing on near-infrared (NIR) spectroscopy, hyperspectral imaging (HSI), and electronic noses (E-noses). Overall, this review seeks to deliver a unified blueprint, arguing that sustainable postharvest preservation can benefit from context-specific hurdle-technology concepts that align accessible postharvest treatments with monitoring networks. We synthesise current evidence on individual thermal, non-thermal, and sensing technologies and use this to motivate potential hurdle strategies and treatment-monitoring pairings for diverse fruit supply chains.

title: Environmental health literacy of local villagers in Northern Thailand with high seasonal PM 2.5 air pollution; a mixed method study
abstract: Seasonal PM2.5 air pollution remains a major public health challenge in northern Thailand. Environmental health literacy (EHL) may influence how communities understand pollution-related health risks and adopt protective behaviors; however, little is known about EHL among rural populations living in highly affected areas. We conducted a mixed-methods study from December 2023 to August 2024 among villagers residing in a rural district of Chiang Mai Province, Thailand, where seasonal air pollution occurs annually. Eligible participants lived in the area for at least two years. Data were collected using a paper-based questionnaire and focus group discussions to assess knowledge, perceptions, and responses to air pollution. Forty villagers participated; 25 (63%) were female, with a median age of 39 years (interquartile range [IQR] 34–56). Most participants completed primary or secondary education (83%), and 80% were maize farmers. Hypertension, allergy, and asthma were reported by 15%, 12.5%, and 7.5% of participants, respectively. Villagers demonstrated good awareness of seasonal air pollution, recognized both short- and long-term health consequences, and reported modifying daily activities to reduce exposure. Participants described complying with government recommendations and measures aimed at reducing burning practices. However, they perceived that air quality had not improved despite these efforts. While recognizing agricultural burning and forest fires as major contributors to PM2.5 pollution, participants emphasized that eliminating burning was difficult because of livelihood and economic constraints. They expressed willingness to participate in community-based solutions but highlighted the need for sustainable support systems, including alternative agricultural practices, reliable water supplies, occupational training, and market access. Villagers living in a high-exposure area of northern Thailand demonstrated meaningful EHL and willingness to adopt protective behaviors. However, individual and community actions alone may be insufficient to address a complex environmental problem driven by structural and socioeconomic factors. Sustainable, multi-sectoral approaches that combine public engagement, livelihood support, and effective policy implementation are needed to reduce air pollution and protect community health.

title: How Does Agricultural Labor Return Migration Affect Farmland Abandonment Among Rural Households?
abstract: The return migration of agricultural labor has emerged as a notable demographic shift in rural China, yet its association with farmland abandonment has received limited empirical attention. Using household-level microdata from the China Household Finance Survey (CHFS), this study empirically examines the association between agricultural labor return migration on farmland abandonment among rural households and explores the underlying channels. The results indicate a negative association between agricultural labor return migration and the area of farmland abandoned by rural households, and this pattern remains stable across a series of robustness checks. Mechanism analyses suggest that this association is consistent with two channels, namely farmland transfer-out and household investment in farmland. This negative association appears stronger in villages with well-developed specialty agricultural industries, relatively limited non-agricultural employment opportunities, and village cooperatives. These patterns suggest that policy efforts could pay greater attention to the role of labor return migration in improving the efficiency of rural farmland resource utilization. A combination of policy measures is recommended to improve farmland transfer markets, strengthen incentives for agricultural investment, and foster locally adapted specialty rural industries.

title: Determinants of farmers’ intention to adopt agricultural e-commerce livestreaming: a sequential mixed-methods study in Beijing
abstract: Agricultural e-commerce livestreaming provides farmers with a new digital means of connecting with consumers, expanding sales channels, and improving market access. However, farmers differ in their willingness to adopt this marketing channel. This study employs a sequential mixed-methods design, integrating grounded theory, structural equation modeling (SEM), and artificial neural networks (ANN) to examine the factors influencing farmers’ willingness to adopt agricultural e-commerce livestreaming in Beijing. First, semi-structured interviews with 26 farmers from suburban Beijing were conducted and analyzed using grounded theory, identifying five antecedent constructs: individual livestreaming readiness, perceived technological feasibility, agricultural product–livestreaming fit, livestreaming ecosystem support, and perceived economic value. Second, based on 300 valid questionnaires, SEM was used to examine the relationships between these constructs and adoption intention. An ANN model was subsequently developed to assess the nonlinear predictive contributions of the factors.
